chapters.name: Rill Below the Cliffs
chapters.content:
By the third day, Ash could stand without trembling when Elianor entered the stable.

The mare still favored her hind leg, and Tomas still refused to let anyone saddle her. He had moved her into a stall near the back wall, where the other horses could not crowd her and the wind came through a crack in the boards smelling of salt. Elianor visited before breakfast, after lessons, and once at midnight when sleep would not come. Each time, Tomas made her wait before touching Ash.

“Patience is becoming an expensive habit,” she told him one gray morning.

“It costs less than a surgeon.”

“Master Vey says everything costs more than expected.”

“Master Vey says that because he has to pay for things.”

Elianor held out a carrot. Ash took it delicately from her fingers.

The simple success pleased her more than it should have. She looked toward Tomas, expecting him to notice. He did, but only smiled faintly and began cleaning the water trough.

“Is that all the praise I receive?”

“You wanted the horse to take the carrot.”

“I wanted you to acknowledge that I helped.”

“You held a carrot.”

“I held it patiently.”

“Then you have earned another carrot.”

She threw the second one at him. He caught it against his chest, and for a moment they were both laughing. The sound seemed dangerous in the dim stable, too alive for a place where every wall belonged to her father.

A groom entered through the main doors and stopped when he saw them. Elianor straightened. Tomas lowered his eyes. The ordinary shape of the world returned at once.

The groom carried a message from Captain Harl: Lord Marrow required Elianor in the west solar before noon, and her escort would meet her at the house.

She should have gone directly to the solar. Instead, she said, “How far is Rill?”

The groom glanced at Tomas.

“Three miles by the cliff path,” Tomas answered.

“On foot?”

“Less, if the tide is out.”

“I have not asked about walking.”

Tomas's expression changed. “Ash cannot be ridden.”

“Not Ash.”

His eyes moved toward the row of horses. “Lady Elianor—”

“You said you knew the coast.”

“I know the coast.”

“Then show it to me.”

He looked toward the doors, where the groom was pretending not to listen. “Your father assigned guards.”

“Your father did not assign guards to you.”

“I do not belong to your father.”

The words were mild, but they touched the place where her anger had been waiting. “You belong to his stable.”

“Until I do not.”

She had no answer to that. The words followed her to the west solar, where Lord Corvin spent an hour discussing the proper arrangement of household accounts as though no one in Avelune had ever gone hungry. She listened, replied when required, and looked through the tall window toward the sea.

At midday, she told Captain Harl she was taking the bay gelding down the coast to inspect the lower pasture.

“There is no inspection scheduled,” he said.

“There is one now.”

“Shall I send Pell?”

“No.”

His face hardened. “My lady.”

“I am not riding beyond Greyhaven's boundary. The pasture is estate land, and the horse is estate property. If you believe I am unsafe among my father's fields, you may explain to him why you refuse to let me see them.”

It was not defiance exactly. It was the kind of language her father used when he wanted to make refusal seem unreasonable. Captain Harl recognized it and disliked her for it, but after a pause he gave orders for the gelding to be saddled.

Tomas was waiting near the stable gate with a smaller brown horse.

“You told them you were going to the lower pasture,” he said.

“I am going to the lower pasture.”

“Rill is not the lower pasture.”

“It lies beyond it.”

“That is not the same thing.”

Elianor mounted. “Will you come?”

Tomas rested a hand on the brown horse's neck. He wore a serviceable cloak over his patched wool, and a rolled blanket was tied behind his saddle. He had also brought two small sacks, which he tried to conceal beneath the blanket.

“What are those?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“Nothing appears to be leaking flour.”

He sighed. “Barley cakes.”

“For whom?”

“For the horse.”

“The horse is not carrying them.”

His jaw tightened. “If you are going to Rill, you should know that you may not like what you see.”

“I have seen the ledgers.”

“Ledgers do not look back at you.”

They rode out through the postern before the guards could question the route. The path climbed first, winding between black rocks and grass flattened by weeks of hard wind. Below them, the sea beat against the cliffs in long white bursts. The sky was the color of old pewter, and rain hung in the distance like a curtain not yet drawn.

Elianor had known the coastal road all her life, but she had known it from a saddle surrounded by retainers, with a cloak wrapped around her and a basket of luncheon fastened to the packhorse. She had seen the villages as clusters of roofs below the cliffs, picturesque from a height and easily forgotten once the road bent inland.

Tomas did not take the road.

He guided his horse down narrow tracks between the rocks, where the grass had been worn away by feet and cartwheels. At one bend, he dismounted to open a gate made of rope and driftwood. Beyond it stood three cottages with roofs patched in sailcloth.

A woman came out carrying a bucket. She saw Tomas and stopped.

“Morning, Lysa,” he called.

The woman looked at Elianor, then back at him. Her face was narrow and brown from wind, though she could not have been more than thirty. “You brought the lady.”

“I did not bring her. She followed me.”

“I did not,” Elianor said.

Lysa gave a tired smile. “Then you have both come where you were going.”

Tomas dismounted. “How is Nerrin?”

“Fever has gone down. The little ones are worse.”

“What little ones?” Elianor asked.

Lysa's hand tightened around the bucket handle. “Mine.”

The cottage door opened behind her. Two children stood in the shadow, one perhaps six and the other no more than four. The older child had a swollen belly beneath a shirt too large for him. The younger leaned against the doorframe, eyes enormous in a pale face.

Elianor looked away first.

Tomas untied one of the sacks. “I brought some cake.”

Lysa shook her head. “You cannot keep doing this.”

“I can today.”

“Master Vey will count the stores.”

“Master Vey counts the stores at Greyhaven. He does not count what I carry.”

“He will if someone tells him.”

“Then do not tell him.”

His voice remained light, but Elianor heard the danger beneath it. Tomas broke the barley cakes into pieces and handed them to the children. The older boy accepted his share cautiously, as if it might be taken back. The younger child did not reach for hers until Lysa knelt and guided the food into her hands.

Elianor felt a question rise in her and did not ask it. The answer was visible in the children's fingers.

They ate too quickly. Tomas murmured for them to slow down, and Lysa gave them water in small sips. The younger began to cough. Elianor dismounted and went to the saddlebag.

“What do you need?” she asked.

Lysa looked startled. “Nothing.”

“That is not an answer.”

“Nothing you can give.”

Elianor opened the bag. Inside were gloves, a comb, a flask, and three wrapped honey biscuits left from breakfast. She took them out and held them toward Lysa.

The woman did not move.

“They are mine,” Elianor said. “I am giving them to you.”

Lysa glanced at Tomas before accepting them. “Why?”

Because she was hungry. Because Greyhaven had full granaries. Because Elianor had been taught to call charity a favor, and the word now seemed obscene.

“Because you need them,” she said.

Lysa's eyes did not soften. Need had taught her not to trust easy kindness. “The last lady who came here asked us to pray.”

Elianor closed her hand around the empty wrapper. “I am sorry.”

It was the first apology she had ever given to someone who could not punish her for it.

They left after Lysa promised to send word if Nerrin's fever returned. The path descended toward the village proper. Rill lay in a hollow below the cliffs, its houses crowded around a stream that had once turned a mill wheel. The wheel stood still. Nets hung from poles, stiff with salt and useless without fish. A row of boats rested upside down on the beach, their hulls split where winter storms had thrown them against the stones.

No smoke rose from several chimneys.

Elianor slowed her horse. “How many people live here?”

“Used to?”

She looked at him.

“Nearly four hundred,” Tomas said. “Now perhaps three hundred. Some went inland looking for work. Some died. Some went to the levy and never came back.”

“Why has no one told Greyhaven?”

“Greyhaven knows.”

They passed a square where a woman had laid out onions, two turnips, and a strip of dried kelp on a cloth. No one stopped. Near the well, an old man sat with a child asleep against his shoulder. He raised two fingers when he saw Tomas.

Tomas raised two in return.

“You know everyone,” Elianor said.

“Not everyone.”

“You knew Lysa's children. You knew the fever. You knew the boats.”

“I work at Greyhaven, not in the clouds.”

He led her down an alley to a shed with a broken door. Three children were crouched inside, trying to keep out of the wind. One wore a red ribbon tied around her wrist. She stared at Elianor's clean gloves, then at the horse beneath her.

Tomas took the second sack from behind his saddle. “Mara, Pellin, Joss. Come here.”

The children came, though the smallest kept one hand on the wall. Tomas gave them pieces of cake and asked whether Joss's cough had improved. He knew that Mara's mother had gone to the salt sheds and that Pellin's brother had lost two fingers to a rope winch. He knew which child would eat slowly and which would hide food in a pocket.

Elianor watched him move among them. There was no performance in it. He did not look toward her to make sure she understood his goodness. He simply knew their names, and because he knew them, their suffering could not remain abstract.

When they rode out of Rill, the rain had begun. They stopped beneath an overhang in the cliff, where water dripped from the stone in a steady silver line.

Elianor said, “You stole the cakes.”

“Yes.”

“From Greyhaven.”

“Yes.”

“You could be whipped.”

“Yes.”

“Dismissed.”

“Yes.”

“Imprisoned.”

Tomas looked at her. “That is less likely.”

“You do not know that.”

“I know the cells are full.”

She studied the rain beyond him. “Why risk it?”

He leaned back against the rock. “Because they are hungry.”

“That is not enough for you?”

“It is enough for me.”

“For punishment?”

“For the risk.”

Elianor felt frustration tighten her throat. “You speak as though the two things are separate.”

“They are. Punishment is what the powerful do after they discover a person has done what was necessary.”

“And if everyone stole from the stores?”

“Then perhaps the stores would belong to everyone.”

“That sounds like rebellion.”

“Sometimes the word is used to make hunger sound criminal.”

She turned on him. “You think I do not know what is happening?”

“I think you know now.”

The gentleness of it hurt more than accusation.

He continued, “Before today, you knew figures. You knew that grain went away. You knew people gathered at the gate. But you could still believe that hunger was a condition, like rain or fog. Something unfortunate, something managed by men with ledgers.”

Elianor said nothing.

“Hunger makes a person invisible to the powerful,” Tomas said. “Not because the hungry are unseen. They are seen all the time. They are seen as crowds, as trouble, as mouths, as a number that must be reduced. But no one sees Lysa's daughter coughing, or Joss hiding cake in his sleeve, or the old man whose grandson is asleep because there is no strength left for crying.”

The rain ran from his hair to his jaw. Elianor wanted to look away, but she had spent enough of her life looking away without knowing she was doing it.

“My father says a ruler must choose who can be saved,” she said.

“Perhaps he has never had to watch the people he did not choose.”

She thought of the First Seed loaf beneath her floorboard, the remembered figures and the words diverted in Master Vey's hand. Evidence had seemed powerful when it lay hidden in her room. Here, beside a cliff above Rill, it seemed terribly small.

“Could Greyhaven feed them?” she asked.

“For a while.”

“How long?”

“Long enough to decide whether they live.”

“And if the crown takes the grain?”

“Then we hide what we can and carry what we cannot hide.”

He said it without bravado. It was not a plan, only a fact about the world as he had learned it.

Elianor drew off one glove. The leather was damp and cold. “If I gave you food openly, my father would stop you.”

“He would stop you first.”

“I have authority.”

“You have a name.”

“Is there a difference?”

“To people in Rill, perhaps. To the guards, yes. To your father, no. He can take one away and use the other.”

She closed her bare hand around the glove. “Then I will not give it openly.”

Tomas stared at her.

“I am not promising to become a thief,” she said.

“You already altered a delivery order?”

The question struck like a thrown stone. “How do you know that?”

“I do not. I asked.”

She should have been offended. Instead she heard the careful boundary in his voice. He was offering neither approval nor betrayal.

“I have not altered one,” she said. “Not yet.”

“Then you should learn exactly how many sacks leave Greyhaven, who records them, and which roads they take.”

She looked at him. “You are telling me to commit a crime.”

“I am telling you to learn the shape of the thing before you try to break it.”

The storm shifted over the sea. For a moment, sunlight broke through the clouds and laid a bright road upon the water, though no boat could follow it.

On the ride back, Elianor saw Rill differently—not transformed, only made impossible to forget. She saw the patched roofs and the stopped mill, the empty fish racks and the children who watched every passing hand. She saw the distance between Greyhaven and the village measured not in miles but in permission: who could enter, who could speak, who could be counted.

At the postern, Tomas dismounted and took the brown horse toward the stable.

Elianor remained in her saddle. “Tomorrow,” she said.

He looked back. “Tomorrow what?”

“Tell me which stores are counted as waste.”

His expression sharpened. “Why?”

“So I can learn the shape of the thing.”

For the first time, he smiled without restraint. “Tomorrow, then.”

She rode toward the house. The guards saw only Lord Marrow's daughter returning from the lower pasture with mud on her boots and rain on her cloak. They did not see the children in Rill, because they had not been there. They did not see Tomas's hands breaking bread into equal pieces. They did not know that Elianor had carried the village back with her, not as a burden she could set down, but as a collection of names that would no longer let her pretend she was protected by ignorance.

chapters.name: A Lesson in Accounts
chapters.content:
Elianor began with the waste ledger because it was the least guarded.

Master Vey kept it in a narrow cabinet beside the kitchen office, where the pages smelled of flour, lamp smoke, and the damp wool of servants waiting to be paid. Anyone might have seen it. No one, she had learned, thought it worth seeing. The great ledgers went under lock in the granary office; the waste ledger recorded what had spoiled, cracked, been eaten by rats, or been issued to household kitchens. It was the account by which abundance disguised itself as loss.

She waited until the noon bell drew most of the household toward dinner. Then she entered the office carrying a basket of folded napkins.

Bryn, the kitchen maid, stood at the table sorting onions.

“You are early,” Bryn said.

“I am carrying linen.”

“You are carrying linen toward the account books.”

Elianor set down the basket. “Do you object?”

“I object to onions. They make my eyes hurt, and nobody thanks the cook for not making soup from them.”

“That is not an answer.”

Bryn looked at the closed door, then lowered her voice. “If you are looking for something, look quickly. Master Vey has gone to the lower yard, and he walks faster when he is angry.”

Elianor opened the cabinet.

The waste ledger was thin compared with the others, its leather cover softened by use. She carried it to the window and turned the pages. Barley: forty sacks spoiled by damp. Oats: twelve sacks unfit for horses. Wheat: six sacks lost to vermin. The entries repeated at intervals so regular that they ceased to resemble accident.

“Can grain spoil in a sealed store?” she asked.

Bryn did not look up. “Not forty sacks at once.”

“Could rats eat twelve sacks of oats?”

“Only if the rats had learned to read the inventory.”

Elianor turned another page. The dates were three days before shipments left Greyhaven. The quantities marked waste nearly matched the amounts recorded in the delivery orders. What failed inspection in the morning became saleable grain on the road by nightfall, though not under Greyhaven’s name. It vanished first into the column marked loss, then reappeared in Master Vey’s external accounts as a consignment to Merrit & Sons.

She took a scrap of paper from her sleeve and copied the figures.

“Do not write too much,” Bryn said. “Paper has ears.”

“Paper has ink.”

“And ink has a way of reaching fathers.”

The words should have startled her. Instead, Elianor closed the ledger and went to the shelves beneath the window. Her memory held the earlier figures, but memory could be challenged. She needed the shape of the theft, not merely its outline.

Behind a stack of old household menus she found a packet of delivery orders tied with blue thread. The top sheets bore Lord Marrow’s seal. Beneath them were duplicates, stamped with the seal of the crown’s grain office and countersigned by a noble intermediary: Sir Edric Pell, Baron of Westmere. The recipient was Merrit & Sons, Capital Provisioners. The destination was not Avelune’s famine districts but the royal depots beyond the eastern road.

The price written beside each shipment was more than double the amount used in Greyhaven’s public accounts.

Elianor felt the room grow cold around her.

This was not merely grain being taken by the crown. Greyhaven was selling it. Lord Marrow was receiving coin for the shortages he described as unavoidable.

She copied the names, dates, quantities, and seals. Then she replaced every sheet exactly as she had found it.

Bryn watched her with an expression too old for her young face. “What will you do?”

“Find out where the next shipment goes.”

“That sounds like a question.”

“It is a beginning.”

She left through the kitchen passage and crossed the inner court with her head high. At the archway, Master Vey emerged from the granary yard. His coat was powdered with chaff, and his tired eyes moved from her face to the basket of napkins she was not carrying.

“My lady,” he said.

“Master Vey.”

“Were you seeking something?”

“Bryn’s onions.”

Bryn, visible through the open office door, began coughing.

Master Vey’s mouth tightened. He was not fooled, but neither did he call her back. “The household is not improved by curiosity.”

“Nor by false arithmetic.”

The steward glanced toward the granaries. “Arithmetic is only false when the person reading it has been given the wrong question.”

“What is the right question?”

“Who profits from the answer.”

For a breath they stood facing one another, the sea wind pushing chaff across the stones. Then Master Vey bowed and went past her.

It was not permission. It was not forgiveness. It was the closest thing to an ally she had yet found in Greyhaven.

That evening Elianor met Tomas in the stable after the last groom had left. Ash stood in her stall with her head lowered, one hind leg eased forward. The mare accepted a hand along her neck, then turned to examine Elianor’s sleeve for carrots.

“I have found the waste,” Elianor said.

Tomas was carrying a brush. “Did it look hungry?”

“It looked profitable.”

She told him about the ledger, the repeated losses, and the orders bearing Sir Edric Pell’s name. Tomas listened without interruption, his scarred hand moving slowly through Ash’s mane.

“Tomorrow night,” he said, “a wagon leaves through the north gate.”

“How do you know?”

“Because I was told to oil its traces.”

“How much?”

“Thirty sacks of barley. Six of wheat.”

“Destination?”

“Westmere road first. After that, the driver does not know.”

“Then we change the order.”

His hand stopped. “You said you wanted to learn the shape of the thing.”

“I have learned it.”

“And now you want to put your hand inside it.”

“I want to put food in Rill.”

Tomas looked toward the stable doors. “If the order bears your father’s seal, altering it is treason.”

“If it bears no seal, it is only a blank page.”

“Elianor.”

She heard her name as he said it—not Lady Elianor, not my lady. It made the danger intimate.

“We can take a portion,” he said. “Not the whole wagon. A missing sack may be blamed on damp or theft. Thirty-eight missing sacks will bring soldiers.”

“Rill needs more than a portion.”

“Rill needs to still be alive when we can bring more.”

She hated the prudence of this. It sounded too much like her father’s language, yet Tomas used it to protect the people her father abandoned.

“How do we make the driver go south?” she asked.

Tomas’s gaze returned to her. “You have already decided.”

“I am asking how.”

He set down the brush. “The stable office keeps route slips for every cart. Drivers collect them from the yard clerk. If the slip says the lower road, he follows it unless Captain Harl stops him. The lower road bends toward Rill before it rejoins the coast road.”

“And the seal?”

“Master Vey’s office has wax.”

“That is not enough.”

“No. But your father’s seal is kept in the west solar.”

“I cannot take it.”

“You need not. A delivery order signed by the steward is accepted for provisions moving between estate stores. The driver will not question a mark he sees every day.”

She studied him. “You have thought about this before.”

“I have thought about food.”

They worked after dark.

Elianor returned to the house, changed into a plain wool dress, and waited until the corridor outside the solar emptied. Lord Marrow had gone to dine with Captain Harl and two visiting landowners. The solar door was locked, but the side cabinet where household forms were stored was not. She took a blank route slip and one of the official delivery orders she had copied earlier, then carried both to the kitchen office.

Bryn stood watch in the passage.

“You are becoming a criminal,” Bryn whispered.

“I am becoming accurate.”

“That is what all criminals say when they have good handwriting.”

Master Vey’s wax sat beside the lamp. Elianor warmed it, pressed the steward’s seal into the red pool, and wrote the new route in a hand close enough to the clerk’s that only a careful reader would question it: Lower Pasture Store, Rill coastal depot, thirty sacks barley, six sacks wheat. Emergency issue by order of household relief.

The last phrase made her pause.

There was no household relief office. There should have been.

She signed with the abbreviated mark she used for estate inventories, folded the slip, and sealed it. When she looked up, Master Vey stood in the doorway.

Bryn went white.

Master Vey’s eyes settled on the wax. “That is a dangerous amount of accuracy.”

Elianor did not move. “You knew.”

“I suspected.”

“You could stop me.”

“Yes.”

“Will you?”

He entered and shut the door. For the first time she saw how tired he truly was. The skin beneath his eyes had the gray cast of old illness.

“Thirty-eight sacks,” he said. “No more. Send the wagon back before dawn. If it is found in Rill after that, the whole village will be searched.”

“Why help me?”

“I am not helping you. I am correcting an account.”

He took the route slip, examined the writing, and handed it back. “The driver is called Noll. He drinks when frightened and talks when drunk. Do not let him speak to the villagers. Have the sacks unloaded before he sees where they go.”

“Will you report this?”

Master Vey opened the door. “I have reported many things. They became orders.”

At the stable, Tomas had prepared a second wagon beneath the loft. He and another stable hand, Pell, waited beside the hay racks. Pell was broad-shouldered, freckled, and silent. Elianor had seen him at the gate but had never before learned his name.

“Pell knows the south track,” Tomas said. “He does not know why we are using it.”

“I know why,” Pell replied. “I am simply not interested in being asked.”

The grain wagon arrived near midnight. Noll, the driver, held the route slip close to the lantern. He squinted at the seal, spat into the mud, and shrugged.

“Lower road,” he said. “That road’s half washed out.”

“Then you will drive carefully,” Elianor told him.

He stared at her fine cloak. “Who are you?”

“Someone whose order you are carrying.”

That was enough. He climbed down to open the rear gate.

They moved quickly. Tomas and Pell carried the sacks from one wagon to the other while Elianor counted aloud. One, two, three. The numbers became a rhythm, a promise made physical. Grain dust settled in her hair and coated her tongue. Her gloves tore at the fingertips. Tomas’s shoulder brushed hers each time they turned, and once his hand closed around her wrist to keep her from falling beneath a shifting sack.

“Careful,” he said.

“I am careful.”

“You are standing under thirty pounds of barley.”

“Then tell the barley to behave.”

He laughed, breathless. The sound was swallowed by the dark stable.

At thirty-eight, they covered the sacks with old blankets and led the second wagon through the postern. Pell drove. Tomas went beside him on foot, guiding the wheels over the stones. Elianor remained in the stable with Noll, who had not noticed the alteration.

“Why does a lady care about village grain?” he asked.

“Because the village is part of the estate.”

Noll shook his head. “That is not what I meant.”

“No,” Elianor said. “It is not.”

By dawn, the wagon was gone.

Tomas returned as the eastern sky paled. Mud streaked his boots and blood showed where a sack had split the skin of his palm. He carried no report from Rill, only the empty grain hooks that had held the sacks.

“Did they receive it?” Elianor asked.

“Lysa did. So did the miller’s widow. We left the wheat for the children.”

“How many?”

“Enough to make tomorrow possible.”

She looked at the blood on his hand. “You are hurt.”

“It is a scratch.”

She took his hand before he could withdraw it and wrapped the torn edge of her glove around his palm. His skin was warm, rough, and unexpectedly still beneath her fingers.

For a moment neither spoke.

Then bells rang from the house.

Tomas pulled away. “You should go.”

“I know.”

“What will you tell your father?”

“The truth.”

His face sharpened.

“I inspected the lower pasture,” she said. “The road was muddy. The wagon reached its destination.”

“That is not the truth.”

“It is the part he has earned.”

At breakfast, Lord Marrow summoned her before she had removed the grain dust from her hair. He stood by the window with a letter in his hand. His expression was controlled, which meant he was angry.

“Your behavior has become difficult to manage,” he said.

“I was unaware that I was a parcel.”

“You are twenty years old, the heir to Greyhaven, and increasingly visible beyond its walls. The court has begun asking whether you are prepared to inherit.”

“I am prepared to read an account.”

“You are prepared to challenge men who have governed longer than you have lived.”

“Perhaps they should govern better.”

His eyes hardened. “A woman with property is not free to indulge every moral impulse. Your future must secure this house.”

“By marrying it to someone?”

He did not answer directly. He folded the letter. “There are families who would value your position. Families with ships, soldiers, and influence at court.”

Elianor understood then that his concern had shifted. He no longer saw only a daughter disobedient in small ways. He saw an heir whose name might be placed beside another name, whose marriage could protect the estate—or whose refusal could weaken it.

“I am not a shipment,” she said.

“No,” Lord Marrow replied. “You are more valuable than one.”

She left before he could see how deeply the words frightened her.

In her room, she lifted the loose floorboard and placed the copied figures beside the First Seed loaf. The new route slip remained in her sleeve, its wax seal cracked from use. She should have destroyed it. Instead she kept it with the evidence.

Outside, the sea struck the cliffs. Somewhere below, in Rill, thirty-eight sacks of grain were being opened beneath a roof that had known too many empty mornings.

Elianor touched the torn place in her glove where Tomas’s hand had been.

For the first time, the accounts held something besides numbers. They held his blood, Bryn’s silence, Pell’s unwilling courage, and the names of people who might see another day. The secret was no longer hers alone. It belonged to the stable, the road, and the dark between Greyhaven’s walls and the sea.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Greyhaven in her room after secretly redirecting a grain shipment to Rill. She is twenty, Lord Corvin Marrow's only child and heir. She has confirmed that grain marked as waste is sold through Sir Edric Pell and Merrit & Sons, copied the figures and delivery details, and preserved them with the First Seed loaf and altered route slip beneath a loose floorboard. She collaborated with Tomas, Pell, Bryn, and tacitly Master Vey to redirect thirty-eight sacks to Rill, creating a shared secret among the stable network. She outwardly answers her father and has learned he is considering a politically useful marriage for her; inwardly she is frightened, angry, increasingly committed to hidden relief, and emotionally affected by Tomas's trust and touch. She possesses her riding and plain wool dresses, damaged glove, copied evidence, altered route slip, authority as heir, and knowledge of the grain network.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven, maintaining authority over the estate and watching Elianor's conduct more urgently. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, and armed, seeking to preserve Greyhaven, its stores, political standing, and crown ties through controlled distribution, grain sales, and strategic alliances. He does not know that Elianor altered a delivery order or that Tomas and the stable network moved grain to Rill, but he now recognizes Elianor as a politically consequential heir and is considering a marriage alliance with families possessing ships, soldiers, and court influence. He possesses the Marrow signet bearing a white bone and the authority of the household guard.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven, moving between the granary office and household administration. Lord Marrow's long-standing steward manages ledgers, servants, schedules, stores, waste records, and delivery orders. He knows Elianor confirmed the grain was being sold through noble intermediaries, witnessed her altered route slip, and chose not to report her, instead limiting the diversion to thirty-eight sacks and warning her about the danger. He remains cautious, composed, observant, physically tired, morally conflicted, and a quiet potential ally. He possesses the steward's seal, administrative knowledge, and access to Greyhaven's records.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after helping Elianor redirect thirty-eight sacks of grain to Rill. He is a young stable servant slightly older than Elianor, with rain-dark brown hair, a serious narrow face, patched stable wool, and a burn scar on his left hand. He knows the hidden routes, drivers, Rill villagers, and the danger of grain theft; he helped Pell move the sacks and personally delivered grain to Lysa, the miller's widow, and the children. His palm is scratched from the work, and his trust and intimacy with Elianor have deepened, though he remains practical and wary of her father's power. He possesses stable tools, practical horse knowledge, a brown riding horse, knowledge of hidden coastal paths, and the first shared secret binding him to Elianor and sympathetic servants.

set.name: Ash
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable in her quiet stall or paddock. She is a tall gray mare with a white blaze, raw rope wound beneath her jaw, swollen hind leg, and scars from mistreatment. She remains frightened but accepts food and touch from Tomas and Elianor, and is not fit to ride until her leg heals. Tomas continues tending her patiently.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Greyhaven's kitchen and service passages. She is a clever young kitchen maid who noticed Elianor studying the waste ledger, kept watch, and witnessed the route slip being sealed. She now knows Elianor is diverting grain and has joined the secret through her silence, though she fears discovery and Lord Marrow's punishment. She remains practical, quick-witted, and wary. She possesses access to kitchen offices, servants' passages, and household routines.

set.name: Pell
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after driving the diverted grain wagon along the south track toward Rill. He is a broad-shouldered, freckled stable hand who knows the southern route and agreed to help without asking for the full reason. He now shares the stable's secret with Tomas and Elianor, remains silent and cautious, and possesses practical cart-driving and coastal-road knowledge.
Elianor confirmed that grain marked as waste was being sold through Sir Edric Pell and Merrit & Sons, then altered a delivery order to redirect thirty-eight sacks of barley and wheat toward Rill.
Tomas, Pell, and Elianor moved the redirected grain through the stables and delivered it to Rill; Master Vey discovered the alteration and quietly limited the diversion rather than reporting it.
Lord Marrow learned that Elianor's conduct and public visibility were becoming politically consequential and began considering a marriage alliance involving ships, soldiers, and court influence.
Elianor will preserve the altered route slip and copied delivery evidence, while concealing the stable network's role in the diversion from Lord Marrow and the guards.

chapters.name: The Chapel Doors
chapters.content:
The storm announced itself before noon.

All morning the sea had worn a color Elianor had never seen before, a green-black darkness that seemed to rise rather than fall beneath the clouds. Gulls flew inland in ragged lines. The kitchen fires smoked despite the chimneys being swept, and Ash struck once against the wall of her stall when thunder muttered beyond the cliffs.

By afternoon, rain began.

It came sideways at first, needling the windows and rattling the leaded panes. Then the wind found the angles of Greyhaven and howled through them. Servants hurried across the inner court with their heads bent. A shutter tore loose from the west tower. In the lower village, bells began to ring—not the measured bells of prayer, but a frantic clanging that made every face in the household turn toward the sea.

Elianor stood beneath the gallery arch and watched the gates.

People were coming up the road.

They appeared in groups between curtains of rain: women carrying infants beneath cloaks, old men leaning on oars used as walking sticks, boys with rope tied around their waists so they would not be separated in the wind. Behind them came two carts, one with a broken wheel. A black dog ran beside the first and vanished under the wheels whenever lightning struck.

“Why are they leaving Rill?” Elianor asked.

The gate guard beside her wiped rain from his mouth. “The lower lanes are flooding.”

“Then open the gate.”

He looked toward Captain Harl, who stood in the gatehouse beneath a covered passage. “That is not my order.”

Elianor crossed the court.

Captain Harl had three guards with him, all armed and wearing the estate’s blue-gray cloaks. The iron portcullis remained lowered. Beyond it, villagers pressed against the bars, shouting to be heard over the storm.

“Captain,” Elianor said, “raise the gate.”

Harl bowed, though his hand stayed on the pommel of his sword. “My lady, Lord Marrow has ordered the gates secured.”

“Against a storm?”

“Against disorder.”

“Those people are not disorder.”

One of the villagers, a girl no older than twelve, lifted a child above the mud. The child’s face was gray with cold. Elianor saw the girl’s lips move, though no sound reached the gatehouse.

Harl followed her gaze. “They cannot enter the estate.”

“On whose authority?”

“His lordship’s.”

“I am his daughter.”

“You are not his voice.”

The words struck harder than the wind. For one instant she was again in the chapel on the day of the First Seed, standing beside her father while the doors closed on hungry villagers. She remembered the polished brass, the incense, the little loaf resting on the altar, and Corvin Marrow saying that a household survived by keeping its thresholds guarded.

Outside, someone fell.

The crowd surged toward the bars. A guard lowered his spear, and the metal point flashed between the iron ribs.

“Back!” Harl shouted. “Back, or you will be driven back.”

Elianor turned on him. “If you raise that weapon against them, I will see you stripped of command.”

Harl’s face tightened. “And if I raise the gate without permission, I will be stripped of more than command.”

A crack of thunder shook the stones. From the road came a cry, followed by another. The black dog had been swept into the drainage ditch. A stable hand ran from the lower yard and caught it by the collar before it disappeared.

Elianor looked at the gate, then at the chapel tower.

“Open the chapel,” she said.

Harl stared at her. “The chapel?”

“It is dry. It has a hearth. Saint Orra’s house was built for those in distress.”

“It is an estate chapel, not a public shelter.”

“Then today the estate has a public distress.”

She left him before he could answer and climbed the chapel steps. The door was barred from within. She struck it with her fist until Chaplain Orren opened it a hand’s breadth, his round face appearing in the gap.

“My lady?”

“Open the chapel.”

His eyes moved past her toward the gate and the crowd beyond it. “Lord Marrow has given no instruction.”

“Lord Marrow is not standing in the rain.”

“His lordship has entrusted the chapel to my care.”

“Then care for it.”

Orren swallowed. Behind him, the sanctuary waited in its familiar dimness: whitewashed walls, dark pews, the painted figure of Saint Orra holding a lamp over a shipwreck. The storm made the little flames before the altar tremble.

“I cannot admit them without permission,” he said.

“You can.”

“I must obey the house.”

“Which house?” Elianor asked. “The one built of stone, or the one Saint Orra was meant to shelter?”

He flinched as if she had spoken blasphemy. She lowered her voice.

“Chaplain, if those people remain outside, children will die before night. You know it. I know it. Captain Harl knows it. My father’s order does not make the cold less cold.”

Orren looked at the altar. For a long moment the rain hissed against the chapel roof.

“Temporary shelter,” he whispered.

“Yes.”

“No fires in the nave.”

“We will use the side hearth.”

“No food from the sacramental stores.”

“I will provide food.”

“And if Lord Marrow asks who gave the order?”

Elianor pushed open the door herself. “Tell him I did.”

Orren’s hand closed around the edge of the door. Then he stepped aside.

Elianor returned to the gate with the chaplain behind her. Captain Harl had not moved. The villagers were now kneeling in the mud, not from prayer but because the wind had taken their balance.

“Raise it,” Elianor said.

“My lady—”

“Open the chapel. No one enters the house proper. Search them for weapons if you must, but do not make the sick stand in the rain.”

Harl’s gaze went to Orren. The chaplain nodded once.

It was not obedience. It was surrender to the fact that there were more witnesses than orders.

The portcullis groaned upward.

The villagers did not rush through. They hesitated, astonished by the space suddenly offered to them, as though Greyhaven had opened a mouth and they feared it might bite. Then the first woman crossed, clutching a soaked bundle against her breast. Elianor recognized her from Rill, though she did not know her name. Behind her came the girl with the child, the old men, the families from the lower lanes.

Captain Harl’s guards searched them quickly. One found a fish knife and took it. Another pulled a length of rope from a boy’s coat and laughed until Elianor told him to return it.

“Everyone to Saint Orra’s,” she called. “Keep together. Do not stop in the court.”

The wind seized her cloak and snapped it like a flag.

At the chapel, confusion became labor. Wet clothing steamed near the hearth. Children coughed beneath pews. A man with a split scalp sat against a pillar while blood diluted with rainwater and ran down his cheek. Someone had brought a basket of turnips, most of them bruised. Someone else carried a hen beneath a coat.

Elianor sent a footman to the kitchen for blankets and was told the kitchen stores were locked.

“Then find the key,” she said.

“Master Vey has it.”

“Find Master Vey.”

She had just begun sorting the villagers by need when Tomas appeared in the chapel doorway, soaked through, his brown hair plastered to his forehead. He had come from the stable yard with Pell and three other servants carrying folded horse blankets.

His eyes found Elianor immediately.

For a heartbeat the storm seemed to recede.

Then he looked at the crowd and understood.

“What do you need?” he asked.

“Blankets. Dry wood. Anyone who knows how to treat fever.”

“Bryn knows the kitchen medicine cabinet.”

“Bryn is in the kitchen.”

“She will not be for long.”

He turned and shouted into the court. “Pell, take the north passage. Bring every blanket not nailed down. Joss, get the stable buckets and fill them at the rain barrel. Mara, find the old nurse in the laundry. Tell her there is work.”

The servants moved before anyone could object.

Elianor watched him organize them with the same unadorned certainty he used with frightened horses. He did not ask who was noble, who belonged to Rill, or whose name appeared in the estate books. He asked who could carry, who could mend, who could boil water. The distinction shamed her more than any accusation.

A girl began to seize near the altar.

Elianor dropped to her knees. “Tomas.”

He was beside her at once. The girl’s teeth chattered violently, her eyes rolled white. Her mother kept saying that she had been well that morning, that the flood had taken their bed, that she had not eaten since yesterday.

“Fever,” Tomas said. “Or cold. Bring a blanket.”

Elianor took off her own cloak and wrapped the girl in it. Tomas lifted the child with careful arms and carried her toward the hearth. Elianor followed, holding the cloak closed around the small body.

“Her name?” he asked.

“Dessa,” the mother said. “Her name is Dessa.”

“Elianor,” Tomas said, “remember that.”

She looked at him. “Why?”

“Because names keep people from becoming a crowd.”

The words entered her with the force of recognition. She repeated the name to herself: Dessa. Not a petitioner. Not a village child. Dessa.

Master Vey arrived with two keys and a face like a locked door. Behind him came Bryn, carrying bottles, linen, and a sack of dried willow bark.

“His lordship is asking what is happening,” the steward said.

“Elianor opened the chapel,” Bryn replied before Elianor could speak.

Master Vey looked at her. “So I see.”

“You can close it again,” Elianor said. “After the storm.”

A distant boom rolled over the cliffs. The chapel windows shuddered.

Master Vey glanced toward the villagers crowded beneath the saints’ painted eyes. “No. I cannot.”

It was the first open act of support he had given her. Elianor felt its weight.

“His lordship may dismiss you,” she said.

“He has threatened that for eleven years.”

Bryn gave a quick, frightened laugh and began arranging the medicines.

By evening, the chapel had become a world of wet wool, smoke, and whispered names. The storm tore at Greyhaven so fiercely that the household bells rang without anyone touching them. A section of the outer wall collapsed near the lower yard. The guards abandoned their posts there and came to the chapel for instructions, finding servants already carrying water and villagers binding wounds.

Lord Marrow did not come.

His steward appeared twice with messages. The first ordered that no villager be admitted to the upper house. The second demanded a count of all persons sheltered in the chapel and warned that provisions must not be wasted.

Elianor read the message by candlelight, then handed it back.

“Write that the count is being made,” she said, “and that no provisions are being wasted.”

Master Vey’s mouth twitched. “That is technically true.”

“It is morally true as well.”

He studied her, perhaps measuring how far she had traveled from the girl who once believed obedience was the highest shape of love.

Near midnight, the fever broke in Dessa. Her mother wept without sound. Tomas sat beside them, his back against the chapel wall, while Elianor changed the cloth on the girl’s forehead. Their hands met over the basin.

Neither withdrew.

“You should sleep,” Tomas said.

“So should you.”

“I am a servant. We are trained to remain inconveniently alive.”

“And I am the heir. We are trained to look rested while everything burns.”

His mouth curved despite his exhaustion. “Then we are both badly trained.”

Lightning filled the chapel white. In its afterimage she saw every face around them: frightened, hungry, exhausted, alive. The walls that had seemed so strong from the inside were only stone. The rain had crossed them. The suffering had crossed them. Her own certainty had crossed them.

Tomas’s thumb brushed the grain dust still caught at the edge of her torn glove.

“You opened the door,” he said.

“Chaplain Orren opened it.”

“You told him to.”

“I used my father’s name.”

“No,” Tomas said quietly. “You used your own.”

She looked toward the altar. “I do not know what that means yet.”

“It means the gate captain heard you.”

“It means my father will hear me too.”

“Yes.”

There was no comfort in the answer, only honesty. She found she preferred it.

Before dawn, the storm weakened. Rain still fell, but the wind no longer battered the chapel doors. Villagers slept wherever there was floor. Bryn had distributed the last of the clean bandages. Pell had brought in a crate of apples from the stores, claiming the lid had broken. Chaplain Orren stood before the altar, staring at the mud tracked across the holy tiles.

Elianor went to him.

“I am sorry,” she said.

“For the mud?”

“For making you choose.”

Orren looked at the sleeping children. “I have been choosing for years. I merely called it obedience.”

At the chapel doors, Tomas was fastening a blanket around an old man’s shoulders. He looked exhausted, and there was a fresh cut across his cheek. Elianor joined him without speaking. Together they lifted the bar when the first gray light reached the eastern windows.

Outside, Greyhaven was battered but standing. The road below had become a brown torrent. Roofs showed where tiles had been ripped away. Beyond the walls, the sea boiled beneath a sky the color of ash.

The chapel doors remained open.

Elianor stood beside Tomas on the threshold. Neither of them said that the doors might close again when Lord Marrow gave the order. Neither said that the night had changed anything that could not be changed back.

A child sleeping inside stirred and called for her mother. From somewhere in the courtyard, a horse whinnied. The sound made Tomas turn toward the stable, and Elianor saw the old reflex of care move through him.

“Go,” she said. “I will stay with them.”

He hesitated. “You are not accustomed to staying.”

“I am learning.”

He looked at her then—not as a lady, not as an ally whose seal could open a storehouse, but as someone standing in the same cold doorway.

“Come back when the mare is fed,” she said.

“I will.”

He went into the rain.

Elianor watched him cross the court, his figure growing smaller beneath the torn banners of Greyhaven. Behind her, the chapel breathed with the sleep of the displaced. Before her, the fortress waited for her father’s anger.

She turned back to the people inside.

For the first time, the walls did not feel like protection. They felt like a question.

And the open doors were her answer.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Greyhaven's Chapel of Saint Orra after opening it as an unauthorized temporary shelter during a violent storm. She is twenty, Lord Corvin Marrow's only child and heir. She has preserved the grain diversion evidence and altered route slip beneath her floorboard, and remains bound to Tomas, Pell, Bryn, and Master Vey by the secret Rill diversion. She defied Captain Harl and her father by ordering the chapel opened to villagers fleeing flooded Rill, used her own authority and cloak to aid the refugees, worked beside Tomas through the night, and now understands more sharply that Greyhaven's walls protect privilege rather than people. She expects Lord Marrow's anger and is frightened but increasingly willing to use her own name against his orders. She possesses her riding and plain wool dresses, damaged glove, copied evidence, altered route slip, heir's authority, and knowledge of the grain network and chapel shelter.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven, informed through messages that Elianor opened Saint Orra's Chapel to storm refugees against his gate policy. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, and armed, seeking to preserve Greyhaven, its stores, political standing, and crown ties through controlled distribution, grain sales, and strategic alliances. He still does not know the full truth of Elianor's grain diversion, but now faces her visible public defiance and is likely to tighten control over her and the household. He possesses the Marrow signet bearing a white bone and the authority of the household guard.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's Chapel of Saint Orra and its administrative passages after helping sustain the storm shelter. Lord Marrow's long-standing steward manages ledgers, servants, schedules, stores, waste records, and delivery orders. He knows Elianor altered the grain route, witnessed the chapel opened against Lord Marrow's order, and chose not to close it or report her directly. He remains cautious, composed, observant, physically tired, morally conflicted, and now a more active quiet ally. He possesses the steward's seal, administrative knowledge, keys to household stores, and access to Greyhaven's records.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven's gate and guard posts after being overruled by Elianor during the storm. He is responsible for enforcing Lord Marrow's orders and keeping petitioners outside the estate. He refused the villagers entry at first, citing Lord Marrow's command, but raised the portcullis when Elianor ordered the chapel opened and Chaplain Orren supported the decision. He remains loyal to the Marrow hierarchy, resentful of public embarrassment, and a possible obstacle to Elianor's movements. He possesses the authority and weapons of the estate guard.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At the Chapel of Saint Orra in Greyhaven, where he has allowed storm refugees to shelter temporarily after Elianor persuaded him to open the doors. He serves the Marrow household's religious traditions and remains subordinate to Lord Marrow, but has begun recognizing that obedience can become an excuse for moral cowardice. He helped authorize the shelter and may now face Lord Marrow's displeasure. He possesses the chapel keys, religious authority, and responsibility for the sanctuary and its displaced guests.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable and Chapel of Saint Orra after organizing care for villagers driven from Rill by the storm. He is a young stable servant slightly older than Elianor, with rain-dark brown hair, a serious narrow face, patched stable wool, and a burn scar on his left hand. He coordinated Pell and other servants to bring horse blankets, water, food, medicine, and an old nurse; he carried and cared for the feverish child Dessa alongside Elianor, and their trust and intimacy deepened through the night's work. He remains practical, wary of Lord Marrow's power, emotionally affected by Elianor's willingness to act, and still tending Ash. He possesses stable tools, practical horse knowledge, a brown riding horse, knowledge of hidden coastal paths, servant connections, and the first shared secret binding him to Elianor and sympathetic servants.

set.name: Ash
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable in her quiet stall or paddock while the storm-damaged estate shelters villagers. She is a tall gray mare with a white blaze, raw rope wound beneath her jaw, swollen hind leg, and scars from mistreatment. She remains frightened but accepts food and touch from Tomas and Elianor, and is not fit to ride until her leg heals. Tomas returned to feed and check on her after organizing the chapel response.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Greyhaven's kitchen and Chapel of Saint Orra after bringing medicines, linen, food, and bandages to the storm shelter. She is a clever young kitchen maid who knows Elianor is diverting grain and witnessed the route slip being sealed. She joined Tomas's effort openly enough to distribute medicine and supplies, increasing her risk if Lord Marrow investigates the chapel. She remains practical, quick-witted, frightened, and loyal to the small network. She possesses access to kitchen offices, servants' passages, household routines, and medicine stores.

set.name: Pell
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable, lower yard, and Chapel of Saint Orra after helping organize the storm shelter. He is a broad-shouldered, freckled stable hand who knows the southern route and helped move the diverted grain to Rill. During the storm he carried blankets and brought food from the stores under a pretext, sharing the servants' secret and risking discovery. He remains silent, cautious, and dependable, and possesses practical cart-driving, stable, and coastal-road knowledge.

During a violent storm, Elianor defied Captain Harl and Lord Marrow's gate policy, persuaded Chaplain Orren to open Saint Orra's Chapel, and sheltered villagers driven from flooded Rill without admitting them to the upper house.

Tomas organized Pell, Bryn, and other servants to bring blankets, medicine, water, food, and care to the storm refugees; Elianor and Tomas worked together through the night and treated a feverish child named Dessa.
Master Vey chose not to close the chapel or report Elianor's defiance directly, and Chaplain Orren acknowledged that obedience had become his excuse for avoiding moral choices.

Lord Marrow will respond to Elianor's unauthorized opening of the chapel by tightening control over her movements and the household, while the sheltered villagers and servants become evidence of her public defiance.

chapters.name: Names at the Table
chapters.content:
By the third evening after the storm, Greyhaven had dried enough to pretend it was whole.

The west tower still wore a black wound where lightning had struck it. Tiles lay in heaps along the lower court, and the chapel doors remained open because the road to Rill was broken in two places and the villagers had nowhere else to go. Yet Lord Marrow ordered the great dining room prepared.

“His lordship says the dinner will proceed as planned,” Master Vey told Elianor that afternoon.

She was standing at the chapel window, watching Pell carry a basket of turnips from the kitchen. “What dinner?”

“The one arranged three weeks ago.”

“For whom?”

Master Vey’s expression did not alter. “For the people who will complain if it is canceled.”

Elianor looked at the refugees sleeping beneath the gallery of Saint Orra’s. Dessa was awake now, though still pale, sitting against her mother’s knees and tracing the pattern of the borrowed blanket with one finger.

“Let them complain,” Elianor said.

“His lordship believes complaints are less dangerous when made over a full table.”

“And the people in the chapel?”

“Will have soup.”

“The soup is made from the same stores they say are too scarce to share.”

“Yes.” Vey glanced toward the chapel doors. “Scarcity has always been a matter of accounting, my lady.”

He left her with the sentence. It followed her upstairs while two maids fastened her into a dark green gown. They brushed the salt from her hair and pinned a narrow chain of pearls at her throat. She had slept in fragments since the storm, waking to coughing, to the sound of rain striking the roof, to Tomas’s voice somewhere below asking for clean water. Her body was tired, but Lord Marrow had sent word that she was to dine in the great room and make herself agreeable.

Make herself agreeable.

The words seemed to belong to another language, one spoken by people who had never watched a child shake with fever beside an altar.

When she descended, the dinner guests had already arrived.

Lord Corvin sat at the head of the table beneath the Marrow banner, his silvering hair tied neatly at his nape. The storm had not softened him. If anything, the wreckage around Greyhaven had sharpened the lines of his face. To his right sat Lady Merrow of Dunscar, whose husband had died two winters earlier and whose estates had somehow expanded since. Beside her was Sir Edric Pell, broad and pink from the cold, with a gold chain heavy enough to pay for several fishing boats. Three lesser nobles occupied the other side of the table.

Elianor took her place beside her father.

“You are late,” Corvin said.

“I was at the chapel.”

“So I was informed.”

“The villagers still need—”

“They need to understand that shelter is temporary. Not become accustomed to the notion that Greyhaven is a public granary.”

His voice was low enough that the musicians at the far end of the room continued playing. A lute and two viols made a sweet, careful sound beneath the clatter of plates.

Elianor folded her hands in her lap. “No one has suggested they remain forever.”

“No one needs to suggest it. People remember an open door more readily than a closed one.”

A footman poured wine. Elianor saw the red liquid tremble in the crystal as the wind pressed against the windows.

Lady Merrow leaned across the table. “Is it true the lower village lost half its boats?”

“Nearly half,” said Sir Edric. “Though the fishermen claim the sea took them. I am told three were found in the cove below the eastern cliffs.”

“Then the sea did not take them,” Lady Merrow said. “The fishermen abandoned them.”

“They were frightened,” Elianor said.

Sir Edric smiled at her. “Fear is costly, my lady. It makes poor men careless with property.”

A servant set down a dish of roasted goose. The scent of fat and rosemary filled the room. Elianor thought of the soup in the chapel, thin with turnip water, and of Dessa asking whether there would be bread in the morning.

Lord Marrow raised his cup. “To Greyhaven standing.”

The guests echoed him.

“To Greyhaven standing.”

Elianor lifted her cup but did not drink.

Corvin noticed. “You have something to say.”

“I have several things to say.”

“Then choose one that can survive the table.”

The musicians played on.

Sir Edric broke the silence. “The storm is a small matter compared with the news from the north. Two tax offices burned last week. A royal courier was found hanging from a bridge near Varrow. The crown calls it organized rebellion.”

Lady Merrow sighed. “Rebellion. The word is becoming fashionable.”

“It is not fashion,” said Corvin. “It is contagion. Hungry villages listen to anyone who promises them an easier world.”

Elianor turned toward him. “Perhaps they listen because the world is difficult for them.”

The room quieted.

Her father’s eyes rested on her. “Difficulty does not excuse treason.”

“Nor does obedience excuse hunger.”

Lady Merrow gave a nervous little laugh. “The young always mistake discomfort for injustice.”

Elianor looked at the goose. “Did the people of Rill mistake the flood for discomfort when their children were carried from their beds?”

“No one is discussing children,” Corvin said.

“That is precisely the problem.”

Sir Edric cut into the goose. “The problem is that levies cannot be collected from people who spend their strength arguing over the fairness of them. The crown requires men for the northern roads. If the coast refuses, soldiers must be sent.”

“For what?” Elianor asked. “To force fishermen to become soldiers?”

“To preserve the kingdom.”

“Whose kingdom?”

The question landed with a dullness more terrible than a shout.

Corvin placed his knife beside his plate. “Enough.”

She felt every eye in the room move between them. Her father had taught her that a lady’s courage consisted in knowing when to be silent. She had once believed him. Now silence seemed less like grace than a servant carrying a covered dish from one room to another.

Lord Marrow turned to the guests. “There are larger matters than village complaints. The western fleet has been ordered to patrol the coast. Duke Alistair Veyne is expected at court within the fortnight.”

Lady Merrow’s eyebrows rose. “Veyne himself?”

“His flag captain will accompany him. The duke wishes to inspect the harbor defenses.”

Sir Edric swallowed a mouthful of goose. “He has put down two mutinies this year.”

“Three,” said Corvin. “The third never became public.”

“That is a distinction only the dead would make,” Elianor said.

Her father’s gaze hardened.

Lady Merrow reached for the wine. “Duke Veyne is a powerful man. An alliance with him would secure Greyhaven against the crown’s suspicion.”

Elianor’s pulse stumbled. “An alliance?”

No one answered immediately. That pause was answer enough.

Corvin spoke as if reading from an account book. “The Marrow lands require protection. The coast is unsettled. Veyne commands ships, soldiers, and considerable influence with the ministers.”

“I see.”

“Do you?”

“I see that you have invited me to dinner so I could be informed in front of witnesses.”

The lady of Dunscar looked down at her plate. Sir Edric studied the pattern of his knife.

Corvin’s face remained composed. “I invited you because you are my daughter and heir, and because there are decisions in which your cooperation is useful.”

“Useful.”

“You prefer indispensable?”

“I prefer to be asked whether I wish to marry a man who puts down mutinies by making sure they are never spoken of.”

A flicker passed across his face—not shame, but irritation at the inconvenience of her hearing.

“Duke Veyne is not yet a proposal,” he said. “He is a possibility.”

“Then let the possibility die.”

“Possibilities do not die because an heir finds them unpleasant.”

“I am not an account to be balanced against ships.”

“No. You are the person who may one day have to defend every person dependent upon those ships.”

He leaned closer. “You think kindness is governance because you have opened a chapel and handed out blankets. Do not confuse a night of compassion with the burden of keeping a house alive.”

Elianor felt heat rise behind her eyes. “Perhaps the house would be easier to keep alive if it stopped selling its food.”

Sir Edric’s knife halted.

Corvin’s voice fell to a whisper. “You will not discuss storehouses at this table.”

“Why? The grain is at the heart of every matter you have named.”

“Because you know nothing of what you are saying.”

“I know that there is enough to fill the granaries and not enough to fill the bowls in Rill.”

For one instant, fear showed itself in his face. It vanished so quickly she might have imagined it.

He rose.

The musicians stopped.

“Dinner is concluded,” Lord Marrow said.

No one moved until he left the room.

Elianor remained seated, her untouched wine before her. Through the high windows she could see the chapel lanterns burning below. Tiny points of gold in the dark. She thought of Tomas carrying Dessa through the storm, of the way he had said her name as if it mattered that she remember one child among many.

The guests departed by the side passage. Lady Merrow paused beside Elianor.

“You are very like your mother,” she murmured.

“Was that meant as praise?”

“No. Your mother also believed that feeling deeply was the same as seeing clearly.”

When she was gone, Elianor stood and walked out into the night.

She found Tomas in the stable, rubbing Ash’s swollen hind leg with a warm cloth. The mare’s ears turned toward Elianor, then back toward Tomas. A lantern hung from the beam above them, gilding the rain-dark strands of his hair.

“You should be asleep,” he said without looking up.

“So should you.”

“I am badly trained.”

She almost smiled, but the memory of the dinner held her rigid. “My father means to marry me to Duke Veyne.”

Tomas’s hand stopped.

“Not means,” he said. “Considers.”

“Does the distinction make it less true?”

“No.” He set down the cloth. “It makes it less immediate.”

She had come seeking sympathy. His caution felt like a refusal.

“They spoke of the people in Rill as if they were spilled grain,” she said. “They discussed forced levies over roast goose. My father called opening the chapel a night of compassion, as though compassion were a weakness I had indulged.”

“Was he wrong?”

She stared at him. “What?”

“About the chapel. You opened it because people were freezing. That was right. But you keep speaking as though one right act has made you different from the house that gave you the power to do it.”

The stable seemed suddenly too small. Ash shifted in her stall.

“I know what my house is.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“You still believe you can repair it from inside.”

“I can change things.”

“You changed one night.”

“I changed the gate.”

“And who closes it tomorrow?”

His words struck with the same force as Harl’s had, but there was no rank between them to absorb the blow. Tomas looked at her with anger she had never seen directed at her before.

“You think if you speak kindly enough, your father will become kind,” he said. “You think if you persuade the right noble, the stores will open and the levies will stop. You want the power of Greyhaven without admitting what that power has done.”

Elianor’s face burned. “That is unjust.”

“Is it?”

“I have risked more than you know.”

“I know exactly what you risked. Your father’s anger. Your reputation. Perhaps a lock on your door.”

“And you have risked nothing?”

His expression changed, wounded beneath the anger. “I risk being seen beside you.”

The truth of it silenced her.

Tomas turned away first. “I am sorry.”

“No. Do not apologize because you have made me uncomfortable.”

“I am not apologizing for that.”

“Then what do you want from me?”

He faced her again. “I want you to stop calling mercy a solution. Mercy keeps someone alive until morning. It does not ask why they were starving. It does not take the hand from the throat.”

She thought of her father’s face at the table, of the frightened flicker when she named the grain. “What would you have me do?”

“Know what you are doing.”

“I am trying to help.”

“Yes. And sometimes helping is how people like you forgive themselves for remaining powerful.”

The words opened something in her that she had kept carefully shut. She wanted to deny them. Instead she remembered the first time she had entered the granary, how astonished she had been by the sacks stacked to the rafters, and how quickly she had turned astonishment into action. She had wanted to be good. She had wanted goodness to be enough.

“I do not know how to leave,” she said.

Tomas’s anger softened, but did not disappear. “Neither do I.”

Between them, Ash breathed heavily.

Elianor stepped toward the stall. The mare watched her, wary but no longer wild. Elianor held out her hand. After a moment, Ash lowered her head and touched it with her muzzle.

“I thought kindness was the opposite of cruelty,” Elianor said.

“It is not nothing.”

“No. But it is not enough.”

Tomas shook his head. “Not by itself.”

Outside, rain ticked against the stable roof. Somewhere in the fortress, a bell marked the hour. The sound traveled through stone built to outlast the people beneath it.

“My father will tighten the household,” Elianor said. “After the chapel, he will watch the servants. He may move me under guard.”

“Then we should assume he already is.”

“We?”

Tomas met her eyes. “You asked what I want. I want you to understand that whatever comes next, you cannot stand between the people and the house forever. At some point you must choose which side of the door you are on.”

She looked toward the stable entrance, where the dark courtyard opened onto the fortress. For years she had believed doors were boundaries. Now they seemed like decisions.

“I am not ready to choose sides,” she said.

“No,” Tomas replied. “But you are no longer allowed to pretend there are none.”

He returned to Ash’s leg. Elianor remained until the cloth cooled, then took the lantern and left him in the stable’s amber hush.

At her room, she knelt beside the floorboard where the altered route slip and copied grain figures lay hidden. She lifted the board and checked them both. The papers were dry. The ink had not run.

She had preserved evidence because she believed truth could force her father to change.

Now she understood that truth might instead force her to act.

Below, a chapel door creaked in the wind. Elianor replaced the floorboard, extinguished her candle, and stood in darkness while Greyhaven listened to the sea.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At her room in Greyhaven after a formal dinner and a serious argument with Tomas in the stable. She is twenty, Lord Corvin Marrow's only child and heir, physically exhausted from the storm shelter but emotionally sharpened by the nobles' casual discussion of famine and forced levies. She openly challenged her father at dinner, learned that Duke Alistair Veyne is being considered as a political match, and now understands that kindness alone cannot repair Greyhaven's system; she is not ready to choose a side but can no longer pretend there are none. She expects tighter control of the household and possibly her movements after the chapel defiance. She remains bound to Tomas, Pell, Bryn, Master Vey, and the servants' network by the grain diversion and chapel shelter. She possesses her riding and plain wool dresses, damaged glove, copied grain evidence, altered route slip hidden beneath her floorboard, heir's authority, and knowledge of the grain network and chapel shelter.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven after presiding over a formal dinner where he publicly discussed rebellion, forced levies, the western fleet, and Duke Alistair Veyne as a possible political match for Elianor. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, and determined to preserve Greyhaven, its stores, political standing, crown ties, and control over his heir. He was angered when Elianor challenged the nobles' treatment of famine and linked the grain stores to policy, and is likely to tighten control over her and the household; he still does not know the full location of her copied evidence and altered route slip. He possesses the Marrow signet bearing a white bone and the authority of the household guard.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's administrative passages and stores after helping sustain the chapel shelter and observing the formal dinner's aftermath. Lord Marrow's long-standing steward manages ledgers, servants, schedules, stores, waste records, and delivery orders. He knows Elianor altered the grain route, witnessed the chapel opened against Lord Marrow's order, chose not to close it or report her directly, and understands that her public challenge may provoke tighter household controls. He remains cautious, composed, observant, physically tired, morally conflicted, and a quiet ally. He possesses the steward's seal, administrative knowledge, keys to household stores, and access to Greyhaven's records.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven's gate and guard posts after the storm shelter and Lord Marrow's dinner gathering. He remains responsible for enforcing Lord Marrow's orders and keeping petitioners outside the estate, and resents being overruled by Elianor when she opened Saint Orra's Chapel. He is loyal to the Marrow hierarchy and may help restrict Elianor's movements or investigate servants after her public defiance. He possesses the authority and weapons of the estate guard.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At the Chapel of Saint Orra in Greyhaven, where storm refugees remain temporarily because Rill's road is damaged. He serves the Marrow household's religious traditions but now recognizes that he has used obedience to avoid moral choices; he supported Elianor's shelter decision and remains subordinate to Lord Marrow, whose displeasure he expects. He possesses the chapel keys, religious authority, and responsibility for the sanctuary and displaced guests.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable with Ash after a serious argument with Elianor. He is a young stable servant slightly older than Elianor, with rain-dark brown hair, a serious narrow face, patched stable wool, and a burn scar on his left hand. He remains practical, wary of Lord Marrow's power, emotionally affected by Elianor's willingness to act but frustrated by her belief that noble mercy can reform the system. He told her that mercy is not a solution and that she must eventually choose which side of the door she is on, while admitting he does not know how to leave either. He remains connected to Pell, Bryn, and the hidden relief network, tends Ash's injuries, and possesses stable tools, practical horse knowledge, a brown riding horse, knowledge of hidden coastal paths, servant connections, and the shared grain and chapel secrets.

set.name: Ash
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable in her quiet stall or paddock while storm refugees remain sheltered in Saint Orra's Chapel. She is a tall gray mare with a white blaze, raw rope wound beneath her jaw, swollen hind leg, and scars from mistreatment. She remains frightened but accepts food, treatment, and touch from Tomas and Elianor; she is not fit to ride until her leg heals. Tomas is tending her swollen hind leg with warm cloths.

set.name: Lysa
set.description: At her patched cottage in Rill below the cliffs with her fever-recovering child Nerrin and two hungry younger children. She remains wary of Greyhaven's charity after repeated neglect, but knows Elianor has seen her need directly and that Tomas's network has brought aid. Her family's survival remains uncertain after the storm damaged Rill and its roads.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Greyhaven's kitchen and Chapel of Saint Orra after bringing medicines, linen, food, and bandages to the storm shelter. She is a clever young kitchen maid who knows Elianor is diverting grain, witnessed the route slip being sealed, and remains part of the servants' relief network. She is practical, quick-witted, frightened, loyal to Elianor and Tomas, and increasingly at risk if Lord Marrow investigates the chapel or tightens household surveillance. She possesses access to kitchen offices, servants' passages, household routines, and medicine stores.

set.name: Pell
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable, lower yard, and Chapel of Saint Orra after helping organize the storm shelter and carry supplies from the kitchen. He is a broad-shouldered, freckled stable hand who knows the southern route and helped move the diverted grain to Rill. He remains silent, cautious, and dependable, shares the servants' secret, and may face investigation as Lord Marrow responds to Elianor's public defiance. He possesses practical cart-driving, stable, and coastal-road knowledge.
At a formal dinner, Lord Marrow revealed that Duke Alistair Veyne was being considered as a politically useful match for Elianor because of his fleet, soldiers, and influence with the ministers.

The nobles discussed famine victims and forced levies as matters of property, taxation, and military necessity; Elianor openly challenged them and Lord Marrow ended the dinner when she linked their policies to the grain stores.

Tomas confronted Elianor in the stable, warning that mercy and noble kindness could not repair the system that caused hunger, and forced her to admit that truth might require action rather than merely persuading her father to change.
Elianor will confront Lord Marrow's marriage plans and investigate Duke Alistair Veyne as a possible political match, while recognizing that her father's control over her movements may increase.

chapters.name: The Sea Garden
chapters.content:
The sea garden had once been designed to prove that Greyhaven could make anything grow.

It lay below the eastern wall, on a shelf of land carved into the cliff where the wind came hard from the water. In the old days, gardeners had trained pear trees against warmed stone and planted herbs in geometric beds. A narrow channel brought fresh water from a spring above the kitchens, dividing into little branches that fed beans, onions, cabbages, and the vines that climbed the garden walls.

Now the garden was mostly weeds.

The pears had gone wild. Salt had silvered the leaves of the sage. One section of the irrigation channel had collapsed during the storm, and water ran in a brown ribbon through the nearest bed before spilling over the cliff. The vegetables that had survived were small, bitter-looking things, hidden beneath broad leaves and tangled grass.

Elianor came at dawn wearing a plain brown dress, an old cloak, and boots borrowed from the stable.

She had not told anyone where she was going. That was no longer as simple as it had been. Since the dinner, Captain Harl had stationed two men near the western stair and one outside the chapel passage. Her maid had asked twice whether she intended to visit the refugees. Master Vey had sent word that Lord Marrow wished to see her after breakfast, which meant he had not yet decided whether to question her or merely remind her that questioning was unnecessary.

The sea garden offered the only route from the house that did not pass a guard.

Tomas was already there.

He stood knee-deep in the weeds, holding a shovel over one shoulder. His hair was damp with mist, and a streak of black soil crossed his cheek. When he saw her, his expression shifted from relief to amusement.

“You stole Pell’s boots,” he said.

“They were in the stable.”

“That is not a denial.”

“They fit.”

“One is larger than the other.”

Elianor looked down. “That explains the walking.”

He laughed, and the sound loosened something in her chest. Their argument had left an ache between them, one she had carried through the night. She had expected him to be guarded. Instead, he pointed at her feet as though unequal boots were the most urgent matter in Avelune.

“You could have told me the garden was full of mud,” she said.

“I thought the boots might warn you.”

“Pell’s boots have betrayed me.”

“Pell has betrayed you many times. Usually by snoring.”

She took the shovel from him. “What are we doing?”

“Repairing the channel. Then carrying vegetables down to the lower path before the kitchen finds them.”
