“Those are two separate crimes.”

“Only if Master Vey catches us.”

“He knows everything.”

“He knows the difference between a crime and an unrecorded kindness.”

She studied him. “Is that how the servants’ network describes itself?”

“No. We call ourselves people who are tired of watching food rot.”

He moved to the broken section. The channel had been built from flat stones sealed with clay, but the storm had torn away the bank and left a gap wide enough for Elianor to place both hands inside. Below it, the bed of cabbages had flooded, while the farthest beds were dry.

Tomas knelt and began clearing silt from the stones. Elianor pushed her shovel into the bank. The earth was wet and stubborn. Twice the blade struck a buried root and jolted her shoulders.

“Do not fight it,” Tomas said.

She looked at him. “You are going to have to find a new lesson.”

“I have several. You have not learned the first one.”

“I learned patience.”

“You learned to touch one frightened horse.”

“That is patience.”

“That is Ash having better judgment than you.”

Elianor scooped mud toward the broken channel. “If you insult my character while I work, I may redirect the water into your boots.”

“Pell’s boots?”

“They are already treacherous.”

They worked in silence for a time, passing stones between them. The garden smelled of wet earth, crushed mint, and the iron tang of the sea. Far below, waves broke against the black rocks, each one vanishing into white foam. The clouds were thinning, but the horizon remained a bruised gray line.

When the gap was cleared, Tomas showed her how to set the stones at an angle, overlapping them so the water would press them together rather than pull them apart.

“Like this,” he said, leaning across her shoulder. “No, turn that one. The flat side faces the current.”

His hand closed over hers.

It was not the first time he had touched her. He had steadied her near Ash’s stall, taken a lantern from her, brushed rain from a length of rope between them. But this was different in its ordinariness. His fingers were warm despite the cold, rough at the knuckles, and close enough that she could feel the movement of his breath against her hair.

“The flat side,” he murmured.

“I heard you.”

“You are holding it upside down.”

“I was considering the stone’s feelings.”

“Stones have no feelings.”

“Then you should be kinder to them.”

His thumb moved once against her hand before he withdrew. The absence seemed larger than the touch.

They packed clay into the seams. When Tomas opened the spring gate, water shuddered through the channel, hesitated at the repair, and then ran clear toward the garden. Elianor crouched beside it, watching the stream divide around the stones.

“It works,” she said.

“It leaks.”

“Everything leaks.”

“An encouraging philosophy.”

“I learned it from the roof.”

He smiled. “You have become very practical.”

“I spent the morning in stolen boots.”

“That is not practicality. That is rebellion with poor footwear.”

The first bed had cabbages nearly ready to cut, along with onions, carrots, and a handful of pale winter greens. Tomas gave her a basket. They moved along the rows, pulling what could be spared and leaving the smaller plants to grow. He showed her how to twist an onion free without breaking its green stem. She attempted it, lost her grip, and sent the onion rolling down the path.

Tomas caught it against his boot.

“Your enemy has been defeated,” he said.

“I allowed it to escape so you could feel useful.”

“A noble act.”

“Do not say noble as if it is a dirty word.”

“Today I meant it as a muddy one.”

She threw a carrot at him. He caught that too.

“You see?” he said. “I am indispensable.”

“Only to root vegetables.”

“And to horses.”

“Ash would disagree.”

“Ash has not yet learned to speak.”

“She has learned not to trust you.”

“Ungrateful creature. I have spent three weeks tending her leg.”

“You frightened her with a bucket.”

“The bucket was unexpected.”

“You were carrying it.”

They were both laughing when the sound traveled up the stone terraces. Elianor stopped first. The basket hung from her hand, onions and greens spilling over its edge. Tomas’s laughter faded as he looked toward the upper path.

For a moment neither moved.

Beyond the garden wall, a servant’s voice called, “Master Vey said the eastern beds were to be checked.”

Another voice answered, closer, “There is water running below.”

Tomas set down his basket. “We need to go.”

“Where?”

He pointed toward the old potting shed, a low structure half-hidden behind pear branches. Its door had fallen from one hinge, and the roof sagged toward the sea.

They ran without speaking. Elianor caught her cloak on a thorn and nearly fell. Tomas seized her wrist, pulled her behind the shed, and pressed them into the narrow space between its wall and the cliffside. The stone was cold against her back. His body blocked the open path.

The servants came into view above them.

One carried a rake. The other was a kitchen boy Elianor recognized, though she could not remember his name. They stood at the edge of the garden, looking down at the repaired channel.

“Someone’s been here,” the boy said.

“Obviously. The channel did not mend itself.”

“Could have been Pell.”

“Pell has been ordered to the lower yard.”

Tomas’s hand remained around Elianor’s wrist. His thumb rested over her pulse. She could feel her heartbeat striking against it, quick and treacherous.

The kitchen boy began down the steps.

Tomas leaned close to her ear. “Do not breathe.”

“I am familiar with the practice.”

His mouth twitched. “You are doing it badly.”

The boy came nearer. Elianor could smell the wet wool of Tomas’s cloak and the crushed thyme beneath their boots. A loose strand of his hair had fallen across his forehead. She wanted, absurdly, to brush it away.

The servant stopped beside the first bed. “The vegetables are gone.”

“Not gone,” said the other. “Taken.”

“Then tell Master Vey.”

“Tell him what? That someone stole three cabbages and a basket of onions from a garden no one has tended since autumn?”

The boy crouched, studying the earth. “There are footprints.”

His gaze turned toward the shed.

Tomas’s fingers tightened around Elianor’s wrist. His other hand came up, not quite touching her shoulder, ready to cover her mouth if she cried out. She understood the necessity. It still sent a shiver through her that had nothing to do with cold.

The boy took one step.

Then a bell sounded from the upper house. Once, twice. The call for the kitchen staff to prepare the midday meal.

“Leave it,” the older servant said. “If Vey wants to know, he can come look himself.”

The boy hesitated, then followed him back up the path.

They waited until the voices disappeared.

Tomas released her.

Elianor did not move. “You nearly strangled me.”

“I barely touched you.”

“Your hand was over my—”

“I know where my hand was.”

The words were quiet. His face had lost its humor. In the cramped shadow of the shed, the danger had changed the air between them. They had been laughing a moment before, stealing vegetables like children. Now the walls of Greyhaven seemed to press down through the stones, reminding them what would happen if anyone understood why they were here together.

Elianor looked at their joined shadows on the wall. “They will search the garden.”

“Not today. The storm has given everyone too much work.”

“And tomorrow?”

“We use a different path.”

“You have planned this before.”

“I plan most things.”

“Do you plan every conversation?”

“Only the ones with you.”

She looked at him.

He seemed startled by his own answer. “That was not—”

“It was a very poor plan.”

“Yes.”

“Because you said what you meant.”

“That is why it was poor.”

She smiled despite herself. Then the smile faded. “You told me you did not know how to leave.”

“I do not.”

“Do you know where you came from?”

The question had been waiting beneath the others. She had wondered about him since the first day in the stable: the caution in his movements, the way he knew every path, the way he could name the needs of people who had never entered Greyhaven’s upper rooms.

Tomas looked beyond the shed toward the sea.

“Not clearly,” he said. “There are pieces. A house with a red door. My mother singing while she kneaded bread. A dog that slept beneath the table. I remember my sister’s ribbon, blue with white stitching.”

“You had a sister?”

“I think so.”

“You think?”

“I was small. The memories do not stay in order.”

“What happened?”

He rubbed his scarred hand with the fingers of the other. “People left. Or were taken. I remember carts on the road and men in armor. I remember being told not to speak my name. After that, I was in three villages before I came here.”

“Who told you?”

“I do not know.”

The uncertainty in his voice was more painful than a clear tragedy. Elianor understood, suddenly, that he had not lost one home but the certainty that a home had ever existed.

“My mother died when I was eight,” she said.

Tomas turned to her.

“She had a cough all winter. Everyone said she would recover when spring came. Then spring came, and she did not.” Elianor folded her hands against the cold. “My father moved her things from the west rooms before the funeral. He said the house needed to continue. I thought that meant grief was a kind of disobedience.”

“Did you obey?”

“I tried.”

“Were you good at it?”

“No.”

“What did you do?”

“I hid one of her gloves.”

He glanced at her. “A glove?”

“It was blue silk, embroidered with little white flowers. I kept it beneath my pillow until the seam came apart.”

“What happened to it?”

“I wore it while climbing the kitchen roof.”

Tomas stared. “Why?”

“I was nine. The roof seemed lonely.”

He laughed again, softer this time. “You climbed roofs in silk gloves?”

“One glove.”

“That explains everything.”

“It explains nothing.”

“It explains why you stole Pell’s boots.”

She nudged his knee with hers. “You are making a theory from insufficient evidence.”

“I am a stable servant. We are experts in judging temper from a single hoofprint.”

“And what is my temper?”

“Difficult.”

“Wrong.”

“Expensive.”

“Cruel.”

“Only when cornered.”

She should have been offended. Instead she found herself watching the curve of his mouth. The memory of her mother’s glove had made the garden feel less like a hiding place and more like a room where the dead could be invited without being announced.

Tomas picked up the basket. “We should take these down.”

“To Rill?”

“To the fisher families waiting near the lower path. The kitchen will not miss them. There is enough in the upper stores to feed a duke for a week.”

“Is that your estimate?”

“No. It is my hope.”

They carried the vegetables through a narrow cleft in the wall, down steps cut into the cliff. At the bottom, three women waited beside a broken cart. One was Lysa. Her face brightened when she saw Elianor, though suspicion remained in her eyes.

“We have cabbages,” Elianor said. “And onions.”

Lysa looked at Tomas. “From the garden?”

“From somewhere the garden will not mind,” he said.

The women divided the vegetables carefully. Lysa touched Elianor’s sleeve before she left.

“You should not come here alone,” she said.

“I was not alone.”

“That is what I mean.”

Lysa’s gaze moved between them. She said nothing more, but the warning remained after she turned away.

On the climb back, Tomas walked ahead with the empty basket. Elianor followed, suddenly conscious of every distance between them. At the garden gate, he stopped.

“Your father will send for you,” he said.

“He already has.”

“Then go before he sends someone to fetch you.”

“You sound almost concerned.”

“I am concerned about the boots.”

“Pell’s boots?”

“They may be missed.”

She took one step toward him. “Tomas.”

He looked back.

The words she wanted had no safe shape. Thank you was too small. I am sorry belonged to another conversation. Stay was impossible.

So she said, “Next time, we should repair the pear trees.”

His eyes softened. “Next time, bring your own boots.”

“Next time, bring a better plan.”

“I will plan to fail more quietly.”

She left him in the sea garden, standing among the wet stones and the newly running water. At the top of the path, she glanced back once. He was still watching her.

The garden was neglected, but not dead. Beneath the weeds, roots held fast to the earth. Water found its way through every crack in the wall.

Elianor returned to Greyhaven with mud on her hem, soil beneath her nails, and the dangerous knowledge that being seen beside Tomas would soon matter less than wanting to be seen beside him.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Greyhaven after secretly visiting the neglected sea garden at dawn and returning to the house with mud on her hem and soil beneath her nails. She remains twenty, Lord Corvin Marrow's only child and heir, under increasing household scrutiny after challenging her father at dinner. She repaired the garden irrigation channel with Tomas, helped harvest and distribute vegetables to Lysa and other fisher families, and shared intimate memories of her mother's death; her attachment to Tomas has deepened into a dangerous desire to be seen with him despite the class boundary. She knows servants nearly discovered them and understands that future meetings must be concealed. She remains bound to Tomas, Pell, Bryn, Master Vey, Chaplain Orren, Lysa, and the servants' relief network through the grain diversion, chapel shelter, and sea-garden aid. She possesses her riding and plain wool dresses, borrowed and returned stable boots, damaged glove, copied grain evidence, altered route slip hidden beneath her floorboard, heir's authority, and knowledge of the grain network, chapel shelter, and sea-garden route.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven after the formal dinner, continuing to tighten control over his daughter and household. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, and determined to preserve Greyhaven, its stores, political standing, crown ties, and control over Elianor. He knows Elianor challenged the nobles' treatment of famine, linked grain stores to policy, and may suspect servants are aiding her, but does not know she secretly repaired the sea garden or distributed its produce. He has ordered or permitted increased watch around household passages and expects Elianor to answer his summons. He possesses the Marrow signet bearing a white bone and the authority of the household guard.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's administrative passages, stores, and household gardens, where he continues managing ledgers, servants, schedules, stores, waste records, and delivery orders. He remains a cautious, composed, observant, physically tired, morally conflicted quiet ally who knows Elianor altered the grain route, helped shelter refugees, and works with the servants' network. He may learn that someone repaired and harvested the sea garden, but has not been told Elianor and Tomas were there. He possesses the steward's seal, administrative knowledge, keys to household stores, and access to Greyhaven's records.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven's gate and guard posts after the storm shelter and Elianor's public challenge. He remains responsible for enforcing Lord Marrow's orders and resents being overruled by Elianor when she opened Saint Orra's Chapel. He has increased or supports increased watch on household passages and may investigate missing produce, servants, and Elianor's movements. set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At the Chapel of Saint Orra in Greyhaven, where storm refugees remain temporarily because Rill's road is damaged. He serves the Marrow household's religious traditions but recognizes that obedience can become an excuse for avoiding moral choices. He supported Elianor's shelter decision and remains subordinate to Lord Marrow, whose displeasure he expects; he is not involved in the sea-garden meeting. He possesses the chapel keys, religious authority, and responsibility for the sanctuary and displaced guests.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable and the neglected sea garden after secretly repairing its irrigation channel with Elianor and distributing harvested vegetables to Lysa and other fisher families. He is a young stable servant slightly older than Elianor, with rain-dark brown hair, a serious narrow face, patched stable wool, and a burn scar on his left hand. He remains practical, wary of Lord Marrow's power, emotionally affected by Elianor's willingness to act, and increasingly attached to her after sharing fragments of their childhood losses and nearly being discovered together. He knows their association now carries immediate danger and intends to use more cautious routes while continuing covert relief. He remains connected to Pell, Bryn, Lysa, and the hidden relief network, tends Ash's injuries, and possesses stable tools, practical horse knowledge, a brown riding horse, knowledge of hidden coastal paths, servant connections, and the shared grain, chapel, and sea-garden secrets.

set.name: Ash
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable in her quiet stall or paddock while storm refugees remain sheltered in Saint Orra's Chapel. She is a tall gray mare with a white blaze, raw rope wound beneath her jaw, swollen hind leg, and scars from mistreatment. She remains frightened but accepts food, treatment, and touch from Tomas and Elianor; she is not fit to ride until her leg heals. Tomas continues tending her swollen hind leg with warm cloths.

set.name: Lysa
set.description: At her patched cottage in Rill below the cliffs with her fever-recovering child Nerrin and two hungry younger children, after receiving vegetables from Elianor and Tomas at the lower sea-garden path. She remains wary of Greyhaven's charity after repeated neglect, but recognizes that Elianor has seen her need directly and that Tomas's network brings aid. She warned Elianor not to come to the lower path alone, implicitly noticing the danger of Elianor and Tomas's closeness. Her family's survival remains uncertain after the storm damaged Rill and its roads; she possesses the vegetables received for her family.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Greyhaven's kitchen and Chapel of Saint Orra after bringing medicines, linen, food, and bandages to the storm shelter. She is a clever young kitchen maid who knows Elianor is diverting grain, witnessed the route slip being sealed, and remains part of the servants' relief network. She is practical, quick-witted, frightened, loyal to Elianor and Tomas, and increasingly at risk if Lord Marrow investigates the chapel, missing produce, or tightens household surveillance. She possesses access to kitchen offices, servants' passages, household routines, and medicine stores.

set.name: Pell
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable, lower yard, and Chapel of Saint Orra after helping organize the storm shelter and carry supplies from the kitchen. He is a broad-shouldered, freckled stable hand who knows the southern route and helped move the diverted grain to Rill. His stable boots were borrowed by Elianor for the sea-garden visit and are now returned or presumed recoverable; he remains silent, cautious, and dependable, shares the servants' secret, and may face investigation as Lord Marrow responds to Elianor's public defiance and unexplained garden harvest. He possesses practical cart-driving, stable, and coastal-road knowledge.
Elianor and Tomas secretly repaired the broken sea-garden irrigation channel, harvested vegetables, and distributed them to Lysa and other fisher families on the lower path.

Servants nearly discovered Elianor and Tomas together in the sea garden, making the danger of their association more immediate and personal.
Elianor and Tomas's presence together in the sea garden and their vegetable distribution may draw household scrutiny, requiring them to use more cautious routes and conceal their growing attachment.
Elianor and Tomas will continue repairing neglected parts of the sea garden and using its produce as a covert source of aid for Rill and coastal families.

chapters.name: The Price of Mercy
chapters.content:
By the third morning after the sea garden, the bells of Saint Orra began before dawn.

Elianor woke to their uneven tolling and lay still beneath the coverlet, listening. The bells did not ring for prayer. They rang in the manner Chaplain Orren had established during the storm: three strokes for the dead, a pause, then three again. The sound traveled through the stone of Greyhaven and entered her room as a tremor.

Three strokes.

She dressed without calling for her maid. Her hands were unsteady as she fastened the collar of her dark blue gown. Outside, rain dragged itself across the windows, fine and cold. The sea had not settled since the storm. Even from the upper rooms she could hear it striking the cliffs below, a constant concussion beneath the household's waking noises.

At the chapel doors, Captain Harl stood with two guards.

He looked at Elianor's face, then at the plain wool cloak over her gown. “My lady.”

“Who has died?”

His jaw tightened. “Chaplain Orren is inside.”

“That was not my question.”

“Three children from Rill.”

The words seemed to hang between them, too small for what they meant.

“Names.”

Harl looked toward the chapel, as if the answer might be written on the doors. “I do not have them.”

“Then find them.”

“My orders are to keep the chapel clear until the household is assembled.”

“Are the dead dangerous?”

A flicker crossed his expression. It might have been shame. It might have been anger at being made to feel it. “My lady, I said—”

“And I heard you.” Elianor placed her hand on the latch. “Open the door.”

For one breath, he did not move. Then the guard behind him stepped aside. Harl unlocked the chapel.

The air inside smelled of wet wool, extinguished candles, and sickness. Refugees still occupied the side aisles and the back benches, wrapped in blankets issued from Greyhaven's stores. A child coughed beneath the gallery. Someone was crying quietly near the altar, but most of the villagers sat in the stunned silence of people who had exhausted their tears.

Chaplain Orren came toward her, his gray hair untidy, his stole hanging crookedly over his robe.

“You should not have come alone,” he said.

“I am not alone. I have an entire guard at my back.”

“That is not what I meant.”

She looked beyond him. Three small bodies lay beneath linen on the chapel floor. The cloth made them seem ceremonial, almost peaceful. One narrow foot showed below an edge. It was brown with mud.

“Who are they?” she asked.

“Two brothers,” Orren said. “Perrin and Cal. Their mother brought them from Rill yesterday. The third is a girl called Miri. She had been ill since the flooding.”

“Why were they not given food?”

Orren lowered his eyes. “They were given what we had permission to give.”

The answer struck harder than an accusation. Permission. A ration counted and measured while children weakened within sight of Greyhaven's walls.

“Where is their mother?”

“Perrin and Cal's mother is with them. Miri's father has gone to Rill to find a place for the burial.”

Elianor approached the bodies. She did not lift the linen. She could not bear to discover what death had made of their faces. At the altar, Saint Orra's painted hands were raised in blessing, her gold halo bright in the candlelight.

“Ring again,” Elianor said.

Orren looked at her. “The household has not yet been summoned.”

“Ring for them.”

He hesitated only a moment before turning toward the bell rope.

By breakfast, everyone who mattered had heard the bells. The household assembled in the great hall beneath the banners of the Marrow line. Lord Corvin stood at the head of the long table, already dressed in black. Master Vey occupied his usual place below the salt, with a ledger closed beneath one hand. Captain Harl remained near the doors. Several lesser officials and two visiting landowners had been drawn from their rooms by the funeral tolling.

Elianor entered last.

Her father did not ask whether she had slept. “You were in the chapel.”

“I was.”

“You gave an order to ring the household bells without consulting me.”

“Three children died.”

“I am aware.”

“Are you?”

The room tightened around them. Master Vey's gaze dropped to the table. Harl shifted his weight.

Lord Marrow's face revealed nothing but fatigue. “This is not the place for dramatics.”

“It is precisely the place. The household eats beneath banners while children die on our chapel floor.”

“The refugees are being sheltered.”

“They are being rationed.”

“They are being kept alive.”

“Not all of them.”

Her father looked toward the nearest servant. “Leave us.”

“No,” Elianor said.

His eyes returned to her. “What did you say?”

“If you mean to refuse me, do so before them.” She turned slightly, taking in the servants along the walls: Bryn near the sideboard, Pell by the service door, two kitchen men, a laundress, and Master Vey with his hand still resting on the ledger. “They carry every sack. They wash every bowl. They know what hunger looks like. They should hear what you call necessary.”

Lord Marrow's mouth became a hard line. “You are making a spectacle of grief.”

“I am asking for grain.”

“How much?”

“Enough to feed Rill until the roads reopen. Open the eastern granary. Release the stores marked for sale and the sacks held for the next levy. Send flour, barley, and dried peas to the village. Give the chapel a full ration for every refugee, not half portions calculated to keep them quiet.”

Master Vey's fingers moved once against the ledger.

“That would empty the eastern granary within a fortnight,” Lord Marrow said.

“It is full.”

“It is assigned.”

“To whom? The villagers who grew it? The ministers in Auvray? Merrit and his sons?”

A silence followed the merchant's name. Elianor saw it pass through the room like a draft beneath a door. Her father had not expected her to say it publicly.

“Those stores are pledged,” he said.

“Pledged against what? The lives of children?”

“Against the survival of Greyhaven.”

She stared at him. “Greyhaven is not a person.”

“It is a fortress, an estate, a garrison, a harbor, and the only reliable storehouse for twenty miles of coast. If I empty it because three children have died, I may condemn three hundred when the next storm comes.”

“Then replenish it.”

“With what? The sea has taken the roads. The fields are drowned. The crown takes its levy whether the harvest succeeds or fails. If I send out everything we possess, the next hungry men at these gates will not ask for bread. They will come with knives.”

“Perhaps they will come with knives because you have left them nothing else.”

Captain Harl's hand moved toward his sword. Lord Marrow raised two fingers, stopping him.

“Your compassion has made you careless,” he said.

“My compassion has made me look.”

“Looking is not governing.”

“No. But refusing to look is not governing either.”

Her father came down from the head of the table. He did not raise his voice. That was worse. Lord Corvin's quiet had always been the sound of doors closing.

“You believe a ruler saves everyone,” he said. “That is a child's understanding of power. A ruler chooses who can be saved. He protects the storehouse, the walls, the soldiers, the seed grain, and the roads. He lets one village suffer so the whole coast may survive.”

“Who chooses which village?”

“The one responsible for it.”

“Rill did not flood itself.”

“They neglected the sea wall.”

“They begged for stone.”

“They were given stone.”

“Not enough.”

“Nothing is ever enough to people who believe the world owes them rescue.”

The words landed among the servants. Bryn's face went still. Pell lowered his head.

Elianor felt something inside her go cold—not the shock of hearing cruelty, but the recognition of how long he had practiced calling it wisdom.

“You think this is responsibility,” she said. “It is only cruelty wearing a steward's coat.”

Lord Marrow's expression changed then. Not anger. Fear, swiftly mastered.

“Be careful.”

“Open the granary.”

“No.”

“Father—”

“No. I will not sacrifice Greyhaven to prove that you possess a generous heart. The grain remains where it is. The chapel will receive its allotted ration. The dead will be buried. The living will be fed according to the stores available.”

“According to the stores you permit.”

“According to law.”

“Your law.”

“My responsibility.”

He turned from her. “Master Vey, amend the chapel count. No additional distributions without my seal. Captain Harl, increase the watch on the eastern passages and granary doors. I will not have panic dressed as charity.”

“Yes, my lord,” Vey said.

Harl bowed.

Elianor stood in the center of the hall, surrounded by people who had heard her ask and heard him refuse. Her blood beat hard in her throat. She wanted to seize the ledger, break the seal, and march to the granary with every servant behind her.

But she saw the guards at the doors. She saw Pell's shoulders tense, Bryn's frightened eyes, Master Vey's warning glance. Open defiance would not free a single sack. It would only give her father names to punish.

She lowered her gaze.

“As you command,” she said.

Her father watched her carefully. “That is all?”

“For now.”

She left before he could hear how much the words cost.

In the corridor, Bryn caught up with her carrying a tray of untouched breakfast.

“My lady.”

“Do not call me that.”

Bryn glanced toward the hall. “Then what should I call you?”

“Someone who has just agreed to starve a village.”

“You did not agree.”

“I bowed.”

“People bow before they steal.”

Elianor stopped. Bryn's face was pale, but her eyes were steady.

“Who taught you that?” Elianor asked.

“Everyone who has ever lived beneath a locked door.”

A footstep sounded at the far end of the passage. Bryn immediately lowered her head and continued toward the kitchen. Elianor followed at a measured pace, hands folded, her face composed as she had been taught since childhood.

At the chapel, the bells stopped.

The children were buried before noon in a strip of ground beyond the eastern wall. Rain fell through the service, darkening the linen and the earth. Elianor stood beneath an umbrella while the villagers stood without shelter. Her father did not attend. Master Vey came, as did Chaplain Orren, Captain Harl, and six servants carrying spades.

Lysa was there. Her eyes met Elianor's only once.

The grave for Miri was shallow because the ground was still waterlogged. When the first clod struck the linen, a woman behind Elianor made a sound like an animal caught in a trap.

Elianor did not look at her father’s absence. She looked at the granary roof beyond the wall, its slate black with rain.

That evening, she returned to her rooms and placed a chair beneath the door handle—not because it would stop a determined guard, but because the act gave her hands something to do. She removed the copied grain figures from beneath the floorboard and spread them across her desk. The papers smelled faintly of dust and hidden wood.

Thirty-eight sacks had once reached Rill. It had fed some families for days. The sea garden could yield vegetables, but not enough. The chapel stores could be stretched, but not without someone noticing. Greyhaven's granaries held hundreds of sacks.

Her father's refusal had not ended the question. It had clarified it.

A soft knock came at the panel behind the wardrobe.

Elianor extinguished the lamp, waited, then moved the wardrobe aside. Tomas slipped through the narrow servants' passage, rain shining on his hair. He closed the panel behind him and stood listening.

“Your father knows?” he whispered.

“He knows I asked. He does not know you are here.”

“Then we have a little time.”

“Three children died.”

“I know.”

“No,” she said. “You know the fact. I heard the bells.”

His face tightened. “I was in the lower yard when they began.”

She told him what had happened in the hall. He listened without interrupting. When she repeated her father's argument—that a ruler must choose who can be saved—Tomas looked toward the dark window.

“He says the same thing as every man who has ever held a key,” he said. “There is always a larger danger. Always a future famine more important than the hunger in front of him.”

“We need the eastern granary.”

“We need more than that.”

He came to the desk. Together they bent over the papers.

“The chapel kitchens have two weeks of dried beans if Bryn can make the count appear smaller,” Elianor said. “The sea garden may provide greens in three days, if the weather holds.”

“Pell can move sacks through the old ash yard. The guard there changes at midnight.”

“Not enough sacks.”

“Not if we take them one at a time.”

She met his eyes. “How many can the stable carry without notice?”

“Four sacks in a feed cart. Six if we hide them under straw. More if the cart leaves as waste.”

“Master Vey controls the waste records.”

“He might help.”

“He might already be watched.”

“So are you.”

The words settled between them. Through the walls came the distant clatter of dishes, the ordinary sounds of a household continuing to eat.

Elianor touched the edge of the copied ledger. “We cannot ask everyone to risk themselves for me.”

“Tomas shook his head. “Not for you.”

“For Rill?”

“For the children who are still alive.”

She looked at the route slip hidden among the papers, its altered seal a small, damning mark. “If we are caught, my father will call it theft.”

“It is theft.”

“Then what do we call his keeping the grain?”

Tomas's gaze did not leave hers. “Law.”

She almost smiled, but grief made the expression fail. “We need a list. Stores, carts, watches, names of those who will carry and those who can receive. No improvising.”

“You are making a plan.”

“I am learning to govern.”

“No,” he said. “You are learning to disobey without getting people killed.”

The distinction frightened her because it was true.

She gathered the papers. “Tomorrow I will speak to Master Vey.”

“Carefully.”

“Bryn can alter the kitchen count. Pell knows the ash yard. You know the stable routes.”

“And you know how to make a sealed order look official.”

“I will need more than one order.”

His hand came to rest on the desk beside hers. Not touching. Close enough that she felt the warmth of it.

“Elianor,” he said, “if this begins, there may be no way back.”

“There was no way back when Miri was buried.”

He looked as if he wanted to argue. Instead, he turned his hand palm upward.

She placed her fingers in it.

For a moment they stood in the dark room, joined not by promises of escape or a future neither could name, but by the cold arithmetic of bread. Outside, the bells remained silent. Beyond the walls, the sea struck the cliffs. In the granaries, grain waited behind locks.

Elianor closed her hand around his.

“Tomorrow,” she said, “we begin with four sacks.”

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Greyhaven in her rooms after attending the burial of three Rill children and publicly confronting Lord Corvin Marrow. She remains twenty, his only child and heir, outwardly submitting to his refusal while secretly planning grain relief with Tomas and sympathetic servants. She is grieving, angry, frightened, and newly committed to disobeying without exposing others recklessly. She knows the eastern granary is full but locked by policy, the chapel ration is restricted, the guards have been increased, and the ash yard and stable routes may permit covert movement. She remains bound to Tomas, Bryn, Pell, Master Vey, Chaplain Orren, Lysa, and the servants' relief network. set.description: At Greyhaven after refusing Elianor's public demand for grain. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, and determined to preserve the estate, garrison, crown obligations, stores, and control over his daughter. set.description: At Greyhaven's kitchen and Saint Orra's Chapel after witnessing the burial and hearing Corvin restrict rations. She remains clever, frightened, practical, and loyal to Elianor and Tomas. She knows Elianor publicly defied Corvin and has begun a larger covert plan; she can alter kitchen counts and access food, linen, medicine stores, servants' passages, and household routines. She has not yet agreed to a specific theft but is positioned to conceal reduced kitchen inventories.

set.name: Pell
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable and lower yard after attending the children's burial and remaining part of the servants' relief network. He remains broad-shouldered, cautious, dependable, and at risk from increased investigation. He knows the southern route, carts, stable movements, and the ash yard, and Tomas intends to rely on him for covert grain transport. He possesses cart-driving and coastal-road knowledge, practical stable skills, and his connection to the earlier grain diversion.

Three refugee children from Rill—brothers Perrin and Cal and a girl named Miri—died in Saint Orra's Chapel after receiving only the ration Lord Marrow permitted; Elianor ordered the bells rung and attended their burial.

Elianor publicly demanded that Lord Marrow open the eastern granary and release grain to Rill and the chapel refugees; he refused, ordered stricter rationing and increased watches, and framed selective deprivation as responsible governance.

After outwardly submitting to Lord Marrow, Elianor met Tomas through the wardrobe passage and began a covert plan with him, Bryn, Pell, and possibly Master Vey to move four sacks from Greyhaven toward Rill.

Elianor, Tomas, Bryn, Pell, and potentially Master Vey will execute a covert distribution beginning with four sacks moved through the ash yard and stable routes to Rill, while concealing the theft as waste or ordinary household movement.
Elianor will recruit or test sympathetic household servants and map guard changes, carts, stores, and receiving families before attempting larger grain diversions.

chapters.name: The Servants' Network
chapters.content:
The next morning, Elianor began with a list of things no lady of Greyhaven was supposed to know.

She wrote them in the margin of a household requisition: lamp oil, clean linen, willow bark, dried peas, salt, turnips, vinegar, and four empty flour sacks. Beneath those she added names—not the names of nobles or officials, but those of people who carried, counted, mended, cooked, ferried, and buried. Bryn. Pell. Lysa. Orren. Master Vey, with a question mark beside him.

The question mark remained after she folded the paper.

At breakfast, Lord Marrow was absent. Elianor ate alone beneath the painted ancestors, while servants moved around her with the careful silence that had settled over Greyhaven since the children's burial. No one spoke of Perrin, Cal, or Miri. Their names had become dangerous because names made a policy resemble a death.

Bryn poured her tea.

“Did the kitchen receive my requisition?” Elianor asked.

“The one for the chapel?”

“The one for the household.”

Bryn's eyes flicked toward the gallery. “The kitchen received three requisitions this morning. One for the household, one for the chapel, and one from Captain Harl for the guards.”

“And which one was filled?”

“The captain's.”

Elianor folded her napkin. “Bring me the kitchen inventory.”

Bryn's hand paused on the teapot. “My lady, Master Vey keeps—”

“Then tell Master Vey that I require it for a household audit.”

“A household audit?”

“It is not a lie.”

“No,” Bryn said. “It is merely a truth wearing a better coat.”

Elianor looked at her. Bryn was small and square-shouldered, with brown hair escaping the white cloth wrapped around it. Her hands were red from lye and winter water. She had served at Greyhaven since she was twelve and had learned, as Elianor had learned lessons in deportment, exactly how much could be said without appearing to say anything.

“Can you get the inventory?”

“If I cannot, I can get you a version of it.”

“Would that version be accurate?”

“It would be useful.”

For the first time since the bells, Elianor nearly smiled. “Then bring me the useful one.”

Bryn inclined her head and moved away.

By noon, Elianor had used her father's authority three times. The first time, she signed an order for willow bark, honey, vinegar, and clean bandages from the infirmary stores, describing them as supplies for the household's winter coughs. The second time, she requisitioned dried peas and salt fish from the kitchen, citing the increased number of servants required to maintain the chapel. The third time, she summoned Captain Harl and asked for a written accounting of the guards assigned to the eastern passages.

Harl arrived with suspicion already arranged on his face.

“You have no authority over the watch,” he said.

“I have authority over household provisions. If the chapel is to be supplied, I must know when its carts can pass.”

“No carts are to pass the eastern gate without Lord Marrow's seal.”

“Then write that plainly.”

His mouth tightened. “There is no need.”

“There is always a need for plain writing when men are later blamed for following unclear orders.”

Harl studied her. She could see the calculation behind his eyes: whether this was merely another challenge, whether her father had sent her, whether she was trying to discover what he had been told not to reveal.

At last he produced a small slate from his belt and read from it. “Eastern passage: two men from sunset to midnight. Three from midnight to dawn. Granary doors: four men at all hours. Ash yard: one man until midnight, two during the change, then one again.”

“During the change?”

“The old watch leaves before the new one arrives.”

“For how long?”

“Less than a quarter hour.”

“Thank you, Captain.”

His eyes narrowed. “For what?”

“For making the household safer.”

When he had gone, she copied the figures onto the back of the requisition. Her hand did not tremble. The fear had not lessened. It had simply become part of the work.

Tomas found her after dusk in the stable, where the smell of hay and horse sweat softened the cold. Ash stood in her stall with one hind leg lifted, her gray head turned toward the door. The swelling had diminished, but the raw rope wound beneath her jaw was still angry and red.

“Elianor,” Tomas said quietly. “You should not be here.”

“Neither should you, apparently, but you have made a habit of it.”

He glanced toward the yard. “I mean that the guards have been asking questions.”

“Then let them ask why the lord's daughter is inspecting a sick mare.”

“They might ask why she is inspecting the mare with a stable servant.”

“Would the answer surprise them?”

His expression shifted, almost amusement and not quite. “You have been speaking to Bryn.”

“I have been speaking to everyone.”

“That is not the same thing.”

Tomas closed Ash's stall and led Elianor through the rear of the stable, past the tack room and a stack of broken yokes. Pell waited beside a narrow cart whose wheels were caked in old ash. He was joined by a woman Elianor had seen carrying baskets from the lower kitchens and an elderly fisherman with a missing finger.

“This is Nessa,” Tomas said. “She washes linen at Greyhaven and knows which cottages in Rill still have roofs. This is Oric. He fishes the north cove when the sea allows it.”

The woman curtsied, but only barely. The fisherman touched two fingers to his brow.

“Lady Elianor,” Nessa said, “we were told you could be trusted with names.”

Elianor looked at Tomas. “Who told you?”

“Everyone tells someone,” Oric said. “That is how news travels when the lord owns the roads.”

They left the stable by a postern door and crossed the lower yard to an abandoned net shed pressed against the cliff wall. The roof leaked. Old nets hung from the rafters like gray cobwebs, and the floor smelled of tar, damp rope, and fish gone bad. Yet six people were waiting inside: two fishermen, a cooper, a washerwoman, a boy with a bundle of firewood, and Lysa.

Elianor stopped short.

Lysa rose from an overturned crate. Her face was thinner than it had been at the burial, and a red scarf covered her hair.

“Nerrin's fever broke,” she said before Elianor could ask. “He still cannot stand for long.”

“I ordered medicine.”

“I know. It reached us this afternoon.”

Elianor felt the answer as a small relief. “How?”

Lysa gave Tomas a look. “Through the hands that know where to go.”

Tomas set the willow bark and bandages on a barrel. “This is not an organization with a name,” he said. “Names are what soldiers look for. It is a path. Someone hears of a family in need. Someone else has a little flour, a blanket, a boat, a cousin in the kitchens, a brother on a cart. We pass what we can and remember who has helped.”

“Who began it?” Elianor asked.

“The famine,” said the washerwoman.

“Before that,” said Oric. “The levies. Before the levies, the taxes. There is always something.”

The boy with the firewood unwrapped a heel of bread and broke it into pieces. He gave the largest piece to Lysa, who tried to refuse it. He put it into her hand anyway.

Elianor watched the exchange. In the great hall, Lord Marrow spoke of stores, walls, and the survival of Greyhaven as if the fortress were a living creature and every person beyond it an expendable limb. Here, no one asked whether a piece of bread would preserve the coast. They asked who was hungriest and divided the bread accordingly.

“How many families?” she asked.

“Forty-two in lower Rill,” said Nessa. “More if the northern boats cannot launch.”

“Twenty-seven roofs damaged. Nine entirely gone,” Lysa added. “The chapel holds some of those people, but not all.”

“And medicines?”

“Willow bark for fever,” said Nessa. “Honey for the children. Clean cloth. Anything for infected wounds.”

Elianor drew out her requisition. “I can obtain more. Not openly from the granaries, but from the infirmary and kitchens. I can sign for it.”

No one celebrated. That, more than gratitude would have, unsettled her.

Oric shook his head. “A signature is a trail.”

“I know.”

“Your father will see it.”

“Perhaps. But he cannot punish every fever in Rill.”

“He can punish the hands that carry the bottles.”

The warning was not an insult. It was a fact offered by someone who had survived by attending to facts.

Tomas placed four marks on the barrel with a bit of charcoal. “Tonight: four sacks from the ash yard. One cart. Pell drives. Nessa takes the medicine and supplies through the laundry passage. Oric carries word to the families. Lysa receives at the old mill and divides it.”

“Why the old mill?” Elianor asked.

“Because everyone knows it is empty,” Lysa said. “Which means no guard thinks to look there.”

“The mill is not empty,” Oric said. “There are three families sleeping in the grain room.”

“Then they will help unload,” Tomas answered. “No one is made a spectator to their own rescue.”

Elianor looked at him. The phrase lodged in her mind.

At Greyhaven, servants had carried blankets into the chapel while nobles watched from dry corridors. Here, the people receiving aid were part of the work. There was no clean division between giver and given, no illusion that one class possessed virtue and another merely needed it.

The cart left after midnight.

Elianor did not go with it. That had been Tomas's condition, and she understood why. Her presence would make the cart memorable. Instead, she returned to the upper household and sat in the accounting room beside Master Vey while he copied figures by candlelight.

He did not look up when she entered. “You have acquired a talent for appearing wherever records are vulnerable.”

“I need a waste authorization.”

“For what?”

“Four flour sacks damaged by damp.”

“There are no damaged flour sacks.”

“There will be.”

His quill stopped.

Elianor placed the requisition before him. Beneath the listed supplies she had written the names of the chapel's remaining fever cases, the number of blankets needed, and the count of bowls Bryn claimed had broken during the storm.

Vey read it all.

“You are using household authority to falsify stores,” he said.

“I am using household authority to correct a false account. The sacks are being wasted by remaining behind a lock.”

“You sound like your mother.”

Elianor stiffened. “You knew her?”

“I knew that she believed a record was a promise.” He dipped his quill again. “Your father believes a record is a wall.”

He signed the waste authorization, then pressed his seal into the wax.

“Why?” Elianor asked.

“Because four sacks will not empty Greyhaven. Because I am tired of counting grain for people who have forgotten what it is.”

He lifted his eyes to hers. “And because if you are caught, I would prefer the blame to fall on a document I deliberately made unclear.”

“Master Vey—”

“Do not thank me. Gratitude makes allies visible.”

The cart returned before dawn without the four sacks. It carried instead four empty flour bags, a broken axle pin, and Pell asleep beneath the driver's cloth. The grain had reached the old mill. No guard had challenged it. The medicines had gone with Nessa through the laundry passage, and Bryn had already made the kitchen count show a quantity of salt fish spoiled by damp.

At breakfast, Lord Marrow complained that the kitchen had become careless.

Bryn stood behind him with the coffee pot and said nothing.

Elianor looked down the long table at her father. The banners above him displayed generations of Marrows, each painted with a sword, a seal, or a hand resting possessively upon a map. They had taught her that Greyhaven was her home because it belonged to her blood.

But that night, while the household slept behind its locked doors, four sacks had crossed the coast through hands that belonged to no lord. A maid had risked her place. A steward had risked his seal. A fisherman had carried news through rain. A mother had divided grain among strangers and called it ordinary.

Elianor understood then that Greyhaven was not the house her father defended.

It was the people who kept the house standing.

Bryn came to her rooms after breakfast with the useful inventory tucked into her sleeve. “There are twelve sacks of peas in the lower kitchen, six jars of honey, and enough salt fish for nine days if the guards stop eating like soldiers at war.”

“Will they?”

“No. But I can make them believe the barrels are empty.”

Elianor took the inventory. “I will need you to decide what can be spared.”

Bryn met her gaze. “No, my lady. You will need me to decide what can be taken without the wrong people going hungry.”

Elianor nodded. The correction did not offend her. It felt like another door opening.

“Then decide,” she said.

Bryn tucked the cloth more firmly around her hair. “I already have.”

Outside, the sea struck the cliffs and Greyhaven endured another day. Within its walls, quietly and without permission, the servants began to move the kingdom toward mercy.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Greyhaven in her rooms and the lower household passages after entering Tomas's hidden coastal relief network and helping complete the first covert four-sack delivery to Rill. She remains twenty, Lord Corvin Marrow's only child and heir, outwardly composed but grieving, watchful, and increasingly alienated from her father's authority. Her goal is to sustain Rill and the chapel refugees while preserving the servants who help her and building evidence against the policies that keep grain locked. She now knows the servant network's routes, the old mill receiving point, the needs of forty-two lower-Rill families, the damaged roofs and fever cases, Captain Harl's watch rotations, and Master Vey's willingness to obscure records. She is allied with Tomas, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, Chaplain Orren, and cautiously Master Vey; her loyalty is shifting toward the people who sustain Greyhaven rather than the Marrow household. She possesses copied grain figures, the altered route slip beneath her floorboard, new supply requisitions, Harl's copied watch figures, Vey's waste authorization, household authority, and access to rooms, wardrobe passage, kitchen and infirmary requests. She is physically safe but under growing suspicion.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven's great hall and inner household after imposing stricter control over grain and watches. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, and determined to preserve the estate, garrison, crown obligations, stores, and control of Elianor. He believes unauthorized charity threatens Greyhaven's survival. He knows Elianor has requested household supplies and watch information, but does not yet know the full network or that four sacks reached Rill. He possesses the Marrow signet, household authority, armed guards, and control of the granaries; he has begun noticing kitchen inventory discrepancies and complaining that the kitchen is careless.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's accounting room after signing a deliberately unclear waste authorization that enabled four sacks and other supplies to leave for Rill. He remains cautious, composed, observant, morally conflicted, and now covertly committed enough to shield Elianor's relief work, though he insists that visible gratitude would expose him. He knows the servants' network is active, knows Elianor is using household authority to divert medicine and food, and suspects Lord Marrow may soon investigate. He possesses the steward's seal, keys and records for stores, waste accounts, delivery orders, household logistics, and the ability to obscure accounts.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven's gate, chapel, eastern passages, and granary watch after giving Elianor the current guard rotations. He remains loyal to the Marrow hierarchy, suspicious of Elianor, and responsible for preventing panic, unauthorized distributions, and access to stores. He knows Elianor requested watch information and may suspect she is testing the ash-yard change, but he does not know the four-sack delivery succeeded. He possesses weapons, guard authority, and knowledge of watch rotations, including the brief changeover when the ash yard has two guards.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and the burial ground beyond Greyhaven's eastern wall, caring for refugees and maintaining burial and ration records. He remains morally troubled, subordinate to Lord Marrow, and sympathetic to Elianor's defense of the hungry. He knows supplies and medicine are being moved covertly to Rill and the chapel's vulnerable people, though he is not directly coordinating the network. He possesses chapel keys, religious authority, burial records, and responsibility for the displaced.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable and on the covert coastal routes between the estate and Rill after introducing Elianor to the hidden servants' network and coordinating the successful four-sack delivery. He remains a wary young stable servant, practical, emotionally attached to Elianor, and alert to the danger of discovery. He knows the network's contacts, the old mill receiving point, the damaged and occupied buildings in lower Rill, stable routes, cart capacities, and guard changes. He is allied with Elianor, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, and other servants and coastal families; he tends Ash and possesses stable tools, horse knowledge, a brown riding horse, carts, and coastal paths. He is physically tired but encouraged by the delivery.

set.name: Ash
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable in her quiet stall or paddock while storm refugees remain sheltered in Saint Orra's Chapel. She is a tall gray mare with a white blaze, raw rope wound beneath her jaw, swollen but improving hind leg, and scars from mistreatment. She remains frightened but accepts food, treatment, and touch from Tomas and Elianor; she is not yet fit to ride. Tomas continues tending her with warm cloths.

set.name: Lysa
set.description: At the old mill and then her damaged cottage in Rill with her fever-recovering child Nerrin and hungry younger children. She remains wary of Greyhaven but now actively receives and divides covert grain and medicine among lower-Rill families. She knows the servants' network, the old mill's hidden occupants, the needs of forty-two families, and that Elianor's supplies can arrive despite Lord Marrow's refusal. She possesses the delivered grain, medicines, local knowledge, and contacts among receiving households; she is exhausted but cautiously hopeful.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Greyhaven's kitchen and Elianor's rooms after openly joining the covert relief network. She remains clever, frightened, practical, and loyal to Elianor and Tomas. She has begun altering kitchen counts, reporting salt fish as spoiled, and deciding which peas, honey, linen, and other supplies can be diverted without starving guards or household dependents. She knows the servants' routes, the four-sack delivery, the chapel's needs, and household routines. She possesses access to kitchen inventories, food, linen, medicine stores, servants' passages, and plausible cover records; Lord Marrow has begun noticing discrepancies.

set.name: Pell
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable and lower yard after driving the covert cart that carried four sacks toward the old mill. He remains broad-shouldered, cautious, dependable, and at risk from increased investigation. He knows the southern and ash-yard routes, the cart, the guard change, the old mill's receiving arrangements, and the wider servants' network. He is allied with Tomas, Elianor, Bryn, Lysa, Nessa, and Oric and possesses cart-driving and coastal-road knowledge, practical stable skills, and experience concealing grain movements.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: At Greyhaven's laundry and on the route to Rill after carrying medicine and supplies through the laundry passage. She remains practical, wary, and committed to the coastal relief network. She knows which Rill cottages still have roofs, the families needing medicine, and the laundry route through Greyhaven. She is allied with Tomas, Elianor, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, and Oric and possesses access to linen, washing supplies, clean cloth, and servant passages.

set.name: Oric
set.description: At the north cove and Rill routes after carrying news and helping coordinate the covert delivery. He remains an elderly one-fingered fisherman, weathered, observant, and cautious. He knows the northern boats, coastal news, the families needing food, and the old mill's occupants. He is part of the unnamed servants' and fishermen's network and possesses a fishing boat when the sea permits, local contacts, and knowledge of tides and coves.
Tomas introduced Elianor to a hidden network of servants, fishermen, laborers, and Rill families operating through the coast; they exchanged news and aid without a formal name or organization.

Elianor used household authority to requisition medicines, bandages, salt, and food supplies, while Captain Harl's watch information and Master Vey's sealed waste authorization enabled a covert four-sack delivery through the ash yard to the old mill in Rill.
Bryn openly allied herself with Elianor and Tomas, taking responsibility for altering kitchen inventories and deciding which supplies could be spared without harming vulnerable household dependents.
Elianor recognized that Greyhaven's servants and coastal poor sustain the estate through communal courage and mutual aid, shifting her loyalty away from Lord Marrow's household hierarchy.

The servants' coastal network now has known routes, receiving families, and supply contacts; Elianor, Tomas, Bryn, Pell, and their allies will need to protect it from the increased scrutiny that follows repeated unauthorized distributions.
Bryn will continue manipulating kitchen inventories and ration records to conceal supplies diverted to the chapel and Rill without starving the guards or household dependents.

chapters.name: The Signet
chapters.content:
The first warning was not the bell.

It was the dogs.

They began barking below the eastern wall just after midnight, not with the lazy complaint they gave to foxes in the rubbish yard, but in a ragged, rising fury that seemed to pass from kennel to kennel. Elianor woke beneath the heavy coverlet and listened. Wind pressed rain against her shutters. Somewhere in the lower household a door slammed, then another. A man shouted a name she could not make out.

Then the bell began.

Three strokes. A pause. Three more.

Raid.

Elianor was already out of bed when Bryn pushed through the wardrobe passage. The kitchen maid wore a wool cloak over her nightdress, and her hair had been tied so hastily that half of it had escaped around her face.

“Lady Elianor,” she whispered. “Soldiers at the east gate. More coming from the road.”

“Whose soldiers?”

“Marrow colors, mostly. I saw blue coats among them. Captain Harl says they are searching for rebels.”

The answer struck colder than the rain. Duke Veyne's men had not yet come to Greyhaven, but his colors were known along the coast: blue wool, silver braid, and a willingness to call every hungry fisherman a conspirator. Frightened soldiers were worse than disciplined ones. Fear made a weapon of every door and a traitor of every shadow.

“Where is Tomas?”

Bryn's eyes flickered toward the passage, then away. “The stable. Pell was sent to bring the carriage horses into the inner yard. Tomas refused to leave Ash.”

For one breath Elianor imagined the stable: the dark stalls, the smell of hay and damp leather, Ash's white blaze lifting in alarm. She imagined soldiers searching among the bridles, overturning feed bins, demanding names from boys who had no names worth giving.

“I am going down.”

“Your father ordered every member of the household to remain in place.”

“Then he should have ordered the soldiers not to frighten the household.”

Bryn caught her sleeve. “If they see you in the lower passages—”

“They will see Lord Marrow's daughter. That may be useful.”

“It may also make them search more carefully.”

Elianor pulled on a dark dress over her linen shift and fastened a plain cloak at her throat. Beneath the floorboard, the altered route slip and copied grain figures lay where she had hidden them. She touched the board with one bare foot as she passed, a gesture too small to be prayer and too deliberate to be chance.

“Listen to me,” she said. “If anyone asks, you came to tell me that the chapel roof is leaking.”

“It is leaking.”

“Good. Truth is a stronger disguise than invention.”

They slipped into the wardrobe passage. The narrow stones held the night's damp. At its end, Elianor paused beside the little door opening toward the servants' stair. Voices rose from below.

“Open it!”

“It is the lord's household!”

“Then the lord's household has nothing to fear.”

A fist struck wood. Bryn flinched.

Elianor descended.

The east corridor had become a river of confusion. Servants stood against the walls in nightclothes and aprons. Two soldiers held spears across the passage while Captain Harl argued with a broad-shouldered officer whose blue coat was darkened by rain. Behind them, more men crowded through the open door, bringing the smell of mud, horse sweat, and cold iron.

Lord Corvin had arrived in a dressing gown beneath a fur-lined coat. His silver hair was unbound, but his face had assumed the hard calm he wore in council.

“What authority brings armed men into my house?” he demanded.

The blue-coated officer bowed without humility. “Search authority issued by the western command. A rebel courier was seen near the coastal road. We have reason to believe he passed through Greyhaven.”

“You have reason,” Lord Marrow said, “to disturb my household at midnight?”

“We have reason to suspect that your household shelters sympathizers.”

Elianor stepped into the corridor. “Then search mine first.”

Her father turned sharply. “Go back upstairs.”

“Not while armed men are questioning servants who cannot defend themselves.”

The blue-coated officer looked her over. “Lady Elianor Vale.”

“Lady Elianor Marrow,” her father corrected.

She felt the correction like a hand laid around her throat. She had been Vale by her mother's name until it became politically inconvenient, and Marrow whenever her father needed to remind the world whose property she was.

The officer smiled thinly. “Forgive me. I have heard of your charity.”

“I have heard of your searches.”

His smile disappeared. Captain Harl shifted his weight. He was loyal to Lord Marrow, but even he disliked the blue coats. They had no knowledge of Greyhaven's passages, stores, or people, and therefore treated ignorance as permission.

“Search the servants' quarters,” the officer ordered. “The stable, kitchens, chapel, and lower yard. No one leaves.”

“My captain will accompany you,” Lord Marrow said.

“Your captain will not interfere.”

“My captain will do precisely what I instruct.”

The standoff lasted only a moment, but Elianor understood its shape. Her father could not expel the soldiers without making himself appear disloyal to the crown. The blue-coated officer could not openly insult him without losing access to the estate. Between them, the servants would pay for every word.

“Search the stable first,” Elianor said.

Her father's eyes fixed on her. “Why?”

“Because the stable servants sleep near the road. If a courier passed through, they are the likeliest to have seen him.”

It was plausible. It was also a warning.

Tomas, she thought. Hide what you can.

The officer gestured to four men. Captain Harl followed with two of his guards. Elianor went as well, despite her father's command. Bryn remained behind, drawing the other servants toward the kitchens with a muttered complaint about the chapel roof, as if the leak had suddenly become the household's greatest emergency.

Rain swept through the archway into the stable yard. Lanterns swung in the soldiers' hands, making the wet stones leap and settle. Pell stood beside the cart shed with both hands raised. Tomas was near Ash's stall, one palm against the mare's neck.

Ash trembled beneath him.

“Search every stall,” said the blue-coated officer. “Look under the straw. Open the tack chests.”

One soldier kicked the door of Ash's stall. The mare lurched sideways, striking her injured hind leg against the partition. Tomas moved between them.

“Easy,” he murmured. “Easy, girl.”

The soldier grabbed his shoulder and spun him around. “You heard the order.”

“She is lame,” Tomas said. “If you drive her into the wall, she will break the leg.”

“Then she will not run.”

Elianor stepped forward. “Remove your hand.”

The soldier looked at her, surprised. “My lady, stand aside.”

“That is an order.”

He hesitated. Not because he respected Tomas, but because he understood the cost of laying hands on a noblewoman's servant in front of her. The officer snapped, “Search him.”

A second soldier seized Tomas by the arms. The first patted him down roughly, pulling at his coat, reaching beneath the hem. Tomas's face stayed still, but Elianor saw the pulse in his throat.

The soldier found a leather cord at his neck.

“What is this?”

He yanked.

Something struck the wet stones.

The lantern light caught a brief circle of gold.

Tomas went utterly still.

Elianor saw the ring before anyone else did. It lay half beneath the edge of the straw mat, its face dark with grime, a raised mark carved into it: not the crowned hawk of Greyhaven, but a broken sun—or perhaps a wheel, its spokes cut deep and worn smooth by years of touch.

The soldier bent.

Elianor moved first.

She stepped between him and the stones, letting her cloak sweep over the ring. When she bent, it appeared that she had slipped in the mud. Her fingers closed around the metal.

“Careless,” she said, straightening. “You have broken my stable floor.”

The soldier frowned. “I dropped nothing.”

“You dropped your manners.”

A few of Harl's men looked away. Pell coughed into his fist.

The blue-coated officer approached. “What did you pick up?”

“A piece of tack.” Elianor held out her empty hand as proof. “Unless your search authority extends to taking ornaments from my household.”

His eyes moved from her face to her clenched left hand. She kept it hidden in the folds of her cloak.

“Open it.”

The rain seemed to stop.

Tomas's gaze met hers. There was no plea in it. That frightened her more than pleading would have. He looked not at the officer but at her, with the terrible concentration of someone already measuring the distance to death.

Lord Marrow's voice cut across the yard. “You will not command my daughter.”

The officer turned. “My lord, if she possesses evidence—”

“She possesses nothing. Search the stable and be done with it.”

For the first time that night, Elianor was grateful for her father's possessiveness. It had built the wall that shielded her hand.

The officer stared at her a moment longer, then nodded toward the stalls. “Continue.”

The soldiers overturned feed bins, opened chests, and thrust spears into hay. One dragged Pell toward the cart and demanded to know why an empty sack smelled of barley. Pell answered that barley had once been in it, as was the purpose of sacks. Another soldier found the ash-yard route board, but Captain Harl called it a stable inventory and sent him toward the harness room.

Tomas did not move until the search passed beyond Ash's stall. Then he bent to the mare, his hands steady again. Elianor felt the ring cutting into her palm.

She needed to return it before anyone noticed its absence. She needed to know why it mattered. She needed, above all, not to look at Tomas as if the small object had opened a door behind him.

When the search moved to the lower yard, she slipped behind the stall partition.

“What is it?” she whispered.

Tomas stared at her closed hand. “Where did you put it?”

“Here.”

“Give it to me.”

“Not until you tell me what it is.”

His jaw tightened. “Elianor.”

It was the first time he had spoken her name without title in the hearing of danger, and the intimacy of it passed through her more sharply than the ring's edge.

“Your father is not looking,” she said. “The soldiers are not looking. Tell me.”

“It belonged to my father.”

The answer was so simple that it became a refusal.

“Who was he?”

Tomas glanced toward the yard. A soldier shouted at someone near the well. Rain ran from his hair into his eyes.

“Someone who died.”

“Many people have died.”

“Yes.”

“Was he a servant?”

His silence told her that the question had struck too near the truth, though not which truth.

The officer called for Captain Harl. Boots splashed closer.

“Give it back,” Tomas said.

Elianor reached inside her cloak. “Turn around.”

He did, placing his body between her and the yard. She laid the ring in his palm. His fingers closed over it, but hers remained beneath them for one suspended moment.

His hand was cold. So was hers.

Neither moved.

A soldier appeared at the end of the partition. “You there!”

Tomas pulled Elianor into the narrow space between the stall and the wall.

Her back struck rough timber. His chest pressed against hers, one arm braced beside her head, the other holding the ring against his heart. Ash shifted in the stall behind him, blowing warm breath into the dark. Elianor could hear Tomas breathing, fast and controlled, and beneath it the pounding of his heart.

The soldier's lantern passed across the gap.

“Nothing here,” Tomas called.

“Come out.”

“In a moment. The mare is frightened.”

The lantern moved away.

But Tomas did not.

Elianor's hands had found the front of his coat. She felt the wet wool, the hard line of his shoulder, the trembling he was trying to conceal. His face was inches from hers. A strand of damp hair clung to his cheek. She could have lifted her hand and touched it.

“You are hurt,” she whispered.

“Not mine.”

There was blood on his cuff, perhaps from the soldier's rough grip. She brushed it with her thumb. His breath caught.

For a moment the raid, the soldiers, the locked granaries, and every wall between them fell away. There was only the warmth of Ash behind him and the narrow dark holding them together. Elianor felt how easily fear could become something else when there was no room to keep the two apart.

Tomas lowered his forehead until it nearly touched hers.

“Do not,” he said.

She did not know whether he meant do not touch him, do not ask, or do not make him want a life he could never offer. Her fingers tightened in his coat.

“Why?”

“Because they are still here.”

“That is not what I meant.”

“I know.”

His eyes lifted to hers. There was tenderness there, and anger, and an old grief she had not yet been permitted to name. He leaned closer—not enough to kiss, only enough that she felt his breath against her mouth.

Then he withdrew.

The loss of him was immediate and physical. Cold rushed into the space he left.

“We cannot do this,” he said.

“Do what?”

“Pretend the danger makes us honest.”

Before she could answer, he stepped into the stall and began calming Ash. Elianor gathered her cloak, hiding the shaking of her hands.

The soldiers searched for another quarter hour. They found no courier, no weapons, and no rebel papers. In the chapel they frightened the refugees awake and overturned three bedding chests. Chaplain Orren protested until Captain Harl told him to be silent. In the kitchen they discovered the missing salt fish and the false spoilage tally. Bryn stood beside the pantry shelves with an expression of injured innocence so convincing that Elianor almost admired the cruelty of it.

At last the blue-coated officer returned to the corridor.

“The courier escaped,” he announced. “If he was ever here.”

Lord Marrow's mouth hardened. “Then your men have enjoyed an unnecessary tour of my house.”

“We will return if evidence appears.”

“You will request permission.”

The officer bowed, and the soldiers filed out into the rain. Their boots faded toward the gate. The bell gave one final stroke.

Only then did the household breathe.

Elianor found Tomas in the stable after dawn. The storm had thinned to a gray drizzle. Ash stood with her head lowered while he changed the cloth around her leg. The ring hung again from its leather cord, tucked beneath his shirt.

“You should have let them take it,” he said without looking up.

“Would you have?”

“No.”

“Then do not ask me to be braver than you.”

He tied the bandage and rested his hand against Ash's neck. “You do not know what you saved.”

“Then tell me.”

“I told you. It belonged to my father.”

“Your father was not a stable servant.”

“No.”

“Was he a rebel?”

Tomas's hand went to the ring beneath his shirt. His face closed as if a door had been barred inside it.

“I cannot tell you.”

“You cannot, or you will not?”

“Both.”

She felt anger rise, not because he owed her every secret, but because he had allowed her to stand between the ring and the soldiers without giving her enough truth to understand the danger. She had risked herself instinctively. He had trusted her only with the edge of the blade.

“You ask me to conceal a thing that may destroy us,” she said. “You ask me to help you, and then call knowledge a danger.”

“Knowledge is a danger.”

“So is ignorance. My father has made a kingdom of it.”

Tomas looked at her then. The weariness in him was deeper than the night's fear.

“I know what your father does with names,” he said. “He writes them down. He sends men to find them. He makes a dead man's family carry the punishment. If I give you mine, you may not be able to keep it from him.”

“I have kept worse things.”

“Not this.”

The certainty in his voice wounded her. She wanted to tell him that she was no longer merely Lord Marrow's daughter, that the hidden sacks and copied figures had already made her complicit in a life beyond his walls. But the words sounded like pride, and pride had no place beside his fear.

“What do you want me to do?” she asked.

“Forget the ring.”

“I cannot.”

“Then forget what you saw.”

“I cannot do that either.”

He looked away first.

Outside, a gull cried over the sea. Somewhere above them, Greyhaven's household began its morning rituals: doors opening, fires being lit, bells marking the hours as though the night had not entered the walls at all.

Elianor stepped toward him. “I will not ask again today.”

Tomas's shoulders loosened by the smallest degree.

“But one day,” she continued, “you will tell me.”

He did not promise. That was answer enough.

She reached for Ash's bridle, though the mare was not ready to be led. Tomas caught her wrist—not hard, only to stop her.

“Thank you,” he said.

The words were inadequate. They were also the nearest thing to tenderness he allowed himself.

Elianor looked down at his hand around her wrist. His thumb rested over her pulse. For one suspended instant, neither of them moved.

Then Tomas released her and turned back to the mare.

Elianor left the stable alone, carrying the shape of his hand with her and the unanswered weight of the signet hidden beneath his shirt.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable and lower household after surviving a midnight raid by Marrow and western-command soldiers. She remains twenty, Lord Corvin Marrow's only child and heir, outwardly controlled but shaken, angry, and increasingly emotionally attached to Tomas. Her goal is to sustain Rill and the chapel refugees, protect the servants' relief network, preserve evidence of grain diversions, and understand the hidden history represented by Tomas's signet without exposing him. She is allied with Tomas, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, Chaplain Orren, and cautiously Master Vey; her loyalty remains shifting toward the coastal people and servants rather than her father's hierarchy. She now knows soldiers are actively searching Greyhaven for rebels, that Tomas carries a dangerous signet inherited from his father, and that he will not yet explain his father's identity. She possesses copied grain figures, the altered route slip beneath her floorboard, supply requisitions, Harl's copied watch figures, Vey's waste authorization, household authority, and access to rooms, wardrobe passage, kitchen and infirmary requests. She is physically safe but under greater suspicion and privately unsettled by her first intense physical closeness with Tomas.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven's great hall and inner household after permitting a midnight search by armed Marrow and western-command soldiers. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, possessive of his daughter, and determined to preserve the estate, garrison, crown obligations, stores, and control of Elianor. His goal is to prevent rebellion and unauthorized relief while maintaining political authority. He knows soldiers searched the stable, chapel, kitchens, and lower passages for a rebel courier, but does not know Elianor concealed Tomas's signet or the full extent of the relief network. He possesses the Marrow signet, household authority, armed guards, and control of the granaries; he is increasingly aware that Greyhaven's servants and supplies contain irregularities.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's accounting room and steward's offices after the household raid. He remains cautious, composed, observant, morally conflicted, and covertly committed to shielding Elianor's relief work while avoiding exposure. His goal is to obscure the network's supply movements and protect the estate's records from both Lord Marrow's investigation and military suspicion. He knows the raid found no courier, that scrutiny of household stores and servants is increasing, and that unauthorized distributions remain dangerous.
