He possesses the steward's seal, keys and records for stores, waste accounts, delivery orders, household logistics, and the ability to obscure accounts. He is physically safe but under pressure.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven's gate, eastern passages, chapel, stable, and granary watch after accompanying the midnight search for a supposed rebel courier. He remains loyal to the Marrow hierarchy, suspicious of unauthorized movement, and responsible for preventing panic, unauthorized distributions, and access to stores. He knows the soldiers searched the stable and lower household, that no courier was found, and that Elianor intervened during the search; he does not know she concealed Tomas's signet or the full network's activities. He possesses weapons, guard authority, and knowledge of watch rotations, including the ash-yard changeover. He is physically safe and more wary of Elianor and the servants.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after surviving the midnight raid, tending Ash and concealing his father's signet beneath his clothing. He remains a wary young stable servant, practical, exhausted, emotionally attached to Elianor, and frightened that his past will endanger everyone near him. His goal is to protect the coastal relief network, Ash, and Elianor while keeping his true family identity hidden. He knows soldiers are searching Greyhaven for rebels, that Elianor saved his signet, and that she now understands it belonged to his father; he still refuses to tell her who his father was. He is allied with Elianor, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, and other servants and coastal families. He possesses the signet on a leather cord, stable tools, horse knowledge, a brown riding horse, carts, and coastal paths. He is physically uninjured except for a bloodied cuff and fatigue, but emotionally exposed after pulling Elianor into close hiding and withdrawing before they could name their feelings.

set.name: Ash
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after being frightened during the midnight raid. She remains a tall gray mare with a white blaze, raw rope wound beneath her jaw, swollen but improving hind leg, and scars from mistreatment. She remains frightened by soldiers and lanterns but accepts Tomas's calming touch and continued treatment; she is not yet fit to ride. Tomas continues tending her with warm cloths and bandages. She is physically unsettled but not newly injured.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Greyhaven's kitchen and servants' passages after helping the household endure a midnight military search. She remains clever, frightened, practical, and loyal to Elianor and Tomas. Her goal is to maintain kitchen cover records and protect supplies diverted to the chapel and Rill without exposing the network. She knows soldiers searched the kitchens and discovered the missing salt fish and false spoilage tally, though they did not uncover the network; she does not know the details of Tomas's signet. She possesses access to kitchen inventories, food, linen, medicine stores, servants' passages, and plausible cover records. She is physically safe but more alert to household scrutiny.

A midnight raid by Marrow and western-command soldiers searched Greyhaven's stable, chapel, kitchens, and lower household for a supposed rebel courier; no courier was found, but the raid increased the danger to the servants' network.

When soldiers searched Tomas, his father's signet fell from beneath his clothing; Elianor concealed and recovered it before the soldiers noticed, and Tomas refused to explain more than that it belonged to his dead father.

During the raid, Tomas pulled Elianor into hiding beside Ash's stall; their physical closeness revealed their growing attachment, but Tomas withdrew and warned that they could not mistake danger for honesty.
Tomas will eventually reveal that the signet belonged to his father and disclose the hidden identity and history he has been protecting, while asking Elianor to keep it secret.

chapters.name: Arlen Rusk
chapters.content:
For three days after the raid, Greyhaven behaved as if silence could mend what soldiers had broken.

The household doors opened at the proper hours. Fires were lit in the great hall. The bells marked prayers, meals, and the changing of the watch. Captain Harl doubled the guards at the eastern gate and sent men to count sacks in the granaries, while Lord Marrow received reports behind the closed doors of the council room. In the chapel, refugees slept beneath blankets that smelled of smoke and damp wool. In the kitchens, Bryn made the missing salt fish appear to have been eaten by rats of exceptional discipline.

Only the stable refused to pretend.

Ash startled whenever boots crossed the yard. She jerked against her halter at the sound of a lantern being lifted, then stood trembling until Tomas's hand found the place beneath her mane where fear gathered hardest. He worked more slowly than usual, and the blood on his cuff had darkened to a brown stain that would not wash out.

Elianor watched him from the open stable door.

She had told herself she came to ask about Ash's leg. She had told herself she came to bring clean linen from the infirmary. She had told herself many things, and none survived the sight of the leather cord disappearing beneath Tomas's shirt.

He saw her in the reflection of the water bucket.

“You should not stand in the doorway,” he said. “The wind is cold.”

“It is colder where I am going.”

His hand paused against Ash's neck. “Where are you going?”

“To ask you a question.”

“You have asked it.”

“Not the question I came to ask.”

Tomas turned. The stable was empty except for them, Ash, and the old brown gelding in the far stall. Dusty light entered through the high slats and laid pale bars across his face.

“What question is that?”

“Who was your father?”

The gelding shifted in its straw. Somewhere beyond the walls, a guard laughed, and the sound made Tomas's expression tighten.

“Elianor—”

“Do not call me away from it.”

“I am trying to keep you alive.”

“My father has been trying to keep me obedient. You are not the same man.”

“No,” Tomas said. “I am worse at it.”

She stepped inside and closed the door. The latch fell with a small, definite click. Tomas glanced toward the yard as if the soldiers might hear the sound through the wood.

“You said the ring belonged to your father,” she continued. “You said he was not a servant. You said my father writes names down and sends men to find them. I know enough to understand that you have been afraid for a long time.”

His eyes lowered.

“How long?”

“Since I was six.”

The answer struck her with the force of an unexpected blow. She had been six when her mother died, when the west wing was hung in black cloth and servants learned to lower their voices. Six when Lord Marrow had begun bringing her to council meetings and telling her that the house was all that remained of their family.

Tomas rubbed his thumb over a white scar in his palm.

“My father was killed fourteen years ago,” he said. “I was six. That is all you need to know.”

“No.”

He looked at her.

“No,” she repeated. “It is not all I need to know.”

For a moment anger crossed his face. Then it gave way to fatigue. He took a stool from beside the tack table and sat, elbows on his knees. The stable seemed to contract around him, holding its breath.

“His name was Arlen Rusk.”

The name had lived in Greyhaven before Elianor did.

She knew it from the half-burned histories in the schoolroom, from a passage in the chapel chronicle that her tutor had told her to skip, from the winter stories servants stopped telling when a noble foot entered the room. Arlen Rusk, rebel commander. Arlen Rusk, traitor to the crown. Arlen Rusk, hanged at Greyhaven after the coastal rising.

She knew the name because it had been used to explain her father's greatness.

The first Lord Marrow, the story said, had broken the rebellion and saved Avelune's western coast. The current Lord Marrow had inherited the fortress, the lands, and the gratitude of the crown. The executions had been necessary. The famine, when it came, had been unfortunate. The walls had stood because men like Corvin Marrow had been willing to do what gentler men could not.

Tomas watched her remember.

“Yes,” he said. “That Arlen Rusk.”

Elianor's mouth had gone dry. “You are saying—”

“I am his son.”

Ash gave a low, uneasy sound. Tomas rose immediately and went to her, but Elianor could not move. The name seemed to fill the stable, larger than the rafters, larger than the fortress above them.

“Your father was executed here,” she said.

“On the eastern green.”

“By order of Lord Marrow.”

“By order of the crown. Carried out by your father.”

The correction did not lessen anything. It made the truth more precise.

Elianor looked at Tomas's hands. Those hands had mended harness, carried sacks, cleaned wounds, and calmed a horse that had learned to fear every human touch. She tried to place them against the image of a six-year-old boy watching a crowd gather beneath a gallows. The two pictures would not join.

“Where were you?” she asked.

“Near the chapel.”

“Who was with you?”

“My mother. My sister had died the winter before. My mother told me not to look.”

He spoke without ornament, which made each word harder to bear.

“She looked,” he continued. “I looked because she did. There were soldiers around us. Marrow soldiers. Their cloaks had the black thorn clasp. I remember that more clearly than his face.”

“Lord Marrow's face?”

“My father's face.”

Elianor flinched.

Tomas noticed. “I am not asking you to mourn him.”

“I am not mourning him.”

“Then what are you doing?”

She had no answer that did not condemn her. She was thinking of her father in the great hall, silver-haired and severe, telling her that a ruler must choose who could be saved. She was thinking of Arlen Rusk beneath the eastern sky. She was thinking of a boy who had survived because his name had been taken from him.

“My father never told me,” she said.

“Of course not.”

“Did he know you lived?”

“I do not know.”

“You must know whether he knew.”

“Not everything is known.” Tomas's voice sharpened. “That is what the soldiers taught me first. They came to our house after the execution. They searched for papers, weapons, names. My mother gave them nothing. They took our land anyway. When she died, a cooper in Rill hid me among his apprentices. I became Tom Vale because a dead rebel's son could not safely remain Arlen Rusk's son.”

“Tom Vale.”

“The name on the stable rolls. Tomas came later. It sounded less like a lie when people said it quickly.”

Elianor put a hand against the nearest stall door. The wood was rough beneath her palm.

“Why Greyhaven?”

“Because no one looks closely at a servant who has learned not to be seen. Because the fortress always needs stable boys. Because I wanted to know the place where my father died.”

“And did you?”

“Know it?”

“Know why he died.”

Tomas's gaze went to the high window, beyond which the sea showed as a strip of hard silver.

“They called him rebel commander,” he said. “He was a village captain before that. He asked for limits on the levies. He wanted the coastal villages to send delegates to the crown's councils. He wanted soldiers to stop taking children for labor when the fishing failed. Your father promised negotiation.”

Elianor closed her eyes.

“Then he broke the promise.”

“He invited my father to Greyhaven under a flag of truce. Marrow's men arrested him before he reached the hall.”

“How do you know?”

“My mother knew. Two fishermen saw it. One of them told me when I was older. The other was found dead in a ditch before winter.”

The stable door rattled under a gust of wind.

“Your father signed the warrant,” Tomas said. “He stood on the steps while Arlen Rusk was hanged. I do not know whether he watched the whole time. I do know he kept the land.”

Elianor's hand fell from the stall door.

“That is not what the histories say.”

“The histories were written by the men who inherited the land.”

She wanted to defend the records, though she had not seen them. She wanted to say that Lord Marrow was not a murderer, not only a murderer, that duty had made him hard and fear had made him cruel. But every defense sounded like an echo of his own voice.

“I am his daughter,” she said.

“Yes.”

“His only child.”

“Yes.”

“If anyone learns who you are—”

“They will use it.”

“Who will?”

“Everyone. Your father will call me proof that the old rebellion has returned. The crown will call me a banner and send troops after anyone who stands near me. The coastal people may call me an heir, though I have inherited nothing but a ring and a grave. Men who want revenge will put words in my mouth and knives in my hands.”

He came toward her, stopping just beyond reach.

“I have spent fourteen years making myself too ordinary to fear,” he said. “Do you understand? I learned to bow before anyone with a sword. I let men forget my face while they remembered my labor. I buried the name Rusk so deeply that sometimes I thought it had never belonged to me.”

“And now the ring has been seen.”

“Not by the soldiers.”

“By me.”

“That is what frightens me.”

She looked up. “That I know?”

“That you care.”

The honesty of it left no room for anger.

Tomas reached beneath his shirt and drew out the signet. In the dim stable light, its worn device appeared less like a symbol than a wound: a broken wheel, its outer rim chipped, its center darkened by years of handling.

“My father pressed this into my hand the night before he died,” he said. “My mother kept it after. When she was dying, she gave it to me and told me never to show it unless I was ready to lose the life I had made.”

“You showed it to me.”

“I did not mean to.”

“But you did.”

He closed his fingers around the ring. “Then you must keep silent.”

The command was almost a plea.

“About all of it?”

“About my name. About the ring. About what I have told you.”

“What if my father asks?”

“Lie.”

The word seemed impossible in her mouth. She had lied about grain, about routes, about kitchens and carts. Those lies had been acts, brief bridges thrown over danger. This would be a lie about blood, murder, and the foundation of Greyhaven itself.

“Can you ask that of me?”

“I can ask anything. I have very little else to offer.”

She stared at him until his face blurred.

He mistook the tears for rejection and stepped back. “If you cannot, go now. Tell Lord Marrow. Let him lock me in the old cells and finish what he began with my father.”

“Stop.”

“I would rather die once than spend another year waiting for the door to open.”

“Stop.” Her voice broke. “I am not going to tell him.”

Tomas stood motionless.

“I am not going to tell anyone,” she said. “Not Bryn. Not Vey. Not Chaplain Orren. No one.”

“You should not promise what you cannot keep.”

“I have kept promises made to men who never deserved them. I can keep this one.”

His eyes shone, though whether from grief or distrust she could not tell.

“I am still Lord Marrow's daughter,” she said. “That does not vanish because your father died beneath my father's sword. But I will not become another weapon against you.”

Tomas's breath left him slowly.

Elianor crossed the remaining space between them. She did not reach for the ring. She laid her hand over his closed fist instead.

“Your name is safe with me,” she said.

He looked down at their hands. “Names are never safe.”

“Then I will be unsafe with it.”

For one terrible moment, he leaned into her touch. His forehead lowered until it rested against hers, as it had during the raid, but this time there were no soldiers outside the stall and no lantern sweeping the darkness. There was only the knowledge between them, and the knowledge made the closeness more dangerous, not less.

“If they discover this,” he whispered, “they will say I used you.”

“Did you?”

“No.”

“Then let them say it.”

He shut his eyes. “They will kill you.”

“Perhaps.”

His head lifted sharply.

Elianor forced herself to meet his gaze. “Do not ask me to pretend that your fear is more important than my choice. I know what I am choosing.”

“No, you know what you feel.”

“Is there a difference?”

“There must be.”

She almost smiled, though there was nothing joyful in her. “You said danger should not make us honest. It has done worse than that. It has made honesty unavoidable.”

A bell sounded above them, calling the household to morning prayers.

Tomas released her hand. The signet vanished beneath his shirt.

“Forget the name when we leave this stable,” he said.

“I will remember it.”

“Then hide the remembering.”

Elianor opened the door. The gray morning waited beyond it, full of guards, ledgers, hunger, and the enormous fortress her father had built upon another man's death.

Before she stepped outside, Tomas said, “Elianor.”

She turned.

“Arlen Rusk was not a hero.”

“Perhaps not.”

“He was a man. He made mistakes. He was afraid. He left my mother and me with nothing.”

“Then I will remember that too.”

Tomas nodded, as if the answer pained him but did not insult him.

She went back toward the house alone. At the corridor's end, Lord Marrow stood beneath the family crest, speaking with Captain Harl about the new watch. His eyes moved to her, then to the stable door behind her.

Elianor kept walking.

For the first time, she carried a name her father had tried to bury. She carried it silently, not as a banner, not yet as a weapon, but as a living wound shared between her and the man she loved.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable and lower household after the midnight raid and Tomas's revelation. She remains twenty, Lord Corvin Marrow's only child and heir, outwardly controlled but shaken by learning that Tomas is the surviving son of Arlen Rusk, the rebel commander her father had executed fourteen years earlier. Her goal is to sustain Rill and the chapel refugees, protect the servants' relief network, preserve evidence of grain diversions, secretly investigate the official history of Arlen's execution, and protect Tomas without exposing him. She is allied with Tomas, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, Chaplain Orren, and cautiously Master Vey; her loyalty is shifting decisively toward the coastal people and servants rather than her father's hierarchy. She knows Tomas's true identity, his assumed name since childhood, his mother's account of Arlen's cause and arrest, and that the signet may make him a symbol for competing factions. She has promised to keep his identity and confession secret. She possesses copied grain figures, the altered route slip beneath her floorboard, supply requisitions, Harl's copied watch figures, Vey's waste authorization, household authority, and access to rooms, wardrobe passage, kitchen and infirmary requests. She is physically safe but emotionally burdened, frightened for Tomas, and increasingly aware that her family's authority rests on a buried crime.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven's great hall, council room, and inner household after permitting the midnight search by armed Marrow and western-command soldiers. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, possessive of his daughter, and determined to preserve the estate, garrison, crown obligations, stores, and control of Elianor. His goal is to prevent rebellion and unauthorized relief while maintaining political authority. He knows soldiers searched the stable, chapel, kitchens, and lower passages for a rebel courier, found no courier, and increased scrutiny of stores and servants; he has noticed Elianor's continued presence near the stable but does not know she concealed Tomas's signet or that Tomas is Arlen Rusk's son. He possesses the Marrow signet, household authority, armed guards, and control of the granaries. He remains unaware that Elianor now understands his role in Arlen Rusk's execution and is concealing Tomas's identity.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven's gate, eastern passages, chapel, stable, and granary watch after accompanying the midnight search for a supposed rebel courier. He remains loyal to the Marrow hierarchy, suspicious of unauthorized movement, and responsible for preventing panic, unauthorized distributions, and access to stores. He knows the soldiers searched the stable and lower household, that no courier was found, that Elianor intervened during the search, and that the watch has been doubled; he does not know Elianor concealed Tomas's signet or that Tomas is Arlen Rusk's son. He possesses weapons, guard authority, and knowledge of watch rotations, including the ash-yard changeover. He is physically safe and more wary of Elianor, Tomas, and the servants.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after surviving the midnight raid and revealing his identity. He remains a wary young stable servant, practically known as Tomas Vale, but is truly Tomas Rusk, the surviving son of Arlen Rusk, the rebel commander executed at Greyhaven fourteen years earlier. He is exhausted, emotionally exposed, and frightened that his father's signet and name will endanger Elianor, the servants' relief network, and himself. His goal is to protect Ash, Elianor, and the coastal network while keeping his identity hidden and preventing the rebellion from turning him into a banner or heir. He is allied with Elianor, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, and other servants and coastal families. He knows his father sought limits on levies, coastal representation, and an end to forced labor; that Lord Marrow's men arrested Arlen under a promise of negotiation; that Arlen was executed at Greyhaven; and that his family's land was taken afterward. He has asked Elianor to keep silent, and she has promised to conceal his name, signet, and history. He possesses Arlen's signet on a leather cord, stable tools, horse knowledge, a brown riding horse, carts, and coastal paths. He is physically uninjured except for a bloodied cuff and fatigue, but emotionally vulnerable after trusting Elianor with the truth and acknowledging how much her care frightens him.

Tomas revealed to Elianor that his true identity is Tomas Rusk, surviving son of rebel commander Arlen Rusk, executed at Greyhaven fourteen years earlier; he has lived under the assumed name Tomas Vale since childhood.

Tomas told Elianor that Arlen Rusk sought limits on levies, coastal representation, and an end to forced labor before Lord Marrow's forces arrested and executed him under a broken promise of negotiation.

Elianor promised to conceal Tomas's identity, signet, and account of Arlen's death from Lord Marrow and the household, accepting that her father's rule was built upon the execution and dispossession of Tomas's family.
Elianor will conceal Tomas's identity as Arlen Rusk's son while investigating the official records of Arlen's execution and the seizure of rebel lands, without exposing Tomas or the relief network.

chapters.name: The Sealed Archive
chapters.content:
The archive lay behind three locks and a door of black oak at the end of the west gallery, where the windows had been narrowed to slits and the sea could be heard but not seen.

Elianor had passed it all her life without wondering what it contained. That was one of the privileges of being raised inside a fortress: walls became furniture, guards became weather, and locked doors acquired the harmlessness of old habits. Now every time she crossed the gallery, she felt the records behind the oak pressing against her like a second silence.

For six days she waited.

She waited until Lord Marrow summoned Captain Harl to the gatehouse. She waited until the household had eaten its evening meal and the servants began their quieter work. She waited until Master Vey left the accounting room carrying the eastern granary ledgers beneath his arm. Then she took the small key from her mother's writing desk.

It was not an archive key. Elianor knew that. It opened a cabinet in the dead lady's room, a cabinet that had held sealing wax, old letters, and a silver comb blackened by disuse. But when she had been a child, she had seen her father use the same key on the archive's inner lock. He had removed it from her mother's ring after her death and never explained why.

The key turned.

The outer lock opened with a reluctant click.

Elianor entered and closed the door behind her. The air smelled of dust, leather, and the bitter mineral scent of old ink. Shelves climbed to the ceiling. Bundles of correspondence were tied with faded ribbons; estate maps stood rolled in pigeonholes; royal decrees slept beneath boards weighted with stones. A narrow table waited beneath the single lamp, its surface scarred by generations of clerks.

She lit the wick with shaking hands.

Arlen Rusk.

The name had been written nowhere in the first three shelves. She found records of salt tariffs, boundary disputes, marriages, shipwrecks, and three separate quarrels over the rights of gulls nesting on the western cliffs. She found a register of levies from the year of the failed harvest. She found a list of men conscripted from Rill, with ages beside their names and a column marked returned.

Most of the spaces in that column were blank.

Elianor swallowed and kept searching.

The oldest papers had been arranged according to Lord Marrow's own system: crown correspondence, military reports, household grants, confiscations. She pulled down a ledger bound in green hide and laid it open. The first pages concerned the coastal rising fourteen years before. The handwriting changed halfway through, from a neat clerk's hand to the angular script of a military secretary.

Arlen Rusk: apprehended while in armed rebellion against the Crown.

Elianor read the line twice.

Apprehended. Not invited. Not promised negotiation. Not seized beneath a flag of truce.

She turned the page. There should have been depositions from the men who had witnessed the arrest. Instead, three pages had been cut out cleanly at the stitching. The remaining text referred to testimony attached elsewhere, but no attachment had survived.

On the next page, a royal order authorized the execution of Rusk and eleven named associates. The order called them pirates, extortionists, and enemies of lawful commerce. It did not mention levies, delegates, or forced labor.

A second document contradicted it.

This one was folded into the ledger, not bound. It was a copy of a letter from a crown magistrate in Avelune City, written two weeks before the execution. The magistrate asked Lord Marrow to delay judgment until the coastal petitions could be reviewed. At the bottom, in a different hand, someone had written: Negotiation withdrawn. Example required.

Elianor sat down.

The lamp flame leaned as wind found a crack around the window. Shadows moved along the shelves like men passing beyond a wall.

Example required.

She thought of her father telling her that a ruler must choose who could be saved. She thought of Tomas saying that his father had been invited under a promise of negotiation. The words did not merely agree. They locked together.

She searched for the names of the eleven associates. Some had been executed at Greyhaven. Others had been transported inland. Beside five names appeared a later notation: lands reverted to Marrow administration pending crown review.

Pending review.

The review had lasted fourteen years.

Elianor found the corresponding land rolls in a lower drawer. The families were not names to her father. They were acreage, pasture, mill rights, and coastal access. Rusk holdings: three hundred and twenty acres above the north cove. Pell holdings: fishing sheds and salt racks. Sella holdings: a cottage, two fields, and a right of passage to the sea. The lands had been transferred in batches to the Marrow estate, to Sir Edric Pell, and to merchants who supplied the capital.

Her hand went cold.

The wealth that had paid for new battlements, imported glass, and the carved cedar doors of the great hall had a shape beneath it. Not money. Not crown favor. Houses. Boats. Fields. The right to walk down to the water without asking permission.

She searched the margin for a signature and found Lord Marrow's seal impressed in dark red wax.

Elianor leaned back as if the paper had struck her.

At the bottom of the drawer lay a thin packet marked RUSK, ARLEN—CLOSED. The seal had been broken long ago and repaired with ordinary wax. Inside were four depositions, each written by a different hand. One fisherman claimed that Rusk had ordered villagers to hide weapons. Another said Rusk had forbidden the burning of a tax office. A third stated that soldiers under Marrow command had taken children from three villages after the arrests.

The fourth deposition ended halfway through a sentence.

I was present when Lord Marrow promised the captain safe conduct, and I heard him say—

The rest of the sheet had been torn away.

Elianor pressed her fingertips to the ragged edge. She could almost hear the missing voice continuing in the dark.

A floorboard creaked outside.

She extinguished the lamp.

The archive vanished. In the blackness, her breath sounded enormous. The outer lock had not moved, but a shadow crossed the strip of light beneath the door.

“Lady Elianor?”

Master Vey.

She did not answer.

The handle turned once. Then again, more gently.

“I know you are inside,” he said. “If you intend to hide, you have chosen a poor room.”

Elianor relit the lamp. “How did you open the door?”

“I did not. You did.”

She stood between him and the table. Vey entered and closed the door with care. His eyes moved over the open ledger, the land rolls, and the broken packet. He did not look surprised. That frightened her more than anger would have.

“You should report me,” she said.

“I should report a great many things.”

“Did you come here to do so?”

“I came to see whether you were stealing from the archives or merely reading what your family had stolen from others.”

The words landed softly. Their softness made them cruel.

Elianor glanced toward the documents. “You knew.”

“I suspected.”

“Since when?”

“Since I was twenty-three and asked why the Rusk lands appeared in three different books under three different descriptions.” Vey removed his gloves one finger at a time. “Your grandfather's clerk told me the discrepancies were clerical. He died before he could explain them. Your father promoted the next clerk.”

“Why did you remain?”

Vey looked at the shelves. “Because suspicion is not proof. Because I had a family to feed. Because men who ask honest questions in this house are given dishonest answers until they learn silence.”

“And now?”

“Now you have proof enough to be dangerous and not enough to be safe.”

Elianor lifted the magistrate's letter. “This says the negotiations were withdrawn.”

“Yes.”

“This says the land was seized after the executions.”

“Yes.”

“This says my father knew.”

Vey's face tightened. “It says he signed. It does not tell us what he believed he was signing.”

“He signed the deaths.”

“I did not say otherwise.”

The archive seemed suddenly too small for the two of them and the dead crowding its shelves.

“Why are some depositions missing?” Elianor asked.

“Because someone wanted the story to be clean.”

“Was it my father?”

“I do not know.”

“You know enough to doubt him.”

“I know enough to doubt everyone who profits from a single version of history.”

She turned toward the table. “I need copies.”

Vey's expression changed at last. “No.”

“I need copies of the magistrate's letter, the land transfers, and the depositions.”

“If you remove them, they may be missed.”

“I will not remove them.”

“Then what do you intend?”

“My mother's writing room has a press. I can copy them there.”

“By morning, the archive clerk will see that the documents were disturbed.”

“Then help me disturb them properly.”

Vey stared at her. Beyond the walls, the watch bell sounded once. Neither of them moved until the echo died.

At last he crossed to a shelf and took down a blank folio, a bottle of ink, and a small packet of vellum sheets.

“Copy only the pages that bear dates, names, seals, or references to land,” he said. “Do not copy the royal order in full. Its wording is already recorded in the crown register, and repetition will make the collection look deliberate.”

Elianor looked at him. “You have done this before.”

“I have preserved things before.”

“Is that what you call it?”

“It is what I call the part of theft that can still be opposed.”

He helped her arrange the papers, placing a blotter beneath each sheet. His hands were steady. Hers were not. She copied the magistrate's letter first, then the notation about the withdrawn negotiation. She copied the land transfers, including the names of families whose descendants might still be living in Rill. When she reached the unfinished deposition, she copied every word and marked the torn edge with a careful line.

The ink dried slowly.

“Do you know what happened to these people?” she asked.

“Some were sent inland. Some took work under other names. Some remained in the villages and paid rent for land their fathers had owned.”

“Tomas's family?”

Vey's pen stopped.

Elianor felt the pause like a hand at her throat. She had said too much.

“Which family?” he asked.

“The Rusks.”

“Most of the Rusk holding was transferred to Greyhaven. A portion went to the crown's preferred merchants.”

“And the family?”

“Dead, dispersed, or silent. Those are the usual choices left to a defeated household.”

He did not ask why she wanted to know. That mercy was its own kind of alliance.

When the copies were finished, Elianor folded them beneath the lining of her sleeve. The original papers returned to their places. Vey replaced the ledgers, then moved one bundle of ship manifests a finger's width to the left.

“Why?” she asked.

“So that anyone searching for your disturbance will find evidence of my incompetence first.”

A reluctant breath escaped her, almost a laugh. It died before becoming one.

At the door, Vey held out his hand. “The key.”

She gave it to him.

He studied the old brass, then returned it. “Your mother's?”

“Yes.”

“Then do not use it again.”

“Will you report me?”

“No.”

“Why?”

Vey's gaze settled on the sealed packet. “Because I have spent half my life adding columns to accounts that were designed to conceal the truth. Because I have watched hungry families pay rent to the men who took their fields. Because if Lord Marrow learns you are asking the right questions, he will stop answering even the wrong ones.”

He opened the door.

“Elianor,” he said, without turning, “doubt is not the same as courage.”

“I know.”

“Good. Doubt carefully.”

She left the archive carrying the copied pages against her skin. The west gallery was empty, but the fortress no longer felt empty. Every stone seemed to contain a buried name. Every polished surface reflected a hand reaching for something that had once belonged to someone else.

At the turn toward her mother's rooms, she stopped and looked back.

The black oak door stood closed again. Behind it lay the missing depositions, the altered histories, and the proof that Greyhaven's prosperity had been fed by confiscation as surely as its granaries were fed by diverted grain.

Her father had taught her that inheritance was a duty passed from the dead to the living.

For the first time, Elianor understood that inheritance could also be an accusation.

She went on through the dark, carrying the copies toward a hiding place beneath her floorboards, and felt the old house watching her as if it had finally recognized her as an enemy.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Greyhaven after secretly entering Lord Marrow's sealed archive and returning toward her rooms. She remains twenty, Lord Corvin Marrow's only child and heir, outwardly controlled but shaken by evidence that Arlen Rusk's execution followed a withdrawn negotiation and that rebel families' lands were transferred to Greyhaven and favored merchants. Her goal is to sustain Rill and chapel relief, protect the servants' network, preserve grain and archive evidence, compare the records with Tomas's memories, and protect Tomas without exposing him. She is allied with Tomas, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, Chaplain Orren, and cautiously Master Vey; her loyalty is decisively shifting toward coastal people and servants rather than her father's hierarchy. She knows Tomas is Arlen Rusk's son, knows his account of the arrest and execution, and now possesses copied records concerning the withdrawn negotiation, missing depositions, and confiscated lands. She also retains copied grain figures, the altered route slip beneath her floorboard, supply requisitions, Harl's copied watch figures, and Vey's waste authorization. She is physically safe but emotionally frightened, morally burdened, and increasingly convinced that her family's inheritance rests on theft.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven's great hall, council room, and inner household, unaware that Elianor entered the sealed archive or that Master Vey protected her. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, possessive of his daughter, and determined to preserve the estate, garrison, crown obligations, stores, and control of Elianor. His goal is to prevent rebellion and unauthorized relief while maintaining political authority. He knows soldiers searched the stable, chapel, kitchens, and lower passages for a rebel courier, found no courier, and increased scrutiny of stores and servants; he has noticed Elianor's continued presence near the stable but does not know she concealed Tomas's signet or that Tomas is Arlen Rusk's son. He possesses the Marrow signet, household authority, armed guards, and control of the granaries. He remains unaware that Elianor now holds copied evidence connecting Greyhaven's wealth to the seizure of rebel lands.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's accounting room and steward's offices after helping Elianor investigate the sealed archive. He remains cautious, composed, observant, morally conflicted, and covertly committed to shielding Elianor's relief work and preserving evidence while avoiding exposure. His goal is to obscure the network's supply movements, protect estate records, and now help prevent Lord Marrow's official history from erasing the truth about Arlen Rusk and confiscated coastal lands. He knows Elianor entered the archive, copied records, and is investigating the execution and land transfers; he also doubts the official history and has chosen not to report her. He possesses the steward's seal, keys and records for stores, waste accounts, delivery orders, household logistics, and knowledge of archive procedures. He is physically safe but under increased personal risk.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after revealing his identity and while Elianor secretly investigates the archive. He remains a wary young stable servant, practically known as Tomas Vale, but is truly Tomas Rusk, surviving son of Arlen Rusk, the rebel commander executed at Greyhaven fourteen years earlier. He is exhausted, emotionally exposed, and frightened that his father's signet and name will endanger Elianor, the servants' relief network, and himself. His goal is to protect Ash, Elianor, and the coastal network while keeping his identity hidden and preventing the rebellion from turning him into a banner or heir. He is allied with Elianor, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, and other servants and coastal families. He knows his father sought limits on levies, coastal representation, and an end to forced labor; that Lord Marrow's men arrested Arlen under a promise of negotiation; that Arlen was executed at Greyhaven; and that his family's land was taken afterward. He does not yet know Elianor has copied archive evidence and plans to compare it with his memories. He possesses Arlen's signet on a leather cord, stable tools, horse knowledge, a brown riding horse, carts, and coastal paths. He is physically uninjured except for a bloodied cuff and fatigue, but emotionally vulnerable and fearful of the consequences of Elianor's care.

set.name: Ash
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after the midnight raid and during Tomas's continued care. She remains a tall gray mare with a white blaze, raw rope wound beneath her jaw, swollen but improving hind leg, and scars from mistreatment. She remains frightened by soldiers and lanterns but accepts Tomas's calming touch and treatment; she is not yet fit to ride. She is physically unsettled but not newly injured.

Elianor entered Lord Marrow's sealed archive using her mother's old key and found missing depositions, conflicting records about Arlen Rusk's arrest, and a crown magistrate's letter indicating that negotiation was withdrawn before his execution.
The archive showed that lands belonging to Arlen Rusk and other executed or displaced coastal families were transferred to Greyhaven, crown-favored merchants, and Sir Edric Pell after the executions.
Master Vey caught Elianor in the archive but chose not to report her, admitting that he doubts the official history and helping her copy records concerning the executions and land transfers.
Elianor concealed copied archive documents beneath her sleeve and carried them toward the hiding place beneath her floorboards.

Elianor will compare the copied archive records with Tomas's memories to reconstruct the truth of Arlen Rusk's arrest, execution, and the seizure of rebel lands, while keeping Tomas's identity concealed.

chapters.name: The Rebel's Son
chapters.content:
Elianor did not go directly to the hiding place beneath her floorboards.

The west gallery was empty, but emptiness in Greyhaven had never meant safety. A servant might be kneeling behind a tapestry, polishing a candlestick in the dark. A guard might be standing at the far stair with his back turned, listening. The fortress had been built to survive storms and sieges; it had also been built so that every passage could be watched from another.

She walked slowly, one hand pressed against the papers hidden beneath her sleeve.

At the turn toward her mother's rooms, she heard voices below. Lord Marrow and Captain Harl were crossing the lower hall. Their words rose through the stairwell in fragments.

“...no courier found.”

“Then search again.”

“The servants are frightened.”

“Fear makes them careless. I want the lower passages watched until morning.”

Elianor waited in the shadow of a pillar until the voices receded. She felt the copied pages warming against her skin. They were thin things, easily burned, easily denied. Yet they seemed heavier than the stone fortress around her.

She had copied the magistrate's letter, the notation—Negotiation withdrawn. Example required—and the rolls that transferred the Rusk lands to Greyhaven, the crown's favored merchants, and Sir Edric Pell. She had copied the names of the dead and displaced, the measurements of fields, the rights to salt racks and fishing sheds. She had copied the unfinished deposition of a man who had heard her father promise safe conduct.

The pages did not tell her everything.

They told her enough.

In her room, she locked the door, knelt beside the bed, and lifted the loose floorboard. Beneath it lay the grain figures, the altered route slip, Harl's copied watch rotations, and Vey's waste authorization. She placed the new papers among them, wrapping the archive copies in oilcloth before lowering them into the narrow dark.

For several moments she kept her hand beneath the board.

Her family had called this inheritance. It was a collection of wounds with seals pressed upon them.

A soft knock came at the door.

Elianor replaced the board and rose. “Who is it?”

“Tomas.”

His voice was low, but she heard the strain in it. She opened the door only far enough to admit him. He slipped inside carrying the smell of hay, rain, and the sharp ointment used on Ash's leg.

His hair was damp. A blood-dark stain marked one cuff, though there was no wound on his hand when she caught his wrist and examined it.

“Ash?” she asked.

“Not hers. She kicked the stall wall when the soldiers came through again.”

“Is she worse?”

“Frightened. Not worse.” He glanced at the locked door. “You found something.”

It was not a question.

Elianor crossed to the table. “I copied records from the archive.”

His expression closed, as if he had drawn a shutter across his face. “You should not have gone back.”

“I did not go back. I went for the first time.”

“That is not what I mean.”

“I know.”

She laid out the copies one by one. The magistrate's letter. The land rolls. The names attached to the execution order. The torn deposition. Tomas stood on the other side of the table, not touching anything.

For a while, only the rain spoke against the windows.

“Read this,” Elianor said.

He looked at the letter but did not reach for it. “I know what happened.”

“You know what you were told happened.”

His eyes lifted to hers. “My mother told me my father went to Greyhaven under a white flag. She told me he believed Marrow would hear the petitions. Then soldiers took him, and three days later his head was displayed above the eastern gate.”

“The record says the negotiation was withdrawn before the execution was ordered.”

“Records say whatever the person holding the pen requires.”

“This one was written by a crown magistrate.”

“Then the crown required a cleaner lie.”

His anger was not loud. That made it more dangerous. It moved through him like a current beneath black water.

Elianor pushed the land roll toward him. “Your family held three hundred and twenty acres above the north cove.”

Tomas stared at the figure.

“My father had fields,” he said.

“You remembered a hill.”

“I remembered a hill because I was four.” His mouth tightened. “There was a stone wall. My mother used to hang fish beneath the eaves. I thought it was all one house.”

“It may have been part of the north holding.”

“May have been.” He gave a short, joyless laugh. “You want the papers to give me back a childhood?”

“No.”

“You want them to tell me that I am right to hate him.”

“I want them to tell us what happened.”

“Us?”

The word struck harder than she expected. Tomas turned away, staring toward the window where the sea was hidden by rain.

“My father was not a saint,” he said. “He could be proud. He could make men follow him when caution would have kept them alive. He believed that if the villages stood together, Greyhaven and the crown would have to listen. He said the taxes could not be collected from empty nets. He said men should not be taken from their families for levies decided by people who had never seen the coast.”

Elianor said nothing.

“He wanted each coastal village to send a representative to the crown's council,” Tomas continued. “Not a lord's man. Someone who knew the boats, the tides, the fields. He wanted the forced labor ended—the road gangs, the military carts, the winter levies. He did not begin by calling for a crownless kingdom. He asked them to stop treating us as a storehouse of bodies and coin.”

His hand moved toward the papers and stopped above them.

“He sent petitions?”

“Bundles of them. Names, marks, accounts of what had been taken. My mother said he carried them in a leather case. When the soldiers came, he told everyone not to fire unless they were attacked. He believed the meeting at Greyhaven would be a negotiation.”

“And Lord Marrow promised safe conduct.”

“He promised that the petitions would be heard.”

The distinction was small, and terrible.

“He was arrested outside the chapel,” Tomas said. “Or near it. The memories change there. I remember my mother's hand pulling me behind a cart. I remember my father kneeling in the mud with a soldier's sword against his neck. I remember him looking toward us, though I do not know if he saw me. Then my mother carried me north through the rain.”

He pressed his fingers to his eyes.

“She said we could not go home. We went from cottage to cottage. People gave us crusts, but no one could keep us. Later she told me the land was gone. Later still she stopped speaking of him.”

Elianor looked at the unfinished deposition. “Someone heard the promise.”

“Someone heard many things.”

“Someone tried to record them.”

“And someone tore out the rest.”

Tomas lifted the page. His thumb traced the ragged edge. “This is what I have feared. Not that my father was innocent. That he was ordinary.”

She did not understand.

He lowered the paper. “If he was a monster, then surviving him means nothing. If he was a hero, then I have a shape to fill. But if he was a tired man asking for a fair hearing, and they killed him because his demands were inconvenient...”

His voice failed.

“If he was ordinary,” Elianor said gently, “then they killed a man who should have been allowed to live.”

Tomas looked at her. The guardedness in his face had broken, revealing something younger beneath it.

“I survived because my mother ran,” he said. “Others did not. Sometimes I think I am carrying the wrong life. The children taken in the levies. The men hanged beside him. The families driven from their fields. They should be here. I am only here because I was small enough to hide.”

“You were a child.”

“That does not make it feel earned.”

“No life is earned by being better than another.”

“You speak as if you believe that.”

“I am trying to.”

His laugh was barely a breath. “You are Lord Marrow's daughter.”

“I know.”

“You slept beneath a roof built from my family's land.”

“I know.”

“You ate from kitchens supplied by fields taken after my father's death.”

“I know.”

The words gathered between them, each one a stone neither could move.

Tomas looked down at the land roll again. “Did you come here to apologize?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“I came because I needed to know whether your memory and the records agreed.”

“And do they?”

“They agree where it matters. Your father sought limits on taxation and levies. He sought representation for the coastal villages. He came believing there would be negotiation. The negotiation was withdrawn. He was executed. His land was taken afterward.”

“Afterward,” Tomas repeated.

The word seemed to open beneath him.

“He did not even have to be dead before they decided what his death would purchase,” he said. “They had the transfers ready.”

Elianor thought of the cedar doors, the imported glass, the new battlements. “The estate profited.”

“Your father profited.”

“Yes.”

Tomas's eyes flashed. “Do not make that easier by saying it as if it belongs to a dead man alone. You still wear his name. You still have his guards outside your door. You still have a choice about whether this becomes a secret kept by the daughter of the man who ordered it.”

Elianor flinched, but did not look away.

“You are right,” she said.

He seemed almost startled.

“I cannot undo what he did,” she continued. “I cannot return your family's fields, bring back the men executed with your father, or give your mother the years taken from her. I cannot make myself innocent by discovering the truth.”

Rain ran down the glass in crooked lines.

“But I can refuse to help conceal it.”

Tomas's anger faltered.

“I can preserve the records,” she said. “I can learn the names. I can keep my father from turning their deaths into a cleaner story. And if he asks me to repeat that Arlen Rusk was merely a traitor, I will refuse.”

“That may put you in danger.”

“It already has.”

“It may put the others in danger too.”

“Then we will be careful. But I will not put safety above truth simply because I was born on the profitable side of the wall.”

He moved around the table. Not toward her, exactly, but nearer than before.

“Truth is not enough,” he said.

“No.”

“It will not feed Rill.”

“No.”

“It will not stop the soldiers.”

“No.”

“It may make men hungry for revenge.”

Elianor thought of the torn deposition and the names on the land rolls. “Then we must be honest enough not to replace one lie with another.”

Tomas studied her. “You would tell them?”

“Not yet. Not carelessly. But I will not destroy these papers, and I will not let my father bury the history again.”

He reached for the magistrate's letter at last. His hand shook once as he lifted it.

“My father wanted a council,” he said. “Not a throne.”

“Then neither should you.”

His gaze sharpened. “You think I want one?”

“I think the dead can become dangerous when the living need them to command.”

For a moment, something like grief passed between them, too intimate to call agreement.

Tomas folded the letter with care. “If anyone learns who I am, they will use his name.”

“I know.”

“They may use me.”

“I know.”

“And if Lord Marrow learns that you have these—”

“He will know I am no longer merely asking questions.”

Tomas set the paper down. “You should leave Greyhaven.”

“Where would I go?”

“Anywhere beyond your father's reach.”

“And leave the servants here? The chapel? The grain?”

“You cannot save everyone.”

“No,” Elianor said. “But I can stop pretending that obedience saves anyone.”

He looked toward the door. “You sound like him.”

“Your father?”

“Not his words. His certainty that a wall could be made to answer for the people behind it.”

Elianor folded the copies together. “Was that what he believed?”

“He believed people could.”

The watch bell rang below. Tomas stepped back into the room's shadows.

“Hide the papers somewhere else,” he said. “If they search your room, the floor will be the first place they look.”

“I will ask Vey for another method.”

“Do not ask too much of him.”

“I will not.”

At the door, Tomas paused. “Elianor.”

She waited.

“I am angry with your father.”

“You should be.”

“I am angry with you.”

“I know.”

“I do not know whether I am angry because you are his daughter or because you are the first person who has made me believe the truth might matter.”

Her throat tightened. “Those are not the same thing.”

“They feel the same tonight.”

He left before she could answer.

Elianor stood alone beside the table. Beyond the walls, the sea struck the cliffs with the slow force of something that had been refused for too long.

She returned the copied records beneath the floorboard, then covered it with the rug and her mother's cedar chest. The hiding place was inadequate. The truth was inadequate. Her promise was inadequate.

Still, she had made it.

She could not undo the past. She could refuse to conceal it.

For the first time, that refusal felt less like innocence than the beginning of a war.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At her private room in Greyhaven after meeting Tomas and comparing his memories with copied archive records. She remains twenty, Lord Corvin Marrow's only child and heir, outwardly controlled but shaken by confirming that her father withdrew negotiation with Arlen Rusk, enabled his execution, and profited from confiscated coastal lands. Her goal is to sustain Rill and chapel relief, protect the servants' network, preserve grain and archive evidence, refuse to conceal her family's crimes, and protect Tomas without exposing him; she now also intends to find a safer place for the copied records. She is allied with Tomas, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, Chaplain Orren, and cautiously Master Vey, while her loyalty is decisively shifting toward coastal people and servants rather than her father's hierarchy. She knows Tomas is Arlen Rusk's son, knows his memories of the arrest and his survivor guilt, and possesses copied records concerning the withdrawn negotiation, missing depositions, and confiscated lands, along with copied grain figures, the altered route slip beneath her floorboard, supply requisitions, Harl's copied watch figures, and Vey's waste authorization. She is physically safe but emotionally burdened, morally committed, and increasingly in danger from Lord Marrow.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven's great hall, council room, and inner household, still unaware that Elianor entered the sealed archive, that Master Vey protected her, or that she has confirmed his role in Arlen Rusk's execution and land seizures. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, possessive of his daughter, and determined to preserve the estate, garrison, crown obligations, stores, and control of Elianor. His goal is to prevent rebellion and unauthorized relief while maintaining political authority. He knows soldiers searched the stable, chapel, kitchens, and lower passages for a rebel courier, found no courier, and increased scrutiny of stores and servants; he has noticed Elianor's continued presence near the stable but does not know she concealed Tomas's signet or that Tomas is Arlen Rusk's son. He possesses the Marrow signet, household authority, armed guards, and control of the granaries. He is physically safe and politically powerful, but his hidden history is now preserved in Elianor's copies.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's accounting room and steward's offices after helping Elianor investigate the sealed archive. He remains cautious, composed, observant, morally conflicted, and covertly committed to shielding Elianor's relief work and preserving evidence while avoiding exposure. His goal is to obscure the network's supply movements, protect estate records, prevent Lord Marrow's official history from erasing the truth about Arlen Rusk and confiscated coastal lands, and help Elianor preserve the evidence safely. He knows Elianor entered the archive, copied records, confirmed the withdrawn negotiation and land transfers with Tomas's memories, and intends to keep the truth from being buried; he also doubts the official history and has chosen not to report her. He possesses the steward's seal, keys and records for stores, waste accounts, delivery orders, household logistics, archive procedures, and knowledge of how to make searches find his apparent incompetence first. He is physically safe but under increased personal risk.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after meeting Elianor in her room and comparing his memories with the archive records. He remains a wary young stable servant, practically known as Tomas Vale, but is truly Tomas Rusk, surviving son of Arlen Rusk, the rebel commander executed at Greyhaven fourteen years earlier. He is exhausted, emotionally exposed, angry at Lord Marrow, and burdened by guilt that he survived while other families and children were destroyed. His goal is to protect Ash, Elianor, the coastal network, and the truth of his father's cause while keeping his identity hidden and preventing the rebellion from turning him into a banner, revenge cult, hereditary ruler, or heir. He is allied with Elianor, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, and other servants and coastal families. He knows his father sought limits on levies and taxation, coastal representation, and an end to forced labor; that Lord Marrow's men arrested Arlen under a broken promise of negotiation; that Arlen was executed at Greyhaven; that his family's land was taken afterward; and that Elianor will not conceal these crimes. He possesses Arlen's signet on a leather cord, stable tools, horse knowledge, a brown riding horse, carts, and coastal paths. He is physically uninjured except for fatigue and a bloodied cuff from Ash's frightened kick, but emotionally vulnerable and fearful of the consequences of his name becoming a weapon.

set.name: Ash
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after soldiers passed through again and after Tomas continued her care. She remains a tall gray mare with a white blaze, raw rope wound beneath her jaw, swollen but improving hind leg, and scars from mistreatment. She remains frightened by soldiers, lanterns, and renewed disturbance, kicking the stall wall during the latest search, but accepts Tomas's calming touch and treatment; she is not yet fit to ride. She is physically unsettled but not newly injured.

Elianor compared the copied archive records with Tomas's memories and confirmed that Arlen Rusk sought limits on taxation and forced levies, representation for coastal villages, and negotiation rather than a crownless revolt; Lord Marrow's forces withdrew the negotiation, executed Rusk, and transferred his lands afterward.
Tomas described his childhood memories of Arlen's arrest, his mother's flight, and the guilt he carries for surviving when other families and children were destroyed by the executions and levies.
Elianor told Tomas she cannot undo the past but will refuse to help conceal Lord Marrow's crimes, preserve the records, and reject any official claim that Arlen Rusk was merely a traitor.
Elianor will seek a safer hiding place and preservation method for the copied archive evidence after recognizing that the floorboards may be searched.
Elianor and Tomas will guard the truth of Arlen Rusk's cause against being turned into a revenge cult or hereditary claim to power.

chapters.name: Duke Veyne
chapters.content:
The announcement came at breakfast, beneath the painted ceiling where Greyhaven’s founders were shown receiving a crown from a kneeling king.

Lord Marrow stood at the head of the table with one hand resting on the back of his chair. He had dressed for ceremony though no ceremony had been named: dark coat, silver chain, the Marrow signet bright against his finger. Elianor saw that and thought of the papers beneath her floorboards, of fields measured in ink and transferred under seals like that one.

“Duke Alistair Veyne will arrive before noon,” he said.

The household’s attention gathered around him. Master Vey looked down at his plate. Captain Harl, seated among the senior officers, did not move at all.

Lord Marrow continued. “His western fleet has been recalled from the outer coast. He will remain at Greyhaven for several weeks.”

Elianor’s hand tightened around her spoon.

“For what purpose?”

Her father looked at her, and she knew before he spoke.

“To formalize the understanding between our houses.”

The room seemed to lose its warmth. A coal shifted in the grate.

“You have not asked me whether I understand it.”

“I am informing you of it.”

“Then inform me plainly.”

A thin silence spread among the servants. Bryn stood near the sideboard with a coffee pot in her hands, her face composed with effort.

Lord Marrow’s voice became official. “You are to be engaged to Duke Alistair Veyne. The announcement will be made at supper, with the chaplain present and witnesses from both households.”

Elianor set down her spoon.

Across the table, a courtier named Sir Rennick smiled as if he had been waiting for the pleasure. “A splendid alliance. Greyhaven’s walls and Veyne’s ships. The western coast will sleep soundly.”

“The western coast has not slept soundly in years,” Elianor said.

Her father’s expression hardened. “You will show the duke courtesy.”

“I have not met him.”

“You have met the consequences of refusing useful men.”

There it was: not a marriage, but another accounting. Ships against inheritance. Soldiers against grain. Her life entered into a column beside harbor tolls and crown obligations.

“And if I refuse?” she asked.

Lord Marrow leaned slightly toward her. “You will not.”

He dismissed the table with a glance. Conversation resumed in careful fragments, but Elianor could no longer hear it. The painted king above them offered a crown to a kneeling man. No one had painted what happened after the crown was accepted.

She left before breakfast ended.

In the passage outside, Tomas waited with a bucket of clean water for the stable. He had not been meant to hear the announcement, but servants heard everything in Greyhaven. His eyes went first to her face, then past her to the dining room.

“What happened?”

“My father has arranged my engagement.”

Tomas stopped.

“To whom?”

“Duke Alistair Veyne.”

The water in the bucket trembled as his grip changed.

For one instant she saw the boy he had been, hiding behind a cart while soldiers took his father. Then the expression vanished, replaced by the wary stillness he wore when danger approached.

“The fleet commander,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I know the name.”

“Everyone does.”

“He put down the mutiny at Blackwater Reach.”

“So I am told.”

“He hanged twelve sailors from the mainmast.”

Elianor looked toward the stair. “Not here.”

“Why not? The walls already know.”

A groom emerged from the lower passage, and Tomas lowered his voice.

“Does your father know you will refuse?”

“He has not allowed refusal to become part of the conversation.”

Tomas’s mouth tightened. “Then the conversation is not about you.”

Before she could answer, Captain Harl called from the courtyard. The duke’s escort had been sighted on the western road.

Greyhaven changed in the hour before their arrival. Servants swept stone that had already been swept. Kitchen boys carried wine up from the cellars. The chapel bells were tested, though no blessing had been requested. Guards doubled along the gatehouse and hung the Marrow banners from the battlements.

Elianor watched from an upper window as the procession climbed the road through blown sea grass. Six mounted officers came first, followed by two wagons and a line of soldiers in blue-gray coats. Behind them rode the duke beneath a black pennant marked with a silver trident.

He was not old. That surprised her. She had expected some soft, jeweled court figure whose strength existed only in inherited titles. Alistair Veyne looked scarcely thirty-five, broad through the shoulders, with wind-browned skin and a pale scar cutting from his left temple into his hairline. He rode easily, one gloved hand on the reins, as though every road belonged to him.

The escort halted in the lower court.

Veyne dismounted before anyone could bring a mounting block. He laughed when a stable boy hurried toward his horse and clapped the boy’s shoulder hard enough to make him stumble.

“Take care of her,” he said. “She cost more than your village.”

The boy bowed.

Veyne turned toward the steps. Lord Marrow descended to meet him, smiling in a way Elianor had not seen since the last royal delegation.

“My lord duke,” he called.

“My lord Marrow.” Veyne embraced him as if they were brothers, though his gaze traveled immediately over the walls, the towers, the gate mechanism, and the guard positions. He counted everything before he accepted the wine offered by a servant.

Then he saw Elianor.

His smile altered. Not softened; sharpened.

“Lady Elianor,” he said, climbing toward her. “I have heard that Greyhaven’s beauty is defended by a greater beauty.”

“You have heard too much from flattering people.”

“Then I am fortunate to meet the truth.”

He took her hand and kissed it. His lips barely touched her knuckles, but his fingers closed around them with proprietorial confidence before releasing her.

Lord Marrow’s satisfaction was almost visible.

Inside, Veyne charmed the household with the ease of a man who had never needed to wonder whether welcome might be withdrawn. He told stories of storms, foreign ports, and royal banquets. He knew which wines to praise and which servants to remember by name. To Bryn, he said, “Your kitchens smell better than most admirals’ cabins.” To Master Vey, he asked questions about Greyhaven’s stores that sounded like compliments until Elianor noticed the steward’s careful pauses.

He asked Chaplain Orren whether the chapel still kept its east-facing doors open during storms. When Orren answered that they opened when the desperate needed shelter, Veyne smiled without warmth.

“Generosity is admirable in a priest,” he said. “In a commander, it is usually a breach in the wall.”

Orren’s fingers tightened around his cup. Elianor noticed. So did Master Vey.

At luncheon, the duke spoke of the western coast.

“The villages there have grown insolent,” he said, carving pheasant with a silver knife. “They mistake famine for an argument. Every failed harvest becomes an excuse to resist the crown.”

“Some villages have lost half their boats,” Elianor said.

“Then they should have guarded the boats.”

“Storms are not rebels.”

“No, but rebels learn to hide behind storms.” Veyne dipped a piece of meat into sauce. “At Blackwater Reach, the sailors complained that their rations were rotten. When I inspected the stores, I found they had sold the good meat and invented the complaint to cover it.”

“Did you?”

“Hang them?” He smiled. “I hanged twelve. The rest remembered their loyalty.”

Lord Marrow lifted his cup. “Necessary firmness.”

“Exactly. A ship cannot be governed by asking every deckhand what he thinks of the captain.”

Elianor looked at the duke. “A ship is not a village.”

“A village is not a person, either.”

The words landed quietly.

He went on eating. Sir Rennick laughed, though a moment too late. Bryn came to replace Veyne’s plate and kept her eyes upon the tablecloth. The duke watched her hands.

“Your people are well trained,” he said to Lord Marrow.

“They know their duties.”

“Duties are easier to teach than loyalty.” Veyne glanced toward the servants. “But fear is a useful beginning.”

Elianor felt something cold move beneath her ribs. Her father did not object. He only asked for more wine.

After luncheon, Lord Marrow took Veyne to inspect the eastern tower. Elianor followed because no one had told her not to, and because she wanted to see what her father had purchased with her future.

The duke studied the sea through the arrow slit.

“With Greyhaven under my protection,” he said, “the crown can secure the whole coast. Your father’s stores, my fleet, and a little discipline among the villages. The ministers will be pleased.”

“You speak as if the coast were an empty board.”

“It is a board. Every lord who refuses to see that loses his estate.”

“Do you see people anywhere on it?”

Veyne turned to her. “People are what the pieces represent.”

Her father gave a low warning sound. “Elianor.”

But Veyne only laughed.

“I admire spirit,” he said. “A wife who thinks is a rare advantage, provided she understands when thought has ended.”

He said wife as if testing the fit of a uniform.

Later, in the gallery, he showed her a miniature of a western harbor painted on ivory. His thumb rested beside the little ships.

“Your dowry will include the Marrow salt rights and the lower harbor revenues,” he said.

“My dowry?”

“Your father and I have discussed the terms.”

“Without me.”

“Without burdening you with figures.”

“I am not burdened by figures.”

“No,” he said, looking at her with renewed interest. “That may be useful.”

She understood then. The marriage was not merely an alliance of houses. He had assessed the grain, the harbor, the roads, the servants, and now her. Her intelligence was another resource to be placed under his command.

“And what will you require of me?” she asked.

“Presence at court when required. A household that reflects discipline. Children, eventually. Discretion always.”

“Do you require affection?”

For the first time, he seemed genuinely puzzled.

“Affection is pleasant,” he said. “Reliability is essential.”

Across the courtyard, Tomas came from the stable carrying a bridle. He stopped beneath the arch when he saw them.

Veyne did not notice him. He was explaining the ceremony he preferred, the fleet officers who would attend, the western estates she would be expected to visit. Elianor heard almost none of it. She watched Tomas’s face as he watched Veyne stand close beside her.

Tomas looked at the duke’s hand resting near her elbow. Then he looked at her.

There was no accusation in his expression. That was worse. There was recognition—the cold understanding that whatever shelter their secrecy had offered was ending.

Elianor took one step away from Veyne.

The duke’s eyes followed the movement. “Is something wrong?”

“No.”

Tomas turned before she could say more and crossed toward the stable.

She wanted to follow him. Every instinct pulled her down the steps, across the yard, through the familiar smell of hay and leather to the place where she could speak without being measured. But Veyne was watching now, and Captain Harl stood at the gate, and two of the duke’s soldiers had begun to notice the stable servant’s haste.

So she remained where she was.

At the stable, Tomas set the bridle on a peg and found Ash watching him from her stall. Her ears had gone back at the unfamiliar soldiers in the yard. He laid a hand against her neck, though his own fingers shook.

He had known, in the abstract, that Elianor would be married. A lord’s daughter did not remain unclaimed because she had learned to listen to a frightened mare. He had told himself that secrecy could be a kind of mercy, that a few stolen hours might be enough for people who had no right to ask for a future.

Seeing Veyne beside her made the lie impossible.

The duke had not looked at Elianor as Tomas did. He had looked at the estate reflected in her. He had seen doors, accounts, ships, and an heir. Tomas had no doors to offer her, no inheritance except a dead man’s name and a history that could get her killed.

Ash breathed against his sleeve.

“Easy,” he whispered. “It is only another storm.”

But he knew storms could enter through every wall.

That evening, Lord Marrow announced the engagement in the great hall. The chaplain blessed the wine. Courtiers applauded. Veyne raised his cup to Elianor, and her father spoke of continuity, security, and the preservation of Greyhaven.

Elianor heard only the sea beyond the windows.

At the far end of the hall, Tomas stood among the servants. He did not look at her again.

The secret between them had once felt like a small room they could enter together. Now soldiers occupied the corridors, a duke had placed his hand upon the door, and her father had given the room a name: marriage.

When the applause rose, Tomas lowered his eyes.

Elianor understood that love could be discovered without being spoken, and destroyed without anyone admitting it existed.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Greyhaven after Duke Alistair Veyne's arrival and the formal announcement of her engagement. She remains twenty, Lord Corvin Marrow's only child and heir, outwardly controlled but inwardly alarmed and angry. Her goal is to sustain Rill and chapel relief, protect the servants' network, preserve grain and archive evidence, refuse to conceal her family's crimes, protect Tomas, and now resist or investigate the political and material terms of the Veyne marriage. She is allied with Tomas, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, Chaplain Orren, and cautiously Master Vey; her loyalty remains shifted toward coastal people and servants rather than her father's hierarchy. She knows Tomas is Arlen Rusk's son, knows the truth of Arlen's broken negotiation and execution, possesses copied archive and grain records, and now knows Veyne intends to treat her, Greyhaven's harbor, stores, and inheritance as assets. She is physically safe but under greater surveillance, emotionally threatened, and publicly bound to an engagement she has not accepted.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven's great hall and inner household after formally announcing Elianor's engagement to Duke Alistair Veyne. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, possessive of his daughter, and determined to preserve the estate, garrison, crown obligations, stores, and control of Elianor. His goal is to prevent rebellion and unauthorized relief while securing Greyhaven through Veyne's fleet and crown favor. He knows Veyne has arrived with soldiers and courtiers and that the household has heard the engagement; he remains unaware that Elianor entered the sealed archive, that Master Vey protected her, that she confirmed his role in Arlen Rusk's execution and land seizures, or that Tomas is Rusk's son. He possesses the Marrow signet, household authority, armed guards, granaries, and the new political alliance. He is physically safe and politically strengthened, though increasingly reliant on military power.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's accounting room and steward's offices after Duke Veyne's arrival. He remains cautious, composed, observant, morally conflicted, and covertly committed to shielding Elianor's relief work and preserving evidence while avoiding exposure. His goal is to obscure the network's supply movements, protect estate records, prevent Lord Marrow and now Veyne from controlling or falsifying the truth about Arlen Rusk and confiscated coastal lands, and help Elianor preserve evidence safely. He knows Elianor entered the archive, copied records, confirmed the withdrawn negotiation and land transfers, and intends to keep the truth from being buried; he now recognizes that Veyne's questions about stores and defenses increase the danger. He possesses the steward's seal, keys, stores records, delivery orders, household logistics, archive procedures, and knowledge of how to make searches find his apparent incompetence first. He is physically safe but under increased personal and political risk.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven's gate, eastern passages, chapel, stable, and granary watch after Duke Veyne's arrival. He remains loyal to the Marrow hierarchy, suspicious of unauthorized movement, and responsible for preventing panic, unauthorized distributions, and access to stores. He knows soldiers previously searched Greyhaven for a rebel courier, that no courier was found, that Elianor intervened during the search, and that Veyne's soldiers now supplement the garrison; he does not know Elianor concealed Tomas's signet or that Tomas is Arlen Rusk's son. He possesses weapons, guard authority, and knowledge of watch rotations, including the ash-yard changeover. He is physically safe and more wary of Elianor, Tomas, servants, and the duke's military presence.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and the burial ground beyond Greyhaven's eastern wall after witnessing Veyne's contempt for generosity and the poor. He remains morally troubled, subordinate to Lord Marrow, and sympathetic to Elianor's defense of the hungry. He knows supplies and medicine are being moved covertly to Rill and the chapel's vulnerable people, though he is not directly coordinating the network, and now understands that Veyne may treat mercy as a security breach. He possesses chapel keys, religious authority, burial records, and responsibility for the displaced. He is physically safe but worried that military control will close the chapel again.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after seeing Elianor with Duke Veyne. He remains a wary young stable servant, practically known as Tomas Vale, but is truly Tomas Rusk, surviving son of Arlen Rusk. He is exhausted, emotionally wounded, jealous without feeling entitled to Elianor, angry at Veyne, and newly convinced that their attachment cannot remain safely hidden. His goal is to protect Ash, Elianor, the coastal network, and the truth of his father's cause while keeping his identity hidden and preventing the rebellion from turning him into a banner, revenge cult, hereditary ruler, or heir. He is allied with Elianor, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, Nessa, Oric, and other servants. He knows his father's cause and history, knows Elianor will not conceal it, and now knows Veyne's marriage and soldiers threaten their secrecy. He possesses Arlen's signet on a leather cord, stable tools, horse knowledge, a brown riding horse, carts, and coastal paths. He is physically uninjured except for fatigue and emotionally vulnerable.

set.name: Ash
set.description: At Greyhaven's stable after Duke Veyne's soldiers and escort entered the yard.
