Her goal is to preserve or conceal the lists, kitchen inventories, and cover records, protect the relief network, and help pass warnings while surviving Lord Marrow's investigation. She knows Elianor was confined, the wedding was moved to six days, and she is among the first servants named for questioning. She possesses kitchen inventories, food, linen, medicine stores, servants' passages, and plausible cover records. She is physically safe for the moment but highly exposed and afraid of soldiers' scrutiny.

set.name: Pell
set.description: At Greyhaven's carts, stable, and relief routes after driving survivors and grain through the eastern gate. He remains broad-shouldered, cautious, dependable, and at high risk from Lord Marrow's investigation. He knows the lower road is impassable, the sea wall has failed, the cart routes and guard changes, Elianor's public pledge, and that he is specifically named for questioning. He is allied with Tomas, Elianor, Bryn, Lysa, Nessa, and Oric and possesses cart-driving and coastal-road knowledge, practical stable skills, and experience concealing grain movements. He is physically safe but faces immediate danger from the expanded military watch.

set.name: Nessa
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel after helping treat survivors and distribute grain from the opened eastern granary. She remains practical, wary, and committed to the coastal relief network. She knows Elianor was confined, the wedding accelerated, the gate opened, and the servants' network is under investigation. She is allied with Tomas, Elianor, Bryn, Pell, Lysa, and Oric and possesses access to linen, washing supplies, clean cloth, and servant passages. She is physically safe but must avoid soldiers and protect the displaced from military control.

set.name: Oric
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and the Rill routes after witnessing Elianor's public pledge and advising villagers to take the offered grain. He remains an elderly one-fingered fisherman, weathered, observant, and cautious. He knows the northern boats, coastal news, the families needing food, and the old mill's occupants, and now knows Elianor has openly committed her inheritance to relief. He possesses a fishing boat when the sea permits, local contacts, and knowledge of tides and coves. He is physically safe but will face greater danger moving relief or news after Elianor's defiance.

Before the eastern gate, Elianor publicly pledged her inheritance and Greyhaven's diverted stores to the survivors of Rill, making her political break with Lord Marrow and her commitment to coastal relief visible to villagers and servants.

Lord Marrow confined Elianor to her rooms, ordered guards placed outside, moved her wedding to Duke Veyne forward to six days, and ordered an investigation of Bryn, Pell, Tomas, and other servants who handled the grain.
Captain Harl and his guards hesitated to use force against Elianor and the gathered villagers, allowing the eastern granary to remain open and the grain to pass through Greyhaven's gate.
Lord Marrow's investigation into the servants who handled the opened grain will uncover evidence implicating Tomas, leading to his arrest and beating unless the network intervenes.
Bryn must protect the distribution lists and cover records created during the public granary opening from Lord Marrow's investigation.

chapters.name: The Beating
chapters.content:
By dawn, the eastern granary had become a wound in Greyhaven’s order.

The doors stood open beneath the watchtower, their iron bands dark with rain. Beyond them, the floor lay swept almost clean, though a few kernels of barley clung in the cracks like pale teeth. The last carts had gone before sunrise, carrying sacks toward Rill and the chapel, and the villagers who had waited beside the road had dispersed into the wet hills. What remained was mud, straw, and the knowledge that everyone had seen the granary opened.

Lord Marrow meant to close the wound with a blade.

Tomas knew it from the moment he entered the stable and found Captain Harl waiting beside Ash’s stall. Harl had brought six guards. Their cloaks dripped onto the straw, and their hands rested near their swords, though none had yet drawn one.

Ash lifted her head at the unfamiliar voices. The raw place beneath her jaw had begun to heal, but fear still moved through her like a second pulse. Tomas stepped between her and the men.

“What do you want?” he asked.

“Your hands,” said Harl.

Tomas looked past him. Pell stood by the cart shed with two stable hands, both pale and silent. One of the men held a pitchfork, though he held it as if he had forgotten what it was for. Bryn was nowhere in sight. That frightened Tomas more than the guards.

“On whose order?”

Harl’s mouth tightened. “Lord Marrow’s.”

“Then let him come and ask.”

“He has asked.”

Harl nodded toward the tack room. A guard opened the door and threw something into the straw between them.

It was a strip of blue cloth, torn from a grain sack. Sewn into its edge was a thread of red wool.

Tomas did not move. He remembered the night they had shifted the first sacks through the stables, Elianor’s hand holding the lantern while Pell cut the household seal from a damaged bundle. He remembered the public distribution yesterday, when the eastern doors had been crowded with bodies and voices, and when every servant who carried a sack had believed, for one bright hour, that the walls no longer belonged to the people who had built them.

The strip was from one of those sacks.

Harl watched his face. “We found it beneath the loose boards in the tack room.”

“Then you have found a piece of cloth.”

“We found three delivery marks scratched on the wall beside it. Yours, Pell’s, and the steward’s.”

Pell swore softly.

Tomas glanced at the stable hands. They had not made those marks. Someone had wanted the evidence to be discovered, or had been careless in a hurry. It did not matter. Lord Marrow needed a name, and Tomas’s was already attached to too many roads.

“Where is Master Vey?” Tomas asked.

“Under examination.”

“And Bryn?”

“Kitchen.”

Harl’s eyes shifted toward the gray sky beyond the open doors. “Come quietly. No one else has to be hurt.”

Tomas thought of Elianor behind her locked door, of the guards stationed outside her rooms, and of the way she had stood before the eastern gate with rain running from her hair. My inheritance, she had said. My stores. My house, if it can be made to serve the living.

He had admired her for making the promise. He had feared her for making it where everyone could hear.

“If I come quietly,” he said, “you’ll hang me quietly.”

Harl looked down.

That was answer enough.

The first guard reached for Tomas’s shoulder. Tomas struck the man’s wrist away, not hard enough to break it but hard enough to make the guard curse. Harl shouted. The stable erupted in motion: boots slipping in straw, Ash kicking at the stall wall, Pell driving his shoulder into a guard who had turned toward him.

For three breaths, the servants had the advantage of confusion.

Then a sword hilt struck Tomas beneath the ribs.

He folded. Someone seized his hair and dragged him upright. He saw Pell pinned against the cart shed, his face bleeding from the mouth. One of the stable hands had dropped the pitchfork and raised both hands. The other was on his knees.

“Stop!” Harl shouted. “Stop, damn you!”

The guards stopped because he was a captain, but they did not release Tomas. His arms were twisted behind him and bound with a leather strap. The blow beneath his ribs had become a hot, spreading weight. He tasted iron.

“Take him to the old weighing room,” Harl said.

“Not the keep?” one guard asked.

“Lord Marrow wants him questioned before the duke’s officers arrive.”

Tomas looked at Harl then. The captain’s face was gray.

The duke’s officers.

Veyne had not yet arrived, but his men were expected. Once they took charge, a servant’s life would be worth less than a broken tool.

As they led him away, Tomas looked back at Ash. The mare pressed herself against the rear of the stall, eyes wide. He wanted to tell her to be still, to wait, to trust the hands that had taught her not every approach meant pain.

But he could not speak around the blood in his mouth.

The old weighing room stood between the granary and the inner court, a low stone chamber where sacks had once been measured before entering the stores. Its windows were narrow, barred, and filmed with salt. The scales had been removed years ago. A ring fixed in the wall remained.

They chained Tomas to it.

Lord Marrow entered alone.

He had changed from the dark coat he wore during the public distribution, but there was still mud on the hem of his boots. His silver hair was tied neatly at the nape. He carried no weapon. He did not need one.

“You have brought shame to this house,” he said.

Tomas leaned against the wall. “Your house was full of shame before I entered it.”

Marrow’s expression did not alter. “You mistake a servant’s cleverness for courage.”

“I mistake nothing.”

“The grain was released under my daughter’s authority.”

“Then question your daughter.”

“I am questioning you.”

“Because you think beating a stable hand will make her order disappear?”

A flicker passed through Marrow’s eyes. “You know what happens to men who incite disorder during famine.”

“Do I?”

“Your father knew.”

The room seemed to contract.

Tomas pulled against the chain before he could stop himself. The iron ring groaned in the wall.

Marrow came closer. “Did you imagine I did not know who you were? Did you think the years had made the records vanish? Tomas Vale. Tomas Rusk. The name is not difficult to trace when one has access to Greyhaven’s books.”

The old fear, buried beneath years of work and assumed silence, rose in Tomas’s throat. It was not fear for himself. It was the image of a child running through reeds while soldiers shouted behind him. His mother’s hand had been hard around his wrist. His father’s signet had been pressed into his palm. Do not let them make you into what they say you are.

Marrow’s voice softened. “You have been tolerated because you were useful. Do not confuse tolerance with protection.”

“Did you tolerate my father?”

“My men executed a traitor.”

“My father asked for negotiation.”

“Your father gathered men against the crown.”

“After you withdrew the promise.”

Marrow struck him.

The blow opened the cut at Tomas’s lip. He turned with it, shoulder scraping stone. The chain bit into his wrists.

“You will tell me who planned the distribution,” Marrow said.

“You know.”

“Names.”

“Ask the woman who opened the doors.”

Marrow’s hand closed into a fist. “My daughter believes she can shame me into surrender. You have encouraged her.”

“No. She saw what you were doing.”

A guard entered carrying a short length of ash wood. Tomas’s body reacted before his mind did. He pulled against the wall, but the chain allowed only a handspan of movement.

Marrow did not look at the wood. “Tell me where the remaining lists are. Tell me who carried the sacks. Tell me which villages have been contacted. In return, I will have you transported north and placed in a labor garrison. You will live.”

Tomas laughed, though the sound hurt. “You offer me the mercy you denied children.”

The guard struck him across the thigh.

Pain flashed white. His knee buckled, and the chain held him upright.

“Names,” Marrow said.

Tomas closed his eyes.

He saw Elianor in the sea garden, mud on her sleeve and sunlight caught in her hair. He saw her holding out her hand to Ash, learning not to force what was frightened. He heard her ask, almost angrily, whether a person could love a place that kept demanding obedience from the starving.

No names.

The wood came down again.

Outside, bells began to ring.

Not the chapel bell. The kitchen bell, clanging in a frantic uneven rhythm. Someone shouted that smoke had risen from the west stores. Another voice cried that a section of the granary roof had collapsed. Men ran past the weighing room. The guard holding the ash wood turned toward the door.

Lord Marrow’s head snapped up. “What is happening?”

The door flew open. A stable boy stood there, breathless. “Fire in the hay loft!”

“There is no fire,” Marrow said.

The boy’s face went blank.

From somewhere beyond the courtyard came the crash of breaking glass, then a horse screaming.

Bryn, Tomas thought.

She had a talent for making a lie sound like an emergency.

Marrow seized the boy by his collar. “Who sent you?”

The boy stared at him, terrified. That terror was real. Bryn had probably told him only enough truth to make him run.

Harl appeared behind him. “My lord, the west watch has abandoned its post. We need men there.”

“Take two.”

“We need all of them.”

Marrow looked toward Tomas. For the first time, uncertainty disturbed his control. The diversion had not defeated him, but it had forced him to choose between guarding a wounded servant and guarding the estate.

“Leave two,” he said. “He cannot go far.”

When Marrow departed, Harl remained by the door.

For several heartbeats neither spoke.

Then Harl crossed the room, drew a knife, and cut the chain from the wall.

Tomas nearly fell. Harl caught his arm, keeping him upright.

“Do not mistake this,” the captain whispered. “I am not joining your rebellion.”

“Then why?”

“Because I have watched men obey orders until there was nothing human left in them.” Harl glanced toward the corridor. “Move.”

The two remaining guards were outside, distracted by shouting from the courtyard. Harl pushed Tomas through the rear door into a passage that smelled of wet stone and old grain.

A figure waited in the darkness.

Bryn.

Her cap was gone, her braid coming loose. She carried a ring of keys in one hand and a bloodied ladle in the other.

“Is that yours?” Tomas asked.

“The ladle?”

“The blood.”

“Guard’s nose. He deserved worse.” She looked him over and went pale. “Can you walk?”

“If I must.”

“You must.”

She led them down a narrow stair behind the weighing room. The stone steps were slick, and Tomas had to brace himself against the wall. Every movement drew pain from his ribs and leg. At the bottom stood a rusted grate half hidden by sacks of spoiled salt.

Bryn knelt and fitted a key into the lock.

“This tunnel runs beneath the old cistern,” she said. “It empties outside the northern cliff road. Pell found it on a drainage map Master Vey kept under the counting desk.”

“Pell?”

“Alive. Harl left him tied in the cart shed. Nessa and Oric are getting him out through the kitchen passage.”

“And Vey?”

“Still in the accounting room.”

Tomas gripped her shoulder. “You cannot leave him.”

“We are not leaving anyone we can reach.”

The grate opened with a shriek.

Cold water ran through the tunnel ankle-deep. Tomas crouched and entered. The ceiling was low, forcing him to bend. Bryn followed, pulling the grate closed behind them.

They had gone only a short distance when voices sounded above. A guard shouted Tomas’s name. Another demanded that the passage be searched.

Bryn shoved him forward. “Faster.”

“I am trying.”

“You have always been annoyingly slow when bleeding.”

He almost smiled. It hurt too much.

At the tunnel’s end, a stone hatch opened onto a ravine choked with gorse. Rain swept across the cliff road. Beyond it, the sea was a gray, boiling expanse.

A covered handcart waited among the bushes. Pell stood beside it, one eye swollen, holding the reins. Nessa was there too, with a bundle of clothes and a small flask.

“Get in,” Pell said.

Tomas looked back toward Greyhaven.

At the upper windows, guards moved like black figures behind the rain. Somewhere inside those walls was Elianor. He could not leave without seeing her.

Bryn understood before he spoke. “No.”

“I need to say goodbye.”

“You need to live.”

“Those are not separate things.”

Bryn’s face tightened. “If they catch you—”

“They will use me to reach her.”

Nessa touched Bryn’s arm. “Let him go.”

They returned through the drainage tunnel while Pell took the cart toward the northern road. Bryn led Tomas up a servants’ stair and through the laundry court. The diversion still held, though smoke now rose from the hay loft in thick black coils. No fire had taken the building; Bryn had burned damp wool and lamp oil in a brazier, enough to make the household panic.

Elianor’s guards had been drawn toward the west passage.

Bryn unlocked the door to her rooms.

Elianor stood beside the window, still wearing the plain blue dress in which she had been confined. A guard’s key had turned in the lock, but she had not expected Bryn. Her face changed when she saw Tomas.

For one moment she did not move.

Then she crossed the room and caught him as his injured leg gave way.

“God,” she whispered.

“I have looked better.”

Her hands hovered over his face, his ribs, the blood darkening his shirt. She touched neither at first, as if any contact might break him. Then she pressed her forehead to his.

“They beat you.”

“They asked questions.”

Her breath shook. “I heard them. I tried to get out.”

“I know.”

“How?”

“Because you are still here.”

The corridor outside filled with boots.

Bryn went to the door. “We have less than a minute.”

Elianor gripped Tomas’s coat. “Come with me. There must be another way. I can threaten them. I can call the household together.”

“They will imprison you.”

“Let them.”

“They will execute everyone who helped us.”

Her eyes flashed. “Then I will tell them to begin with me.”

“That is not courage,” he said. “That is grief trying to make itself useful.”

She flinched, but she did not release him.

He took the signet from beneath his shirt. The leather cord was wet with sweat and rain. He placed it in her palm and folded her fingers around it.

“Keep it hidden.”

“I will not keep you hidden.”

“You cannot save me here.”

“Then take me with you.”

The words broke something in him. For one impossible instant he imagined it: the two of them running down the northern road, beyond the cliffs, beyond Greyhaven’s reach. But behind that image lay the chapel, Rill, the names of the hungry, the records still threatened by Marrow’s hands. And beside him stood a woman whose inheritance had become a promise to people she could no longer abandon.

“I love you,” he said.

She closed her eyes.

“I know,” she answered. “I love you. That is why I cannot let you go alone.”

“You are not letting me go. You are giving me a chance to return.”

Boots struck the stair below.

Tomas kissed her once, quickly, desperately. Her tears touched his cheek. He wanted to remember her as she was in the sea garden, laughing at his ruined boots, but he could not keep the present from him: her hand at his neck, her heart racing beneath his palm, the door between them and the men who would kill them both.

Bryn pulled the inner latch.

“Now.”

Tomas stepped away. Elianor caught his sleeve.

“If you find the coast,” she said, “find Oric. Find Mara if you can. Do not let them turn your father’s name into another throne.”

He looked at the signet in her closed hand.

“And you,” he said, “do not let them turn your blood into a chain.”

The door shuddered under a fist.

He kissed her knuckles, then let go.

Bryn opened the concealed panel behind the wardrobe. Tomas entered the passage. Elianor remained in the room, upright and pale, the signet pressed against her heart.

The panel closed.

Through the narrow dark, Tomas heard the guards break into her chamber. He heard Lord Marrow demand to know where she had hidden him. He heard Elianor answer in a voice that did not tremble.

“I have no servant to surrender.”

Then the tunnel swallowed the rest.

Outside, the rain came down harder, washing blood from Tomas’s hands as the cart carried him north. Behind him, Greyhaven’s bells rang and rang, calling men to defend a house that had already begun to lose its walls.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: Confined at Greyhaven under guard after publicly opening the eastern granary and pledging her inheritance and diverted stores to Rill. She remains twenty, controlled but shaken, newly in love with Tomas, and more openly committed than ever to defying Lord Marrow. Tomas was arrested, beaten, and escaped through a drainage tunnel; she saw him briefly before his flight, gave him no surrender, and received Arlen Rusk's signet from him. Her goal is to protect the servants' network, preserve the grain and archive evidence, expose the crown-Veyne-Marrow alliance, and turn her inheritance toward relief and resistance. She is allied with Bryn, Pell, Nessa, Oric, Chaplain Orren, Master Vey, Captain Harl, and Tomas's coastal contacts, though Tomas is now fleeing north. She knows Marrow has discovered Tomas's Rusk identity and threatened execution for everyone involved. She possesses the signet hidden in her hand/room, copied archive records, her mother's key, and the moral authority of her public pledge. She is physically safe but isolated, watched, grieving, and under immediate threat of imprisonment and forced marriage.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven directing the investigation after confining Elianor and ordering the accelerated wedding. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, enraged, and convinced necessity justifies coercion. He discovered Tomas's identity as Arlen Rusk's son, ordered him beaten and interrogated for names and records, and failed to prevent his escape during Bryn's diversion. His goal is to preserve Greyhaven, the garrison, harbor, stores, inheritance, crown obligations, and control of Elianor by suppressing the relief network and completing the alliance with Duke Veyne. He knows Tomas escaped north through an old drainage tunnel, Harl compromised the arrest, and Elianor refuses to surrender him. He possesses the Marrow signet, household authority, armed guards, maps, remaining stores, and Veyne's alliance. He is physically safe but publicly challenged, furious, and increasingly dependent on military force.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's accounting room under examination or intensified surveillance after Lord Marrow's investigation into the public grain distribution. He remains cautious, composed, observant, and committed to shielding Elianor's relief work while preserving evidence. He knows Tomas was arrested and escaped, Marrow learned Tomas's Rusk identity, Bryn disrupted the search, and the grain books remain dangerous evidence. His goal is to copy and protect grain books, distribution lists, archive links, and marriage records while misleading searches and protecting the remaining servants. He possesses the steward's seal, keys, stores records, delivery orders, archive procedures, and knowledge of the drainage map. He is physically safe for the moment but at acute risk of arrest or coercion.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven after compromising Lord Marrow's investigation by cutting Tomas free from the weighing room and guiding him toward Bryn's drainage escape. He remains loyal in language to the Marrow hierarchy but morally shaken and unwilling to watch a wounded servant be destroyed for obeying a relief order. He knows Tomas is Arlen Rusk's son, Marrow ordered the beating, and Tomas escaped north. He possesses guard authority, weapons, watch rotations, and knowledge of the ash-yard and old passages. He is physically safe but politically compromised and vulnerable to Veyne's officers and Marrow's retaliation.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: Fleeing north from Greyhaven in a covered handcart after being arrested and beaten in the old weighing room for helping move grain. He remains exhausted, injured with bruised ribs, a bloodied mouth, and a damaged leg, newly in love with Elianor, and determined to protect her and the coastal network. Lord Marrow discovered that he is Tomas Rusk, surviving son of Arlen Rusk, and demanded the names of the grain distributors; Tomas revealed nothing. Captain Harl cut him free, and Bryn led him through the drainage tunnel while Pell and Nessa helped him escape. Before leaving, he gave Elianor Arlen's signet and they shared a desperate farewell. His goal is to reach Oric and the coastal rebels, protect Ash and the network, preserve evidence through trusted allies, and prevent the Rusk name from becoming a hereditary throne or revenge banner. He possesses Arlen's signet only through Elianor now, stable knowledge, coastal paths, and the support of Pell, Nessa, Bryn, Harl, and the wider network. He is physically wounded, hunted, frightened for Elianor, and uncertain whether they will meet again.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Greyhaven after creating a false hay-loft fire, kitchen alarm, and other diversions that disrupted Lord Marrow's investigation and enabled Tomas's escape. She remains clever, frightened, practical, bloodied at the hand from striking a guard, and fiercely loyal to Elianor and Tomas. She helped Tomas through the old drainage tunnel and returned with him to Elianor for their farewell. Her goal is to protect the relief network, preserve or conceal distribution lists and kitchen cover records, shield Elianor during the intensified confinement, and help extract threatened servants. She is allied with Pell, Nessa, Harl, Master Vey, Orren, and the coastal network. She possesses keys, servant passages, kitchen inventories, cover records, and knowledge of the diversion routes. She is physically safe for the moment but exposed, hunted, and likely to face interrogation.

set.name: Pell
set.description: At or moving away from Greyhaven with Nessa after being beaten and briefly restrained by guards during Tomas's arrest. He remains broad-shouldered, cautious, dependable, and injured with a swollen eye and split lip. He helped sustain the stable disruption and stood ready to move Tomas through the northern route. His goal is to protect the servants' network, get Tomas safely to coastal allies, and keep grain and people moving despite Lord Marrow's investigation. He knows the drainage route, cart roads, guard confusion, and Tomas's escape. He possesses cart-driving and coastal-road knowledge and practical stable skills. He is physically hurt but mobile, endangered by Greyhaven's search.
Captain Harl cut Tomas free after Lord Marrow's guards beat and interrogated him, allowing Bryn to lead him through an old drainage tunnel beneath Greyhaven.
Bryn, aided by stable hands and the servants' network, created a false fire and other diversions that disrupted the investigation long enough for Tomas to escape with Pell and Nessa's help.
Before fleeing Greyhaven, Tomas and Elianor shared a desperate farewell; Tomas gave Elianor Arlen Rusk's signet, and they reaffirmed their love without knowing whether they would meet again.
Lord Marrow learned that Tomas was Arlen Rusk's surviving son and ordered him interrogated for the names of the grain distributors and the location of the remaining lists.
Tomas must reach the coastal rebel network and decide whether to reveal himself as Arlen Rusk's surviving son while carrying the memory of Greyhaven's relief network.
Elianor must preserve the grain records and archive evidence while confined and under intensified searches, using the wedding preparations as her remaining access to Greyhaven's political secrets.

chapters.name: Ashes in the North
chapters.content:
The first news came in on a horse too tired to stand.

It reached Greyhaven at dawn, when the sea was the color of old iron and the wind worried the shutters of the eastern tower. A groom found the animal collapsed beneath the gatehouse arch, its flanks trembling, its mouth white with foam. The rider slid from the saddle and struck the stones on one knee. He wore the red-and-black badge of the northern garrison, though the badge had been torn nearly in half.

By the time Elianor heard the bells, three guards had carried him into the lower hall.

She was not meant to hear anything. Since her confinement, the household had become a series of doors closing before she reached them. Guards stood outside her chamber at all hours, changing watch with murmured passwords. Meals came on covered trays. Even the servants who entered to tend the fire kept their eyes lowered, as if a glance might be counted as treason.

But Greyhaven had always carried sound through its stone. A bell rung in the gatehouse traveled along the walls and trembled in the silverware of the upper rooms.

Elianor stood beside her narrow window, one hand pressed against the cold glass. Below, the courtyard was filling with soldiers.

“Bryn,” she called.

The door opened only after one of the guards looked through the hatch. Bryn entered carrying a basin that did not need carrying. Her left hand was wrapped in linen from the knuckles to the wrist, and the guard watched her as though she might draw a blade from the water.

“What happened?” Elianor asked.

Bryn set down the basin. “A messenger came from Northwatch.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“No.” Bryn glanced at the guard’s boots beyond the door. “It is what I can say while he is listening.”

Elianor crossed to the hearth. The fire had been built high, though the room was not cold. “Then say it loudly.”

Bryn’s mouth tightened. “Northwatch mutinied three nights ago. The soldiers refused the levy order. They broke open the stores and gave the grain to the town.”

A pulse beat in Elianor’s throat. “The whole garrison?”

“Enough of it. The officers who would not join them were locked in the powder house. The tax office burned. The crown’s ledgers went with it.”

The words seemed to brighten the room and darken it at once. Somewhere beyond the walls, men were shouting orders. A horse screamed.

“Who holds Northwatch now?”

“Those who took it, perhaps. Or no one. The messenger said villages south of the garrison have declared for the rebellion.”

“The rebellion.” Elianor repeated the word, and heard how easily it entered her mouth. “There is no single rebellion.”

Bryn looked at her. “There may be by tonight.”

That was the danger. Not that the hungry had risen, nor that soldiers had discovered their hunger was shared by the people they were ordered to punish. The danger was that every grievance might now reach for the same banner, and every man carrying a banner might claim the right to decide what came after.

A knock sounded. Captain Harl entered with two guards behind him. He had removed his cloak, but rain darkened the shoulders of his uniform. His face looked older than it had the day before Tomas escaped.

“Lady Elianor,” he said. “Lord Marrow requires you in the west council room.”

“Requires?”

“He has ordered it.”

“Then I suppose the distinction is academic.”

One of the guards shifted his grip on his spear. Harl noticed and gave him a warning glance. “You will be escorted.”

Elianor looked at Bryn. “Bring the basin.”

Bryn blinked. “The basin?”

“If I am to be displayed before my father, I will not go with my hands empty. It may remind him that the household still contains work worth doing.”

Harl’s expression did not change, but something moved behind his eyes. “Leave it.”

“Then carry it yourself.”

For a moment no one spoke. The wind struck the window with a flat palm.

At last Harl stepped aside. “Bring the basin.”

The west council room had been rearranged overnight. Maps covered the long table, pinned beneath knives and inkpots. The coastal map was marked in red charcoal: Rill, Northwatch, Bracken Cove, Saint Orra’s road, the old mill, and the fishing villages scattered along the cliffs. Some names had been circled. Others had been crossed through.

Lord Marrow stood at the far end with Master Vey and three officers Elianor did not know. One wore the blue braid of the royal ministry. Another had a scar that divided his eyebrow. The third was a young lieutenant whose hand rested constantly on the hilt of his sword.

Master Vey did not look at Elianor. That frightened her more than if he had.

“You have heard,” Marrow said.

“I have heard that Northwatch has given its stores to the hungry.”

“I asked whether you have heard the truth.”

“I doubt we would agree on what that is.”

The lieutenant’s fingers tightened around his sword. Marrow raised one hand, stopping him before he spoke.

“Northwatch has been seized by mutineers,” Marrow said. “They have killed two officers, imprisoned four more, and invited armed bands from the surrounding villages to join them. Tax offices have been burned at Hallowmere and Durn. The roads are cut. Three coastal villages have declared themselves outside crown authority.”

“Because the crown has abandoned them inside it.”

“Because agitators have taught them that disorder is freedom.”

“Are the grain stores at Northwatch disorder?”

His jaw hardened. “You will not turn this meeting into another performance of conscience.”

“I did not ask to attend.”

“No. You forced your way into governance, emptied an eastern granary, encouraged disobedience among the servants, and made yourself the public face of a movement whose aims you do not understand.”

Elianor looked at the map. “What are its aims?”

The scarred officer gave a humorless laugh. “That depends which rebel you ask. The northern soldiers want pay and an end to being sent against their own kin. The village councils want the levies abolished and the tax collectors driven into the sea. Some of the coastal captains demand representation. Others speak of taking every noble estate and dividing it among the people. A few want Lord Marrow’s head displayed over his own gate.”

Marrow’s gaze flicked toward Elianor. “And you have supplied them with a story.”

“I supplied Rill with grain.”

“You supplied rebellion with proof that Greyhaven can be made to yield.”

Master Vey’s hand moved a fraction over the map, covering the mark beside Rill. Elianor saw the gesture and understood: he was hiding something, perhaps a route, perhaps a name. Even under suspicion, he was still working.

The ministry officer unfolded a sealed letter. “A royal order arrived before sunrise. Duke Veyne is to take the western fleet north and suppress the coastal insurrection. All ports from Blackwater Reach to the Greyhaven headland are to be searched. Vessels suspected of carrying rebels, weapons, or stolen crown grain may be seized. Settlements that refuse inspection are to be treated as hostile.”

Elianor felt the room tilt.

“Veyne is at sea?” she asked.

“His lead ships departed Blackwater Reach yesterday,” the officer said. “The rest will assemble at the western harbor.”

Marrow turned on him. “You were not ordered to discuss fleet movements with my daughter.”

“I am not your daughter,” Elianor said, “when the fleet comes for the coast. I am one of the people it will burn.”

The young lieutenant drew half an inch of steel. Harl’s hand went to his own sword, not drawing it, but making the warning plain. In the charged silence, the basin on the floor gave a soft metallic tremor as water slopped over its rim.

Marrow looked at Harl. “Remove Captain Harl from this room.”

Harl did not move. “My lord?”

“You have become unreliable.”

The words struck more deeply than an accusation. Harl’s face went still.

Elianor turned toward him. “Because he refused to watch an injured man die?”

“Because he permitted a known rebel to escape.”

“Your orders were to beat names out of him.”

“My orders were to obtain information.”

“You call it information when a man’s blood is on the floor.”

The scarred officer stepped forward. “My lord, the captain should be relieved of command until—”

“No,” Marrow said. He did not take his eyes from Harl. “He will retain command of the inner watch. I need men who know these walls.”

That was not mercy. It was a leash.

“Double the watch at the harbor,” Marrow continued. “Seal the lower road. No servant leaves without inspection. Search the chapel, the stables, and the accounting rooms again. Confiscate all private correspondence.”

“Even letters from the crown?” Elianor asked.

“Especially letters from the crown.”

She understood then that the fortress was not being prepared only against rebels. It was being prepared against truth. Marrow no longer trusted his servants to obey, his officers to remain loyal, or the papers in his own possession to survive the week. He was building walls around every fact that might accuse him.

“Will you search my room?” she asked.

“If necessary.”

“Then you should have done it before coming here.”

A faint color rose beneath his skin. “You mistake defiance for strength.”

“And you mistake walls for safety.”

He stepped closer. “The coast is burning, Elianor. Men who have never governed are promising to remake the kingdom with knives. If Veyne fails, the crown will send another fleet. If that fails, it will send an army. You think your documents will save anyone?”

“No. But they may prevent you from calling the dead liars.”

For the first time, fear showed plainly in his face—not fear for himself, but fear of a world in which his explanations could no longer command belief.

“Take her back,” he said.

The guards moved toward her. Bryn bent quickly and seized the basin. Water ran over her bandaged hand, turning the linen pink where an old cut had reopened.

In the corridor, they passed a line of servants being searched against the wall. Kitchen maids stood with their aprons lifted. A stable boy had been made to empty his boots. Two soldiers were examining the chapel keys while Chaplain Orren argued with them in a voice that remained calm only because it had become exhausted.

At the end of the passage, a bell rang from the harbor tower.

Once. Twice. Then a third time.

Everyone stopped.

A lookout’s cry came down from the battlements. “Sail to the west! Three ships!”

The guards ran. Servants abandoned the wall. Harl emerged from the council room and shouted for the harbor chain to be raised.

Elianor reached the nearest arrow slit before anyone could stop her. Far beyond the black rocks, three vessels moved beneath the low clouds, their sails dark against the gray sea. They were too distant to show their flags, but the sight of them changed Greyhaven more surely than any order.

The fortress began to close.

Gates slammed. Chains groaned. Men carried powder from the stores. The chapel doors were barred from within and without. In the courtyard, Lord Marrow’s guards formed ranks facing the harbor, while other soldiers faced inward toward the servants.

Bryn came to stand beside Elianor, still holding the basin.

“Do you think it is Tomas?” she whispered.

Elianor stared at the ships until her eyes burned. “No.”

She did not know whether that answer was hope or fear. Tomas was fleeing north in a wounded body and borrowed cart, carrying no banner but the memory of what had been done at Greyhaven. The ships belonged to Duke Veyne, or to men who hated him, or to some faction neither of them had imagined.

Below, Harl ordered the inner doors locked.

The sound traveled through the stone like a verdict.

Elianor touched the hidden signet beneath her sleeve. Its edge pressed into her palm, small and hard and warm from her skin. Tomas had given it to her because he believed she could keep a name from becoming a weapon. Now every road seemed to lead toward weapons: the crown’s fleet, the villagers’ torches, the soldiers’ mutiny, the old hunger gathering new language.

Greyhaven had once been a house above the sea. By noon it was a garrison. By evening, perhaps, it would be a prison for everyone inside it.

She turned from the ships.

“Bryn,” she said, “find Master Vey.”

“He is being watched.”

“Then find the person watching him.”

Bryn studied her face. “What do you want me to tell him?”

“That the walls are closing from both sides.” Elianor looked toward the locked corridor, where her father’s footsteps receded into the heart of the fortress. “And that we must decide what can still be carried through them.”

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: Confined but temporarily brought under armed escort to Lord Marrow's west council room at Greyhaven, then returned to her guarded chamber as the fortress sealed itself. She remains twenty, controlled, defiant, grieving Tomas, and newly aware that northern mutiny and coastal rebellion have made the political crisis open warfare. Her goal is to protect Bryn, Master Vey, Harl, Orren, and the servants' network; preserve the grain books, copied archive records, and marriage evidence; and prevent Lord Marrow and the crown from calling the coming repression lawful. She knows Northwatch mutinied, tax offices burned, several villages declared for rebellion, rebel factions disagree over reform, noble abolition, and revenge, and Duke Veyne's fleet has orders to suppress the coast. She also knows Marrow suspects the servants, wants all correspondence confiscated, and is preparing Greyhaven against both rebels and internal disobedience. She possesses Arlen Rusk's signet hidden beneath her sleeve, copied archive evidence, her mother's key, and the moral authority of her public pledge. She is physically safe under guard but isolated, watched, emotionally strained, and in immediate danger of forced marriage, imprisonment, and searches.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: At Greyhaven's west council room and inner keep directing the emergency response after Northwatch's mutiny and the spread of coastal rebellion. He remains lean, silvering, authoritative, enraged, and convinced that necessity justifies coercion. He knows Tomas escaped north as Arlen Rusk's son, that Harl compromised the arrest, that Elianor openly defied him, and that royal orders have assigned Veyne's fleet to suppress the coast. His goal is to keep Greyhaven, its harbor, stores, inheritance, and crown obligations intact, complete Elianor's alliance with Veyne, suppress the relief network, and prevent incriminating records from surviving. He possesses the Marrow signet, household authority, armed guards, maps, remaining stores, and Veyne's military alliance. He has ordered the gates sealed and renewed searches of the chapel, stables, accounting rooms, servants, and private correspondence. He is physically safe but politically challenged, increasingly distrustful, and dependent on a fortress mentality and military force.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's accounting and council rooms under intensified surveillance after the public grain distribution and the northern news. He remains cautious, composed, observant, and committed to shielding Elianor's relief work while preserving evidence. He knows Tomas escaped, Marrow learned Tomas's Rusk identity, Bryn disrupted the investigation, the grain books remain dangerous, Northwatch has mutinied, and Veyne's fleet is coming to suppress the coast. He aims to copy and protect grain books, distribution lists, archive links, and marriage records while misleading searches and preserving routes for the remaining servants. He possesses the steward's seal, keys, stores records, delivery orders, archive procedures, and knowledge of the drainage map. He is physically safe for the moment but under acute surveillance and at risk of arrest or coercion.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven retaining command of the inner watch after Lord Marrow accused him of unreliability for freeing Tomas. He remains outwardly bound to the Marrow hierarchy but morally shaken, politically compromised, and unwilling to watch wounded people be destroyed for obeying relief orders. He knows Tomas is Arlen Rusk's son and escaped north, Marrow ordered the beating, Elianor defied her father, Northwatch has mutinied, and Veyne's fleet is approaching. His goal is to protect the walls and the servants where he can, prevent indiscriminate violence, and decide how far he can undermine Marrow's searches without exposing the people he helped. He possesses guard authority, weapons, watch rotations, and knowledge of the ash-yard and old passages. He is physically safe but under suspicion, watched by Marrow's officers, and vulnerable to Veyne's command.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel within Greyhaven, now facing soldiers examining the chapel keys and threatening tighter control of the refugees. He remains morally troubled, subordinate to Lord Marrow in theory, and openly sympathetic to Elianor's defense of the hungry. He knows Elianor pledged her inheritance, Tomas escaped, Northwatch mutinied, Veyne's fleet is being sent against the coast, and Marrow is sealing the estate against both rebels and servants. He possesses chapel keys, religious authority, burial records, and responsibility for the displaced. He is physically safe but understands the chapel and its people may become targets of military control or collective punishment.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Greyhaven moving between Elianor's guarded rooms and the servants' passages after helping Tomas escape. She remains clever, frightened, practical, bloodied at the hand, and fiercely loyal to Elianor and Tomas. She knows the northern mutiny has opened a wider rebellion, Veyne's fleet is ordered against the coast, Greyhaven's gates are sealed, and Marrow has ordered searches and confiscations throughout the household. Her goal is to protect Elianor, conceal or relocate distribution lists and kitchen cover records, find Master Vey or the person watching him, and preserve a route for threatened servants. She is allied with Pell, Nessa, Harl, Master Vey, Orren, and the coastal network. She possesses keys, servant passages, kitchen inventories, cover records, and knowledge of diversion routes. She is physically safe for the moment but exposed, hunted, and at high risk of interrogation.
News reached Greyhaven that Northwatch's garrison had mutinied, opened its stores to the town, imprisoned resisting officers, and that tax offices at Hallowmere and Durn had been burned.
Royal orders assigned Duke Veyne's western fleet to suppress the coastal insurrection, search ports and vessels, and treat settlements refusing inspection as hostile.

Lord Marrow sealed Greyhaven's gates and ordered renewed searches of the chapel, stables, accounting rooms, servants, and private correspondence while positioning guards against both outside attack and internal disobedience.
Lord Marrow accused Captain Harl of unreliability for allowing Tomas to escape but retained him in command of the inner watch under suspicion.
Elianor and the trusted servants must move or conceal the grain books, archive copies, and marriage evidence before Greyhaven's renewed searches reach the accounting rooms and private chambers.
Master Vey and Captain Harl must decide whether to cooperate with Greyhaven's internal defense or quietly undermine the searches as Veyne's fleet approaches the coast.
Elianor must learn which faction controls the northern mutiny and determine whether the coastal rebellion can protect civilians rather than becoming a campaign of revenge or noble seizure.

chapters.name: Saint Orra's Abbey
chapters.content:
Tomas woke to the smell of wet wool and blood.

For several breaths he did not know whether the cart was moving. His ribs hurt when he breathed, his leg burned from hip to ankle, and the boards beneath him rose and fell with a slow, uneven rhythm. Then a wheel struck a rut. Pain opened his eyes.

The cart stood beneath a stand of wind-bent alder trees. Rain whispered through the leaves. Pell was crouched beside the rear wheel, one hand pressed to his swollen eye, while Nessa held a lantern beneath her cloak. Beyond them, the road climbed into a country Tomas had never seen except in old stories: black moorland, broken stone walls, and hills folded beneath a sky the color of ash.

“How long?” Tomas asked.

“Since Greyhaven?” Pell said. “A day and a half.”

Tomas tried to sit. Nessa pushed him back with surprising force.

“Do not make me bind you to the cart,” she said.

“Where are we?”

“North of Oric’s old mill. Near Saint Orra’s.”

He closed his eyes again. Saint Orra’s Abbey had been ruined before he was born. In Rill, people spoke of it as a place where the dead still kept watch. Its bell tower had fallen during the great winter quake, and the crown had taken its stone for roads, leaving only the chapel shell and a cloister open to the weather.

“Why here?”

Pell looked toward the hills. “Because the people waiting there have been asking for Arlen Rusk’s son.”

The name entered the cart like a draft.

Tomas remembered Elianor’s face in the drainage passage: pale beneath the soot, her hair unpinned, her hand closing around the signet he had placed in it. He had wanted to give her something that could outlast him. Now the absence beneath his shirt felt like a wound deeper than the bruises.

“She has it,” he said.

Nessa’s expression softened. “Who?”

“The signet. Elianor.”

Pell’s mouth tightened. He had not asked about the farewell. None of them had. Their kindness was a form of silence.

“Then they will have to believe you without it,” Nessa said.

“They should not believe me at all.”

“People rarely ask permission before believing what they need.”

The cart began to move again. Tomas lay beneath a horse blanket while rain ticked against the canvas. Pell drove slowly, avoiding the worst of the ruts. Nessa sat beside Tomas with a cup of water and a knife tucked into her sleeve.

By dusk, smoke appeared between the hills.

They left the road before the abbey, pushing the cart through heather until the ruins emerged from the mist. Saint Orra’s had once been built to command the valley. Its roof had fallen, its windows were empty arches, and ivy covered the carved saints along the western wall. Fires burned beneath the cloister. Figures moved between them carrying bows, sacks, and bundles of blankets. Some wore the remnants of garrison uniforms. Others had come in fisher coats, shepherd’s wool, or patched leather armor.

No one cheered when Tomas arrived. That frightened him more than a cheer would have done.

They watched him as Pell and Nessa helped him down. A woman with a crossbow stepped forward, her gray hair braided close to her skull. She was not tall, but everyone near her made room.

“Mara Quill,” Pell said. “This is Tomas.”

“Which Tomas?” she asked.

“The one from Greyhaven.”

“That is not an answer.”

Tomas leaned on Pell’s shoulder. His leg nearly gave way. “It is the name I have used.”

Mara studied him. Her gaze traveled over his bruised mouth, his torn coat, and the blood stiffened at his cuffs. “And the name you were born with?”

“I was born in a house that burned.”

“That is also not an answer.”

A man rose from beside the largest fire. He was broad and heavily bearded, with a broken nose and a soldier’s posture. One sleeve of his coat bore the faded badge of Northwatch. He carried no visible weapon, though Tomas suspected he needed none.

“Let him sit before you question him to death,” the man said.

Mara did not look at him. “Joren Pell, if he is to lead men, he can stand long enough to say who he is.”

“I am standing,” Tomas said.

“On another man’s shoulder.”

“That is still more standing than Greyhaven intended me to do.”

For the first time, something like approval touched Mara’s face. It vanished quickly.

They brought him into the roofless chapel. A fire had been built in a stone baptismal basin, and rain fell through the open rafters beyond it. Someone gave him broth. Someone else cleaned the cut at his temple. Tomas noticed that the hands tending him were young and callused, and that the woman who wrapped his ribs had a red thread tied around her wrist—a sign he had seen in Rill among families who moved food along the coast.

The rebels did not look like an army. They looked like all the people an army had failed to kill.

At the far end of the chapel stood a woman in a dark coat. She had Tomas’s narrow jaw and his father’s black hair, though silver showed at her temples. Her left hand rested on the stone altar. She had been watching him without blinking.

“Your name,” she said.

“Tomas.”

“Your other name.”

He looked at Mara. “You brought me here to be judged?”

“No,” Mara said. “We brought you here because the coast is splitting, and every faction believes the split can be healed by putting its own hand on the knife.”

The woman at the altar stepped closer. “You have his eyes.”

Tomas felt the broth turn in his stomach. “Whose?”

“Arlen’s.”

The chapel seemed to contract around them.

“My father’s name has been used by Greyhaven to frighten children,” Tomas said. “I would prefer not to use it myself.”

“I am Sella Rusk,” the woman said. “I was your father’s sister.”

He stared at her. He had carried a few fragments of his family all his life: his mother’s hands, his father’s voice, the blue cup that had broken during the soldiers’ search. An aunt had never existed in his memories. No one had told him there was an aunt left to find.

“You were alive,” he said.

“So were you.”

The words were not accusation. That made them worse.

Sella crossed to the table where maps and weapons lay scattered. From beneath a folded sailcloth she took a small wooden box. She opened it and removed a disk of hardened wax.

Tomas’s breath stopped.

Pressed into the wax was the mark of the signet: a rook or tower above a broken wave, enclosed by a circle of thorns. The impression was imperfect, but the shape was unmistakable. He had seen it once on his father’s hand when he was very small. He remembered the cold metal against his cheek as Arlen lifted him from a cradle.

“You have the ring?” Mara asked.

“No.” Tomas touched the empty place beneath his shirt. “I gave it to someone.”

“To whom?”

“Elianor Vale.”

Joren’s face hardened. “Marrow’s daughter.”

“She is not Marrow.”

“She was born in his house.”

“So were the ledgers that proved he stole the coast.”

Joren leaned forward. “And yet she remains behind his walls while you come here wearing the wounds of his justice.”

Tomas rose too quickly. His leg buckled, and he caught himself against the altar. Pain flashed white. “She opened Greyhaven’s granaries. She stood before the gate and gave away her inheritance. She hid the records your people need. She risked her life to get me out.”

“And loved you?”

The question struck more cleanly than any blow.

Tomas said nothing.

Mara glanced between them. “We did not bring you here to measure the purity of your grief. We brought you because Northwatch has risen, the tax houses are ash, and the coast is about to be hunted by Veyne’s fleet.”

Joren spread a map across the altar. Red marks ran from the northern garrison to the harbors. Blue ink showed roads, coves, and old smuggling paths. “The village councils will not answer to the soldiers. The soldiers will not answer to fishermen. The harbor captains refuse to follow anyone who calls himself a lord. We have three forces moving in three directions, and Veyne has enough ships to turn our divisions into graves.”

“Then form a council,” Tomas said.

“We have.”

“Then let it command.”

“It does not,” Mara said. “Not when every faction suspects the others of wanting the crown’s seat after they break it.”

Sella placed her fingers on the wax impression. “Your father’s cause is remembered in every coastal parish. The old petitions survived. So did the names of the men who signed them. Limits on levies. An end to forced labor. A voice for the villages. Negotiation before bloodshed.”

“His cause,” Tomas said, “not his blood.”

“People do not separate them so easily.”

“They must.”

Joren gave a bitter laugh. “You speak as if you have a better answer.”

“I have a better warning. My father was not a king. He was a man who believed an agreement could restrain power. Marrow proved him wrong. If I arrive here and declare myself his heir, men will not hear the petitions. They will hear a throne waiting to be filled.”

“Some want a throne,” Mara said quietly. “Some want every noble estate burned. Some want revenge on the officers who starved their families. If you refuse the name, they will choose another name for themselves.”

“Then let them choose badly without me.”

Sella’s eyes flashed. “That is what the dead are always told. That their absence is cleaner than their return.”

Tomas looked at her. “Did you preserve my father’s papers?”

“I preserved what I could. The rest I carried in my head.”

“Did he ask you to make a son into a banner?”

“No. He asked me to keep the petitions safe.”

“Then do that.”

“I have.”

“Keep them safe from us too.”

Silence settled beneath the rain.

Mara moved to the broken archway. Beyond it, the valley fires shone like scattered stars. “You are right to fear your name,” she said. “Names have eaten more people than swords. But fear can become another kind of vanity. You may refuse command because you do not trust yourself, while others die under the command of men who trust themselves too much.”

Tomas thought of Elianor in the courtyard, standing before the granary with the wind pulling at her hair. She had not waited to become certain. She had not asked whether her action would preserve her innocence. She had opened the door because people were hungry on the other side.

He had no such certainty. Only pain, memory, and the knowledge that Veyne’s ships were coming.

“I will not be your heir,” he said.

Joren’s hand closed into a fist.

“I will not be a lord, a king, or the keeper of my father’s revenge. I will not order villagers to die so that his name can be spoken louder.” Tomas looked from Mara to Sella. “But I will carry messages between the councils. I will speak for surrendering soldiers if you let them live. I will speak for villages when fighters decide that food is a military supply. If you want me to stand in the road between your factions, I will stand there.”

“And if they call you Rusk?” Sella asked.

“I will tell them my name is Tomas.”

“That may not be enough.”

“It must be.”

Mara watched him for a long moment. Then she took the wax impression from Sella and held it out.

Tomas did not take it.

“Keep it,” he said.

“For what?”

“For remembering what the mark was meant to seal.”

Sella returned it to the box. Her hand trembled only once.

Outside, a horn sounded from the southern ridge. Another answered from the valley. Men rose around the fires, checking bowstrings and powder horns.

Mara rolled up the map. “Rest tonight. At dawn, we send word to Northwatch, Bracken Cove, and the harbor councils. You will speak at the first gathering.”

“I said I would carry messages.”

“Yes,” she said. “That is how command begins when a man is wise enough not to call it command.”

Joren turned away, displeased but listening. Sella remained beside the altar.

As Nessa led Tomas toward a pallet beneath the cloister, he looked back at the wax seal, at the broken wave and the circle of thorns. Somewhere far south, Elianor carried the ring against her skin. Somewhere between them, the coast was choosing what kind of rebellion it would become.

Tomas lay down beneath the ruined saints.

He had come north to disappear into the cause.

By morning, the cause would begin learning his name.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At the ruins of Saint Orra's Abbey north of Greyhaven, recovering on a pallet beneath the cloister after reaching the rebel council with Pell and Nessa in a covered cart. He remains wounded with bruised ribs, a bloodied mouth, a damaged leg, exhaustion, and grief over leaving Elianor; he is frightened by the political power of his father's name but determined not to let it become a throne or revenge banner. He now knows Mara Quill, Joren Pell, and Sella Rusk have preserved Arlen Rusk's petitions and cause, and that Northwatch soldiers, village councils, and harbor captains are divided over reform, noble seizure, revenge, and command while Veyne's fleet approaches. Elianor possesses Arlen's signet, which Tomas gave her before escaping. His goal is to carry messages among the coastal factions, defend civilians and surrendering soldiers, and keep the rebellion from becoming hereditary or indiscriminate. He possesses his stable and coastal knowledge, the support of Pell, Nessa, Mara, Joren, Sella, and the wider network, but no signet or formal authority. He is physically fragile, emotionally attached to Elianor, and newly under pressure to become a symbol.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: At the ruins of Saint Orra's Abbey, directing the rebel council and preparing messages to Northwatch, Bracken Cove, and the harbor councils. She is a gray-haired, sharp-eyed organizer and crossbow bearer who understands the divisions among the coastal factions and recognizes that symbols may be necessary to prevent Veyne from crushing them separately. She knows Tomas is Arlen Rusk's surviving son, that he refuses hereditary authority, and that he will advocate civilian protection and humane surrender terms. Her goal is to test and use Tomas's coordinating role without turning him into a ruler. She possesses rebel contacts, maps, armed supporters, and influence at the abbey. She is physically safe for the moment but under imminent military threat.

set.name: Joren Pell
set.description: At Saint Orra's Abbey with the Northwatch rebels, serving as a broad, bearded former garrison soldier and skeptical military voice within the council. He knows Tomas's identity, Arlen Rusk's remembered cause, the divisions between soldiers and village or harbor councils, and the danger posed by Veyne's fleet. He distrusts Elianor because she was born in Marrow's house, though Tomas defended her relief actions. His goal is to secure effective military coordination and protect the uprising from betrayal, while deciding whether Tomas's refusal of command is wisdom or weakness. He possesses Northwatch connections, battlefield experience, and influence among armed mutineers. He is physically safe at the abbey but expects imminent conflict.

set.name: Sella Rusk
set.description: At Saint Orra's Abbey beside the ruined altar, serving as keeper of Arlen Rusk's surviving memory and petitions. She is Tomas's aunt, a dark-haired woman silvered at the temples who preserved the written cause and a wax impression of Arlen's signet after the old executions. She knows Tomas survived, recognizes his resemblance to Arlen, and wants the petitions' aims—limits on levies, an end to forced labor, village representation, and negotiation—kept alive without losing them to opportunists. She understands Tomas refuses to be an heir or revenge symbol but fears the people may still attach his name to power. She possesses the preserved petitions and wax signet impression. She is physically safe for the moment, emotionally shaken by finding Tomas alive, and protective of both his freedom and Arlen's memory.
Tomas reached the rebel council at the ruins of Saint Orra's Abbey with Pell and Nessa, after traveling wounded from Greyhaven through the northern routes.

At Saint Orra's Abbey, Mara Quill, Joren Pell, and Sella Rusk showed Tomas preserved petitions and a wax impression of Arlen Rusk's signet, confirming that his father's cause survived in the coastal memory.

The rebel council revealed that Northwatch soldiers, village councils, and harbor captains were divided over command, noble privilege, revenge, and reform, while Veyne's fleet threatened to exploit their divisions.

Tomas refused to present himself as Arlen Rusk's heir or accept a throne, but agreed to carry messages and advocate for civilian safety and the lives of surrendering soldiers among the rival rebel factions.

Tomas will coordinate messages among Northwatch, Bracken Cove, and the harbor councils while refusing formal hereditary authority and arguing for civilian protection and humane treatment of surrendering soldiers.
Mara, Joren, and Sella will test whether Tomas's proposed conditions can hold the divided coastal factions together as Veyne's fleet approaches.
Tomas's refusal to claim the Rusk inheritance will not prevent other rebels from using his name as a symbol, creating a continuing danger of vengeance or hereditary leadership.

chapters.name: The Weight of a Name
chapters.content:
At dawn, Saint Orra’s Abbey smelled of wet ash, boiled leather, and the bitter roots Nessa had crushed into Tomas’s broth.

He woke beneath the cloister with his injured leg propped on a rolled blanket. The rain had stopped, but water fell steadily from the broken roof, drop by drop, into the stone channels between the paving slabs. Beyond the arches, the fires had burned low. Men and women slept in their cloaks beside stacked crates, bows, fishing spears, and sacks of grain marked with villages Tomas knew from the coast.

For one breath, before memory returned, he was back in Greyhaven’s stable. He heard Ash shifting in her stall. He felt Elianor’s hand against his cheek, rain cold between them. Then his ribs pulled when he breathed, and the abbey came back.

Mara stood over him.

“Can you walk?”

“Not well.”

“That has not stopped you yet.”

She offered him a stick cut from ash wood. Its handle had been smoothed by someone’s knife. Tomas pushed himself upright, tying his boot around the swollen ankle as tightly as he could bear.

“Where are we going?”

“To the chapter house.”

“The roof fell in.”

“The walls remain. That is more than can be said for most councils.”

He followed her through the cloister, leaning on the stick. Pain traveled up his leg with every step, but he refused Nessa’s arm when she came to meet them. Her expression told him she considered this refusal an act of stupidity rather than courage.

“You will take the crutch,” she said.

“I have a stick.”

“You have a branch.”

“It serves.”

“So does a door bar, until someone tries to walk on it.”

Mara’s mouth twitched. “Let him keep his branch. He will need the argument more than the crutch.”

The chapter house had once been a library. Its shelves stood empty against the walls, and moss filled the joints of the floor. A table had been made from a fallen door. Around it sat representatives of the forces that had gathered in the north: Joren Pell for the mutinied soldiers of Northwatch; a harbor captain named Ruskett with salt-white hair; two village delegates from Bracken Cove; and a narrow-faced woman called Iven who spoke for the mill towns inland.

Tomas recognized none of them. Every one of them recognized him.

The room quieted when he entered.

Joren stood at the far side of the table. His broken nose had been washed, though the bruise beneath one eye had darkened overnight. “There he is. The answer to every problem.”

“I am not an answer,” Tomas said.

“No. You are a delay. We have been waiting two hours to begin because three people wanted to know whether you would sit at the head of the table.”

“There is no head.”

“That is why we have three commands, four supply routes, and no agreement about which road Veyne will take.”

Mara pointed to the map. “Northwatch has sent word that their officers will not march unless the coastal villages accept a military commander. Bracken Cove will not send provisions to a force commanded by officers who once collected levies from them. The harbor captains will not recognize either side. Meanwhile, Veyne’s fleet has left the western anchorage.”

Ruskett’s fingers tightened around the edge of the table. “His ships were seen beyond Blackwater Reach.”

“How many?” Tomas asked.

“Seven warships. Three transports. More behind them, perhaps.”

“And Greyhaven?”

No one answered immediately.

“Still sealed,” Mara said. “Its guns face the sea and the land. Marrow has chosen to defend the walls rather than feed the people outside them.”

Elianor, Tomas thought. Confined behind those walls. He saw her as she had been when he left her: soot on her face, the torn sleeve of her dress caught on a stone, the signet hidden beneath it. He had promised that the coast would hear the truth. He had not promised that he would come back alive.

Joren slapped a folded paper onto the table. “This came from Northwatch.”

Mara opened it and read aloud. “The garrison will march under the son of Arlen Rusk, or it will remain within the walls until the fleet arrives.”

The village delegates exchanged looks.

“That is not a request,” Tomas said.

“No,” Joren replied. “It is a condition.”

“What do they think I can do?”

“Give them a name the soldiers will follow.”

“I have already said I will carry messages.”

“And I have already said messages do not stop men from fighting each other.”

The words struck a deeper place than Tomas wished to admit. At Greyhaven he had known the shape of his duty. A frightened mare. A starving child. A cart that needed loading. The task had been in front of him, and the next task had followed. Here, every road opened onto ten others, each carrying a different claim to justice.

The door of the chapter house stood open to the cloister. A boy no older than fourteen appeared there, soaked to the knees. He carried a red scarf tied around a willow rod.

“From Bracken Cove,” he said. “The council asks whether the Rusk man commands.”

Tomas stared at the scarf. “What is your name?”

“Perrin.”

The answer tightened his throat. He had known a boy called Perrin once, though that child had died in Saint Orra’s Chapel months ago, long before the storm and the siege. For a heartbeat, the two names were one.

“Tell Bracken Cove I command no one,” Tomas said. “Tell them I will come and speak.”

The boy looked at Mara, then at Joren. He seemed disappointed by the answer.

“Tell them,” Tomas added, “that I will not ask them for grain without showing them where it goes. Tell them that no soldier who lays down a weapon will be killed. Tell them that their children will not be taken for labor.”

The boy’s face changed. Not hope, exactly. Attention.

“Will you defend them?”

“If I can.”

“That is not a command.”

“No,” Tomas said. “It is a promise I may have to die keeping.”

Perrin nodded as if that made more sense than anything else in the room, then ran back into the rain.

Joren watched him go. “You see? They want certainty.”

“They want to know whether we will become the thing we are fighting.”

“People want bread and a wall between them and cannon fire. They do not care what words you use to describe the wall.”

“Then build one without making me its lord.”

A low murmur passed among the delegates. Ruskett rubbed his white beard. Iven leaned over the map.

“You speak of limits,” she said. “Who enforces them?”

“The councils.”

“Which councils? The ones with boats? The ones with rifles? The ones who remember your father kindly?”

Tomas had no answer ready. That was the first honest thing he could give them.

Mara came to his side. “This is the difference between inheritance and leadership,” she said. “Inheritance asks people to obey because you were born first in a particular bed. Leadership asks them to judge whether your actions deserve obedience. You are afraid they will confuse the two.”

“I am afraid they already have.”

“Then make the distinction in public.”

Joren gave a harsh laugh. “A speech will not make Northwatch surrender its officers, and it will not persuade harbor captains to put their ships under a village vote.”

“No,” Mara said. “But a visible person can carry terms from one camp to another. Without that, each faction hears only the worst story about the others.”

“Why him?”

“Because they are asking for him.”

“That is not a reason. That is hunger dressed as politics.”

Tomas looked at the map. Red lines marked Veyne’s likely approach. Blue lines marked roads cut by flooding and old military bridges. The coast seemed small beneath the ink. He remembered Elianor saying that hunger made a person invisible to the powerful. Here, the powerful had given the hungry names—traitor, rebel, thief, subject—and called that visibility.

“What exactly would you have me do?” he asked.

Joren answered first. “Take command of the march to Bracken Cove. Bring Northwatch’s men under your banner. Make the harbor captains obey a single order. If Veyne lands, meet him as one army instead of a quarrel.”

“And after?”

“After we win, we decide who governs.”

“That is how thrones begin.”

“Only if you are weak enough to let them.”

Tomas turned on him. “My father believed negotiation could restrain men like Marrow. They killed him for believing it. If I take command because soldiers demand my bloodline, then I have learned the wrong lesson from his death.”

Joren’s face reddened. “Your father’s death taught us that a divided people are easy to hang.”

“And it taught me that a cause can be stolen by the people who claim to defend it.”

The room went still. Even the rain seemed to pause.

Sella entered without knocking. She carried a bundle of papers beneath her coat. Her eyes moved from Tomas to Joren.

“Arlen did not ask men to kneel,” she said. “He asked them to stand in a room together long enough to hear one another. That was his failure, perhaps. Or his courage. I have never decided.”

Joren looked away.

Sella placed the bundle on the table. “These are copies of the petitions. Not the originals. The originals remain hidden.”

Tomas felt a sudden fear. “Where?”

“Somewhere no commander can reach by calling himself necessary.”

Mara smiled faintly. “Your aunt has more sense than all of us.”

“She has had fourteen years to acquire it,” Tomas said.

Sella met his gaze. “And you have had fourteen years to acquire something else.”

“What?”

“The habit of surviving alone.”

He wanted to deny it. Instead he thought of the stable, the assumed name, the careful distance he kept from every household that might ask where he came from. He had believed solitude was a shield. Now people were asking him to turn it into a standard.

Mara unrolled the largest petition. At the bottom, beneath the demands for limits on levies and village representation, Arlen’s name had been written in a firm, slanting hand. Tomas had seen that hand only in memory.

“Here is what I propose,” Mara said. “Not a lord. Not a general. A coordinating voice chosen by the councils and removable by them. You will carry messages, call gatherings, and negotiate terms between the factions. No order is binding unless a village council and an armed council both accept it. You will not command the distribution of food alone. You will not appoint officers. You will not inherit land through your father’s name.”

Joren looked skeptical. “And in battle?”

“Tomas may advise,” Mara said. “The commanders retain their authority.”

“That makes him a messenger with a title.”

“Then let the title be small enough not to become a throne and useful enough to prevent three armies from starving beside one another.”

Tomas studied the petition. His father’s name lay at its bottom, not above the demands but beneath them, as if signing meant bearing responsibility rather than receiving power.

“What will the title be?” he asked.

“Coordinator,” Mara said.

“An ugly word.”

“Ugly words sometimes survive beautiful ones.”

“And if the councils revoke me?”

“They must be able to.”

“If a commander refuses the surrender terms?”

“You will stand against him,” Mara said. “With whatever authority the councils have given you.”

“If that commander is Joren?”

Joren’s eyes narrowed. “Then stand carefully.”

Tomas almost smiled. “And if the people call me Rusk?”

Mara folded the petition. “Correct them when you can. Let them remember when they must. A symbol is a tool. It becomes a weapon when people forget who holds it.”

He thought of the ring against Elianor’s skin. He had given it to her because he wanted one piece of his history to remain with the person who knew him before the name had become a demand. He did not want it returned as a crown.

“I will serve as coordinator,” he said. “On the conditions you named, and two more. No village will be stripped for supplies without its council’s consent or a recorded emergency agreement. And every prisoner who surrenders will be fed, treated, and kept alive until a public hearing.”

Joren opened his mouth.

“No exceptions,” Tomas said.

The Northwatch captain looked toward the broken window, where the gray morning had begun to brighten. “Veyne will not offer us the same mercy.”

“Then let him show the coast what he is,” Tomas replied. “We do not need to become him to defeat him.”

Mara extended her hand, not as a blessing but as a bargain. Tomas took it.

Her grip was hard and dry. “At noon,” she said, “you speak to the gathered councils.”

“Today?”

“Symbols grow heavier when people are left alone with them.”

By noon, the abbey yard held more than two hundred people. Fishermen stood beside mutineers, villagers beside smugglers, and women carrying children beside men carrying muskets. Word had traveled faster than Tomas could imagine. Some had come to see Arlen Rusk’s son. Others had come to decide whether he was dangerous.

He climbed the three remaining steps of the old bell platform. His leg shook beneath him. Mara stood below with the petition. Joren stood farther back among the Northwatch soldiers, arms folded. Sella watched from beside the ruined altar.

Tomas looked over the crowd.

“My name is Tomas,” he began.

A few voices answered, “Rusk.”

He waited until they quieted.

“I was born to Arlen Rusk, whose petitions you have preserved. I will not deny him, and I will not ask you to obey me because he was my father. Blood is an accident. It is not a law.”

The wind moved through the ruined arches.

“I will carry messages between your councils. I will bring your terms to those who fear you and theirs to those who hate them. I will speak against the taking of food, the burning of homes, and the killing of soldiers who surrender. If I fail those promises, remove me. If I ask you to follow me because of my father’s name, refuse.”

No one moved.

Then an old harbor woman raised her fist. “And if we follow you because you keep them?”

“Then follow the promises,” Tomas said. “Not me.”

The first cheer came from the village side of the yard. It was small, almost embarrassed. Another rose from the soldiers. Soon the sound crossed the space between them.

Tomas felt no triumph. Only the weight of two hundred faces, and behind them the unseen faces of those still trapped in Rill, Greyhaven, Northwatch, and every village waiting for a fleet to decide whether it deserved to live.

Mara stepped beside him and raised the copied petition.

“By the councils gathered here,” she called, “Tomas Rusk is appointed coordinating voice of the coastal resistance, subject to recall and bound to the terms he has spoken.”

This time the crowd shouted his father’s name.

Tomas let it pass over him like weather.

He did not lift a hand in salute. He did not claim the name. But neither did he run from it.

Far to the south, beyond flooded roads and armed gates, Elianor waited inside Greyhaven with evidence hidden against the ruin of her house. Veyne’s ships were coming. Marrow’s walls were closing.

Tomas looked toward the sea.

A name could be a chain. It could also be a door, if enough hands refused to let one person own it.

He would spend what remained of his life keeping it open.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: At Saint Orra's Abbey, newly appointed recallable coordinating voice of the coastal resistance, preparing to carry terms among Northwatch, Bracken Cove, and the harbor councils as Veyne's fleet advances. He remains wounded with bruised ribs, a bloodied mouth, damaged and painful leg, exhaustion, and grief over Elianor, but has resumed walking and speaking publicly. He rejects lordship, kingship, hereditary authority, and revenge, insisting that blood is not law and that people follow promises rather than his name.
