He looked down the emptying corridor. “I am trying to keep the morning from becoming an execution.”

“Then when the small bell rings, put your men between my father and the prisoners.”

“That may be seen as mutiny.”

“It may be seen as the difference between law and murder.”

Harl’s eyes hardened. “You ask me to choose.”

“No. My father has already chosen. I am asking whether you will choose after him.”

He said nothing. But when they continued toward the west rooms, he shifted his position so that his body remained between Elianor and the nearest guard.

Master Vey waited beside the marriage table. The room had been cleared of ledgers and replaced with flowers, sealing wax, and instruments written in a clerk’s precise hand. He wore his formal black coat, though his collar was unfastened and his face looked older than it had the night before.

“My lady,” he said.

“Master Vey.”

His gaze touched the gown. “Your mother wore that when she signed the first marriage articles.”

“And what did she receive for signing?”

“An estate already burdened with debt. A husband who believed tenderness was an indulgence. A lifetime of being praised for endurance.”

Harl glanced at him, startled by the answer.

Vey reached beneath the table and produced a narrow strip of parchment. “The grain books have been copied. The original pages are no longer in the accounting room.”

“Where?”

“Somewhere no search of Greyhaven will find them quickly.”

“Will you be safe?”

“No.” He gave a faint, humorless smile. “But I have been unsafe for years. I simply had better furniture.”

Elianor took the parchment. It contained a list of names: servants, fishermen, and chapel workers who had agreed to carry food, testimony, or messages if the gates opened. She read it once, then folded it into the seam beneath her left cuff.

“Burn this list if the household breaks,” she said. “Not before.”

Vey nodded.

“And the west door?”

“Captain Harl’s men hold it.”

“Harl?”

The captain’s face remained turned toward the corridor. “I hold the door.”

“Then hold it for the living,” Elianor said.

A commotion rose from the reception hall: wheels on stone, the sharp call of an officer, and a murmur that passed through the household like a cold draft.

Duke Veyne had arrived.

Master Vey went still. Harl’s hand settled on his sword.

Elianor touched the hidden signet beneath her sleeve. It was warm now from her skin.

“Where are the originals?” Vey asked quietly.

“Under the wardrobe board.”

“And how will you bring them to the chapel?”

She looked down at her mother’s silver gown. “The train is long.”

Vey understood. His eyes filled briefly with something like grief, then steadied.

“Once the small bell rings,” Elianor said, “you will open the archive chest before everyone. Do not argue with my father. Do not accuse him. Show them the seals, the orders, the names.”

“And you?”

“I will read.”

“To the nobles?”

“To anyone who remains.”

Vey bowed. “Then let the record outlive the house.”

Elianor turned toward the corridor. Outside, Greyhaven’s bells began another proclamation. The sound shook dust from the rafters and sent a flock of gulls screaming from the sea wall.

For years she had been taught that duty was the highest form of love: duty to blood, to title, to walls, to the men who called their fear governance. Her father had planned a future in which she would stand beside a duke, bear children, smile at councils, and preserve the shape of the world by surrendering herself to it.

She had once thought that future might be enough.

Now the silver gown showed every crease. It showed the strain at her shoulders, the bruise-colored shadows beneath her eyes, and the place where her sleeve concealed a dead rebel’s signet. It showed that she was not a bride entering a life prepared for her, but a witness being carried toward a public lie.

At the chapel threshold, Elianor stopped.

Beyond the doors waited her father, Duke Veyne, the household, and perhaps the last moment in which Greyhaven could pretend not to know what it had done.

She lifted her chin.

“Open the doors,” she said.

Captain Harl gave the order.

The guards pulled them wide, and the morning entered.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel threshold on the morning of her forced wedding, dressed in her dead mother's silver gown and escorted by armed guards under Captain Harl. She remains twenty, controlled but exhausted, grieving the final destruction of her relationship with Lord Marrow, frightened for Bryn and Tomas, and irrevocably defiant. She knows the original royal, Veyne, and quartermaster letters remain beneath the wardrobe board, copied archive evidence is in her prayer book, copied collective-punishment orders are being placed behind the chapel's loose west lectern panel, copied grain books are preserved outside the accounting room, and Arlen Rusk's signet is hidden beneath her sleeve. She has instructed Bryn to place the packet, Orren to signal with the small bell, Vey to open the archive chest, and Harl to put his men between Marrow and prisoners if violence begins; she intends to retrieve and read the originals before the assembled household. Her goal is to expose the crown and Marrow's crimes, protect Bryn and the servants, prevent an execution, and keep the wedding from becoming a weapon. She possesses the prayer book, her mother's key, the signet, remaining authority as Marrow's daughter, and the silver gown whose train may conceal the originals. She is physically safe for the moment but watched, armed-guarded, politically disinherited, and standing at the threshold of open revolt.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Greyhaven's west marriage rooms and accounting routes on the morning of the forced wedding, wearing formal black while under intensified surveillance. set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven's chapel and west-door watch on the morning of the forced wedding, escorting Elianor while maintaining armed control of the corridors. He remains morally shaken, outwardly obedient, and increasingly willing to prevent indiscriminate violence. He knows Elianor has coordinated a public disclosure, Bryn is being held in chains with an injured hand, Vey has copied the grain books, and the small bell will signal a confrontation; he has agreed to hold the west door and may place his men between Marrow and prisoners if an execution is attempted. His goal is to keep the ceremony from becoming a slaughter and protect prisoners, servants, and refugees without openly declaring mutiny before necessary. He possesses guard authority, watch rotations, weapons, and knowledge of the ash yard and old passages. He is physically safe but under direct suspicion and on the edge of an irreversible choice.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel under guard on the morning of the wedding, constrained but still responsible for the chapel and its records. He remains troubled, compassionate, and sympathetic to Elianor's defense of the hungry. set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Greyhaven's west holding room or being returned there under guard after a brief supervised encounter with Elianor on the wedding morning. She remains clever, wounded in the bandaged left hand, frightened but fiercely loyal. She knows the copied collective-punishment orders are to be passed to her through Hessa with the bride's veil, hidden behind the third panel of Saint Orra's west lectern, and that Orren's small bell will signal Elianor's disclosure; she still does not know or reveal the location of the originals beneath Elianor's wardrobe board. Her goal is to carry out the chapel instruction without betraying Elianor or the servants' network and to survive confinement. She possesses only her servant's clothing and bandage; her keys remain confiscated and chains have been placed on her wrists. She is physically injured, deprived of freedom, and under immediate threat of renewed punishment.

set.name: Duke Alistair Veyne
set.description: At Greyhaven's reception hall and wedding preparations after arriving with military officers on the morning of his forced marriage to Elianor. He remains politically ambitious, militaristic, contemptuous of villagers, and aligned with the crown's collective-punishment campaign. He knows the ceremony is being held under armed control and that Greyhaven's harbor and stores are tied to his military alliance, but does not yet know the full details of Elianor's planned disclosure or the location of the evidence. On the morning of the forced wedding, Elianor was dressed in her dead mother's silver gown and escorted under armed guard through Greyhaven toward the chapel.

Elianor secretly coordinated Bryn, Master Vey, Chaplain Orren, and Captain Harl for a public disclosure: copied orders were to be hidden at the chapel lectern, the small bell would signal the gathering, and Vey would display the surviving records.

Master Vey confirmed that the grain books had been copied and that the originals were hidden beyond the accounting room's immediate searches; Captain Harl agreed to hold the west door and considered protecting prisoners from an execution.
Duke Alistair Veyne arrived at Greyhaven during the wedding preparations, bringing the military presence that made the ceremony and Elianor's planned disclosure immediately perilous.

When the wedding household is assembled, Bryn must place the copied collective-punishment orders behind the loose third panel of Saint Orra's west lectern, while Chaplain Orren rings the small bell as the signal for Elianor's public testimony.

Elianor must retrieve the original royal and military orders from beneath the wardrobe board and carry them into the chapel, where Master Vey will open the archive chest and she will read the evidence before the household.

chapters.name: Signals on the Cliffs
chapters.content:
The first signal fire appeared on the northern cliff just as the chapel bell began to gather the household.

It was not a kitchen fire. It burned too high and too steadily, a red tongue lifting against the gray morning, then bending sharply when the wind came off the sea. A second flame answered from the headland beyond Rill. A third kindled near the old watchtower, where the stone ribs of the ruin showed black against the clouds.

Elianor saw them through the chapel's eastern window.

For one breath she thought of Tomas—not as a memory, not as the wounded man she had last held in the drainage passage, but alive somewhere beyond the cliffs, watching the same flames and knowing what they meant. The thought struck through her with such force that her hand closed around the signet hidden beneath her sleeve.

Arlen Rusk's ring was warm from her skin.

“Lady Elianor,” Captain Harl said quietly, “do not move toward the window.”

She turned. Harl stood between her and the chapel door, one hand resting on the hilt of his sword. His men had formed a loose line along the nave, though several were watching the fires instead of the people. Their helmets and damp cloaks made the chapel seem smaller. Behind them, servants carried benches into rows. Noble guests entered in bright silks and fur-lined coats, speaking too loudly, as though the noise could hold the sea at a distance.

Duke Veyne stood near the altar in white and gold, his military coat worn beneath the ceremonial mantle chosen for the wedding. He had removed his gloves. His right hand rested on the pommel of the short sword at his side.

Lord Marrow had not yet entered.

“Those are rebel signals,” Veyne said.

No one had asked him, but every voice fell silent to hear the answer.

At the western lectern, Chaplain Orren lowered his eyes. Behind the third loose panel, the copied orders waited. The small bell hung above him on its cord. His fingers had already found it once. Now they trembled beside the prayer book.

A boy in the colors of the harbor watch ran into the chapel. He slipped on the wet flagstones and caught himself against a pillar.

“Your Grace,” he gasped. “Ships off the eastern point.”

“How many?” Veyne demanded.

“Six. No—more behind them. Fishing boats among them.”

“Warships?”

“Two cutters. A broadside vessel. The rest are small.”

Veyne smiled without humor. “Small vessels do not take a fortress.”

The boy swallowed. “They are moving toward the transports.”

A sound rolled over the chapel then, so deep that it seemed to come from beneath the floor. The stained glass trembled in its lead. Dust sifted from the ribs of the vaulted ceiling.

A cannon had fired from the sea.

The noble guests cried out. Someone dropped a silver cup. Somewhere beyond the walls, horses screamed.

Elianor felt the impact in her teeth.

“Close the doors,” Veyne ordered.

Harl did not move at once. He looked toward Elianor, and in that hesitation she understood that the order meant more than keeping out rain. It meant sealing the chapel with frightened people inside. It meant allowing Veyne's soldiers to decide who was an enemy and who was merely in the way.

“Captain,” Veyne said, sharper now.

“The west door is already barred from the corridor side,” Harl replied. “The chapel is full.”

“Then clear it.”

“Clear it where?”

Veyne's eyes hardened. “The lower yard. The old stores. Anywhere that is not here.”

A second cannon shot struck the sea. This time it was followed by several smaller reports, quick and irregular. Through the eastern window, a smear of smoke spread above the harbor. Tiny craft darted across the water, their lateen sails dark against the pale waves.

The fishing boats had reached the transports.

Elianor could see no men at that distance, only motion: a transport turning too slowly, a fishing vessel cutting across its bow, another coming close along its side. One of the small boats appeared to break apart. Then a line of flame ran up the transport's rigging.

“They're burning the supply ships,” someone whispered.

“They're boarding them,” said another.

Veyne pushed through the guests toward the chapel door. “Find the fleet signal officer. I want the harbor guns turned on those boats.”

“Your Grace,” Harl said, “the harbor guns are manned by Greyhaven's watch.”

“Then remind them who commands Greyhaven.”

A third explosion boomed from below. The sound was followed by a clatter of bells—not the measured chapel bell, but the frantic ringing of the alarm tower.

This time the servants did not merely flinch. They looked at one another.

Bryn was among them, her bandaged left hand hidden in the folds of her plain brown dress. Two guards had brought her from the side corridor, still wearing the iron at her wrists. She stood beside Hessa, the laundress, and an old scullion Elianor recognized from the lower kitchens. Bryn's gaze found hers across the crowded nave.

The signal had come earlier than planned.

Or perhaps this was the signal they had been waiting for all along.

“Bryn,” Elianor called.

One of the guards seized the chain between Bryn's wrists. “She stays where she is.”

The guard's face was young. He had a bruise along his jaw and fear bright in his eyes. The fear did not belong to Elianor. It belonged to the men outside the walls, to the ships, to the gunfire, to the knowledge that Greyhaven was no longer a house protected by distance.

Bryn twisted her hands. The chain flashed.

Hessa moved first. She lifted the brass candlestick from the edge of the lectern and struck the guard across the temple.

The chapel erupted.

The guard fell against a bench. The second guard reached for his sword, but the old scullion drove a shoulder into his stomach. A noblewoman screamed and climbed onto the altar steps, dragging her skirts through the candle flames. Two servants seized a fallen pike from a sentry near the door. Another slammed the chapel's inner bar into place.

Harl shouted for his men to hold formation, but his voice was swallowed by the noise.

Elianor caught Bryn as she stumbled forward. The iron cuffs cut into the girl's swollen wrist.

“Are you hurt?”

“Not newly,” Bryn said. Her breath shook, but her eyes were clear. “The panel.”

“I know.”

“Orren has not rung.”

“He will.”

Across the chapel, Veyne had drawn his sword. He did not look like a bridegroom now. The mantle had slipped from one shoulder, exposing the dark military coat beneath. He struck at a servant who had lifted a pike, and Harl intercepted the blow with his own blade.

Steel rang beneath the painted saints.

“Stand down,” Harl said.

“You are protecting insurgents?”

“I am preventing a panic.”

“Prevent it with their blood.”

Harl's sword held against Veyne's. “There are children in the chapel.”

As if summoned by the word, a cry rose from beneath the western benches. Refugees from Rill had been gathered there before dawn, those too frightened or too weak to remain in the exposed lower rooms. Lysa crouched over a little boy while two fishermen stood between them and the soldiers. One of the fishermen held a kitchen cleaver. The other had a length of iron chain wrapped around his fist.

The chapel was no longer divided between noble and servant. It was divided between those who believed the walls still belonged to Lord Marrow and those who had discovered that walls could be occupied from either side.

Another cannon shot struck the harbor.

The floor lurched. A section of plaster fell from the north arch and shattered across the aisle. The young guard who had been struck by Hessa groaned. A woman began praying loudly. Someone shouted that the eastern gate had been opened. Someone else shouted that the rebels were already inside.

The second cry was true.

A stable hand burst through the sacristy door with blood on his cheek and a short iron bar in his hands.

“Lower yard is ours,” he said. “The grain men have taken the storehouse. Marrow's soldiers are falling back toward the keep.”

“Who opened the gate?” Veyne demanded.

“Your dead men, perhaps,” the stable hand answered. “They left it unguarded when they ran to the harbor.”

A murmur passed through the chapel.

Elianor knew what it meant. The villagers who had gathered at the eastern gate after the grain distribution had not gone far. The laborers who unloaded carts, mended nets, hauled stone, and slept in rooms beneath the kitchens had been waiting for the moment when Greyhaven's armed authority looked away.

Now they were moving.

From outside came the distant roar of men, then the repeated crack of muskets. It was followed by a cheer that climbed the cliff face and entered the chapel like wind.

“Is it Tomas?” Elianor asked before she could stop herself.

Bryn's expression softened, just once. “If he has reached the coast.”

“He has.”

She did not know how she knew. Perhaps the fires had told her. Perhaps the sea had. Or perhaps love, having been denied every ordinary proof, had learned to recognize itself in danger.

At the chapel's west side, Orren suddenly pulled the cord.

The small bell rang.

Its clear note cut through the shouting with startling force. It was a little sound, almost delicate, but it carried the authority of a decision. The servants nearest the lectern stopped fighting. Harl's men looked toward the chaplain. Even Veyne turned his head.

Orren pulled again.

The bell rang a second time.

Bryn stepped toward the lectern. The guard who had been struck tried to rise, and Hessa kicked his sword away. Bryn crouched before the third panel, worked her bound fingers into the narrow seam, and tore the loosened wood free.

Papers slid into her lap.

Veyne saw them.

“What is that?”

“Evidence,” Elianor said.

He started toward her. Harl moved to block him, but the chapel doors burst inward before either man could speak.

A soldier stumbled through, clutching his shoulder. Behind him came smoke, wet air, and the terrible noise of the harbor. He fell across the threshold.

“Marines at the lower stair,” he gasped. “The duke's transports—three are burning. Fishing boats have cut the chain boom. The rebels are coming up from the quay.”

For a moment no one moved.

Then a horn sounded from the cliffs.

It answered the fires. One long note, two short.

A signal traveled along Greyhaven's walls. From the eastern battlement came another horn, and then another from the old stable yard. The estate, which had spent years speaking through locked doors and official seals, was suddenly full of voices.

Veyne turned toward Lord Marrow's empty place near the altar.

“Where is he?”

No one answered.

Elianor gathered the front of her silver gown in both hands. Beneath its train, wrapped against her mother's old silk lining, lay the original orders. The chapel's disorder had made the journey possible. It had also made every person inside more vulnerable.

She looked at Bryn, at Orren, at Vey, who had appeared in the side aisle carrying the key to the archive chest. She looked at Harl, whose soldiers had lowered their weapons but had not yet chosen whom they served. Beyond them, villagers pressed against the chapel walls while Veyne's officers tried to force a path toward the inner keep.

Outside, another cannon fired.

This time the shot did not fall in the harbor. It struck Greyhaven's eastern tower.

Stone thundered down into the yard. The chapel windows flashed white, and every candle went out.

In the darkness, Elianor heard the servants take up their hidden weapons.

A knife leaving a sleeve. A hammer lifted from beneath a bench. The click of a guard's musket being cocked, followed by another, and another.

Then Tomas's name rose from the lower yard—not as a command, but as a cry passed from mouth to mouth.

“Rusk.”

“Rusk is at the gate.”

“Rusk has come.”

Elianor held the signet beneath her sleeve and listened to the cry grow.

The wedding had not begun.

Greyhaven had begun to fall.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: Inside Saint Orra's Chapel during the interrupted wedding, still wearing her dead mother's silver gown and holding Arlen Rusk's signet beneath her sleeve. She remains controlled, terrified, and irrevocably defiant; the appearance of rebel signal fires and Tomas's advancing forces has turned her planned disclosure into an immediate crisis. She knows Bryn retrieved the copied collective-punishment orders, Orren rang the small bell, Vey has brought the archive-chest key, Harl is resisting Veyne, and servants and villagers have seized the lower yard. The original royal and military orders remain hidden in the train of her gown and must be brought into the chapel; the copied archive evidence remains in her prayer book and copied grain books remain outside the accounting room. Her goal is to complete the public exposure, protect Bryn and the refugees, prevent a massacre, and keep the evidence from Veyne or Marrow. She possesses the prayer book, mother's key, signet, remaining authority as Marrow's daughter, and the concealed originals. She is physically safe but surrounded by armed disorder, with the wedding not begun and Greyhaven beginning to fall.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: Absent from Saint Orra's Chapel and believed to have withdrawn toward the inner keep as Greyhaven's lower defenses collapse. He remains desperate, authoritarian, and committed to preserving his estate and the records of his rule. He knows the wedding has been interrupted by rebel attack and that Elianor's disclosure is imminent, though his exact location and immediate actions are unknown. His goal is to retain the inner defenses, recover or destroy the evidence, and use the garrison to preserve authority. He possesses the Marrow signet, household command, and the keep's remaining guards, but the lower yard and servants have turned against him.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: Inside Saint Orra's Chapel during the uprising, carrying the key to the archive chest and wearing formal black under intensified danger. He remains cautious, composed, and committed to preserving the grain books and archive evidence. He knows the copied orders are now in Bryn's hands, the small bell has signaled disclosure, Elianor carries the originals, and the lower yard has fallen to villagers and laborers. His goal is to open the archive chest before the household, make the records impossible to erase, and protect the servants during the collapse. He possesses the steward's seal, archive key and procedures, copied grain books, drainage map, and hidden-route knowledge; he is physically safe in the chapel but at immediate risk from Veyne or Marrow.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: Inside Saint Orra's Chapel during the attack, commanding a divided watch while standing between Duke Veyne and armed servants. He remains morally shaken but has crossed into open resistance to indiscriminate violence: he blocked Veyne's demand for blood, citing the children and refugees in the chapel, and his soldiers have lowered their weapons without fully choosing sides. He knows Orren's signal has sounded, Bryn has retrieved the copied orders, the lower yard is held by villagers and laborers, and rebel forces are coming from the harbor. His goal is to prevent a massacre, protect prisoners and refugees, and keep his men from becoming Veyne's execution squad. He possesses guard authority, weapons, watch knowledge, and the west-door position; he is physically safe but exposed to arrest or attack from Veyne's marines.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: Inside Saint Orra's Chapel amid the wedding collapse, standing at the west lectern after ringing the small bell twice. He remains frightened but committed to making the chapel a place where truth can be heard rather than a stage for coercion. He knows Bryn has recovered the copied collective-punishment orders, Elianor must bring in the originals, and Veyne's forces are fighting toward the inner keep while villagers and servants hold the lower yard. His goal is to keep the evidence visible, shelter refugees, and support Elianor's testimony. He possesses chapel authority, burial and refugee records, the bell, and knowledge of the lectern panel; he is physically safe for the moment but exposed to the armed struggle.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: With the coastal resistance approaching Greyhaven by sea and cliff routes, leading or coordinating the assault under the Rusk name despite refusing hereditary rule. He remains wounded, exhausted, and committed to civilian protection, while emotionally bound to Elianor; he does not yet know exactly what has happened inside the chapel. He knows the coastal councils' terms, Veyne's campaign, and the need to seize Greyhaven without sacrificing refugees or surrendering soldiers. His goal is to reach the harbor and inner defenses, rescue Elianor if possible, preserve the records, and prevent the revolt from becoming revenge. He possesses the recallable coordinating mandate, coastal knowledge, and the loyalty of ships and fighters, but remains physically endangered in the assault.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: Inside Saint Orra's Chapel during the wedding uprising, still wearing irons and carrying a bandaged injured left hand. She remains frightened, loyal, and newly active in the revolt: with Hessa's help she disarmed a guard and tore open the third loose west-lectern panel to retrieve the copied collective-punishment orders. She knows Orren has given the signal, Elianor still carries the originals, Vey is ready to open the archive chest, and servants and villagers control the lower yard. Her goal is to protect Elianor and the papers, help expose Marrow and the crown, and survive the garrison's collapse. She possesses the copied orders and her servant network's knowledge but remains physically restrained by the cuffs and vulnerable to Veyne's soldiers.

set.name: Duke Alistair Veyne
set.description: Inside Saint Orra's Chapel during the wedding attack, still in his ceremonial mantle over military clothing and armed with a drawn sword. He remains furious, militaristic, contemptuous of servants and villagers, and intent on preserving control of Greyhaven. He knows rebel ships are attacking his transports, fishing boats have cut the harbor chain, the lower yard is held by insurgents, the chapel contains incriminating papers, and Captain Harl has refused to clear the chapel with blood. His goal is to reach the inner keep, rally the garrison, seize Elianor and the evidence, and crush the uprising. He possesses royal authority, officers, marines, and the approaching fleet, but his forces are divided, transports are burning, and he is physically exposed inside a hostile chapel.
Rebel signal fires appeared along the cliffs before the wedding ceremony, announcing that coastal forces had reached Greyhaven and that the assault had begun.
Fishing vessels attacked Duke Veyne's transports in the harbor, setting at least one transport alight and cutting the harbor chain boom while cannon fire struck Greyhaven's defenses.
Villagers, laborers, stable hands, and servants rose inside Greyhaven, seized the lower yard and storehouse, and forced garrison soldiers toward the inner keep.

During the wedding panic, Bryn and Hessa disarmed guards, Chaplain Orren rang the small bell, and Bryn retrieved the copied collective-punishment orders from behind the third panel of the west lectern.
Captain Harl openly prevented Duke Veyne from using lethal force against armed servants and refugees in the chapel, leaving his soldiers divided and the chapel in revolt.

With Greyhaven's harbor and lower yard contested, Tomas and the coastal forces must breach the inner defenses while Elianor and the chapel allies preserve the evidence and prevent the garrison from turning the uprising into a massacre.
Elianor must bring the original orders into the chapel and complete the public reading before Veyne or Lord Marrow can seize or destroy them.

chapters.name: The Surrender
chapters.content:
The chapel doors stood open to the storm.

Rain blew across the threshold in silver sheets, carrying the smell of salt, smoke, and the harbor’s burning pitch. Beyond the doorway, Greyhaven no longer belonged to one command. Villagers crowded the lower yard with fishing hooks, axes, kitchen knives, and lengths of chain. Servants had overturned carts to make a barricade beneath the eastern arcade. On the stair above them, Captain Harl’s soldiers held their weapons in uncertain hands, facing both the armed marines gathered around Duke Veyne and the people who had once brought them food.

The wedding candles guttered along the chapel walls. Wax ran over the brass sconces and hardened like pale tears.

Duke Veyne stood near the west door, his ceremonial mantle darkened by rain and powder smoke. One of his marines had a pistol leveled toward the crowd. Captain Harl’s arm barred the man’s path.

“Lower it,” Harl said.

“You have no authority to command me,” Veyne answered.

“I have enough authority to keep you from shooting children in a chapel.”

A cannon sounded from the harbor. The floor shuddered under Elianor’s slippers. Somewhere outside, men shouted, and a bell began ringing from the lower yard—not the measured signal Orren had given, but a wild peal struck by someone who had forgotten fear.

Elianor stood at the chapel’s center in her mother’s silver gown. The silk was already wet at the hem where rain had crossed the stones. Beneath the train, hidden in a fold sewn into the lining, lay the original letters bearing the crown’s seal. Against her ribs, under her sleeve, Arlen Rusk’s signet pressed a small, hard circle into her skin.

Bryn stood beside Chaplain Orren at the lectern, her wrists still circled by irons. Her bandaged hand held the copied orders. Master Vey waited near the locked archive chest, one hand closed around its key. Hessa, the laundress who had helped Bryn disarm a guard, watched the chapel entrance with a kitchen cleaver tucked through her belt.

The nobles had gathered behind Elianor as if she were still a shield. Lady Fenwick clutched a jeweled rosary. Two of Veyne’s officers whispered about the north stair. Her father’s secretary had abandoned his papers and was trying to hide behind a pillar. No one spoke of fleeing now. They were waiting to discover which way power would turn.

Elianor looked toward the chapel’s upper gallery. From there she could see the black line of the inner keep above the roofs. Lord Marrow was somewhere within it, surrounded by the guards who still obeyed him. He had sent her to be married in silver and obedience. He had expected her to stand beside Veyne while soldiers made a fortress of the coast.

The old instinct came to her then: find the safest path for the household. Preserve the name. Keep the doors closed. Let the violence pass over the walls and call the surviving structure duty.

She saw her mother’s face in memory, pale above a collar of pearls, saying that noblewomen preserved kingdoms by enduring what men demanded of them.

Then she saw Perrin, Cal, and Miri beneath the chapel cloths, their small bodies laid side by side after hunger had taken what the storm left behind.

Duty had not saved them. It had merely taught everyone who remained to call their deaths necessary.

“Elianor,” Lady Fenwick whispered, “we must go. The west passage leads to the sea caves. Your father can still gather the household guard. If you come with us, Veyne will protect you.”

“Protect me from whom?” Elianor asked.

The lady glanced toward the villagers. “From them.”

Outside, a boy no older than ten lifted a length of iron above his head. His face was smeared with soot. Beside him stood Lysa, one hand wrapped around a broken oar and the other gripping the shoulder of Nerrin, who was trembling from exhaustion.

Elianor stepped toward the lectern.

Veyne’s gaze sharpened. “Lady Elianor, this is not the hour for speeches.”

“It is the only hour left to us.”

“You are my promised wife.”

“No.” She felt the word pass through the chapel like a blade drawn from its sheath. “I was the instrument of a promise made between men who meant to use this coast as a battlefield.”

His mouth tightened. “You will not shame your house before servants.”

“I am about to shame it before everyone.”

He moved toward her. Harl shifted at once, placing himself between them. Veyne’s marines raised their weapons. The soldiers along the gallery looked down, frightened now not of the villagers but of the order they might be given.

“Captain,” Veyne said, “remove her.”

Harl did not move.

“I said remove her.”

“And I heard you.” Harl’s voice was rough. “I am choosing not to obey.”

For a heartbeat no one breathed. Then one of Harl’s soldiers lowered his sword. Another followed. The sound of steel touching wood was quiet, yet it traveled farther than the cannon fire.

Elianor climbed the three steps to the lectern. The silver gown dragged behind her, catching on a splinter in the stair. Bryn reached to free it, and Elianor saw blood darkening the maid’s bandage.

“Are you hurt badly?”

“Not badly enough to stop,” Bryn said.

Elianor took the copied papers from her. The first page shook in the wind coming through the open doors. She steadied it with both hands.

“People of Greyhaven,” she called.

Her voice did not carry at first. Rain struck the chapel roof. Men shouted from the yard. Somewhere a horse screamed.

Orren seized the chapel bell rope and rang once.

The noise gathered attention. Faces turned: villagers below, servants in the aisles, soldiers on the steps, nobles pressed against the walls. Even Veyne looked toward her.

Elianor tried again.

“People of Greyhaven.”

This time the words reached the yard.

“I am Elianor Vale, daughter of Corvin Marrow, born to the house that owns these walls by law, by crown grant, and by the labor of those who stand before me. I have been told that those laws are sacred. I have been told that grain may be withheld while children starve, that villages may be searched and emptied, that soldiers may take labor from families, because order is more important than a life.”

She looked down at the silver fabric covering her hands.

“I believed some of it. I believed that if I spoke carefully enough, my father might remember mercy. I believed that the house could be made honorable without surrendering what it had taken. I was wrong.”

A murmur passed through the crowd. Behind her, Lady Fenwick made a sound of protest, but no one turned to her.

Elianor reached beneath the gown and found the seam in the lining. Her fingers worked at the hidden stitches. The originals had been folded into a narrow packet and tied with blue thread. When she drew them out, the royal seals shone red in the gray chapel light.

Veyne went pale.

“Give me those,” he said.

Master Vey stepped forward, holding the archive key high. “The papers will be witnessed.”

Veyne lunged toward the steps. Harl caught his forearm. The duke struck him with his free hand, but Harl held on. Two marines moved to help their commander. Hessa raised the cleaver. Around her, three servants lifted shovels and iron spits.

“Stand down,” Harl ordered his men.

The marines hesitated.

Elianor unfolded the first letter.

“This bears the seal of the royal ministers and is addressed to Duke Alistair Veyne. It orders the entire coast declared treasonous if its villages refuse inspection. It authorizes the seizure of rebel lands, the detention of families, and the displacement of households judged sympathetic to the resistance.”

She turned the page so the seal could be seen.

“It orders children ten years of age and older taken for military labor.”

The chapel changed then. It was not one sound but many: a woman crying out in the yard, a soldier swearing under his breath, the scrape of a weapon being lowered. Lysa’s face went rigid.

“My son is eleven,” someone said.

“And mine is ten.”

“Read it again.”

Elianor read the passage again, slowly. The words were cold and precise. They gave no name to fear, no description to hunger, no room for the face of a child. That was the cruelty of them. They made suffering grammatical.

She lifted the second letter.

“This is from Duke Veyne to Lord Corvin Marrow. It says the marriage will remove noble shelter from the coastal resistance. It says Greyhaven’s harbor and stores will be secured under military protection. It says that once the alliance is completed, no village will be able to claim the protection of my family.”

Veyne stopped struggling. Rain shone on his face.

“Those are military measures,” he said. “The coast is in rebellion.”

“The orders were written before the assault began,” Elianor answered. “They were written before your transports burned. Before the fishing boats cut the harbor chain. Before the people here took up weapons because they understood what you intended to do to their homes.”

“You are speaking under duress.”

“I am speaking because I am no longer under yours.”

The words reached the soldiers more deeply than the accusations. Elianor saw it in their expressions: the calculation of men who had been told they were defending order and had discovered they were being prepared to enforce punishment.

She turned toward Master Vey. “Open the chest.”

He inserted the key into the archive lock. The chest had been brought from the west rooms during the confusion, its iron corners shining with wet. The lock opened with a thick click. Vey drew out the grain books, bound ledgers, route slips, and copied depositions. He set them on the lectern beneath the royal orders.

“These records show grain sent from Greyhaven while Rill was starving,” Elianor said. “They show sacks marked waste and diverted through Merrit & Sons. They show stores carried away from the people who grew and harvested them.”

She lifted one of the books.

“Rill. Hallowmere. Durn. Blackwater Reach. These names appear in the accounts as places of levy, seizure, arrest, or loss. Rill was left without grain after its mill stopped and its sea wall broke. Hallowmere and Durn lost their tax offices to fire after the people there refused further collections. Blackwater Reach lost sailors to the rope when they refused orders that would have sent them against their own coast.”

She did not claim that Lord Marrow had lit every fire or ordered every death. The truth needed no embellishment. His policies had made hunger, confiscation, and military force into the language by which the coast was governed.

“My father called these choices,” she said. “He said a ruler must decide who can be saved. But he did not make those choices from an empty storehouse. He made them beside full granaries. He made them while taking land from families whose names were erased from the archive. He made them because some lives were useful to him and others were not.”

The soldiers were looking at one another now.

A young guard in the gallery stepped down. He removed the red cord that marked Marrow’s household watch and laid it on the chapel floor.

“My mother is from Rill,” he said. “I was told the village had become dangerous.”

Another soldier lowered his crossbow. “My brothers were taken for road work in the spring.”

Veyne’s face twisted. “Cowards. You would abandon the crown because a girl in a wedding dress reads stolen papers?”

“No,” said Harl. He released the duke’s arm. “We abandon the crown because we have read them too.”

The statement broke the last line of obedience. Harl’s remaining watchmen turned their weapons away from the villagers. One marine backed toward the west door. Another dropped his pistol into a puddle.

Outside, the crowd began to chant—not a name, but a demand.

“Open the stores.”

“Open the records.”

“Open the gates.”

Elianor looked toward the inner keep. Smoke had begun to rise behind its battlements. Her father was burning something. Perhaps the archives. Perhaps the granaries. Perhaps both.

She raised her voice again.

“Hear me, then. By the authority my father gave me when he made me the face of this house, and by the authority I take from the people who have sustained it, I surrender Greyhaven.”

The words seemed impossible once spoken. They hung above the chapel like a bell’s final vibration.

“I surrender the estate, its harbor, its granaries, its fields, and its archives. They do not belong to Lord Corvin Marrow. They do not belong to me. They belong to the people whose labor built them and whose hunger filled them with meaning. The stores will be counted publicly. The records will be preserved publicly. No servant will be punished for obeying conscience. No villager will be executed for taking food. Any soldier who lays down his weapon will live to answer before a public hearing.”

Captain Harl bowed his head.

“I will enforce that,” he said.

“And I,” said Master Vey.

Chaplain Orren stepped beside the lectern. “The chapel will witness it.”

Bryn lifted her cuffed hands. “Then take these off me.”

Harl drew a key from his belt and crossed the chapel. He unlocked Bryn’s irons. They fell against the stone with a dull clatter.

Veyne stared at Elianor as though she had become someone he had never met.

“You have destroyed your inheritance,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Your father will disown you.”

“He already has.”

“You will have nothing.”

Elianor thought of Tomas in the storm, of his hands calming Ash, of the signet beneath her sleeve. She thought of the life she had once imagined—a house by the sea, perhaps, with no guard at the door and no ledger deciding who deserved bread. That life had never been promised to her. It had only been glimpsed, and now the glimpse was enough to make every bargain behind her seem unbearable.

“I will have the truth,” she said. “And the work it requires.”

A horn sounded from the harbor.

For one terrible moment, every person in the chapel froze. Then another horn answered from the cliffs, closer than the first. Rebel ships had reached the outer wall. The fighting would come inward soon.

Elianor gathered the papers against her chest.

“To the lower yard,” she said. “Tell them what has been surrendered. Keep the gates open for those who come under terms. Move the grain before the keep can burn it. And send word to the coastal forces that Greyhaven is no longer Marrow’s fortress.”

Harl turned to his soldiers. “You heard her.”

They moved.

Not all at once, and not without fear. Some carried weapons. Some carried wounded men. One soldier stopped to help an old woman over the chapel threshold. A marine threw down his sword and raised both hands. Villagers made room for him, suspiciously but without striking.

Elianor descended the steps. The silver train dragged through rainwater, ash, and wax. At the chapel doors, she looked back once at the altar where the wedding had not begun.

There would be no marriage. No inheritance. No return to the life her father had prepared.

Beyond the threshold, Greyhaven roared with the sound of a world breaking open.

Elianor stepped into it, carrying the crown’s crimes in both hands.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel threshold and moving toward Greyhaven's lower yard, still wearing her dead mother's wet silver gown and carrying the crown's original orders and archive evidence. She has publicly read the collective-punishment orders, named Rill, Hallowmere, Durn, and Blackwater Reach among the harmed coastal settlements, surrendered Greyhaven, and renounced her inheritance in favor of the people whose labor sustained the estate. She knows Lord Marrow is in or near the inner keep and may be burning records or granaries; she knows Tomas's coastal forces are approaching but has not yet reunited with him. Her goal is to enforce the surrender terms, protect grain, archives, servants, villagers, refugees, and prisoners, and prevent the uprising becoming a massacre. She possesses the original orders, grain books and archive records, her mother's key, Arlen Rusk's signet, and moral authority among the chapel crowd. She is exhausted, rain-soaked, frightened, and irrevocably committed to the people over her family name.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: In or near Greyhaven's inner keep while the chapel and lower yard reject his authority. He remains desperate, authoritarian, and committed to preserving his rule and destroying evidence; smoke rising behind the keep suggests he has begun burning archives, granaries, or both. He knows Elianor has publicly exposed the crown's orders and surrendered the estate, and that garrison loyalty is collapsing. His goal is to retain the inner defenses, recover or destroy the records, and use remaining guards to prevent the surrender from becoming effective. He possesses the Marrow signet, the inner keep, and whatever guards remain loyal, but has lost the lower yard, chapel, much of the watch, and public legitimacy.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and moving with the surrender effort toward the lower yard, carrying the archive key and having opened the archive chest before the assembled household. He remains cautious but openly committed to preserving grain books, archive evidence, and humane surrender terms. He knows Elianor has read the original orders and records, renounced her inheritance, and ordered the grain and archives protected; he is allied with Elianor, Harl, Orren, Bryn, servants, villagers, and the approaching coastal resistance. His goal is to move and preserve the records and publicly count the surrendered stores while protecting servants. He possesses the steward's seal, archive key, grain books, drainage map, and hidden-route knowledge. He is physically safe for the moment but exposed to Marrow's remaining guards and Veyne's marines.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and directing former Greyhaven watchmen toward the lower yard under Elianor's surrender terms. He openly refused Veyne's order to remove Elianor, declared that his soldiers would not shoot children, publicly accepted the surrender, freed Bryn from her irons, and ordered his men to protect surrendering soldiers and civilians. He knows the crown's punishment orders are genuine, the garrison's loyalty is breaking, Marrow is in the keep, and rebel forces are entering Greyhaven. His goal is to keep the gates open, prevent retaliation and massacre, move grain and wounded people, and hold his soldiers to the stated terms. He possesses guard authority, weapons, and knowledge of the defenses, but is exposed to Veyne's marines and Marrow's remaining loyalists.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel, having rung the bell to gather witnesses and publicly affirmed that the chapel would witness Elianor's surrender. He remains frightened but resolute, allied with Elianor, Vey, Harl, Bryn, servants, and villagers. He knows the crown's orders and grain evidence have been read aloud, Greyhaven has been surrendered, and fighting is moving inward from the harbor. His goal is to keep the chapel a refuge and witness, protect records and prisoners, and support humane treatment during the transfer of authority. He possesses chapel authority, burial and refugee records, the bell, and knowledge of the lectern panel. He is physically safe for the moment but vulnerable to the continuing battle.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: With coastal resistance forces approaching and entering Greyhaven from harbor and cliff routes, still coordinating the assault under the Rusk name. He remains wounded, exhausted, and committed to civilian protection, unaware of the exact details of Elianor's public surrender but likely to receive her message that Greyhaven is no longer Marrow's fortress. He knows the coastal councils' humane terms and must now breach or secure the inner defenses without allowing revenge. His goal is to reach Elianor, protect civilians and records, and preserve the surrender's promise that surrendering soldiers live. He possesses the recallable coordinating mandate, coastal knowledge, and loyalty of ships and fighters, but remains physically endangered in the assault.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and moving toward the lower yard after Harl unlocked her irons. Her left hand remains bandaged and injured, but she has helped retrieve the copied orders and witnessed Elianor's public disclosure and surrender. She is loyal to Elianor and allied with Harl, Vey, Orren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. Her goal is to protect the evidence, guide the servants' network, move supplies away from the burning keep, and survive the battle. She possesses the copied collective-punishment orders, knowledge of servant routes, and freed hands, but remains physically vulnerable and exhausted.

set.name: Duke Alistair Veyne
set.description: At or near Saint Orra's Chapel under Captain Harl's restraint and facing the collapse of his authority. He remains furious, militaristic, and contemptuous, but his marines and Greyhaven soldiers are divided after Elianor read the crown's orders and renounced the marriage and inheritance. He knows the documents are authentic enough to turn soldiers and that Greyhaven has been publicly surrendered. His goal is to regain control, reach the inner keep, seize or destroy the evidence, and crush the uprising. He possesses royal authority, officers, and some marines, but is exposed, isolated from much of the garrison, and challenged by Harl.

Still wearing her mother's silver gown, Elianor publicly read the crown's collective-punishment orders and the grain and land records before villagers, servants, soldiers, nobles, and Duke Veyne in Saint Orra's Chapel.

Elianor declared Greyhaven surrendered and renounced her inheritance, placing the estate, harbor, granaries, fields, and archives under the people whose labor had sustained them; she promised humane treatment for servants and surrendering soldiers.

Captain Harl, Master Vey, and Chaplain Orren publicly supported Elianor's surrender; Harl freed Bryn and his soldiers lowered their weapons, while several garrison soldiers and at least one marine abandoned the old command.
Elianor named Rill, Hallowmere, Durn, and Blackwater Reach as places harmed by Marrow's levies, seizures, military policies, or neglect, making the estate's crimes publicly legible beyond its walls.

Elianor ordered the lower yard informed, the grain moved from the threatened keep, the gates kept open under surrender terms, and the coastal forces told that Greyhaven was no longer Marrow's fortress.
The surrendered Greyhaven must be defended and its grain, archives, servants, villagers, and prisoners protected as rebel forces fight through the harbor and inner defenses.
Elianor must preserve the public terms of surrender and prevent retaliatory executions as authority passes from Marrow's household to the coastal resistance.

chapters.name: The Harbor Gate
chapters.content:
The harbor gate had been built for a siege that Greyhaven no longer remembered. Its lower stones were black with salt, its iron teeth furred with rust, and beneath it ran the old stable tunnels where horses had once been led from the quay to the lord’s yard without passing through the village streets. In the storm, the sea struck the outer wall hard enough to shake dust from the murder holes. Above the gate, bells and shouting tangled with the boom of cannon.

Tomas reached the harbor road on foot, one hand pressed against the bandage beneath his coat. The wound left by the guards’ beating had opened again during the climb from the western cliff. Warm blood slid along his ribs, but he scarcely felt it. The sight before him had driven pain into a smaller room.

Fishing boats crowded the harbor, their masts black against a sky the color of iron. One of Veyne’s transports burned at the far pier, its ropes snapping in the wind. Rebel fighters poured from skiffs and over the sea wall, while Greyhaven watchmen fired from the gatehouse. Some of the watchmen wore Marrow’s colors. Others had thrown their red sashes into the water.

“Rusk!” someone shouted.

The name crossed the road like a spark finding oil.

“Tomas Rusk!”

“Arlen’s son!”

Men and women turned toward him. A fisherman with blood running from his scalp raised a boat hook. Two Northwatch soldiers lowered their muskets and stared. From the breach near the harbor chain, a young woman cried the name again, and a dozen voices took it up until the stonework seemed to answer.

Tomas stopped beneath the dripping arch.

He had spent half his life hiding that name. He had carried it like a blade sewn into his skin, dangerous even when no one could see it. Now it had become a banner before he had chosen to lift it.

Mara Quill came through the press of fighters, gray hair plastered to her temples, a pistol in one hand and a map tube tied across her back. Joren Pell followed, limping but broad enough to part the crowd by presence alone.

“You were meant to come by the cliff path,” Mara said.

“The cliff path is full of wounded and villagers.”

“Then you came by the right path.” She looked over the harbor. “The gatehouse is still held. Harl’s men have opened the lower sally door, but the chain winch is jammed. We need the harbor gate before Veyne brings the rest of his marines through the eastern quay.”

Joren pointed toward the inner road. “And we need to stop waiting for permission. Marrow’s men are falling back. If we break them now, Greyhaven is ours.”

“Ours,” Tomas repeated.

The word felt heavier than the rain.

A boy no older than sixteen ran past with a sword too long for him. Behind him came three fishermen carrying a wounded woman between them. She was a servant by her gray apron, and one of the fishermen had covered her face with his own cloak.

“Where is Elianor?” Tomas asked.

Mara’s eyes sharpened. “In the lower yard, or moving toward it. She surrendered the estate before the chapel. Publicly. The garrison is divided because she read the orders aloud.”

A fierce relief went through him, followed at once by terror. She was inside the walls. Veyne was inside the walls. Lord Marrow was somewhere in the keep, and smoke had begun rising behind it.

“She told us to keep the gates open,” Mara continued. “She ordered the grain and records protected.”

“Then we take the gate without closing it behind us.”

Joren gave a harsh laugh. “That is a fine phrase for a man standing beneath a gate held by soldiers.”

“It is a command.”

The laughter died.

Tomas climbed onto a toppled cart so the nearest fighters could see him. Rain ran from his hair into his eyes. The old signet, which he had given Elianor in the drainage tunnel and received back only in memory, was not on his hand; he had left it with her. He had no emblem except the blood on his coat and the name others had chosen to shout.

“Listen,” he called.

The harbor was too loud. He raised the pistol Mara had given him, not firing it, but holding it upright until faces turned.

“We are taking Greyhaven to end the rule that made hunger a law. Not to replace one lord with another. Not to make prisoners of every person who wore a uniform. The chapel has declared terms. Servants, villagers, children, and those who surrender are under protection. Anyone who kills a man after he lays down his weapon answers to the councils.”

A voice from the quay shouted, “Marrow killed our fathers!”

Another answered, “Rusk, give us the keep!”

The second cry swelled more quickly than the first.

“Rusk! Rusk! Rusk!”

The fighters struck spear shafts against the stones. A woman held up a hatchet. Someone began to sing an old marching hymn, and the refrain broke apart beneath the roar of the crowd.

Tomas felt the name turning around him, gathering heat. He understood, suddenly, how a man could be carried into a war by people who believed they were carrying him. Arlen had perhaps felt it too, before Greyhaven took him. The thought did not make Tomas proud. It made him sick.

“Joren,” he said, climbing down. “Take the western stair. No fire into the gatehouse if the watchmen yield.”

Joren’s jaw worked. “And if they do not?”

“Then disarm them. Hold them for a hearing.”

“They will shoot at us.”

“Then stop them. Do not execute them.”

Joren stared at him, measuring the order against the dead he had brought from Northwatch. At last he nodded. “You make mercy sound like another wall.”

“It is. Build it.”

Mara touched Tomas’s sleeve. “The stable tunnels?”

“Still open, if the flood has not filled them.”

“They run beneath the old tack room and come up behind the inner gate.”

“I know.”

He knew every turn. He had slept beside the stable through winters when his hands cracked from cold. He knew where the tunnel roof dipped, where water gathered, where Ash had once shied at the hollow sound beneath the floor. He knew the narrow door behind the hay rack, though it might now be barred from within.

He chose forty fighters: Pell, Nessa’s younger assistants carrying bandages, six Northwatch soldiers, fishermen with knives and clubs, and former Greyhaven watchmen who had thrown down Marrow’s colors. He left Mara to hold the harbor road and Joren to take the gatehouse. Before descending, he turned back toward the chapel hill.

For one instant he saw Elianor as she had stood beneath the bell: silver gown soaked dark, one hand raised over the papers, her voice stronger than the cannon. He could not see her now. Smoke dragged across the yard and swallowed the chapel roof.

“Come back,” he whispered, though he did not know whether he spoke to her or himself.

The tunnel door opened beneath three kicks. A smell of wet earth, old straw, and horse rot rose from the dark. Tomas took a lantern from Pell and entered first.

The passage was narrower than he remembered. Water ran over the floor around his boots. Behind him, the fighters moved in a crouch, weapons held close to avoid scraping the brick. Twice they passed alcoves where rusted rings remained in the walls. Once Tomas saw a child’s wooden wheel half buried in mud. He wondered whether it had belonged to a Marrow child or a servant’s child, then despised himself for making the distinction.

At the first bend, voices sounded ahead.

“Hold,” Tomas whispered.

Through the dark came the wet cough of a man and the clatter of a dropped weapon. A Greyhaven soldier appeared around the corner with both hands raised. He was young, pale, and bleeding from the forehead.

“Don’t shoot,” he said. “We’re done.”

Behind him, two more soldiers crouched beside a wounded corporal. One had a broken arm. The other was crying silently.

A fisherman raised his knife. “They shot at the chapel.”

The young soldier flinched. “We were ordered.”

“And you obeyed.”

Tomas stepped between them. “Put the weapons down.”

“They already have,” Pell said.

“Then bind the wounded and take all three to the lower yard. Give them water. No one touches them.”

The fisherman’s face twisted. “My sister is dead.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

Tomas looked at the man until the knife lowered by an inch. “No. I do not. But if we answer every death by making another, Greyhaven will teach us nothing except its own language.”

The man spat into the water and stepped aside.

They carried the corporal between them. The delay was less than five minutes. It felt like an hour.

At the tunnel’s end, a barred door shuddered under blows from the other side. Tomas extinguished the lantern. In the dark, everyone listened.

“Who is there?” a voice called.

“Greyhaven watch,” Pell answered. “We surrender.”

The bar lifted. A woman in a kitchen apron stood beyond it, gripping a cleaver. Behind her were two stable hands and a boy with a crossbow.

“Bryn sent us,” the woman said. “The inner gate is full of Veyne’s marines. They have prisoners from the chapel. Harl’s men are trying to reach them.”

“Where is Elianor?”

“Lower yard. She went after the grain carts.”

The relief in him was so sharp he nearly staggered.

Then a cannon blast struck the outer wall. Dust rained from the ceiling. The woman shouted that the marines had broken through the east passage.

Tomas pushed into the stable yard.

Greyhaven’s old stalls stood open and empty. Ash’s stall door hung from one hinge, and a gray shape moved beyond it. The mare saw him and gave a frightened cry. Tomas crossed the yard long enough to put a hand against her wet neck.

“Stay,” he murmured. “Stay here.”

He wanted Elianor to know Ash was alive. The thought was absurd amid the smoke and gunfire, but love had always made room for such absurdities.

Pell shouted from the archway. “The gate!”

The inner harbor gate had been forced halfway open. Rebels surged through, but marines fired from the parapet above. A former watchman fell backward into the mud. Another rebel raised a torch toward the wooden supports.

“No fire!” Tomas roared.

The torchbearer turned. “They’ll trap us!”

“Use the side stairs. Pell, take the left. Watchmen with me.”

He ran beneath the gate as musket balls chipped stone around him. The marines had placed prisoners in a line against the wall: two stable hands, four garrison soldiers, a fisher boy, and Captain Harl, whose face was dark with blood.

Duke Veyne stood behind them in a breastplate slick with rain. His sword was drawn. Around him, marines formed a disciplined crescent.

“Rusk,” Veyne called. “You came at last.”

The name passed through the rebels again, but this time Tomas heard hunger in it—not for food, but for vengeance.

Veyne smiled. “Your father begged before he died.”

Tomas’s pistol rose. His finger tightened.

Harl, kneeling among the prisoners, met his eyes and shook his head once.

Not for mercy, Tomas thought. For the terms.

He lowered the pistol.

“Duke Veyne,” he called, “you are surrounded. Release the prisoners and surrender.”

Veyne laughed. “You are a stable boy wearing a dead man’s name.”

“I am the man ordering you to lay down your arms.”

The marines shifted. Beyond them, the gatehouse bell began to ring as Joren’s force took the western stair. The rebels pressed from the tunnel and harbor road. For a moment, surrender seemed possible.

Then a marine officer leaned toward Veyne and said something too low to hear.

Veyne glanced at the prisoners.

“Kill the captain first,” he said.

The nearest marine raised his musket.

Tomas fired. The officer fell, but the shot broke the moment. Marines fired together. Harl twisted aside; the ball struck the prisoner behind him. The stable hand collapsed without a sound.

“Hold!” Tomas shouted.

His own fighters surged forward. He struck one man’s rifle aside as the fisherman with the knife lunged toward a fallen marine.

“Alive!” Tomas yelled. “They surrender if they drop weapons!”

“They’re killing ours!” someone screamed.

“I said alive!”

The command cost them. Instead of sweeping across the courtyard, the rebels stopped to drag wounded men from beneath the fire, to bind wrists, to separate prisoners from those who wanted blood. Joren reached the gatehouse and shouted that the winch was free. Pell’s fighters took the parapet, but every step was contested.

Veyne’s marines used the hesitation.

They drove through the inner arch, dragging the remaining prisoners with them. Harl was struck behind the knee and fell. The fisher boy cried out as a marine seized him by the collar.

Tomas ran after them.

The courtyard beyond had become a maze of smoke and overturned carts. He saw Elianor at the far end, silver gown flashing between grain sacks, turning toward the gunfire. Their eyes met across the distance.

Then a marine shoved Harl against the wall and fired into the prisoners.

One body fell. Then another.

Elianor screamed his name. Tomas heard it above the cannon, above the bells, above the triumphant cry of those who called him Rusk.

The inner defenses slammed shut between them.

Tomas reached the bars too late. On the other side, Veyne’s men dragged the surviving prisoners toward the keep. Smoke poured from the upper windows. Somewhere within it, Lord Marrow was destroying the past.

Tomas put both hands on the iron and felt it tremble.

“Break it,” Joren shouted behind him. “Break the damn thing!”

Tomas turned to the fighters. Their faces were wet with rain, sweat, and blood. They were waiting for him to become what the name promised: an heir, a weapon, an answer.

He raised his pistol toward the lock.

“Bring the ram,” he said. “And no one crosses until the prisoners are secured.”

A murmur of disbelief passed through them.

Tomas looked toward the courtyard where Elianor had vanished.

“We are not Greyhaven,” he said.

The ram came forward. Behind the iron gate, another shot sounded.

This time, no one could tell whose prisoner had died.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: Inside Greyhaven's inner yard near the grain sacks after publicly surrendering the estate from Saint Orra's Chapel and directing grain, archives, civilians, servants, and prisoners to be protected. Still wearing her dead mother's wet silver gown, she has seen Tomas across the smoke and heard him named as Rusk, but the inner defenses closed between them before they could reunite. She knows Marrow is burning or preparing to burn records and granaries, Veyne's marines have breached the inner defenses and begun executing prisoners, and Tomas is leading the assault under humane terms. She remains exhausted, frightened, morally resolute, and committed to preventing massacre and preserving evidence. She possesses the original crown orders, grain books and archive records, her mother's key, Arlen Rusk's signet, and authority drawn from the public surrender. Her immediate goals are to reach the prisoners and Tomas, save the grain and surviving records, and enforce surrender terms despite Veyne and Marrow.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: Wounded and inside the inner gate area after being captured with servants, surrendering garrison soldiers, and a fisher boy by Veyne's marines. He had supported Elianor's surrender and Tomas's humane terms, and he remains allied with both despite being struck behind the knee and dragged among the prisoners. He knows Veyne's marines have begun executing captives and that Tomas is trying to breach the inner defenses without allowing revenge. His goal is to survive, protect the prisoners, and help the rebels hold to the surrender terms. He possesses command knowledge of Greyhaven's defenses but is disarmed, injured, and at immediate risk.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: Inside Greyhaven at the barred inner defenses after leading rebel fighters through the harbor gate and old stable tunnels. His identity as Arlen Rusk's son is now known among the fighters, who rally around the Rusk name despite his refusal of hereditary authority. He remains wounded, exhausted, rain-soaked, and emotionally shaken by the name becoming a banner. He knows Elianor publicly surrendered Greyhaven and is somewhere inside the lower or inner yard, knows Veyne's marines are executing prisoners, and has ordered rebels to spare servants and surrendering soldiers even when that restraint costs lives and time. He is allied with Mara, Joren, Pell, Harl, Elianor, the servants, villagers, and coastal resistance. His immediate goal is to break the inner gate, save surviving prisoners, reach Elianor, protect the records and grain, and prevent revenge. He possesses Mara's pistol, coastal authority as recallable coordinator, knowledge of the stable tunnels, and the loyalty of the assault force; Ash remains alive in the old stable.

set.name: Ash
set.description: Alive in the old stable at Greyhaven after the harbor assault, frightened by cannon fire, smoke, and gunshots but comforted briefly by Tomas. She remains a tall gray mare with a white blaze, raw rope wound beneath her jaw, swollen improving hind leg, and scars from mistreatment. The stable has been breached and is exposed to the battle, but no one has removed or ridden her. She is physically unsettled and vulnerable to the spreading fire.

set.name: Pell
set.description: Inside Greyhaven's harbor and inner gate approach with Tomas's assault force. He remains broad-shouldered, injured, dependable, and active after helping lead fighters through the old stable tunnels and take the parapet. He knows Tomas has ordered humane treatment despite rebel anger, Veyne's marines have seized prisoners and retreated into the inner defenses, and Elianor is in the courtyard. He is allied with Tomas, Joren, Mara, Elianor, and the servants' network. His goal is to organize the ram and fighters for the inner breach while extracting wounded people and preventing retaliatory killings.

set.name: Joren Pell
set.description: At Greyhaven's harbor gatehouse and inner defenses with Northwatch fighters after taking the western stair and freeing the harbor winch. He remains injured but active, battle-experienced, and impatient with Tomas's restraint, though he follows the order to spare surrendering soldiers. He knows Tomas's Rusk identity is now public, Veyne's marines are retreating through the inner arch while executing prisoners, and Elianor is inside the courtyard. He is allied with Tomas, Mara, Pell, Harl, Elianor, and the coastal resistance. His goal is to bring the ram to the inner gate, breach it, and support prisoner rescue without permitting indiscriminate revenge.

set.name: Duke Alistair Veyne
set.description: Inside Greyhaven's inner defenses with surviving marines and prisoners taken from the harbor gate. He remains furious, militaristic, contemptuous, and willing to execute captives to regain control. He knows Tomas's Rusk identity is public among the rebels, Elianor has surrendered Greyhaven, and the outer harbor and gatehouse are falling. He has ordered marines to kill prisoners and is using the inner passage and keep as a fighting retreat toward Lord Marrow. He is opposed by Tomas, Harl, Joren, Elianor, and the divided garrison. He possesses royal authority, armed marines, the inner defenses, and access to the keep, but is increasingly isolated and under assault.

Tomas led a mixed force through Greyhaven's harbor gate and old stable tunnels, publicly ordered rebels to spare servants and surrendering soldiers, and halted retaliatory killings despite calls for revenge.
Tomas's identity as Arlen Rusk's son became known to the assaulting fighters, who rallied around the Rusk name and unsettled him by treating it as a banner of authority.

Tomas's restraint in stopping executions and protecting surrendering soldiers slowed the rebel advance; Duke Veyne's marines used the delay to seize the inner passage and execute prisoners, including a stable hand and other captives.
Tomas and the rebels must breach the inner defenses while protecting the surviving prisoners and preventing Veyne's marines from carrying out further executions.
Elianor and Tomas must reunite inside Greyhaven amid the burning archives and granaries while preserving evidence and resisting the transformation of Tomas's name into revenge authority.

chapters.name: The Burning Granaries
chapters.content:
The first fire began in the archive.

Elianor smelled it before she saw the smoke: hot oil, singed leather, and the bitter sweetness of paper taking flame. She was halfway across the inner yard when a gust drove black ribbons from the keep’s upper windows. Ash settled on her mother’s silver gown like gray snow.

“Master Vey!” she called.

He emerged from behind a cart piled with sacks, one hand pressed to his mouth. In the other he carried the steward’s seal and a ring of keys. His face had gone the color of old wax.

“Marrow ordered the archive doors opened,” he said. “The guards are carrying out ledgers and throwing them into the brazier in the records room. He has sent men to the eastern granary.”

“To burn it?”

Vey looked toward the keep. “He said nothing surrendered by a Marrow would remain for a rebel to inherit.”

A crash sounded above them. Through the smoke came the long, collapsing sigh of shelves giving way.

Elianor gathered the wet skirts of the silver gown and ran.

The inner yard had become a battlefield compressed between walls. Rain fell hard enough to flatten the smoke, then the wind lifted it again in choking clouds. Servants dragged grain sacks from the granary doors while villagers formed a chain toward the open lower gate. Garrison soldiers stood uncertainly beneath the covered walk, some with weapons lowered, some staring at the keep as if waiting for their old orders to become possible again.

“Take the sacks to the chapel stores,” Elianor shouted. “Not the upper house. The chapel and the lower yard.”

A kitchen boy froze with a sack on his back. “Lady—”

“Not lady,” she said. “Move.”

He moved.

Bryn came limping from the granary, her bandaged hand tucked against her chest. Two stable hands supported a third servant between them. The wounded man’s apron was dark with blood.

“Marrow’s men barred the eastern doors,” Bryn said. “We broke the side latch. They’re setting fire to the straw loft.”

“How many are inside?”

“Enough to kill us if they decide they remember obedience.”

A shower of sparks rose above the granary roof.

“Get the women and children out first,” Elianor said. “Then the grain marked for Rill.”

Bryn gave her a hard look. “All of it?”

“All that can be carried.”

“Then we’ll need every pair of hands.”

“You have them.”

Bryn turned and began shouting orders. Her injured hand shook, but her voice did not. Hessa seized a hook and pulled burning straw away from the doorway. Orren arrived from the chapel with three villagers and a line of buckets. Behind them came Lysa, soaked to the skin, carrying a child whose face was streaked with soot.

“Put her under the arcade,” Elianor said.

“She won’t leave her mother,” Lysa answered.

“Then bring her mother too.”

Lysa’s expression changed. She thrust the child into Elianor’s arms and ran back toward the flames.

The little girl clung to the silver gown. Her breath smelled of smoke.

“Is this the place where they keep the bread?” she whispered.

“It was.”

“Will it burn?”

Elianor looked at the sacks passing from hand to hand, at the grain dust whitening the servants’ hair, at the orange light licking beneath the granary eaves.

“Not if we can stop it.”

She handed the child to Orren and went inside.

Heat struck her like an opened oven. The granary’s lower chamber was crowded with sacks stacked higher than a man’s head. Fire crawled through the loft above, dropping burning straw between the rows. Water hissed against the floor. A guard lay near the inner wall with his sword beside him, unconscious or dead.

“Pull the eastern stacks first!” Elianor shouted. “The roof will fall there!”

No one questioned why she knew. She had walked these aisles as a girl while Master Vey taught her the difference between barley and wheat, between seed grain and flour, between a household’s wealth and the lives hidden inside its numbers. Her father had told her that a full granary was proof of good governance.

Now the same grain was being turned into a funeral pyre.

She and Bryn seized the end of a sack. The cloth scraped across the floor. A servant took the other side, and together they dragged it into the rain.

“Where are the books?” Elianor asked.

“Vey took the copied ledgers to the chapel,” Bryn said. “The originals are in the accounting room.”

“And the archive?”

“Some are still there.”

Elianor released the sack. “I’m going.”

Bryn caught her sleeve. “The keep is held by Veyne’s men.”

“So is the archive.”

“You cannot save every page.”

“No,” Elianor said. “But I can save the pages they are afraid of.”

She ran toward the keep.

The doors of the records passage stood open. A guard lay facedown across the threshold, his red sash dark with rainwater and blood. Elianor stepped over him. Smoke filled the corridor from floor to ceiling, and somewhere beyond it men were shouting that the rebels had breached the harbor gate.

She covered her mouth with the sleeve of the gown and went on.

The archive room had once been the quietest place in Greyhaven. Its walls were lined with oak cases, its narrow windows glazed against the sea. Now flames shone along the shelves. A brazier had been overturned in the center, and burning papers skittered across the stone like pale birds.

Master Vey had not exaggerated. Marrow’s men had opened every chest and scattered the contents before setting them alight. Tax rolls, land grants, correspondence, depositions: the paper history of the estate was becoming smoke.

Elianor saw the crown orders in her mind, the minister’s careful language about treasonous villages and children taken for labor. She had the originals hidden beneath her bodice, protected in waxed cloth. But the orders alone could be called forged. The grain books proved the diversions. The land transfers proved what had followed Arlen Rusk’s execution. Names, seals, dates—without them, the old regime could claim that Greyhaven had fallen to a rebel’s seduction and a noble daughter’s madness.

A figure moved beside the western shelves.

“Father.”

Lord Marrow turned.

He wore no coat, only a black shirt beneath an ancestral chain. Soot marked his cheek. In his hand he held a bundle of ledgers bound for the fire. Behind him, the portrait of his grandfather burned in its frame.

“You should be in the yard,” he said.

“You should be surrendering.”

His mouth tightened. “To whom? A stable boy with a stolen name?”

“To the people you starved.”

“The people will thank whoever gives them bread today and curse whoever cannot give it tomorrow. That is the whole of their politics.” He threw the ledgers into the flames. “What matters is what survives the telling.”

Elianor felt the truth of his words as a threat rather than an argument.

“You are destroying evidence.”

“I am denying weapons to men who will use them to dismantle the kingdom.”

“You mean weapons against you.”
