“I mean records that can be interpreted by anyone with a grievance.” He stepped toward her. “You have made yourself useful to them by turning private shame into public treason.”

“Private shame?” She pointed toward the burning shelves. “You took families’ lands. You sent grain away while children died in our chapel. You promised Arlen Rusk negotiation and hanged him when he believed you.”

His eyes flashed at the name. “He raised men against the crown.”

“He asked that they be heard.”

“He asked for weakness.”

“He asked for limits.”

A beam cracked overhead. Fire spilled through the ceiling in a curtain of sparks.

Marrow looked up, then back at her. “You have always mistaken refusal for courage.”

“And you have mistaken fear for order.”

He dropped the bundle and moved toward the inner door. For one instant she thought he meant to leave her there. Then he pulled the bar across the door from the outside.

“Elianor,” he said through the smoke, “when the rebels find you, tell them the archive burned because you could not protect it.”

She hurled herself against the wood. “Father!”

His footsteps receded.

She turned back to the room. The fire had reached the eastern cases. Flames ran along the shelves, consuming years in seconds. Elianor seized a water bucket and threw it at the nearest blaze. The water struck the stone below. There was no time to fetch more.

Her mother’s key hung beneath her gown, cold against her ribs. She remembered the sealed chest Vey had shown her in the lower archive: not the copied books, but the original deposition packets kept behind a false panel. The panel was in the north wall, near the case of confiscated lands.

She crawled through the smoke.

The case had collapsed, pinning the false panel beneath a fallen shelf. Elianor pulled until the wood tore her palms. She heard voices beyond the door—servants, perhaps, or men coming to finish the work. She pulled again.

The shelf shifted.

Behind it waited a narrow iron box.

She dragged it free and fitted her mother’s key into the lock. The metal was hot enough to burn her fingers. Inside lay folded depositions, the magistrate’s seal, and three original transfers bearing Lord Marrow’s mark. At the bottom was a packet tied with blue thread: Arlen Rusk’s petition, its last page covered in the neat signatures of coastal villages.

Elianor pressed the packet to her chest.

The door burst inward.

A servant stood there with a wet cloak over his head. “This way!” he shouted. “The passage is open!”

She thrust the iron box at him. “Carry this to Master Vey.”

He stared at it.

“Do not drop it.”

“I won’t.”

They stumbled into the corridor as the archive roof began to fall.

Outside, the courtyard had changed. Veyne’s marines had forced the inner arch and taken the prisoners from the harbor gate. They stood in a crescent before the keep, muskets leveled at Harl, the stable hands, garrison soldiers, and the fisher boy. Captain Harl knelt with one leg bent beneath him, blood running down his face. Veyne stood behind the prisoners, his breastplate shining wetly in the firelight.

“Stop the grain carts,” he called. “Anyone who moves one sack, I shoot a prisoner.”

The servants halted.

A sack slipped from a girl’s arms and burst across the stones. Grain scattered through the mud like pale sand.

Elianor stepped into the open with smoke behind her and the silver gown torn at the hem.

“Duke Veyne,” she called.

He turned. His eyes moved to the iron box in the servant’s arms, then to her face.

“Lady Marrow,” he said. “You have chosen your side.”

“I chose it when you began killing prisoners.”

“Your father has chosen correctly. Greyhaven will not be surrendered to a mob.”

“The estate has already been surrendered.”

“By a disinherited woman.”

The marines laughed. The prisoners did not. Harl lifted his head, and the fisher boy stared at Elianor with a terror so naked that it steadied her.

She walked forward until she stood between the grain carts and the guns.

“Captain Harl,” she said, loud enough for the yard to hear, “you accepted the surrender terms in the chapel. These prisoners are protected.”

“I remember,” Harl answered.

Veyne placed his sword against the fisher boy’s throat. “Then tell your people to lay down their weapons.”

“They are not my people,” Elianor said. “They are criminals carrying out a royal order.”

His expression hardened. “You believe papers will save you?”

“No. People will save the papers.”

Behind her, Bryn began moving again. One sack. Then another. Servants carried grain beneath the arcade while villagers lifted the iron box and ran it toward the chapel. Orren rang the bell—not the small signal from the wedding, but the great bell that called witnesses, mourners, and the whole hungry coast.

Veyne heard it and looked toward the sound.

The prisoners saw the distraction. Harl drove his shoulder into the marine nearest him. A stable hand kicked another’s knee. Muskets came up.

“Do not fire!” Elianor shouted.

But the yard erupted. Rebels struck from the side passage. Marines answered with a volley. The grain carts splintered, sacks burst, and white dust leapt into the rain. Men fell among the stores they had fought to preserve.

Elianor seized the fisher boy as he stumbled free and dragged him behind a cart. A bullet tore through the silver sleeve. Harl crawled toward the wounded stable hands while Bryn and Lysa pulled them beneath the arcade.

Above them, the archive windows glowed red. The eastern granary roof folded inward with a roar, sending a tower of flame into the storm.

For a moment Elianor watched the fire climb. Greyhaven’s wealth, its records, its stolen certainty—all of it could vanish before Tomas reached the yard.

Then she understood what Marrow had understood before she did: walls mattered, but stories decided what happened after walls fell. If the evidence burned, the crown could call the rebellion treason, the famine unfortunate, the dead uncounted. Veyne could return with more ships. Another Marrow could inherit the same justification. Another generation could be told that hunger had been necessary.

“Carry the books!” she cried. “Carry every page that survives!”

Master Vey appeared at the chapel steps, waving the steward’s seal. “The original grain books are safe!”

“Then get them beyond the gates!”

“Where?”

“Rill. Northwatch. Anywhere people can read them.”

A horn sounded from the harbor. Through the smoke came a voice shouting that the inner gate was breaking.

Tomas.

Elianor turned toward the sound, but Veyne’s marines closed around the prisoners again. The duke had regained his footing. His sword was red at the tip.

“You will not leave this yard,” he said.

Elianor looked from him to the burning keep, to the grain sacks passing through the rain, to the chapel bell shaking the air. She had wanted to reach Tomas. She had wanted to save the records. She had wanted, impossibly, to keep every person alive.

The battle had made the choices plain. She could not do all three alone.

“Bryn,” she said, without looking away from Veyne, “take the prisoners to the chapel.”

Bryn’s eyes widened. “And you?”

Elianor stepped toward the duke.

“I will keep him looking at me.”

Beyond the inner gate, iron groaned under the first blow of the rebel ram. The old order had begun to crack. Around Elianor, the servants carried grain and evidence through the smoke while the flames climbed higher, and she understood that Greyhaven’s true surrender would be decided not by who held the walls, but by what the living managed to carry out of them.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: In Greyhaven's smoke-filled inner courtyard beside the burning archive and granaries, still wearing her dead mother's torn wet silver gown and carrying the original crown orders beneath her bodice. She has recovered an iron box containing original depositions, land transfers, and Arlen Rusk's petition, while directing servants to move grain, records, and prisoners toward Saint Orra's Chapel. She has confronted Lord Marrow in the burning archive and Duke Veyne in the courtyard; Marrow fled or remains within the inner keep, and Veyne's marines still hold the courtyard and threaten prisoners. She is allied with Bryn, Master Vey, Orren, Harl, Tomas, villagers, servants, and the coastal resistance, though Tomas has not yet reached her. She knows Marrow deliberately destroyed evidence, Veyne is willing to kill captives, and the political survival of the old regime depends on what records escape. Her immediate goal is to keep Veyne occupied, save prisoners and remaining grain, and get the evidence beyond Greyhaven while exhausted, smoke-stung, frightened, and resolute.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: Inside or retreating through Greyhaven's inner keep after ordering the archives and granaries burned rather than surrendered. He confronted Elianor in the archive, defended the destruction as preventing rebels from possessing political weapons, and then barred her inside before escaping. He remains authoritarian, soot-stained, desperate to erase evidence and preserve the old regime's narrative, and opposed by Elianor, Tomas, the servants, villagers, and coastal rebels. He still possesses access to the inner keep and any loyal guards or remaining records there, but has lost public legitimacy and much of Greyhaven.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and the routes between the inner courtyard and lower gate, carrying the steward's seal and coordinating servants who move grain and surviving records. He knows Lord Marrow ordered the archive and granaries burned, Elianor recovered original land and Rusk records, and the original grain books survived. He is allied with Elianor, Bryn, Orren, Harl, villagers, servants, and Tomas's approaching rebels. His goal is to get the grain books and iron box beyond Greyhaven where coastal communities can read them, while protecting servants under fire. He is exhausted but active and exposed to Veyne's marines.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: Wounded and kneeling in Greyhaven's inner courtyard among prisoners seized by Duke Veyne's marines. His knee and face are injured, but he remains allied with Elianor and Tomas and remembers the chapel surrender terms. He knows Veyne threatens to execute him, the stable hands, garrison soldiers, and fisher boy, while Elianor is confronting Veyne and Bryn is trying to move the prisoners to safety. He is disarmed and physically vulnerable but resisting when openings appear, with command knowledge of Greyhaven's defenses.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and its steps, ringing the great bell as witness and coordinating refuge for prisoners, grain, records, and wounded people. He knows the archive and granary fires have begun, the surrender remains contested, and Elianor has recovered original evidence while servants carry supplies under fire. He is allied with Elianor, Vey, Bryn, Harl, villagers, and the coastal resistance. He possesses chapel authority, refuge space, burial records, and knowledge of the lectern panel; he is frightened but resolute and physically exposed to the battle.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: With the rebel assault force immediately outside or at the breaking inner gate of Greyhaven, having heard the fighting and Elianor's position but not yet reunited with her. He remains wounded, rain-soaked, exhausted, and committed to humane surrender terms. He knows Veyne's marines hold prisoners and that Marrow is destroying the archive and granaries; his goal is to break through, rescue Elianor and the prisoners, and prevent revenge while preserving the evidence. He is allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Pell, Harl, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance, and carries Mara's pistol with the fighters rallying around the Rusk name.

set.name: Ash
set.description: In or near the breached old stable at Greyhaven, alive but frightened amid smoke, fire, cannon, and gunshots. She remains a tall gray mare with a white blaze, raw rope wound beneath her jaw, swollen improving hind leg, and scars from mistreatment. Tomas briefly reassured her before continuing toward the inner gate. The stable and surrounding yard are exposed to the spreading fires, leaving her vulnerable to injury or evacuation.

set.name: Lysa
set.description: In Greyhaven's inner courtyard and arcade with Rill survivors, carrying a soot-streaked child and helping move wounded prisoners and grain away from the burning granaries. She remains exhausted, grieving, wary of Greyhaven, and cautiously committed to Elianor's surrender terms. She knows the archive and granaries are burning, Veyne's marines threaten captives, and evidence and supplies must reach the chapel and coastal villages. She is allied with Elianor, Bryn, Vey, Orren, Tomas, and the servants' network.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: In or beside Greyhaven's inner courtyard and arcade, her left hand bandaged and injured, directing servants and villagers to move grain and wounded prisoners toward Saint Orra's Chapel during Veyne's attack. She knows Elianor recovered the original archive evidence and is deliberately keeping Veyne occupied, while the marines threaten captives. She is loyal to Elianor and allied with Vey, Orren, Harl, Tomas, servants, and villagers. She possesses the copied collective-punishment orders and knowledge of servant routes, and is exhausted, frightened, and fiercely active.

set.name: Duke Alistair Veyne
set.description: In Greyhaven's inner courtyard with surviving marines, standing behind Captain Harl and other prisoners after seizing the inner arch. He has ordered that prisoners be shot if grain carts move or servants resist, and has confronted Elianor while the archive and granaries burn. He remains militaristic, contemptuous, and determined to preserve royal authority through terror; he knows Elianor holds or has recovered politically dangerous records and that Tomas's rebels are breaking the inner gate. He possesses armed marines and a bloodied sword but is surrounded by rebel pressure and a divided garrison.
Lord Marrow ordered the archive and granaries burned, and Elianor recovered an iron box containing original depositions, land transfers, and Arlen Rusk's signed petition before the archive collapsed.
Servants and villagers carried grain from the burning granaries toward the chapel while Master Vey confirmed that the original grain books had survived and were being moved beyond the estate.

Duke Veyne's marines seized the inner courtyard and threatened to execute Captain Harl and other prisoners; Elianor confronted Veyne and created an opening for Bryn and the rebels to rescue them during the ensuing clash.

The surviving archive records and original grain books must be carried beyond Greyhaven and distributed among coastal communities so the crown cannot dismiss the rebellion as treason or erase the famine evidence.
Elianor must keep Duke Veyne occupied in the courtyard while Bryn and the servants move prisoners, grain, and records toward the chapel under fire.

chapters.name: The Duke's Demand
chapters.content:
The courtyard had become a second sky, red and black beneath the storm.

Smoke rolled from the granaries in thick, oily folds, hiding the upper windows of Greyhaven and making the rain shine copper where it fell. Grain popped in the heat like small bones breaking. Men shouted from the inner arch. Somewhere beyond the walls, a cannon answered, and the stones under Elianor's shoes trembled.

She stood before Duke Alistair Veyne with her mother's silver gown torn at the hem and darkened with soot. The fabric clung coldly to her legs. Beneath the bodice, pressed against her ribs, lay the folded crown orders she had carried through fire, along with the knowledge that copies of them were already moving toward Saint Orra's Chapel. In her left hand she held the iron box rescued from the archive.

Veyne watched it as if it were a weapon.

Behind him, two marines dragged Captain Harl toward the wall. Harl's face was swollen, and blood ran from his brow into his beard. A stable hand lay motionless beside the overturned grain cart. Bryn was somewhere in the arcade with the prisoners, if the confusion had not swallowed her. Elianor had seen her last directing Lysa and three servants toward the chapel, one arm wrapped around a child, the other clutching a sack of grain.

“Set the box down,” Veyne said.

Elianor did not move. “Release Captain Harl.”

“You are in no position to bargain.”

“I am the only person here who can give you what you need.”

His expression altered—not softened, but sharpened. Veyne had always looked at her as one might inspect a harbor: measuring its depth, its defenses, the profit of possession. Now he looked at her as a door whose lock he had finally found.

“What I need,” he said, “is order.”

“Order is what brought us here.”

A marine struck Harl behind the knee. He fell hard against the wall. Elianor flinched, but did not look away from Veyne.

The duke drew a sheaf of papers from inside his coat. The pages were protected by waxed leather, though rain had spotted the edges. He tapped them against his palm.

“Your father has withdrawn into the keep. The rebels are at the inner gate. The garrison is uncertain, the servants are armed, and half the coast has decided that murder is a form of government.” He held out the papers. “Yet this can still be contained.”

“Contained?”

“You will sign a declaration.”

He gestured to a marine, who brought a small writing table from beneath the arcade. It was a wedding table, carved with the Marrow crest and still bearing a silver inkstand. One leg had been scorched black. The marine set it down between them and placed a blank sheet upon it.

Elianor stared at the paper. The rain struck its surface, leaving little dark flowers.

“What declaration?”

“That Tomas Rusk entered Greyhaven under false pretenses. That he cultivated your sympathy, exploited your distress, and seduced you into treason. That the grain thefts, the chapel disorder, and the assault upon this estate were organized through his criminal influence.”

For a moment the fire seemed to recede. She heard only the rain, the wet hiss of burning grain, and the pulse beating in her throat.

“You want me to say he used me.”

“I want you to state the truth in a form the ministers can use.”

“He taught me the names of the people your policies starved.”

“Manipulation.”

“He carried children out of floodwater.”

“Calculated theater.”

“He refused command until the council bound him to protect civilians and surrendering soldiers.”

Veyne's mouth curled. “Rebels learn the language of mercy when it helps them recruit. Your testimony will explain that you were deceived by a servant who discovered your loneliness and filled it with fantasies of justice.”

The word servant landed more heavily than the cannon.

Elianor looked beyond him. The courtyard was crowded with the cost of every convenient word. A marine held a musket toward the arcade. Two garrison men had lowered their weapons but remained frozen, unable to decide which oath still owned them. Lysa crouched behind an overturned trough, shielding a boy beneath her body. Grain rolled in the mud around them, each kernel pale and bright as a tooth.

“Sign,” Veyne said, “and I will recommend that the crown treat you as a coerced witness rather than a traitor. Greyhaven may be restored to you after the rebellion is crushed. Your servants will be spared if they submit. The villages—”

“The villages?”

He paused, calculating how much truth would persuade her.

“Those that surrender will be assessed for damages. Those that resist will be cleared.”

“Cleared.”

“Do not make a moral drama of military language.”

“You wrote it.”

Elianor set the iron box on the rain-slick stones and opened it.

The hinges gave a shriek. Inside lay the original depositions, their edges blackened but legible; land transfers bearing the seals of men who had profited from executions; and, beneath them, Arlen Rusk's petition. The parchment was stained, its corner torn away, but his signature remained. The ink had faded to brown. His name looked less like a monument than a hand reaching across fourteen years of darkness.

Veyne took one involuntary step forward.

“You understand what those are,” Elianor said.

“Forged rebel material.”

“The crown magistrate's seal is on the deposition.”

“Seals can be stolen.”

“Your ministers' orders are in my possession. They direct the seizure of rebel lands, the detention of families, and the conscription of children into military labor.”

A flicker passed through his eyes. Not shame. Not fear. Irritation that the evidence had survived.

“You have copies,” he said.

“And originals.”

“Where are the copies?”

“Beyond your reach.”

The duke moved so quickly that the nearest marine startled. He seized Elianor by the wrist and twisted her arm behind her back. Pain flashed white from her hand to her shoulder. The silver gown pulled tight across her ribs, crushing the papers beneath it.

“You mistake possession for safety,” he murmured beside her ear. “There are boats in the harbor. There are soldiers on the roads. I can burn every copy before dawn.”

“And if you kill me?”

“Then you become a martyr. I would prefer you useful.”

He released her with a shove. She staggered against the writing table. The inkstand fell and broke, spilling black across the blank declaration. It ran in branching lines, like veins beneath skin.

Veyne caught her elbow before she could fall.

“Listen to me,” he said. “Your lover has already made you an instrument. He has put a weapon in your hand and called it conscience. He has used your father's failures to turn you against your blood, your name, and the only structure that can prevent this coast from tearing itself apart.”

Elianor pulled free. “You speak of structure while your men kill prisoners.”

“They are not prisoners. They are insurgents.”

“You promised surrendering soldiers a hearing.”

“I promised nothing.”

“You heard me read the orders in the chapel.”

“I heard a frightened girl recite papers she did not understand.”

The old reflex rose in her—the urge to prove herself composed, educated, worthy of being heard. She felt it, and let it pass. Veyne wanted her to stand inside the language of the house, where every accusation could be turned into a breach of decorum. But the house was burning. Its vocabulary had become smoke.

“I understand them,” she said. “I understand that my father sold grain while Rill starved. I understand that he took the lands of families after their men were executed. I understand that the crown intends to punish children for the decisions of their parents. I understand that you came here not to preserve Avelune, but to preserve the right of men like you to decide who may live comfortably and who must disappear.”

The marines shifted. One looked toward the garrison soldiers. Another glanced at the chapel bell, which was ringing without rhythm now—Orren's warning, or a summons, or grief.

Veyne heard the uncertainty and answered it with violence.

He slapped Elianor across the face.

Her head snapped sideways. Heat bloomed along her cheek. For one breath she tasted blood.

“Sign,” he said.

She turned back slowly. “No.”

He struck her again, less from anger than from disbelief. The second blow sent her into the table. The declaration slid to the stones. The inkstand's broken neck cut through the paper, leaving a black slash over the blank place where her name should have been.

“Sign,” Veyne repeated. “Blame Rusk. Blame yourself if you like. Say that you were bewitched by a servant and the crown will call you repentant.”

Elianor heard Harl make a rough sound behind them. She heard Lysa whispering to the child. She heard the great granary roof collapse, and the courtyard filled with sparks.

On the ground near the wedding table lay a broken ceremonial sword.

It had been carried from the chapel as part of the marriage display, a polished relic of Marrow authority, its hilt worked in silver vines. During the first cannon strike it had fallen from its stand and snapped when a fleeing nobleman trampled it. The blade was broken halfway down, leaving a jagged edge bright with rain.

Elianor saw it. Veyne saw only her face.

He seized her gown at the shoulder and dragged her toward the table. The bodice tore. The crown orders slipped partly free beneath the fabric.

“Do you know what happens when the crown loses this coast?” he said. “Every lord who owns a wall will become a king. Every hungry crowd will call a torch a law. I am offering you a place on the side that survives.”

“You are offering me a name with which to bury the dead.”

“I am offering you your life.”

“No,” she said. “You are offering me the life you can control.”

He raised his hand again.

Elianor moved first.

She twisted beneath his grip, seized the broken sword with both hands, and drove its jagged end forward. The blade entered beneath his ribs with a dull resistance. Veyne's breath stopped. His eyes widened—not with pain at first, but astonishment that the object he had treated as ceremonial could still cut.

For an instant they remained joined: his hand clenched in the torn silver cloth, her hands locked around the hilt, rain coursing over them both.

Then she pulled away.

Veyne stumbled backward. Blood spread across his coat, dark and almost purple. He looked down at it as if someone else had been wounded. The marines shouted. One raised his musket toward Elianor, but a garrison soldier struck the barrel aside. The shot tore into the arcade roof.

Veyne fell to one knee.

“You…” he breathed.

Elianor stood over him, shaking so violently that the broken sword rattled in her hands. She had imagined killing no one. Even when she had hated her father, even when Veyne had spoken of villages as obstacles, death had remained an abstraction kept at the edge of every decision.

Now it was looking up at her.

“You attacked me,” she said, though the words sounded thin against the battle.

Veyne tried to rise. His fingers found the wet stones. “They will call you murderer.”

“They called us traitors before we answered them.”

“You think Rusk will forgive this?”

“Tomas does not own my conscience.”

The duke's face had gone gray. “The crown will come.”

“Then let it read what you tried to make me sign.”

He reached for the declaration, perhaps believing even then that paper could save him. His hand stopped short. Blood spilled through his fingers. He tipped sideways and collapsed beside the scorched wedding table.

The courtyard fell into a strange, ragged silence.

Not peace. Only the pause in which everyone understood that one kind of power had ended and no one yet knew what would replace it.

Elianor lowered the sword. The rain washed Veyne's blood from the broken edge, carrying it in thin red threads toward the drain.

“Captain Harl,” she called.

Harl lifted his head.

“Are you alive?”

“Insulted,” he rasped. “Which is not the same as dead.”

A laugh broke from somewhere near the arcade, sharp and frightened. It died quickly.

Elianor turned to the garrison soldiers. “Lay down your weapons. The surrender still stands. Anyone who kills a captive answers to me and to the people gathered at Saint Orra's.”

One marine spat at the ground. Another looked at Veyne's body, then at the burning walls. A third slowly lowered his musket.

From beyond the inner gate came a roar of voices. The rebels had broken through.

“Elianor!”

Tomas's voice.

She turned toward it, but smoke rolled between them. For one terrible moment she could not see him. She feared the voice had been memory, or hope sharpened into hallucination. Then figures surged through the arch—Pell first, bleeding from the temple, followed by Joren and a flood of rain-soaked fighters.

Tomas came behind them with Mara's pistol in one hand and blood darkening his sleeve. He stopped when he saw the duke on the stones and Elianor holding the broken sword.

Their eyes met across the wrecked courtyard.

He did not ask whether she had done it. He understood.

Elianor's strength broke at last. The sword slipped from her fingers and struck the stones.

Tomas crossed the distance between them, but stopped just before touching her, as though the whole courtyard still belonged to rules that could punish them for wanting one another.

She closed the distance herself.

His arms came around her. Smoke, rain, blood, and the familiar warmth of him gathered at once. Against his shoulder she whispered, “I would not sign.”

“I know.”

“I killed him.”

“I know that too.”

Behind them, the chapel bell continued to ring. Servants carried the last grain sacks through the arcade. The iron box lay open in the rain, its documents guarded now by Master Vey and Bryn. Above the courtyard, Greyhaven burned toward the sea.

Tomas held her tighter.

“Come,” he said. “We have to get the records out.”

Elianor looked once at Duke Veyne, once at the blank declaration stained with ink, and then at the keep where her father had vanished behind smoke and stone.

“Yes,” she said.

She picked up the iron box.

Together they turned toward the chapel, while the old order burned behind them.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: In Greyhaven's burning inner courtyard, reunited with Tomas after he broke through the inner gate. She remains in her dead mother's torn, wet silver gown, soot-streaked and bruised on the face and wrist, carrying the iron box of original depositions, land transfers, and Arlen Rusk's petition; the original crown orders remain beneath her bodice. She refused Duke Veyne's demand that she blame the rebellion on Tomas's seduction and criminal influence, denounced the crown's planned atrocities, and killed Veyne with the broken ceremonial sword when he attacked her. She is allied with Tomas, Bryn, Master Vey, Harl, Orren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. She knows Veyne is dead, some soldiers have lowered their weapons, the surrender terms still require protection of captives, and Lord Marrow remains in the inner keep. Her immediate goal is to get the evidence to the chapel and then confront or survive the final struggle in the keep; she is shaken by killing Veyne but resolute.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: In Greyhaven's inner courtyard or the route to Saint Orra's Chapel, guarding the opened iron box's original depositions, land transfers, and Arlen Rusk petition while coordinating servants carrying grain and records. He knows Veyne is dead, Elianor refused the false declaration, Tomas has returned, and Lord Marrow remains in the inner keep with the last threats to evidence. He is allied with Elianor, Tomas, Bryn, Orren, Harl, villagers, servants, and the coastal resistance. Exhausted and exposed to fire and combat, his immediate goal is to get the originals and surviving grain books safely beyond the keep's reach.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: Alive but injured in Greyhaven's inner courtyard after being held prisoner by Veyne's marines. His knee and face are badly hurt, and he remains disarmed and physically vulnerable, but he is conscious and grimly responsive. He witnessed Veyne's failed coercion of Elianor and death by the broken ceremonial sword. He remains allied with Elianor and Tomas and knows the surrender terms must continue despite the collapse of Veyne's command. His immediate concern is protecting the prisoners and helping the garrison choose surrender rather than revenge; he possesses command knowledge of the inner defenses but may need assistance to move.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: In Greyhaven's inner courtyard with Elianor after leading the rebel assault through the harbor and inner gates. He is rain-soaked, exhausted, and wounded with blood darkening one sleeve, but alive and committed to humane surrender terms. He has seen Veyne dead and understands that Elianor killed him in self-defense; he does not judge her. He remains allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Pell, Bryn, Vey, Harl, Orren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance, and carries Mara's pistol while fighters rally around the Rusk name. His immediate goal is to escort Elianor and the iron box to Saint Orra's Chapel, preserve the evidence, rescue prisoners, and reach the inner keep before Marrow destroys the last records.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: In or near Greyhaven's inner courtyard and arcade, alive with her left hand bandaged and injured, helping move prisoners, children, grain, and surviving records toward Saint Orra's Chapel. She witnessed or learned of Elianor's refusal and Veyne's death, and now helps guard the opened iron box and evidence alongside Master Vey. She is allied with Elianor, Tomas, Vey, Orren, Harl, Lysa, servants, and villagers. Exhausted and frightened but fiercely active, she aims to preserve the records and keep captives safe while the rebels push toward the inner keep.

set.name: Duke Alistair Veyne
set.description: Dead in Greyhaven's inner courtyard beside the scorched wedding table. Elianor killed him with the broken ceremonial sword after he assaulted her while trying to force her to sign a false declaration blaming Tomas and the rebellion. His surviving marines and nearby garrison soldiers witnessed his death; some lowered their weapons or turned aside, while others remain dangerous. His body, bloodied sword wound, and declaration papers lie amid rain, smoke, and burning grain.

Duke Veyne attempted to force Elianor to sign a declaration blaming the rebellion on Tomas's seduction and criminal influence, but she refused and denounced the crown's atrocities before him and his troops.
When Veyne attacked Elianor, she killed him with the broken ceremonial sword from the wedding display; the shock caused some garrison soldiers and marines to lower or turn aside their weapons.

Tomas reached the burning courtyard after the inner breach and reunited with Elianor, accepting without reproach that she had killed Veyne; they turned together toward Saint Orra's Chapel to preserve the surviving evidence.

After Veyne's death, Elianor and Tomas must reach the inner keep while preserving the surrender terms, rescuing remaining prisoners, and dividing forces between the last archives and Elianor's safety.

chapters.name: The Inner Keep
chapters.content:
The first marine reached Elianor before Tomas could cross the courtyard.

He came through the smoke with a boarding axe in one hand and a strip of bloodied wedding cloth tied around his arm. Another seized her from behind. The iron box struck the stones, slid through soot and rainwater, and stopped beneath the overturned wedding table.

“Take her!” the marine captain shouted. “The duke ordered her kept alive.”

Elianor twisted hard enough to tear the sleeve of her mother’s gown. The broken ceremonial sword was still in her hand, though its hilt had become slick with rain and Veyne’s blood. She struck backward with the pommel. The man behind her grunted, but his grip tightened around her ribs.

“Tomas!”

His name vanished beneath the roar of the granary roof collapsing.

A wall of sparks lifted into the storm. For one breath the courtyard became a red, wind-torn chamber, every figure cut sharp against the fire: servants carrying sacks toward the chapel, soldiers lowering weapons, rebels forcing open the inner passage, and Tomas in the middle of it all with Mara’s pistol in one hand and a sword in the other.

Then the smoke closed.

Tomas saw only the silver of Elianor’s gown disappearing between two marines.

He fired. The pistol’s report struck the courtyard like a hammer. The marine holding Elianor staggered, not dead but blinded by the powder and flame. She drove her heel into his knee. His arm opened. Elianor dropped, rolled beneath the blade of the second man, and came up on one hand.

Tomas was running toward her.

Three marines came between them.

The first raised a musket. Tomas turned aside as it fired, and the ball tore through his coat near the shoulder. He felt heat, then wetness, but no time to measure the wound. He caught the musket barrel, wrenched it downward, and struck the marine beneath the jaw with the guard of his sword.

The second marine slashed at his back. Pell intercepted the blow. Steel rang. Pell’s wounded arm shook, but he locked the blades together and drove his forehead into the man’s face.

“Go!” Pell shouted. “Get to her!”

The third marine had Elianor by the wrist.

She brought the broken sword across his forearm. He cried out and released her, but a fourth man seized the chain of her gown and dragged her toward the black archway leading into the keep.

Tomas reached the place where she had fallen. He saw the iron box beneath the table and kicked it toward Bryn, who was limping through the smoke with a sack of grain over one shoulder.

“Chapel!” he shouted. “Take it to Orren!”

Bryn dropped the sack. “What about her?”

“I’m going after her.”

“You’ll need more than yourself.”

“I know.”

Mara’s voice came from behind the burning granary wall. “Then stop trying to be one man.”

She emerged with Joren Pell and six Northwatch fighters. Mara’s gray hair was loose, her coat blackened at the hem, and a cut along her temple had filled one eye with blood. She looked first at Elianor, then at the keep, whose narrow windows glowed with the uncertain light of fires inside.

“Joren,” she said, “take the inner stair. No killing unless they refuse surrender.”

Joren lifted his sword. “And if they refuse?”

“Then disarm them. If they keep fighting, stop them. Those are not the same thing.”

His mouth tightened, but he nodded.

“Mara,” Tomas said, “the records—”

“Vey has the grain books moving toward the chapel. Orren has the copies and the prisoners. The originals are with her.” She pointed toward the arch. “You get Elianor. We get the rest.”

Another shot cracked from the keep. A rebel beside Mara spun and fell against the stones.

Mara did not flinch. “Go.”

Tomas ran.

The inner archway had once been painted white. Smoke had turned it gray. Beyond it lay a corridor wide enough for two carts, descending first toward the old armory and then rising into the keep. The marines had barred the inner doors with a length of timber. Elianor was on the far side of them, struggling between two soldiers.

Her silver gown snagged on a hinge. She tore free, leaving a long strip of fabric behind.

“Let me go!”

The marine captain struck her across the face. The blow snapped her head sideways. Tomas saw the mark redden beneath the soot.

He entered the corridor without slowing.

The captain turned. “Rusk.”

The name traveled through the smoke.

One of the marines stared at him. “Rusk’s son?”

“Yes,” Tomas said.

The captain brought up his pistol. “Then you can die as your father did.”

Tomas shot first. The ball struck the captain’s weapon and broke his fingers around it. The man screamed. Tomas crossed the space between them and drove his shoulder into his chest. They went down against the wall.

The marine holding Elianor lifted his sword to her throat.

“Stop!”

Tomas froze.

The man’s breath came fast. He was young—too young, Elianor thought, to have learned how easily a uniform could turn fear into permission. His eyes moved between Tomas’s bloodied face and the woman in the torn silver gown.

“Put down the sword,” he said.

Tomas let his blade fall.

For one instant, the corridor held still.

Then a bell rang in the outer courtyard. Once. Twice. Three times.

Orren’s signal from the chapel.

The young marine glanced toward the sound. Elianor drove the heel of her hand into his nose. His grip loosened. She seized his wrist and twisted. Tomas lunged, caught the falling sword, and struck the wall beside the man’s head rather than his neck.

“Live,” Tomas said. “You can still choose what you are.”

The marine collapsed, clutching his face.

Elianor stepped toward Tomas, but he caught her before she could fall. Her knees had begun to tremble.

“You’re hurt,” she said.

“Not enough.”

“That is not an answer.”

“Later.”

“There may not be a later.”

He touched the bruise on her cheek with two fingers, then drew his hand away as if the corridor itself might accuse them. “There will be if we move.”

A heavy door slammed somewhere above.

Lord Marrow’s voice carried down the stairwell.

“Kill them.”

It was not shouted. That made it worse. The command descended through the keep with the calm certainty of a law already written.

“Kill every rebel who enters. Burn the remaining papers. No surrender is to be accepted.”

Elianor looked at Tomas. “He’s going to the archive.”

“He knows what survived.”

“And the iron box?”

“Bryn has it.”

“Then we have to trust them.”

Tomas looked toward the stairs, where the light of the upper keep flickered against the stone. “I have trusted you with my life since before I knew how to say your name.”

She took his hand. “Then trust me now.”

They climbed.

The first landing opened onto the old armory. Racks of pikes stood empty along the walls, and the floor was strewn with shields bearing the Marrow crest. Two household guards waited behind them, neither in armor. One carried a crossbow; the other held a kitchen cleaver.

Tomas raised his empty hand. “The surrender still stands.”

The guard with the cleaver laughed shakily. “Lord Marrow says there is no surrender.”

“Lord Marrow has been burning his own records.”

“He is still lord here.”

“No,” Elianor said. “He is a man hiding behind a wall.”

The crossbowman’s aim shifted toward her.

Tomas moved in front of her. “Put it down.”

The guard’s finger tightened.

A stone struck his wrist from the side passage. The crossbow fell. Captain Harl limped into the armory with a marine’s short sword in one hand and blood running from his brow. Behind him came four garrison soldiers who had removed the white cords from their sleeves.

“Those who want to live,” Harl said, “stand away from the weapons.”

The guard with the cleaver looked at him. “Captain—”

“I am no longer asking.”

The man let the cleaver fall.

Harl leaned against a rack, breathing hard. “The west stair is blocked. Joren is bringing the ram to the inner doors, but Marrow has men above and below. He’s sent the loyalists toward the archive.”

“How many?” Tomas asked.

“Enough to make a fight of it.” Harl looked at Elianor’s torn gown and the blood on her sword. “Veyne’s marines are breaking. Some are fleeing toward the harbor. Others think they can buy forgiveness by killing everyone they find.”

“Then give them a way to surrender,” Elianor said.

Harl’s expression altered—not softened, exactly, but steadied. “I’ll hold this landing. Take the east stair. It reaches the archive passage.”

Tomas nodded. “Harl, if Marrow reaches the records—”

“He won’t.”

The captain’s knee buckled. One of the disarmed soldiers caught him.

“Captain,” Elianor said.

“I can still stand.”

“You can still command,” she answered. “Those are different things.”

For the first time, Harl almost smiled. “Your father taught you that?”

“No. He taught me the opposite.”

A crash shook dust from the ceiling.

Harl pushed away from the soldier. “Go.”

They took the east stair. It narrowed between walls carved with the names of Marrow ancestors. Elianor had passed those names all her life without reading them. Now they seemed less like history than a procession of locked doors.

At the second turn, they found a body in a red household coat. The man had been stabbed through the chest. Beside him lay a ring of keys and a bundle of papers, already smoking at the edges.

Elianor crouched and snatched up the papers. Most were household inventories. One was a list of names.

Children.

Ages beside them. Ten. Eleven. Twelve.

Military labor assignments.

Her stomach tightened.

“Take it,” Tomas said.

She folded the list into the lining of her gown. “There are always more.”

“Then we save what we can.”

“Is that what you tell yourself?”

He looked at her.

“When you think of your father?” she asked. “When you think of all the people you couldn’t save?”

His face closed, but his hand remained around hers. “No. I tell myself that the dead do not need my guilt. The living need my work.”

Above them, someone shouted. A door opened. Firelight spilled down the stair.

They reached the archive passage.

The great iron doors stood ajar. Smoke poured through the gap, thick and oily. Inside, shelves burned in rows. The last records had been dragged into the center of the room and piled around a brazier. Lord Marrow stood beside them in ancestral armor.

Elianor stopped.

She had seen the armor in portraits: blackened plates, a silver sea-dragon on the breast, the Marrow crest worked into the shoulders. In life it made him look less like her father than like the fortress itself—hard, elevated, built to withstand weather by forcing weather upon everyone beneath it.

In his right hand he carried a long sword with a dark notch near the guard.

Tomas went still.

The blade had been named in the archive records. It was the sword used at Arlen Rusk’s execution.

Marrow saw recognition pass between them.

“So,” he said. “The servant has finally come home.”

Elianor stepped forward. “Put down the sword.”

“Your concern is touching.” Marrow glanced at her ruined gown. “Did Veyne fail to make you obedient?”

“He failed to survive his own violence.”

“And now you stand with murderers.”

“I stand with the people you starved, robbed, and condemned.”

Marrow’s eyes shifted to Tomas. “You should have remained nameless. Your father’s name was a disease. It infected every fool who heard it and believed that order could be negotiated with.”

“Arlen asked you to keep your oath,” Tomas said.

“He asked me to surrender a province to men who mistook hunger for a political argument.”

“He asked for representation.”

“He asked for weakness.”

“He asked you not to execute him.”

Marrow raised the sword slightly. “And yet here I am, carrying the consequence of mercy refused.”

Behind him, a loyal guard thrust a torch into the pile of records. Flames climbed the dry paper.

Elianor moved toward the brazier.

Marrow’s guards leveled weapons.

Tomas stepped in front of her. “You said no surrender?”

“I said no surrender to rebels.” Marrow’s gaze hardened. “You are not rebels anymore. You are an invading army. And she is a traitor who has placed this house in their hands.”

“Greyhaven was never yours to place,” Elianor said. “It was built by hands you never named.”

The fire snapped. Somewhere beyond the archive, the inner doors boomed under Joren’s ram. The sound rolled through the keep like a second heartbeat.

Mara’s voice rose from the stair below. “Tomas!”

He looked back.

Mara stood at the foot of the passage with Joren, Pell, and the fighters from the courtyard. Pell was bleeding from the scalp. Joren carried the ram’s iron hook as a club. Behind them, servants and two garrison soldiers dragged a wounded marine away from the smoke.

“The chapel has the grain books,” Mara called. “Orren has the prisoners. But the west archive room is sealed, and there may be more originals inside.”

Tomas glanced at the burning pile, then at Elianor.

Marrow smiled faintly. “There. Choose, Rusk. The woman or the proof.”

“No,” Tomas said. “We choose both.”

He pointed to Joren. “Break the west room.”

“To save the records?”

“To save whoever is trapped in it.”

Then to Mara: “Get the surviving papers out through the stair and send them to Orren.”

“And you?”

Tomas drew his sword. “I take Elianor.”

Marrow lifted the execution blade.

The guards advanced. The archive doors filled with smoke, fire, and steel. Elianor tightened her grip on the broken ceremonial sword and moved beside Tomas, shoulder to shoulder.

For the first time since Greyhaven’s gates had opened, Lord Marrow looked uncertain.

Then the keep began to fall around them.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: In Greyhaven's inner archive passage with Tomas, wearing her dead mother's torn, wet silver gown, soot-streaked and bruised on the face and wrist, carrying the broken ceremonial sword and a folded list of children marked for military labor hidden in her gown. Bryn has taken the iron box of original depositions, land transfers, and Arlen Rusk's petition toward Saint Orra's Chapel; the original crown orders remain beneath Elianor's bodice. She killed Veyne in self-defense, reached the inner keep after surviving his marines, and now faces Lord Marrow in ancestral armor beside the burning records. She is allied with Tomas, Mara, Joren, Pell, Bryn, Master Vey, Harl, Orren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. She knows Marrow has ordered no surrender and is destroying evidence. Her immediate goal is to stop him, preserve the remaining records, keep surrender terms from collapsing, and survive the final struggle.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: In Greyhaven's burning archive passage, wearing ancestral black armor and carrying the sword associated with Arlen Rusk's execution. He has ordered remaining loyal guards to kill rebels, rejected surrender, and begun burning the last records rather than allowing the coastal resistance to possess them. He knows Elianor has openly rejected him, Tomas is Arlen Rusk's surviving son, and the evidence of his family's crimes is being carried toward the chapel. He is opposed by Elianor, Tomas, Mara, Joren, servants, villagers, and the resistance, with only a shrinking group of loyal guards around him. He remains authoritarian, armed, desperate, and increasingly isolated; his immediate goal is to destroy the archives and kill or defeat the people confronting him.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: Moving between Greyhaven's inner routes and Saint Orra's Chapel with servants and surviving grain records, exhausted and exposed to smoke and combat. He knows Bryn is carrying the iron box's original depositions, land transfers, and Arlen Rusk petition toward the chapel, while Marrow is burning the remaining archive and the original grain books are being protected. He is allied with Elianor, Tomas, Bryn, Harl, Orren, Mara, Joren, villagers, servants, and the coastal resistance. His immediate goal is to get the grain books and surviving evidence beyond Marrow's reach and preserve the factual record of Greyhaven's crimes.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: Holding the old armory landing inside Greyhaven with four garrison soldiers who have abandoned the white cords, injured in the knee and face and leaning on a weapon for support. He has maintained Elianor's surrender terms, disarmed two household guards, and ordered soldiers to stand away from weapons rather than die for Marrow. He knows Veyne's command is breaking, Marrow has ordered no surrender, and Tomas and Elianor have reached the archive passage. He is allied with Elianor, Tomas, Mara, Joren, Master Vey, Orren, servants, villagers, and surrendering soldiers. His immediate goal is to hold the landing, protect prisoners and wavering soldiers, and prevent retaliatory killing while the final fight proceeds.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and its steps, coordinating refuge, prisoners, wounded people, grain, and surviving records while the great bell signals the resistance. He knows Tomas and Elianor have reached the inner keep, Bryn is bringing the iron box, and Marrow is burning the last archive materials while refusing surrender. He is allied with Elianor, Tomas, Vey, Bryn, Harl, Mara, Joren, villagers, servants, and the coastal resistance. He possesses chapel authority, refuge space, burial records, and the lectern; his immediate goal is to receive and protect the evidence, keep prisoners alive, and preserve the public surrender terms.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: In Greyhaven's inner archive passage beside Elianor, rain-soaked, exhausted, and wounded near the shoulder with blood darkening his coat. He carries Mara's pistol, a sword, and the public burden of being Arlen Rusk's son, while refusing hereditary authority or revenge. He fought through the courtyard, rescued Elianor from surviving marines, and ordered a young marine spared when he laid down his weapon. He is allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Pell, Bryn, Master Vey, Harl, Orren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. He knows Marrow carries the execution sword used against Arlen, has ordered rebels killed, and is burning the records; Mara and Joren are dividing forces to save people and archives. His immediate goal is to protect Elianor, stop Marrow, save records and trapped civilians, and uphold humane surrender.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: Moving from Greyhaven's inner courtyard toward Saint Orra's Chapel, alive but exhausted with her left hand bandaged and injured. She abandoned a grain sack to take the iron box containing the original depositions, land transfers, and Arlen Rusk's petition after Tomas ordered her to save it. She knows Tomas and Elianor are entering the keep, Marrow is burning records, and the chapel must become the evidence's refuge. She is allied with Elianor, Tomas, Vey, Orren, Harl, Mara, Joren, Lysa, servants, and villagers. Her immediate goal is to deliver and help guard the originals while keeping grain and prisoners safe.

set.name: Pell
set.description: At the inner archive passage with Mara, Joren, Tomas, and the coastal fighters, broad-shouldered, injured, bleeding from the scalp but dependable and active. He helped Tomas reach Elianor through the courtyard and now supports the divided effort to save the west archive room and preserve records. He knows Marrow has ordered no surrender and the keep is collapsing around the confrontation. He is allied with Tomas, Mara, Joren, Elianor, Harl, Vey, Bryn, Orren, servants, villagers, and the resistance. His immediate goal is to protect the fighters and assist in rescuing anyone trapped while limiting revenge.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: Inside Greyhaven's inner archive passage at the foot of the stair with Joren, Pell, and coastal fighters, gray-haired, bloodied at the temple, and directing the divided resistance. She has ordered Joren to break open the sealed west archive room and is sending surviving papers toward Orren while Tomas protects Elianor. She knows Marrow carries Arlen's execution sword, has rejected surrender, and is burning evidence. She is allied with Tomas, Elianor, Joren, Pell, Vey, Bryn, Orren, and the coastal resistance. Her immediate goal is to save trapped people and records, maintain civilian protection, and prevent the Rusk name from becoming an excuse for revenge.

set.name: Joren Pell
set.description: At the inner archive passage with Mara, Pell, and coastal fighters, injured but active and carrying the iron hook of the ram as a club. He has been ordered to break open the sealed west archive room and rescue anyone inside while avoiding unnecessary killing. He knows Marrow and loyal guards are defending the burning archive and that Tomas and Elianor are confronting them. He is allied with Tomas, Mara, Pell, Elianor, Harl, Vey, Bryn, Orren, and the resistance. His immediate goal is to breach the west room, save civilians and records, and support the final advance under humane surrender terms.

Surviving Veyne marines dragged Elianor toward the inner keep, but Tomas fought through the courtyard and reached her; Bryn received the iron box containing the original depositions, land transfers, and Arlen Rusk petition for transport to Saint Orra's Chapel.

Mara, Joren, and Tomas divided the resistance inside the keep: Tomas went to protect Elianor, while Mara and Joren directed fighters and servants toward the chapel, the burning records, and the sealed west archive room.

Lord Marrow appeared in ancestral armor carrying the execution sword used against Arlen Rusk, ordered his remaining loyalists to kill rebels and reject surrender, and began burning the last records in the archive passage.

Captain Harl held the armory landing with disarmed garrison soldiers while maintaining Elianor's humane surrender terms, and Tomas and Elianor reached the archive passage where Marrow and his guards prepared for the final confrontation.

Elianor, Tomas, and the coastal fighters must survive the confrontation in the archive passage, prevent Lord Marrow from destroying the remaining records, and complete the rescue of anyone trapped in the west archive room.
The surrender terms must be preserved inside the keep while loyal guards and surviving marines are offered a chance to lay down their weapons rather than being killed in retaliation.

chapters.name: The Battlements
chapters.content:
The keep began to fall around them.

A beam gave way somewhere beyond the archive, and the floor lurched beneath their feet. Burning pages rose in a black spiral. One of Marrow’s guards stumbled; Mara’s fighters surged forward, not with a roar but with the terrible efficiency of people who had learned that noise did not stop blades.

“Hold!” Tomas shouted. “Those who lay down their weapons live.”

A loyal guard answered with a crossbow bolt.

It struck the stone beside Tomas’s head. Elianor did not think. She caught his sleeve and dragged him sideways as Mara fired from the stair. The guard dropped behind the brazier, his weapon clattering among the burning records.

“Out!” Mara called. “The roof is going!”

Marrow retreated through a narrow door at the back of the archive. Two guards followed him. The third, a boy with a cut across his mouth, lowered his sword and raised both hands.

“I surrender,” he said.

Pell seized his weapon and pushed him toward the stair. “Then keep your head down.”

The boy obeyed.

Joren and two fighters reached the west archive door. They drove the iron hook into its seam. From within came a muffled cry.

“Someone’s alive!” Joren shouted.

“Break it,” Mara said.

Elianor started after Marrow, but Tomas caught her hand.

“He wants us separated.”

“He is going to the battlements.”

“How do you know?”

“Because there is nowhere else left for him to go.”

A window exploded inward. Wind tore through the archive, lifting sparks and the silver threads of Elianor’s gown. Beyond the window, the sea was a heaving darkness veined with white. The storm had come back upon them, driving rain through the broken opening.

Marrow’s door slammed above.

Tomas looked toward Mara. “The records.”

“Go,” she said. “I’ll bring what we can.”

“And the surrender?” Elianor asked.

Mara’s blood-streaked face turned stern. “It remains, unless the dead make a different law. We’ll hold the stair.”

Tomas nodded once. He and Elianor ran through the rear door.

The passage beyond was narrow and unlit. They climbed a spiral stair that wound through the keep’s thickness, their shoulders scraping damp stone. Smoke followed them upward. Behind, the sounds of fighting diminished: the crash of Joren’s hook, shouts cut short, Mara’s voice repeating the terms of surrender as if words could be mortar.

Elianor’s lungs burned. Her wrist throbbed where the marine had gripped it, and the bruise on her cheek had begun to swell. The folded list of children pressed against her ribs beneath the gown.

Tomas climbed ahead of her, one hand against the wall. Blood had spread across the shoulder of his coat, dark even in the weak light.

“You’re losing too much,” she said.

“I’ve had worse.”

“That is not a measure.”

He turned on the stair. “No, it is the only measure I have at present.”

She reached him and pressed her palm over the wound. He flinched despite himself.

“Then borrow mine,” she said. “I am frightened enough for both of us.”

For a breath, the storm and the battle fell away. His forehead touched hers.

“I thought I had lost you in the courtyard.”

“You did not.”

“I saw the silver vanish.”

“And I saw you come after me.”

“I would have come through the sea.”

“You nearly came through the fire.”

Her laugh broke strangely, almost a sob. He kissed her once, quickly, with the taste of rain and blood between them.

Then the stair above filled with light.

Marrow stood in the open doorway at the top, sword in hand.

“Enough,” he said.

Tomas pushed Elianor behind him. Marrow did not attack. He stepped backward through the doorway, toward the battlements.

“Come and hear the truth before you die,” he said.

“Your truth has burned half the house,” Elianor answered.

“Then you have seen what becomes of sentiment.”

He disappeared into the storm.

Tomas raised his sword. “Stay here.”

“No.”

“Elianor—”

“You are not facing him alone.”

“He carries the execution sword.”

“And I carry the reason he fears it.”

They reached the top together.

The battlements ran along the seaward face of Greyhaven, slick with rain and glazed with blown ash. The parapet had broken in three places. Through the gaps, the sea plunged away beneath them, black water smashing itself white against the cliffs. Signal fires burned along the distant headland, reduced by the rain to trembling red eyes.

Marrow stood beside the central merlon. His ancestral armor gleamed wetly. The sword in his hand looked almost black, except where lightning revealed its edge.

Below, the harbor raged. The chain boom had fallen. Fishing boats and burning transports rolled together in the waves. Farther inland, the lower yard shone with scattered torches. Greyhaven’s walls, once so absolute, had become a series of openings through which the night entered.

Marrow looked past them toward the sea.

“You have brought this upon the house,” he said.

Elianor stepped onto the battlement. “The house was already burning before we came.”

“I kept it standing.”

“You kept its doors shut.”

“I kept you alive.”

“You kept me ignorant.”

Lightning flared behind the clouds. For an instant his face was naked of armor: gray, exhausted, and much older than the man who had walked into the chapel that morning.

Then the hardness returned.

“You believe the people will thank you,” he said. “They will not. They will take the grain, then the rooms, then one another’s throats. Men like Tomas will promise equality until someone asks who commands the army. Then they will discover that blood is the oldest argument.”

Tomas moved beside Elianor. “I have promised no throne.”

“You have not needed to. Your name has done it for you.”

Below them, from the inner keep, a cry rose and was swallowed by thunder.

Marrow pointed the sword at Tomas. “Arlen Rusk was a traitor.”

Tomas’s face tightened. “You executed him after withdrawing the offer to negotiate.”

“He raised armed men against the crown.”

“He raised petitions before he raised men.”

“He gathered villages into a refusal of lawful levy.”

“Lawful?” Tomas’s voice carried over the rain. “You took half the fishing boats for the western fleet. You seized winter stores. You sent soldiers to make examples of families who could not pay. Arlen asked for limits. He asked that villages choose their own representatives. He asked you to keep your word.”

Marrow’s sword trembled, though whether from age or fury Elianor could not tell.

“Your father understood only force,” he said.

“He understood what force was doing to people.”

“He would have torn Avelune apart.”

“No. You tore it apart and called the pieces peace.”

Elianor looked at the walls below. Smoke drifted from the granaries. In the courtyard, people moved among the flames carrying the wounded. Beyond the gate, the villagers who had once begged for entry were now directing the battle inside the fortress.

“Look,” she said to her father. “The world you preserved is already destroyed.”

Marrow’s eyes found hers.

“For them,” she continued. “It was destroyed years ago. At Rill’s empty mill. In the chapel when Perrin, Cal, and Miri died beneath your ration order. In every cottage where a child was marked for labor because you needed soldiers more than you needed children. You called it preservation because you stood on the dry side of the wall.”

His jaw worked.

“You speak like a rebel.”

“I speak like your daughter.”

“You are no daughter of mine if you would hand Greyhaven to men who will destroy its name.”

“I am your daughter because I know exactly what you taught me. I know the names of the dead. I know which rooms were warm while the lower village flooded. I know how many times you said that suffering was necessary when you meant that it was convenient.”

Marrow lifted the sword.

Tomas stepped forward, but Elianor held out an arm.

“Not yet.”

Marrow laughed once. There was no amusement in it. “You think you can stand between us.”

“I am already between you.”

“No. You are between a man and the consequence of his father’s treason.”

Tomas looked at the blade. “You carried that sword all these years?”

“It was the sword of my office.”

“It was the sword that killed Arlen.”

“It killed a traitor.”

“It killed a man who believed your word.”

Marrow’s gaze shifted over Tomas’s face, searching perhaps for the child he had failed to find fourteen years before. “You inherited his curse.”

Tomas took another step. Rain ran from his hair into his eyes.

“I inherited his grief,” he said. “The curse was yours.”

A gust struck the battlement. Elianor caught the merlon with one hand. Marrow’s cloak snapped behind him like a torn flag.

“What do you know of inheritance?” Marrow demanded. “You were hidden in a stable, fed by strangers, taught to curry horses. You have no land, no court, no army. Your father left you a name and a grave.”

“He left me the knowledge that people can be afraid and still refuse to kneel.”

“He left you nothing.”

“He left me people who remembered.”

“And what have they remembered?” Marrow shouted at last. “A failure! A dead commander! Villages that could not defend themselves! I offered them order. I built walls against the sea and the crown alike. I kept ships from taking this coast. I paid soldiers to stand between these families and every worse thing beyond them.”

Elianor stared at him. “You paid them with other families.”

“I made choices.”

“You chose who would suffer.”

“That is what rule is.”

“No,” Tomas said. “That is what power tells itself when it cannot bear to call its own fear by name.”

For the first time, Marrow looked directly at him—not at Arlen’s son, not at a rebel banner, but at the servant who had once stood in Greyhaven’s stable with a frightened mare and patient hands.

“You think mercy will govern?”

“No. People will govern. Mercy will be one of the things they demand of one another.”

“You will be swept aside.”

“Perhaps.” Tomas glanced at Elianor. “But no execution will erase what happened here.”

The words entered the storm and seemed to remain there.

From below came the tolling of Saint Orra’s bell. Once. Twice. Then a long peal. The sound carried across the sea, over the burning harbor, through Greyhaven’s open gates.

Surrender, Elianor thought. Or witness.

Marrow heard it too. His grip closed around the execution sword.

“I gave this house everything,” he said more quietly.

“You gave it everyone else,” Elianor replied.

His expression broke—not into repentance, but into the last shape of refusal.

He turned the sword toward Tomas.

Elianor moved fully between them.

“Father,” she said, “if you raise that blade, you will have to pass through me first.”

Marrow’s eyes rested on her silver gown, torn nearly to the knee, on the blood at her cheek, on the broken sword hanging uselessly at her side.

“You would die for him?”

“No,” she said. “I would live against you.”

Marrow came forward.

Tomas reached for her arm. “Elianor, move.”

She did not.

The old lord raised Arlen Rusk’s sword. Tomas shifted his weight, ready to disarm rather than strike. Wind screamed through the broken battlement. Far below, the sea opened its white mouth against the cliff.

And between father and beloved, with the whole ruined world behind her, Elianor waited for the blade to fall.

For a moment, none of them moved. The sword hovered above the narrow space between their bodies, and the rain ran along its fuller in bright threads. Elianor could hear Tomas breathing behind her, fast and controlled, and beneath that the deep pulse of the sea. She remembered the first time he had placed her hand against Ash’s neck and told her that frightened creatures mistook force for safety. Her father had made a kingdom of that mistake.

“Look at me,” she said.

Marrow’s eyes flicked to hers.

“Not at the walls. Not at the crown. At me.”

He did. She saw the father who had once lifted her onto a pony, the man who had taught her the names of heraldic birds, and the ruler who had measured every human life against the survival of his house. They were not separate men. That was the grief of it. Love had not been false; it had simply been made to kneel before power.

“I will not let you call this preservation,” she said. “Not when the truth is standing here with us.”

Tomas’s hand closed around the hilt of his sword.

Marrow’s face hardened again.

Then he stepped across the line she had drawn.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: On Greyhaven's storm-lashed seaward battlements above the sea, wearing her dead mother's torn, wet silver gown, soot-streaked and bruised on the face and wrist, with the folded list of children marked for military labor hidden in her gown and the broken ceremonial sword at her side. She escaped the burning archive with Tomas and now stands physically between Tomas and Lord Marrow, who has raised Arlen Rusk's execution sword. She killed Veyne in self-defense, renounced her inheritance, and remains allied with Tomas, Mara, Joren, Pell, Bryn, Master Vey, Harl, Orren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. She knows Marrow's crimes, his refusal of surrender, and the truth of Arlen's execution. Her immediate goal is to prevent Marrow from killing Tomas, survive the confrontation, preserve the surrender terms, and ensure the remaining records and trapped civilians are saved. She is exhausted, frightened, resolute, and has finally rejected her father's definition of preservation.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: On Greyhaven's storm-lashed seaward battlements, wearing ancestral black armor and carrying the sword used in Arlen Rusk's execution. He fled the burning archive after ordering records destroyed and loyalists to reject surrender. He has confronted Elianor and Tomas, called Arlen a traitor and Tomas's inheritance a curse, and insists that his coercion and famine policies were necessary choices to preserve Greyhaven. He is opposed by Elianor, Tomas, Mara, Joren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance, with his loyal guards defeated, surrendering, or scattered. He remains armed, isolated, furious, and unwilling to repent; his immediate goal is to kill or defeat Tomas and preserve the authority and narrative of House Marrow.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: On Greyhaven's seaward battlements beside and partly behind Elianor, rain-soaked and exhausted, wounded near the shoulder with blood darkening his coat, carrying a sword and Mara's pistol. He escaped the burning archive with Elianor and has directly confronted Lord Marrow about Arlen Rusk's petitions, execution, and cause, refusing to claim a throne or treat his father's name as hereditary authority. He is allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Pell, Bryn, Master Vey, Harl, Orren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. He knows Marrow carries the execution sword and intends violence, and he is prepared to disarm him rather than kill him if possible. His immediate goal is to protect Elianor, survive Marrow's attack, uphold humane surrender, and prevent the Rusk name from becoming a justification for revenge. He is bleeding, emotionally raw, and determined.

set.name: Pell
set.description: Inside Greyhaven near the archive stair below the battlements, bleeding from the scalp but active, helping Mara hold the passage and directing a surrendered young household guard and wounded marine away from the fighting. He knows Tomas and Elianor have followed Marrow to the battlements, the west archive room may contain survivors and originals, and the surrender terms remain in force. He is allied with Tomas, Elianor, Mara, Joren, Harl, Vey, Bryn, Orren, servants, villagers, and the resistance. His immediate goal is to protect prisoners and fighters, support the breach of the sealed archive room, and prevent retaliatory killing.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: Inside Greyhaven below the seaward battlements, directing Joren, Pell, coastal fighters, servants, and surrendering soldiers at the archive stair. She is bloodied at the temple and exhausted but active. She ordered the resistance to hold the surrender terms, save anyone trapped in the sealed west archive room, and carry surviving papers toward Saint Orra's Chapel while Tomas and Elianor pursued Marrow. She knows the confrontation has moved to the battlements and that Marrow still carries Arlen's execution sword. She remains allied with Tomas, Elianor, Joren, Pell, Vey, Bryn, Orren, Harl, villagers, and the resistance. Her immediate goal is to rescue trapped civilians, preserve evidence, and keep fighters from retaliatory killing.

set.name: Joren Pell
set.description: Inside Greyhaven at the sealed west archive room below the battlements, carrying the iron hook of the ram as a club and working with two coastal fighters to breach the door. He is injured but active, while muffled signs indicate someone remains alive inside. He is allied with Tomas, Elianor, Mara, Pell, Harl, Vey, Bryn, Orren, servants, villagers, and the resistance. He knows Marrow fled to the battlements and that the final confrontation has begun, but his immediate goal remains rescuing trapped people and records under humane surrender terms rather than pursuing revenge.

Elianor escaped the burning archive passage with Tomas and reached Greyhaven's storm-lashed seaward battlements, where she confronted Lord Marrow over the famine, the children marked for military labor, and the destruction of the people outside his walls.

On the battlements, Tomas and Lord Marrow directly confronted the history of Arlen Rusk's execution; Marrow called Arlen a traitor and Tomas's inheritance a curse, while Tomas answered that no execution erased the people's suffering and refused hereditary authority.

Lord Marrow raised Arlen Rusk's execution sword against Tomas, and Elianor placed herself between them, declaring that she would live against her father rather than allow him to call his rule preservation.

chapters.name: The Price of the Gate
chapters.content:
The sword came down with the weight of fourteen years.

Tomas caught it on his own blade, and the impact drove him to one knee. Steel rang against steel. The sound flew over the battlements and vanished into the storm.

Elianor heard the sea below them, though the wind seemed intent on tearing the world apart. Rain streamed from the black plates of her father’s armor. It ran along the execution sword and fell in bright drops from its point. Lord Marrow stood beyond her, broad and terrible, the face she had known all her life hardened into something that no longer resembled a father.

“Tomas,” she said.

“I’m here.”

His voice was strained. Blood had spread farther across his coat beneath the shoulder wound, making the rain seem red where it touched him. He pushed upward, turning Marrow’s blade aside. “Go to the stair.”

“I will not leave you.”

“You are between us.”

“I know.”

Marrow wrenched his sword free and struck again. Tomas rose just in time. Their blades crossed at the hilt, Marrow’s strength forcing Tomas backward over the slick stones. Elianor moved with him, keeping herself in the narrow space between the parapet and the two men.

“Get behind me,” Tomas said.

“That is precisely where he wants me.”

Marrow’s eyes flicked toward her. “You still think this is a story in which choosing the right side saves you.”

“No,” Elianor said. “I think it is a story in which you have chosen the wrong side every time you called it necessity.”

His mouth tightened. He drove forward.

Tomas did not meet the blow head-on. He stepped aside, caught Marrow’s wrist with his free hand, and twisted. The old lord’s sword scraped over the stone. For an instant Marrow’s balance broke. Tomas hooked his boot behind the older man’s ankle and sent him staggering toward the parapet.

Elianor saw the drop beyond it: black water, white violence, no shore visible through the rain.

Tomas could have shoved him.

He did not.

Instead he released Marrow’s wrist and reached for the sword arm. “Yield,” he said. “Your men have laid down their weapons. The keep is lost. Do not make this another execution.”

Marrow recovered with astonishing speed. He struck Tomas across the face with the mailed back of his hand. Tomas reeled. Before he could regain his footing, Marrow slammed his shoulder into him and drove him against the parapet.

Elianor cried out. “Stop!”

The old lord’s forearm pressed against Tomas’s throat. “You know nothing of what must be done.”

Tomas seized the rim of Marrow’s armor. “I know you are afraid.”

Marrow’s expression changed—not into shame, but into fury. He brought the pommel of the sword toward Tomas’s temple.

Elianor stepped between them.

The blow missed Tomas and struck her instead. Pain burst through her wrist and up into her arm. She stumbled, her wet gown dragging around her legs. Marrow’s blade turned in the same motion, its edge passing close enough to cut the silver fabric at her ribs.

Tomas pushed him away.

They separated, breathing hard. The storm filled the space between them. Somewhere below, men shouted. A cannon boomed from the harbor, and the battlement shuddered beneath their feet. Then came another sound: a confused roar rising from the inner keep, followed by the chapel bell.

Not a war cry. A signal.

The fighting was moving toward its end, but here the old order had narrowed itself to three people and a sword.

Marrow lifted the weapon again. “Your father stood where you stand.”

“And you killed him.”

“He raised men against the crown.”

“He asked for limits.”

“He asked for weakness.”

“He asked you to keep your word.”

Marrow lunged.

Tomas parried high. The force of it numbed his fingers. Marrow followed with a cut toward his wounded shoulder, and Tomas turned so the blade passed across his coat without finding flesh. He answered with a short strike at Marrow’s wrist, then another at his knee.

The older man was not merely strong. He was practiced. He had survived years of border wars, court intrigues, and the private violence by which Greyhaven had been kept obedient. He knew how to make every movement costly. Tomas was faster, but the battlement was narrow and the rain made every stone uncertain.

And Tomas was bleeding.

Elianor saw it in the way he favored his left side. Saw the tremor that entered his sword hand and vanished whenever Marrow looked at it. He had escaped the archive, crossed the keep, fought through Veyne’s marines, and climbed into this storm with a wound that should have put him on a table.

“Let me take him,” she said.

Tomas did not look at her. “No.”

“You cannot keep—”

“No.”

Marrow smiled without pleasure. “There. Even now, the servant tells you what you may do.”

Elianor’s anger sharpened. “He is the only person here who has ever told me the truth without asking what it would cost him.”

“Truth is a luxury afforded by people who have never governed.”

“Then let the governed speak.”

Marrow’s gaze moved to the wet silver gown, torn and gray with soot. “You speak as though the people will thank you for destroying them.”

“I did not destroy them.”

“You opened the gates.”

“Yes.”

“You surrendered the stores that kept this house alive.”

“I returned what was taken from them.”
