“You have made Greyhaven a prize for men who will divide it until nothing remains.”

“Perhaps,” she said. “But nothing remained for them while you held it.”

Marrow’s sword lowered a fraction. It was not hesitation. It was calculation. He looked past her toward the stair, measuring the distance, the possible witnesses, the roads by which he might still retreat. His world was collapsing, but he still searched for a door.

Then Tomas moved.

He feinted toward Marrow’s chest, drew the execution sword aside, and caught the older man’s elbow. With his other hand he seized the guard of Marrow’s sword. Their bodies collided. Tomas twisted, using the turn of Marrow’s weight against him.

The sword came loose.

It struck the battlement stones and skidded toward the parapet.

For one breath, no one moved.

Tomas kicked the sword away. It clattered against a raised block and stopped near Elianor’s feet. Marrow stood unarmed, his hands open at his sides. The rain flattened his gray hair against his brow.

“It is over,” Tomas said.

Marrow looked at the sword, then at Tomas. “You think disarming me makes you merciful.”

“It gives you a chance to live.”

“You give me a chance?”

“I give you the chance you refused Arlen.”

The words struck more deeply than the blade had. Marrow’s face went still.

Below them, the bell rang again. Voices carried upward through the wind.

“Surrender!” someone shouted.

Another voice answered, “Lay down your arms!”

Tomas kept his sword lowered but ready. “Your soldiers are being offered hearings. Your servants are under protection. Your daughter has declared the terms. You can live long enough to answer for what you did.”

Marrow’s eyes remained on Elianor.

“You would hand me to them,” he said.

“I would hand you to the people you ruled.”

“You would let them judge me?”

“They already have.”

Marrow laughed once. It was a broken, disbelieving sound. “And you call that justice? A mob with knives? Villages choosing what to do with every man they blame?”

“No,” Tomas said. “That is why I am telling them no executions. That is why Harl is holding the prisoners. That is why the chapel is taking names. You are not being offered mercy because you deserve it. You are being offered the law we mean to build.”

“Law.” Marrow looked at the burning keep. “You stand in the ruin of mine and speak of law.”

“Your law was a locked gate.”

Marrow’s eyes shifted again, this time to the stone arch behind Elianor. Beside it lay a fallen guard, face down in the water, one hand still curled around a dagger. The weapon had slipped free of its sheath during the fighting. Its hilt showed pale against the black stone.

Elianor saw Marrow see it.

“Tomas,” she whispered.

He understood too late.

Marrow sprang not toward the sword but toward her.

Elianor stepped backward. The hem of her gown caught under her heel. Marrow’s hand closed around her upper arm, crushing the bruised flesh beneath his gauntlet. He pulled her against him and reached for the dagger.

Tomas struck Marrow’s wrist. The older man released Elianor, but the movement brought him within the reach of the fallen weapon. His fingers closed around its hilt.

Elianor fell against the parapet.

Marrow rose with the dagger in one hand and seized the execution sword with the other. He had crossed the distance in a single violent motion. Tomas drove forward, but Marrow turned, placing Elianor between them.

“Put down your sword,” Marrow said.

Tomas stopped.

Rain ran into his eyes. His sword was still raised, its point aimed at the floor between them. “Let her go.”

“You have always been willing to sacrifice other people for your principles.”

“No.”

“Your father sacrificed villages.”

“My father did not order their deaths.”

“He brought soldiers to my gate.”

“He came to negotiate.”

“He came to threaten me.”

“And you called the threat rebellion because it was easier than answering him.”

Marrow’s dagger pressed against Elianor’s throat. She felt the cold edge through the wet collar of her gown. Her father’s breath touched her ear. He smelled of iron, smoke, and the bitter oil used to polish old armor.

“Do not make me do this,” he said quietly.

The plea, if it was one, almost broke her. Not because it was tender. Because it was the last remnant of the man who had once held her hand at her mother’s grave and told her that grief was a duty one performed in silence.

“You made this long ago,” Elianor said.

His grip tightened.

Tomas lowered his sword a little. “Corvin. Listen to me. No one else needs to die.”

Marrow’s gaze remained fixed on him. “You sound like him.”

“Then listen.”

“Your father begged.”

“He asked you to remember the people.”

“He cursed me.”

“He named what you were doing.”

Marrow lifted the execution sword. Its blade passed above Elianor’s shoulder, ready to strike Tomas when he came close enough.

Tomas took one step.

“Stop,” Marrow said.

Tomas stopped again.

Elianor felt the dagger shift against her throat. Her father’s sword arm trembled—not with weakness, but with the effort of holding two intentions at once. He wanted Tomas dead. He wanted Elianor alive long enough to witness it. He wanted the world to remain arranged according to his will, though the walls below were falling and the people had already walked through his gate.

His mistake was believing that love made a person still.

Elianor drove her heel backward into his knee.

Marrow cursed and lurched. She seized the dagger wrist with both hands and twisted away. The blade cut her palm, but his grip loosened. She tore free and stumbled toward Tomas.

Marrow recovered almost immediately. He raised the execution sword.

Tomas stepped between them.

The blade entered beneath his ribs.

For a moment the sword seemed to hang in the air, its point hidden in Tomas’s back. Then blood spread across his coat, dark and sudden, and Marrow’s face changed. The fury left it. He looked almost astonished.

Tomas made no sound.

He stood upright because the sword held him there.

Elianor caught him as Marrow pulled the blade free. Tomas’s weight struck her, forcing them both down against the stones. His hand found her shoulder. His fingers closed once.

“Stay behind me,” he breathed.

“You are impossible,” she said, and heard the terror in her own voice.

Marrow raised the sword again.

The world narrowed to the blade, Tomas’s blood, and the hand that had once taught her to calm a frightened mare.

Elianor reached for the fallen dagger.

Her fingers closed around it.

Marrow brought the sword down.

She rose into the blow.

The dagger entered beneath his breastplate, where the armor had shifted at the waist. Elianor felt the hilt strike her palm and the resistance of flesh give way. Her father’s sword stopped halfway through its arc.

He stared at her.

Not at the wound. At her.

“Elianor,” he said.

It was the first time in years he had spoken her name without command in his voice.

She held the dagger between them. “You should have stopped.”

Marrow’s hand opened. The execution sword fell onto the stones.

He swayed once, then sank to his knees. The rain washed the blood from his armor in thin red trails. He looked toward the gate, though the gate could not be seen from the battlement. Perhaps he imagined it closed. Perhaps he imagined it open. Perhaps, at the end, he could not tell the difference.

Elianor released the dagger.

Lord Corvin Marrow fell forward, and the storm took the sound of his body striking stone.

For several breaths, Tomas remained upright against her. Then his knees gave way.

She caught him and lowered him beside the parapet. Blood was flowing too quickly. It soaked through his coat and gathered beneath him, mixing with rainwater in the cracks between the stones.

“Tomas.”

“I know.”

“No. No, you don’t.” She pressed both hands to the wound. “Bryn will come. Nessa will come. Orren has cloth. We can get you to the chapel.”

He looked at her with exhausted tenderness. “You always did make plans after the ending.”

“This is not the ending.”

Below, a horn sounded once. Then another answered from the harbor.

The battle had gone quiet.

Not peaceful. Quiet. The kind of silence that followed a door being forced open and every person on either side realizing there was no way to close it again.

On the stairs, voices called that Marrow was dead. Others called for Tomas. Captain Harl shouted an order to hold the battlement and let no one kill the surrendered. Chaplain Orren’s bell rang from Saint Orra’s Chapel, steady now, marking neither attack nor retreat but the beginning of reckoning.

Elianor bent over Tomas, her silver gown spread around them like a ruined flag.

“I killed him,” she said.

Tomas’s eyes drifted toward the body of Lord Marrow. “You stopped him.”

“I killed my father.”

“You stopped him.”

Rain ran down his face. She wiped it away, though more immediately replaced it.

“Can you stand?”

“No.”

“Can you breathe?”

“For now.”

She pressed harder against the wound. He flinched, and she nearly pulled away.

“Don’t,” he whispered.

“I have to.”

“I know.”

Beyond him, the execution sword lay where it had fallen. The weapon that had killed Arlen Rusk, carried through Greyhaven’s history as proof of authority, was now only a length of steel in the rain.

Elianor looked at it, then at the open stair.

“The gates are open,” Tomas said.

“Yes.”

“The granaries?”

“Being saved.”

“The prisoners?”

“Under the surrender terms.”

He nodded, as if these were the only answers that mattered.

She bent and held him closer while men ran toward them through the storm. The price of the gate was paid in blood, and no victory could return it. Greyhaven had fallen. Her father was dead. The old world had ended beneath her hands.

Tomas’s breathing grew shallower.

Elianor called his name again, and this time the battlements gave it back.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: On Greyhaven's storm-lashed seaward battlements beside Tomas and Lord Corvin Marrow's body, wearing her dead mother's torn, wet silver gown, soot-streaked and bruised with a cut palm and wrist. She killed Duke Veyne in self-defense and has now killed her father with a fallen dagger after Marrow mortally wounded Tomas with Arlen Rusk's execution sword. She has renounced her inheritance and remains allied with Tomas, Mara, Joren, Pell, Bryn, Master Vey, Harl, Orren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. The surrender terms are being upheld, prisoners are protected, the gates are open, and the granaries and surviving records are being saved. She knows Marrow's crimes, the truth of Arlen's execution, and that Tomas is dying. Her immediate goal is to keep Tomas alive long enough for help to arrive, preserve humane surrender, and endure the consequences of killing her father. She is exhausted, horrified, grieving, and resolute.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: Dead on the storm-lashed seaward battlements of Greyhaven, killed by Elianor with a fallen dagger after he mortally wounded Tomas with the execution sword associated with Arlen Rusk's death. He died still refusing surrender or repentance, having ordered the records and granaries burned and rejected the open-gate terms. His body, the dagger, and the execution sword lie on the battlement stones. His death ends his authority and the active fighting within Greyhaven, though his crimes and political legacy remain to be judged by the coastal resistance and surviving communities.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: Inside Greyhaven near the route to the seaward battlements, injured in the knee and face and directing surrendered soldiers and resistance fighters after hearing that Lord Marrow is dead and Tomas is wounded. He remains allied with Elianor, Tomas, Mara, Joren, Master Vey, Orren, Bryn, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. He knows the surrender terms remain in force and has ordered that no surrendered prisoner be killed in retaliation. His immediate goal is to secure the battlements, protect Tomas and Elianor, maintain humane custody, and prevent renewed violence now that Marrow's command has ended.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and its steps, coordinating refuge, prisoners, wounded people, grain, and surviving records while his bell marks the beginning of reckoning rather than battle. He knows Lord Marrow is dead, Tomas is mortally wounded on the battlements, Elianor survived, and the surrender terms are being upheld. He remains allied with Elianor, Tomas, Vey, Bryn, Harl, Mara, Joren, villagers, servants, and the coastal resistance. He possesses chapel authority, refuge space, burial records, and the lectern; his immediate goal is to receive the wounded, keep prisoners alive, protect the evidence, and prepare for the dead and the political aftermath.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: On Greyhaven's seaward battlements in Elianor's arms, rain-soaked and mortally wounded beneath the ribs by Lord Marrow's execution sword after stepping between Marrow and Elianor. He is bleeding heavily, conscious but weak, and has refused to kill Marrow even when he could disarm him. He remains allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Pell, Bryn, Master Vey, Harl, Orren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. He knows Marrow is dead, the fighting inside Greyhaven has fallen quiet, the gates are open, the granaries are being saved, and surrendering prisoners remain protected. His immediate goal is to reassure Elianor that the people and humane terms have survived, while he faces the certainty of his wound. He still carries his sword and Mara's pistol; Arlen Rusk's signet remains with Elianor from their earlier farewell.
Lord Marrow attacked Tomas on the seaward battlements; Tomas repeatedly chose disarmament and surrender over killing him, but Marrow regained the execution sword and used Elianor as a shield.
When Lord Marrow turned the execution sword on Elianor, Tomas stepped between them and was mortally wounded beneath the ribs by the blade used to execute Arlen Rusk.
Elianor killed Lord Marrow with a fallen dagger after Tomas was wounded, ending Marrow's rule and the active fighting within Greyhaven while Tomas remained gravely injured.
Elianor must remain with mortally wounded Tomas on the battlements through the storm, receive Arlen Rusk's signet, and face his final request that his name not become another throne.

chapters.name: No One Expendable
chapters.content:
For a little while after Lord Marrow fell, the storm seemed to forget Greyhaven.

The rain slackened to a cold mist. Smoke drifted low across the battlements, torn into ribbons by the wind. Below, the sea heaved against the cliffs, black and white and without mercy, but the guns had stopped. No orders came from the keep. No boots pounded up the stair. Somewhere within the fortress, a bell began to ring—slowly, unevenly, as if the hand pulling the rope had not yet learned whether it was calling people to prayer or to judgment.

Elianor knelt on the wet stones with Tomas in her arms.

His blood had spread through the front of his coat and beneath her hands. She pressed both palms against the wound, though the pressure made his breath catch and did nothing to stop the warmth leaving him. The sword had gone beneath his ribs. She knew enough of wounds to understand what that meant. She had seen men die in Saint Orra's Chapel from lesser cuts, their faces gray with the knowledge that no prayer could reach what had been opened inside them.

“No,” she whispered.

Tomas's head rested against her shoulder. His hair was plastered to his brow. Rainwater and blood ran together down his cheek, and when she wiped it away her fingers came red.

“Elianor.”

“I am here.”

“You keep saying that as if you are trying to convince someone.”

“I am trying to convince you.”

His mouth moved, almost a smile. “Then you should choose a better argument.”

She bent over him, shielding his face from the wind with her body. Her mother's silver gown, torn at the sleeve and darkened with soot, clung to her knees. The hem dragged through Marrow's blood. The gown had been made for a wedding, for vows spoken before witnesses and a future arranged by other hands. Now it was a bandage, a shroud, and the last bright thing left amid the ruin of Greyhaven.

“You are going to the chapel,” she said. “Orren has clean cloth. Nessa will be there. They will open you and draw the blade's path closed. Master Vey knows medicines. Bryn knows where everything is kept. We have all of them.”

“Tomas,” she corrected herself, hearing the edge of panic in her own voice. “You have all of them.”

He looked past her toward the inner yard. Flames still burned in the granary roofs, but the fire had been beaten down along the lower walls. Figures moved through the smoke carrying sacks, boxes, wounded men, and children. They looked tiny from the battlement, as if the whole world had been reduced to hands passing what could be saved from one pair to another.

“Are the gates open?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Did they hold the terms?”

Elianor swallowed. “Harl is holding them. He put the surrendered soldiers under guard rather than letting the villagers reach them. Orren has the prisoners in the chapel arcade. No one is to be killed.”

“No one?”

“No one who has surrendered.”

“Good.” His breath shuddered. “And the grain?”

“Being carried out of the east store. The granaries are damaged, but not all of them. The sacks that were nearest the chapel are safe. Vey has the books.”

“The books?”

“The original grain records. He got them past the fire.”

Tomas closed his eyes. “Then the gates are open. The grain is saved. The records are saved.”

“Some of them.”

“Enough for the truth to have witnesses.”

She shook him gently. “Do not speak as though you are making a list before leaving.”

“I am making a list because you will forget what matters.”

“I will forget nothing.”

“You will remember the sword. You will remember your father falling. You will remember Veyne.” His eyes opened again, dark and lucid despite the pain. “Those things are loud. They will keep shouting in your head. But remember the gates, too. Remember the grain. Remember that Harl lowered his weapon. Remember Bryn carrying an iron box with one injured hand because she thought paper could save the dead from being lied about.”

“I remember.”

“Remember Lysa's child. Remember the people who came through the lower gate and did not ask whether the person handing them bread had a title.”

“I remember,” she said, louder.

A gust struck them. Elianor nearly lost her balance. She tightened her arms around him, and Tomas cried out despite himself.

“Forgive me.”

“There is nothing to forgive.”

“There is everything to forgive.”

His hand moved weakly against her waist, searching. She caught it and held it between both of hers. His fingers were cold.

Footsteps sounded on the stair below. Elianor looked up sharply, one hand reaching for the fallen dagger beside her knee. Captain Harl appeared first, limping heavily, his face cut and swollen. Two resistance fighters followed him, and behind them came Chaplain Orren with a satchel clutched beneath his cloak.

Harl stopped when he saw Tomas.

“Make room,” Orren said. “We can carry him.”

“No.” Tomas's voice was scarcely more than breath.

Orren came closer and knelt. He opened the satchel, revealing folded linen, a small bottle, and a needle already threaded. His expression changed when he examined the wound. He did not lie, which was one of the reasons Elianor trusted him.

“We need to take him inside,” the chaplain said.

“Can you save him?” Elianor asked.

Orren looked at the sword wound, then at Tomas. “I can make him more comfortable. I can try to keep the bleeding from worsening. Nessa may know more.”

“That is not what I asked.”

The chaplain's face was lined by exhaustion and rain. “I know.”

Tomas turned his head toward Harl. “The inner keep?”

“Quiet,” Harl answered. “Marrow's men have laid down their arms. Some are wounded. Some are hiding. The marines who remain have been disarmed or driven to the harbor. The fighting is over.”

“Because of him?” Tomas asked, looking toward Marrow's body.

“Because his command ended with him,” Harl said. “And because everyone heard Lady Elianor declare the surrender.”

Elianor flinched at the title. It sounded absurd now, like a name from a story told about someone else.

“Harl,” she said, “get Nessa.”

“I have sent a runner.”

“Get her faster.”

“I will.”

He turned, but Tomas caught his sleeve. The movement cost him. His face tightened, and a fresh line of blood appeared at the corner of his mouth.

“Captain.”

Harl bent down.

“Do not let them make an exception for me.”

Harl stared at him.

“If I die,” Tomas continued, “no executions. Not for Marrow. Not for Veyne. Not for any soldier who laid down his weapon.”

“Your death will not be used to excuse murder,” Harl said.

“Say it to Mara.”

“I will.”

“Say it to Joren.”

“I will.”

“And if the crowd calls for blood?”

Harl's jaw worked. “Then I will put myself between them and the prisoners.”

Tomas released his sleeve. “Good.”

Harl looked at Elianor. For the first time since she had known him, the captain seemed to have no command left in him, only a man's grief and the stubbornness that had kept him standing through the day.

“Keep him warm,” Orren instructed. “Do not move him until the litter comes.”

“I will,” Elianor said.

The others withdrew a short distance, leaving the lovers beneath the broken crenellation. Orren stayed near enough to intervene, but he lowered his head as though granting them a final privacy no wall in Greyhaven could have protected.

Tomas's gaze fell to Elianor's clenched hand.

“The ring,” he said.

She had forgotten she was holding it. Arlen Rusk's signet pressed into her palm, its edges biting the cut there. She had carried it since their farewell through the tunnel, beneath the wedding flowers, through smoke and fire and the blood of two men. It had been his gift already. Yet Tomas looked at it as if seeing it for the first time.

“You still have it,” he said.

“I never let it go.”

“Then take it properly.”

She shook her head. “You gave it to me.”

“I gave you a thing I was afraid to keep. That is not the same.”

His fingers fumbled toward hers. She opened her hand and laid the ring upon his palm. The old silver was dull with grime, the carved mark of the Rusk house half-filled with blood. Tomas curled his fingers around it, gathering what strength he had left.

“My father wore this when he signed the petitions,” he said. “Sella kept the wax impression. I thought the ring would make me brave.”

“It did.”

“No. You did.”

“I did nothing.”

“You stood in front of him.”

“I killed him.”

“You stopped him.”

“He was my father.”

“And he was going to kill me.” Tomas's eyes sharpened. “Do not turn that blade against yourself because you were the one who held it. You chose the living person in front of you. That was the right choice.”

Elianor bent her forehead to his. “There was no right choice.”

“There rarely is.”

He lifted their joined hands. With slow effort, he pressed the signet into her fingers and closed them around it. His hand remained there, covering hers.

“Now it is yours,” he said.

“I do not want it.”

“I know.”

“I want you.”

The words broke out of her before she could soften them. Tomas shut his eyes. His breath came shallowly, each inhale a difficult negotiation with the wound.

“We can leave,” she said. “Listen to me. We can leave Greyhaven tonight. There are boats at the harbor. Oric can find us a cove. We can go north, beyond the crown's reach. We can live in a village where no one knows my name. I will work. I can mend nets. I can keep accounts. I can do anything.”

“You hate mending nets.”

“I will learn.”

“You cannot count fish without accusing them of fraud.”

“I will accuse them quietly.”

A small laugh escaped him, and then became a cough. Elianor held him upright while blood darkened his lips. Orren rose, but Tomas waved him back. When the coughing passed, he sagged against her.

“We can go,” she repeated, desperate now. “You can lead the council from somewhere safe. Mara can speak for you. Sella can speak. I do not care what they call me. We will make another life.”

Tomas looked at her for a long time. The tenderness in his face was worse than any refusal.

“Elianor.”

“No.”

“You know.”

“No.”

“The sword went deep.”

“Then we will go slowly.”

“There is too much blood.”

“Then we will use more cloth.”

“Your hands are shaking.”

“Because I am cold.”

“You are not cold.”

She pressed harder against the wound. “Be quiet.”

He obeyed for several heartbeats. The sea thundered below them. The broken clouds opened, and a pale strip of dawn showed beyond the horizon, though the sun itself remained hidden. Rain fell through the light like ash.

Tomas touched the signet in her fist.

“Promise me something.”

“Anything.”

“Do not let them make this a throne.”

She stared at him.

“Your name,” he said. “Mine. My father's. They will come to you with it. They will say the coast needs a Rusk. They will say the blood of Arlen gives us the right to rule. They will put the ring on a table and call it a crown.”

“I will not.”

“You must promise.”

“I promise.”

“Not only you. Make the promise public. Give them the petitions. Give them the names of those who argued with my father and those who disagreed with him. Let them see that the cause was never one man's inheritance.”

“I will preserve everything.”

“Not everything. People are not papers.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

His voice had weakened, but the question held the old Tomas—the man in the stable who had placed a hand against Ash's frightened neck and refused to yank the reins.

“Say it,” he whispered.

Elianor's tears fell onto his face. “No life is expendable.”

“Again.”

“No life is expendable.”

“The starving child?”

“No life is expendable.”

“The frightened soldier?”

“No life is expendable.”

“The servant no lord remembers?”

“No life is expendable.”

“Your enemy?”

She looked toward Marrow's body. The old man's armor was black with rain. His hand lay open beside the execution sword, as if even in death he had been unable to release it.

“No life is expendable,” she said. “But some people choose to spend the lives of others. We will not.”

Tomas breathed in. This time the breath did not catch.

“That is the whole rebellion,” he said.

“No. It is the whole of us.”

His hand slipped from hers. Elianor caught it before it fell. The signet remained between their palms.

“Nessa is coming,” she said, though she could not see anyone on the stair. “Orren will save you. Harl will bring the litter. You will wake in the chapel, and Bryn will scold you for staining her clean blankets. You will complain that the soup is thin. I will tell you that you have no authority over soup.”

Tomas's eyes drifted shut.

“Tomas.”

“I am listening.”

“You must listen harder.”

“I am trying.”

She kissed his brow. His skin was cold now. “Stay.”

“I am here.”

“Stay with me.”

He opened his eyes once more. The dawn had found them, gray and uncertain, reflected in the wet black of his gaze.

“I loved you before I knew what to call it,” he said. “In the stable, I think. You were angry at a horse for being afraid.”

“I was angry at you.”

“You were angry at everyone.”

“Not everyone.”

His smile was faint. “No. Not everyone.”

She held him tighter. “I love you.”

“I know.”

“Say it.”

“I love you.”

The words were barely audible. They entered her like a blade.

Below, the bell continued its slow calling. Voices rose from the yard—orders, prayers, someone crying out for water. The world had not stopped for them. The gates were open. The grain was moving. Prisoners were being counted. The dead waited in corridors and beneath the rain. Every life demanded an answer.

Tomas's fingers tightened once around hers.

“Do not make me beautiful,” he murmured.

Elianor bowed over him. “You are impossible.”

“Tell them I was difficult.”

“I will tell them you were vain, argumentative, and incapable of following an order.”

“Good.”

“And brave.”

“No.”

“And kind.”

“No.”

“And mine.”

His breath trembled. “Only if you say the others first.”

She laughed and sobbed at once. “You were difficult, argumentative, vain, and impossible. You stole food, broke rules, and taught a noblewoman to trust a horse. You were not a king. You were not a saint. You were Tomas.”

His eyes closed.

“Tomas?”

Orren came nearer. “Lady Elianor.”

“No.” She pressed her ear to Tomas's chest. His heartbeat was faint, irregular, but present. “He is alive.”

“Yes.”

“Then bring the litter.”

“It is coming.”

“Tell them to hurry.”

“I have.”

She did not release Tomas. She kept the signet enclosed in one hand and his hand enclosed in the other while the storm passed over Greyhaven. When the first clear light touched the sea, the battlements shone with rain, blood, and the broken pieces of two houses.

The gates stood open below.

And Elianor, holding the man who had taught her that no one could be thrown away for the comfort of the powerful, waited for the footsteps climbing toward them.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: On Greyhaven's storm-lashed seaward battlements, kneeling in her dead mother's torn, wet silver gown and holding Tomas in her arms. She is soot-streaked, bruised, with a cut palm and wrist, exhausted and grieving, and has killed Duke Veyne and Lord Corvin Marrow in self-defense and defense of Tomas. Tomas is mortally wounded beneath the ribs and remains conscious but fading; Elianor is holding his hand and Arlen Rusk's signet, which he has now formally given her. She knows the gates are open, the fighting has ended, surrendered prisoners are being protected, grain and surviving grain records are being saved, and Tomas has asked her to prevent his name becoming a throne and to uphold the belief that no life is expendable. She remains allied with Harl, Orren, Vey, Bryn, Mara, Joren, Pell, Lysa, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. Her immediate goal is to get Tomas to the chapel, preserve humane surrender, and carry out his final political and moral wishes while enduring the consequences of her father's death.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: Dead on the storm-lashed seaward battlements of Greyhaven, killed by Elianor with a fallen dagger after mortally wounding Tomas with the execution sword associated with Arlen Rusk's death. His body, the dagger, and the execution sword lie on the wet battlement stones. His death has ended his authority and the active fighting within Greyhaven, while his crimes and political legacy await judgment by the coastal resistance and surviving communities.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: On or near the route between Greyhaven's interior and the seaward battlements, limping with an injured knee and face, directing surrendered soldiers and resistance fighters after Lord Marrow's death. He has confirmed that the inner fighting is over, prisoners are under guard rather than exposed to revenge, and Elianor's surrender terms are being followed. He has promised Tomas that no surrendered soldier will be executed because of Tomas's death and is sending for Nessa and a litter. He remains allied with Elianor, Tomas, Mara, Joren, Master Vey, Orren, Bryn, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance. His immediate goal is to secure the battlements, move Tomas to medical care, and prevent renewed retaliation.

set.description: On Greyhaven's seaward battlements beside Elianor and mortally wounded Tomas, carrying a satchel of linen, medicine, and a needle while waiting for a litter and Nessa. He has assessed that he can ease Tomas's suffering and attempt to control the bleeding but cannot promise survival. He knows Marrow is dead, the fighting has ended, the gates are open, grain and records are being saved, and surrendering prisoners are protected. He remains allied with Elianor, Tomas, Harl, Vey, Bryn, Mara, Joren, villagers, servants, and the resistance. set.description: On Greyhaven's seaward battlements in Elianor's arms, rain-soaked and mortally wounded beneath the ribs by Lord Marrow's execution sword after stepping between Marrow and Elianor. He is conscious but extremely weak, bleeding heavily, cold, and awaiting a litter and medical care from Orren and Nessa. He has refused to kill Marrow and has insisted that surrendered soldiers not be executed in retaliation. He knows Marrow is dead, the gates are open, the granaries and some grain records have been saved, the fighting has ended, and the surrender terms are being upheld. He has given Elianor Arlen Rusk's signet and asked her to preserve the cause as a program rather than a bloodright, never allowing his name to become another throne or treating any life as expendable. He remains allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Pell, Bryn, Master Vey, Harl, Orren, servants, villagers, and the coastal resistance; his immediate concern is reassuring Elianor and remaining alive long enough to reach the chapel.

As Tomas lay dying on Greyhaven's battlements, Elianor learned that the gates were open, the granaries and grain records had been partly saved, and the surrender terms were being upheld; Tomas gave her Arlen Rusk's signet and made her promise that no life would be treated as expendable or his name turned into a throne.
After Tomas's death, Elianor must publicly preserve his final humane terms and prevent the Rusk name or signet from becoming hereditary authority or a justification for revenge.

chapters.name: After Greyhaven
chapters.content:
By dawn, Greyhaven no longer belonged to the living in any orderly sense.

The storm had gone east, dragging its thunder after it like a chain. In its wake the sea lay bruised and iron-colored below the cliffs. Rainwater ran through the courtyards in red threads, carrying ash, straw, splinters of wedding furniture, and the pale scraps of papers that had escaped the fire. The banners of Marrow and Veyne hung in strips from the towers. One had caught on a gargoyle and fluttered there, blackened and wet, as if the fortress were still trying to announce whose house it was.

Elianor walked beneath it without looking up.

She had changed out of the silver gown only because Bryn and Lysa had cut it from her shoulders. Its hem was stiff with soot and blood. The blood was not all Tomas's, nor all her father's. She wore a plain servant's cloak over a linen shift, and the signet rested on a cord against her chest, hidden beneath the cloth. Her palm was bandaged. Her wrist ached where the marine had seized it. Every step seemed to begin in a dream and end in a body.

There were bodies everywhere.

Villagers lay beside the outer gate, some under blankets, some still where they had fallen. Three fishing men had died beneath the harbor wall when Veyne's marines fired on their boats. A girl in a blue wool cap had been killed by a stray shot near the grain yard. Two stable hands, six household servants, and a cook named Hessa were among the dead within the lower court. Soldiers occupied the spaces between them: rebels, garrison men, marines in Veyne's dark coats. The dead had been stripped of all distinctions that had seemed so important the day before.

A nobleman from Veyne's retinue lay facedown beneath the arcade. His jeweled hand showed from beneath his cloak. Beside him, a kitchen boy no older than fifteen had fallen with a bread knife in his fist.

Elianor stopped.

“Cover them together,” she said.

The men carrying sheets looked at her. One was a fisherman with a bandaged cheek. The other wore the breastplate of Greyhaven's garrison, though he had set his sword on the ground.

“The nobles?” the fisherman asked.

“The soldiers. The servants. Everyone.”

“Some of these men killed ours.”

“I know.” Her voice almost failed. She made it steady. “No one is to be dishonored. No one is to be displayed. We will learn who they were before we decide what their deaths mean.”

The fisherman stared at her as if she had spoken in a foreign tongue.

Then the garrison man picked up a sheet.

Together they covered the dead.

At the chapel, the living had begun to sort themselves into the wounded, the frightened, and the furious. Saint Orra's floor was crowded with pallets. Smoke entered through the broken clerestory and turned the morning light gray. Nessa moved among the injured with her sleeves rolled to the elbow, her hands red to the wrists. Orren had set up a table beside the altar for linen, needles, and strips of boiled cloth. The old carved saint above them had lost her face to a cannon fragment.

In the nave, prisoners sat under guard.

Some were marines. Some were Greyhaven soldiers. A few had thrown down their weapons only after Veyne fell. They watched the rebels with the rigid stillness of men expecting a blade.

One of the younger captives had a split lip and a broken finger. Another shivered violently beneath a cloak. They had been given water, but no food.

Elianor saw the looks passing among the victorious fighters and understood what would happen if hunger and grief were permitted to choose the next command.

“Bring the grain,” she said.

A woman near the door laughed once, without humor. “For them?”

“For everyone.”

“They shot at us.”

“Some did. Some obeyed. Some surrendered. The grain was taken from all of us, and it will not be used to begin another execution.”

The woman stepped closer. She had a cut across her forehead and a dead child wrapped against her chest. Elianor recognized her as one of the families from Rill, though she could not recall the name.

“My brother is outside,” the woman said. “A marine killed him.”

“I am sorry.”

“Sorry is what the lord used to say when he closed the doors.”

The words struck more cleanly than any accusation Elianor's father had made.

“Yes,” Elianor said. “Then let me say something else. The doors stay open. The food is counted in public. The prisoners live until their cases are heard. If I give an order that breaks those promises, you should disobey me.”

The woman's expression did not soften. But she looked toward the open chapel doors, where rainwater and daylight entered together.

Elianor turned to Harl.

The captain stood with his weight braced on a crutch improvised from a spear shaft. His knee was swollen beneath a torn bandage. He had not slept. Behind him, surrendered soldiers sat beneath the watch of coastal fighters and two servants armed with kitchen cleavers.

“Food for the prisoners first,” Elianor said.

Harl's mouth tightened. “First?”

“Alongside the wounded. Their ration must not depend on whether someone hates them.”

“And if my men refuse?”

“Then remove them from the guard.”

He studied her. “You are giving away authority quickly, Lady Vale.”

“I have no authority left to give away.”

“Everyone is calling you lady.”

“Then they are making the same mistake my father made.”

Harl glanced toward the inner court, where Corvin Marrow's body had been brought down from the battlements and laid beneath a canvas. “What shall we call you?”

Elianor looked at the chapel floor, at the prisoners, at the women tearing old altar cloth into bandages.

“Call me when something needs doing.”

That was how the first distribution began. Grain came from the eastern stores in measured baskets. Lysa and Bryn recorded each one on a board salvaged from the ruined wedding table. A portion went to the wounded, a portion to the refugees, a portion to the prisoners, and a portion to the people who had fought through the night. No one received enough. There had never been enough. But no one was made to kneel for it.

When a rebel named Tarrow dragged a marine from the line and struck him with the butt of a musket, Elianor crossed the chapel before anyone could stop her.

“Put it down,” she said.

Tarrow lifted the musket again. “This one was at the inner passage. He helped kill Pell's brother.”

The marine's face had gone white. He could not have been more than twenty.

“Put it down.”

“He deserves—”

“Perhaps he does. That will be decided by witnesses, not by the first hand that reaches him.”

Tarrow looked around the chapel. “You think a hearing brings the dead back?”

“No.” Her grief rose through her like fire, and for a moment she saw Tomas on the battlements, his fingers loosening around hers. “It prevents us from making the living answer for the dead in whatever way our anger chooses.”

Tarrow's grip trembled.

Mara came to stand beside Elianor. Blood had dried at her temple, and one sleeve was stiff with it. “You heard Tomas,” she said to the fighters. “He gave the order.”

The mention of his name altered the room. It traveled through the chapel as both blessing and burden.

Tarrow lowered the weapon.

Harl took it from him. “You will guard the west door without a weapon until the hearing.”

Tarrow opened his mouth, then shut it. The marine was led away to the prisoner line.

By midday, the fires had been contained. The archive was a black wound in the western wall. The granaries had lost a roof and one entire store, but the eastern chambers remained standing. Master Vey brought the surviving grain books to the chapel wrapped in oilskin. Bryn carried the iron box behind him, both hands around its scorched sides.

They placed the records on the altar.

The original depositions were warped by heat, but the names could still be read. The land transfers survived in patches. Arlen Rusk's signed petition was black along one edge and whole along the other. His name remained clear.

Master Vey stared at it for a long time.

“Your father tried to burn this,” he said.

“My father tried to burn everything that could speak after him.”

“Not everything.”

Elianor looked toward the canvas in the courtyard. “No. He left us one witness.”

There was no ceremony for Corvin Marrow. His body was washed only enough to remove the worst of the ash. The execution sword was laid beside him for the public record, though no one permitted it to be carried in procession. Veyne's body was entered in the same list as the other dead. Their names, rank, and acts would be written down, but neither man would receive the honors that had once seemed inseparable from their station.

Tomas received less.

He was carried from the battlements to the old stable before the chapel could be prepared. Ash was still in her stall, trembling but alive. When the litter passed, the mare stretched her neck toward him. Elianor stopped long enough to place Tomas's hand against the white blaze on her face.

“She remembers,” Orren said.

“So do I.”

Tomas had been wrapped in a clean blanket. His face looked almost peaceful, which was worse than the blood. Nessa had closed the wound and washed his hair. There was no saving him. They had known that before the storm ended, but knowledge did not become acceptance merely because daylight arrived.

They buried him beyond the chapel, on a strip of wind-cut ground where the old sea garden had once begun. The soil was thin and full of stones. No priest's vestments were brought. No noble cloth covered him. Elianor refused a carved marker and refused the title Lady Vale when Orren asked how his name should be spoken.

“Tomas Rusk,” she said. “Son of Arlen Rusk. Stable servant of Greyhaven. Friend to Rill. Coordinator of the coastal councils. Do not make him more than he was.”

“And less?” Mara asked quietly.

Elianor looked at the grave. “Never less.”

The people came in uneven groups. Servants stood beside fishermen. Wounded soldiers remained at the edge beneath guard. Sella Rusk arrived before sunset from Saint Orra's Abbey, having crossed the flooded road with two riders. She did not weep before the others. She placed her hand on the earth and whispered something no one heard.

Afterward, the arguments began.

“He should have ruled,” said a young harbor captain. “The coast needs a Rusk.”

“He refused a throne,” Bryn answered.

“He refused it because he was dying.”

“He refused it before he was dying,” Mara said. “Many times.”

An old fisherman shook his head. “He was a hero.”

“A hero is still a kind of statue,” said Sella. “Statues do not answer when the hungry ask who owns the grain.”

A soldier who had surrendered during the assault said, “He saved men who would have killed him.”

“And men who killed others,” someone replied.

“And that is why he must be remembered,” Orren said. “Not because he was pure. Because he knew the difference between justice and the pleasure of punishment.”

Elianor listened from beyond the circle. The signet was warm against her skin. It seemed to carry the shape of his hand, though she knew that was memory and not metal.

At last the harbor captain turned to her. “What was he, then?”

Elianor looked back at Greyhaven. Smoke rose from the broken keep. The gates stood open to the road. Beyond them, people waited for grain, judgment, shelter, and answers that would not come quickly.

“He was Tomas,” she said. “He was loved. He was wrong sometimes. He was brave and afraid. He was a servant, a son, and a man who tried to keep other men from becoming what they hated.”

The captain frowned. “That is not enough for a cause.”

“No,” Elianor said. “It is enough for a life.”

She went to the altar before nightfall and placed the signet beside the surviving petition. Then she ordered that neither be used to appoint a ruler. The records would be copied, read aloud in every coastal settlement, and kept where anyone could examine them. The grain books would be counted by village delegates. The prisoners would face hearings. The dead would be named together.

Outside, the sea struck the cliffs with a sound like distant applause.

Elianor stood in the ruined chapel until the candles burned low. She had lost her father, her home, and the man whose absence made every open door seem cruel. Yet Greyhaven remained full of work. That was Tomas's final mercy, and perhaps his final command.

No life was expendable.

Not even the life of a place built on stolen bread.

Not even hers.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: At the ruined Saint Orra's Chapel and the burial ground beside Greyhaven's old sea garden, wearing a plain servant's cloak over a linen shift with her bandaged palm and aching wrist. She is exhausted, grieving Tomas, and newly responsible for Greyhaven's food, records, prisoners, wounded, and political aftermath. She has publicly ordered equal food distribution, stopped retaliatory violence, confirmed her father's crimes, rejected noble honors for Tomas, and ordered that Tomas's name and signet never become hereditary authority. She possesses Arlen Rusk's signet, which she placed beside the surviving petition at the chapel altar, and remains allied with Mara, Joren, Harl, Vey, Orren, Bryn, Lysa, Sella, villagers, servants, and the coastal resistance. Her immediate goals are to keep the gates open, protect prisoners through public hearings, preserve and publish the surviving archives, distribute grain fairly, and carry Tomas's humane terms without turning him into a ruler.

set.name: Lord Corvin Marrow
set.description: Dead and recorded among Greyhaven's other dead after Elianor killed him on the battlements. His body was washed only enough to remove ash and laid beneath a canvas; the execution sword associated with Arlen Rusk's death was recorded beside him but no noble procession or honor was permitted. His crimes, grain diversion, executions, land seizures, and collective-punishment policies are now publicly confirmed through surviving records.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel with the surviving grain books and scorched original depositions, land transfers, and Arlen Rusk petition. Exhausted and smoke-stained but active, he helped secure the records beyond Marrow's reach and placed them on the chapel altar for preservation. He is allied with Elianor, Bryn, Harl, Orren, Mara, Joren, Lysa, villagers, servants, and the coastal resistance. His immediate goal is to copy and protect the archives and establish transparent accounting of the remaining grain.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: At Greyhaven's chapel and inner routes, limping on an improvised spear-shaft crutch with an injured knee and face. He is directing guards over surrendered soldiers while enforcing Elianor's order that prisoners receive food and survive until public hearings. He is allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Vey, Orren, Bryn, Lysa, villagers, servants, and the resistance. His immediate goal is to maintain order without retaliation, protect prisoners and wounded people, and support the new public hearings.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and Tomas's burial ground, exhausted and smoke-stained, tending wounded people with linen, needles, medicine, and boiled cloth. He supported Elianor's equal food distribution and humane prisoner policy, helped prepare Tomas's body, and witnessed the burial without noble honors. He is allied with Elianor, Harl, Vey, Bryn, Mara, Sella, villagers, servants, prisoners, and the resistance. His immediate goal is to care for the wounded and dead while helping the chapel remain a refuge and public place of record.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: Dead and buried without noble honors in wind-cut ground beside Greyhaven's old sea garden. He died after being mortally wounded by Lord Marrow while protecting Elianor. His body was washed and wrapped in a clean blanket, and Elianor, Sella, Mara, Orren, servants, villagers, and surviving soldiers attended the burial. His signet and Arlen Rusk's scorched petition remain at the chapel for preservation rather than hereditary succession. His memory is disputed as hero, rightful leader, or casualty, while Elianor and the coastal resistance remain committed to honoring his life without making his name a throne.

set.name: Ash
set.description: Alive in the old stable at Greyhaven, trembling but safe after the assault, with her white blaze and old injuries. Tomas's body passed her stall before burial, and Elianor placed his hand against her face; she appeared to remember him. She remains under the care of the stable hands and is vulnerable to the damaged estate and continuing shortages. Her immediate goal, as far as the household can provide, is safety, food, water, and recovery.

set.name: Lysa
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel and Greyhaven's lower routes, exhausted and grieving, helping record and distribute grain to refugees, wounded people, prisoners, rebels, and servants. She witnessed Elianor stop retaliatory violence and remains cautiously allied with her, Bryn, Vey, Harl, Orren, Mara, and the coastal network. Her immediate goal is to protect Rill survivors, help identify the dead, and ensure Greyhaven's stores are shared transparently.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: At Saint Orra's Chapel, exhausted with her injured left hand bandaged, recording public grain distributions on a board salvaged from the wedding table. She carried the scorched iron box and helped secure the surviving records, and remains allied with Elianor, Vey, Harl, Orren, Mara, Lysa, villagers, servants, and the coastal resistance. Her immediate goal is to maintain honest ration records, help copy the archives, and ensure food reaches prisoners, wounded people, refugees, rebels, and household survivors without sacrificing vulnerable dependents.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: At Tomas's burial ground beside the old sea garden and Saint Orra's Chapel, blood dried at her temple and one sleeve stiff with blood, directing coastal fighters and supporting Elianor's humane terms. She helped stop a rebel's retaliation by invoking Tomas's orders and argues against turning Tomas into a hereditary ruler or statue. She is allied with Elianor, Sella, Harl, Vey, Orren, Bryn, Lysa, Joren, villagers, servants, and the resistance. Her immediate goal is to maintain discipline, protect prisoners, and help build a political settlement around Tomas's program rather than his bloodline.

set.name: Sella Rusk
set.description: At Tomas's burial ground beside Greyhaven's old sea garden after traveling from Saint Orra's Abbey, emotionally controlled but grieving, with knowledge of Arlen's surviving petition and Tomas's refusal of hereditary power. She placed her hand on Tomas's grave and publicly rejected reducing him to a statue or ruler. She is allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Harl, Vey, Orren, Bryn, villagers, and the coastal resistance. Her immediate goal is to protect Arlen's cause as a program of representation, limits on levies, and humane government while resisting opportunists who invoke the Rusk name.

After Greyhaven fell, Elianor ordered food distributed publicly to wounded people, refugees, rebels, household survivors, and surrendered prisoners, forbidding rationing or punishment based on rank or hatred.
Elianor stopped a rebel from beating a surrendered marine and established that prisoners would remain alive until public hearings, preserving Tomas's humane surrender terms.

Master Vey and Bryn brought the surviving grain books and scorched original Rusk depositions, land transfers, and petition to Saint Orra's Chapel, where Elianor ordered them preserved and publicly copied.
Tomas Rusk was buried without noble honors in the wind-cut ground beside the old sea garden, and Elianor publicly rejected turning his name or signet into hereditary authority.
The dead of Greyhaven, including villagers, servants, rebels, garrison soldiers, marines, and nobles, were covered and entered into a common public record rather than separated by rank.
Elianor must organize public hearings for surrendered soldiers and accused collaborators, keeping testimony and judgments separate from retaliatory vengeance.
The surviving grain books and Rusk papers must be copied and made accessible to coastal settlements, with village delegates involved in counting and distributing the remaining stores.

chapters.name: The Long Rebellion
chapters.content:
For two years after Greyhaven fell, Elianor learned that a gate could be opened in a single morning and kept open only by a thousand hands.

The first winter, she slept in storehouses, chapels, fishermen's lofts, and once beneath an overturned cart while rain struck its wooden wheels. She carried no household seal. The Marrow signet had been melted with the other silver recovered from the keep and poured into spoons, buckles, and small tools for the settlements. What remained of her wealth traveled ahead of her in ledgers: coin for roof beams, sacks of seed, iron nails, salt, lamp oil, and medicines. Every payment was written twice, once by the person who gave it and once by the person who received it.

The coast did not trust the first record.

It trusted the second only slightly more.

At Rill, Elianor stood in the shell of Lysa's cottage while carpenters fitted a new frame into the blackened walls. The sea wall had been patched with stone, timber, and the ribs of two wrecked boats. Beyond it, gulls screamed over mud where houses had stood.

“Three beams,” said the carpenter. “Not four. The fourth belongs to the cooper's shed.”

“The shed can wait,” Elianor said.

Lysa, thinner than she had been before the flood, shook her head. “The cooper has six children.”

“Then divide the beams.”

“That gives neither roof enough to stand.”

Elianor looked at the open sky above them. The old instinct rose in her—to decide, to command, to make scarcity obey the firmness of her voice. She felt Tomas beside that instinct, patient as a hand held near a frightened mare.

“Ask the cooper whether he would rather have two beams now or one roof in three days,” she said. “Ask me again after he answers. We will not choose for people who are present.”

Lysa studied her face. “You sound like him.”

The words were not praise. They were a wound gently touched.

“I am trying to.”

“No. You sound like yourself when you remembered to listen.”

Together they carried the beams into the rain. By dusk, the cooper had chosen the divided timber. His shed received a temporary brace, Lysa's cottage a roof frame, and no one called the arrangement fair. It was merely visible, and therefore open to challenge. Elianor wrote both names in the account book before she slept.

In Bracken Cove, the fishing fleet had been reduced to eleven boats. Elianor used the last of her private jewels to buy netting from a merchant who had once sold grain through Merrit & Sons. The merchant demanded a noblewoman's guarantee. She gave him a list of his own unpaid debts to three villages and told him the nets would be seized if he cheated them.

Mara, reading over her shoulder, raised an eyebrow. “That was almost a threat.”

“It was an accounting.”

“Your father used to call his threats accounts.”

“Then I will make mine verifiable.”

Mara laughed, though fatigue had hollowed her eyes. She had become a road-worn negotiator, carrying sealed agreements between councils that would gladly have agreed to anything except sitting in the same room. Joren traveled with her when he was not escorting grain caravans, broader now across the shoulders and permanently lame from the injury he received at Greyhaven.

They met in barns, ruined tollhouses, and village kitchens. Northwatch wanted command of the coastal forts. Bracken Cove wanted the forts dismantled. The harbor captains demanded control of customs. The inland farmers wanted the ports taxed to replace the levies that had once been taken from them. Former soldiers wanted pay, land, or both. Some wanted every noble estate broken into fields. Others, especially minor landholders who had abandoned the crown, wanted reform without surrendering their houses.

“There are seven rebellions,” Joren said one night in a rain-darkened guildhall, “and each believes the other six are treason.”

“Eight,” Mara replied. “The prisoners have their own.”

She had insisted that surrendered soldiers be heard publicly, as Tomas had required. Not all were innocent. A captain who had burned a village was named by four witnesses and sentenced by the village assembly to labor rebuilding its sea wall. A conscript who had carried messages under threat was released with food and a place on a fishing crew. The distinction took time. Time was the one thing every faction claimed it could not spare.

Elianor attended whenever she could. She sat below the speaking platform, never above it, and wrote the names of the dead when arguments became too abstract. The list grew until it required three books. At one hearing, a widow interrupted a captain's polished defense by placing a child's shoe on the table. No one spoke for several minutes. The captain was not condemned that day; neither was he released. The assembly sent witnesses to the burned village, and Elianor added a fourth column to the record: what remained to be repaired.

At Saint Orra's Chapel, Master Vey maintained the public archive. Copies of the grain books and Rusk papers were sent by boat and road to every settlement that had a council willing to receive them. Bryn kept the ration accounts in a traveling chest, her once-injured hand stiff but capable. She had become feared by merchants and beloved by hungry children, which she considered a balanced reputation.

“Your expenses are impossible,” Bryn told Elianor after the first year. “You have spent nearly everything.”

“Nearly?”

“There is Greyhaven.”

Greyhaven had become a council house in all but name. Its upper rooms were roofless, its great hall open to the weather, and its old stable repaired before the lord's chambers. Ash lived there still. She had grown calm with age, though she turned her head whenever Elianor entered, as if expecting another hand to reach through the stall bars.

Elianor had not ridden her for months. The mare's back carried scars, and Elianor's wrist still ached in damp weather. But on the anniversary of the assault she led Ash along the cliff road while workers below laid new stones in the harbor wall.

Tomas had taught her the first rule of riding: do not confuse the animal's fear with disobedience.

The rule had outlived him.

By the second spring, royal orders arrived only as rumors. The crown's ministers commanded the northern garrisons to retake the coast, then ordered the confiscation of rebel lands, then promised pardons to any settlement that surrendered its leaders. Each order bore a seal no one trusted and arrived weeks after the conditions it described had changed.

At Northwatch, the soldiers refused to march.

Their commander read the minister's decree from the fort steps. It required them to seize grain from the town, arrest three councilors, and conscript boys for military labor. The rank-and-file listened in silence. Then a young soldier named Perren took the paper from his commander's hand and read aloud the names of the men who had died during the winter retreat.

“My brother is on this list,” he said. “The order says we are to take his family's grain.”

No one raised a weapon when the soldiers opened the stores instead. The commander was escorted to a hearing. Two days later, the garrison sent word that it would defend Northwatch from any force that tried to restore the ministers, but would not enforce royal orders against the town.

The refusal traveled faster than Elianor could.

At Hallowmere, tax clerks laid down their quills. At Durn, cavalry refused to burn the ledgers and instead brought them to the village square. A fleet at Blackwater Reach sailed home without firing on the harbor. One by one, the crown's commands became letters carried into places where no one would obey them.

The crown collapsed not with a single battle but with the sound of doors shutting against its officers. The royal standard vanished from the northern forts first, then from the customs houses. A minister attempted to flee by fishing boat and was returned by the crew, not in chains but with a demand that he answer for the accounts he had signed. Even then, the coast did not agree on what justice required. Some wanted a scaffold. Others wanted the records opened and the stolen revenues returned. Elianor argued for the latter, knowing that a dead minister could not name every accomplice.

When the news reached Greyhaven, people filled the ruined hall. Some cheered. Others stared at one another, suddenly aware that victory had removed the shape of the enemy and left them facing one another across the same empty tables.

Mara placed a packet on the council bench. “The western captains propose that Tomas's name be recognized as the lawful foundation of the new coast.”

Elianor felt the signet beneath her shirt, though she had not worn it publicly since the burial.

“What does recognized mean?” she asked.

Joren opened the packet. “His bloodline would hold a permanent seat in the assembly. The Rusk lands would become a hereditary trust. A successor could be selected from his family if the councils fail to agree.”

“No,” Elianor said.

The word crossed the hall like a thrown stone.

A harbor lord named Venn rose from the benches. “You loved him. You know what he wanted.”

“I know what he refused.”

“He was Arlen Rusk's son.”

“He was Tomas. He spent his life refusing to be made into an inheritance.”

Venn's mouth tightened. “Without a name, factions will tear this coast apart.”

“Then build agreements strong enough to survive without a dead man's name.”

A murmur moved through the hall. Some voices supported her. Others called her a Marrow still, a noblewoman protecting her claim to power by pretending humility. Someone shouted that she had no right to speak for Tomas because she had been born above him.

That accusation was true. It was also not an answer.

Elianor turned toward the benches. “I was born into a house that took food, land, and lives. I benefited from it before I understood it. I cannot make that vanish by saying I loved one man who opposed it. If you give me authority, give it because I can be questioned, removed, and held to an account—not because Tomas kissed me, not because my father is dead, and not because his blood is useful.”

Silence followed. It was not agreement. It was the first space in which agreement might be made.

Mara stood. “The proposal is rejected.”

Venn protested, but Joren was already calling for the next matter: the division of seized lands, the repair levy for the sea wall, the treatment of former crown officers, the winter grain reserve. The work of freedom was less glorious than its announcement. It required measurements, witnesses, apologies, and people willing to return tomorrow after losing an argument today.

That evening, Elianor went alone to the old sea garden. Only a few rows had survived the war. Nettles grew around the broken irrigation channel she and Tomas had repaired long ago. She knelt and cleared mud from a stone with her bare fingers.

Mara found her there.

“You could leave,” Mara said. “You have enough money for a ship and a house somewhere the coast has not heard your name.”

“So could you.”

“I have a bad leg and enemies in six villages.”

“I have a worse reputation.”

Mara sat on the fallen wall. For a while, neither spoke. Below them, the sea garden sloped toward the rebuilt harbor. Children carried baskets of turnips between the rows. A bell rang from the chapel—not for death, but for the evening distribution.

“Does it get easier?” Mara asked.

Elianor watched the children disappear behind the bean poles. “No.”

“Good,” Mara said. “I was afraid grief might make us careless.”

Elianor touched the place beneath her shirt where the signet rested in a small cloth pouch. She had returned it to the chapel archive after the assembly rejected the hereditary proposal. Tomas's petition lay beside it, copied in dozens of hands now. His name was no longer rare enough to belong to one family.

The war had lasted two years. The hunger had lasted longer. The peace, when people called it that, was a collection of unfinished roofs and disputed boundaries, guarded by exhausted soldiers who had discovered that obedience was not the same as honor.

Elianor rose and brushed the soil from her hands.

“There is a meeting in the lower hall,” she said.

“About the grain?”

“About who has counted it.”

Mara groaned. “A terrible subject.”

“The important ones usually are.”

They walked back toward the lights together. Behind them, the sea garden held the dark between its rows, and somewhere in the old stable Ash stamped once against the floor, waiting for morning.

Elianor did not mistake the sound for a promise. She had learned better than that.

Still, she kept walking.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: Based primarily at the ruined Greyhaven, now functioning as an informal council house, while traveling among Rill, Bracken Cove, Northwatch, Hallowmere, Durn, Blackwater Reach, and other coastal settlements. Over two years she has spent nearly all remaining personal wealth on rebuilding homes, sea walls, fishing nets, seed, food, and medicine; she keeps public double-entry records and attends hearings. Emotionally she remains grieving Tomas but has turned grief into accountable work. She rejects the Marrow title as a basis for authority and opposes making Tomas's name hereditary power. She is allied with Mara, Joren, Bryn, Vey, Orren, Lysa, Harl, coastal councils, former soldiers, villagers, and reformers; some factions distrust her as a Marrow noblewoman. She knows the crown has collapsed through military and administrative refusal, but the coast remains divided. She retains access to the surviving public archive, while Tomas's signet and petition are kept in the chapel archive. Her immediate goals are to help build an accountable provisional assembly, preserve transparent grain distribution and hearings, repair the coast, and prevent both old aristocracy and new Rusk hereditary rule.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: Based at Saint Orra's Chapel, maintaining and copying the surviving grain books, Rusk petition, depositions, and land transfers for distribution to coastal settlements. He is aging, smoke-marked by Greyhaven's fall, and committed to public accounting. He is allied with Elianor, Bryn, Mara, Joren, Orren, Lysa, Harl, and the coastal councils. He knows the crown has collapsed and that factions are disputing land and authority. His immediate goal is to preserve the archive, circulate copies, and establish records that can be examined by village delegates.

set.name: Ash
set.description: Alive and safe in Greyhaven's repaired old stable, older and calmer but still attentive to Elianor and the memory of Tomas. She bears old scars and remains under the care of stable hands while the council house and surrounding harbor are rebuilt. Her immediate need is continued food, shelter, and care.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: Based at Saint Orra's Chapel and traveling with the relief network, maintaining ration and expenditure accounts in a traveling chest. Her previously injured hand remains stiff but functional. She is feared by dishonest merchants and trusted by hungry children, and remains allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Vey, Orren, Lysa, Harl, coastal councils, and vulnerable dependents. She has helped make grain accounting public and has seen the crown's administrative collapse. Her immediate goal is to keep food records transparent, prevent hoarding, and support the archive and future assembly.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: Traveling between Greyhaven, coastal villages, forts, guildhalls, and council meetings as a principal negotiator among rival rebel factions. She is road-worn, fatigued, and has witnessed the war's dead and the difficult public hearings, but remains disciplined and committed to Tomas's humane program rather than vengeance. She is allied with Elianor, Joren, Bryn, Vey, Orren, Lysa, Sella, villagers, former soldiers, and coastal councils, while facing factional opponents who want military or hereditary rule. She helped reject a proposal to make Tomas's bloodline the permanent foundation of government. Her immediate goals are to negotiate a provisional assembly, reconcile competing coastal interests, protect civilians, and prevent Tomas's memory from becoming a throne.

set.name: Joren Pell
set.description: Traveling with Mara or escorting grain caravans between coastal settlements and Greyhaven. He remains broad-shouldered but permanently lame from his Greyhaven injury, and is active in negotiations and security. He has helped distinguish culpable officers from coerced conscripts in public hearings and has witnessed the crown's collapse. He is allied with Elianor, Mara, Bryn, Vey, Orren, Lysa, Harl, villagers, former soldiers, and reform factions. He opposes revenge and hereditary Rusk authority. His immediate goals are to protect relief caravans, support public hearings, and help factions agree on accountable local government.

set.name: Sella Rusk
set.description: Based between Saint Orra's Chapel, the Rusk archive network, and coastal councils, preserving Arlen Rusk's petition and Tomas's stated refusal of hereditary power. She is grieving but controlled and opposes using either man's name as a political idol. She is allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Vey, Bryn, Orren, villagers, and reform-minded delegates. Her immediate goal is to protect the Rusk cause as a program of representation, limits on levies, and humane government while supporting a public archive.

Over the two years after Greyhaven's fall, Elianor traveled among coastal settlements, spending her remaining wealth on roofs, seed, nets, medicines, sea walls, and transparent food distribution while refusing to use noble authority as a private claim.

Mara and Joren negotiated among rival coastal factions, including village councils, harbor captains, former soldiers, farmers, and minor landholders, while public hearings distinguished responsible officers from coerced conscripts.

Royal authority collapsed through widespread refusal: Northwatch soldiers opened stores and rejected conscription orders, tax clerks at Hallowmere and Durn stopped enforcing crown demands, and Blackwater Reach's fleet refused to fire on the harbor.

Coastal leaders proposed making Tomas Rusk's bloodline the permanent foundation of the new government, but Elianor rejected hereditary seats, trusts, or succession based on his name and argued for accountable authority instead.
The provisional coastal assembly must be formed and must settle land, taxation, forced levies, and local representation while preserving public records and humane hearings.
Elianor must convert the ruined Greyhaven into an elected council house and formally renounce the Marrow title and inheritance.
The public archive must continue recording the famine, rebellion, Marrow crimes, and Tomas's life without allowing his name or signet to become a political idol.

chapters.name: The Assembly
chapters.content:
The first meeting of the provisional assembly was held in the great hall at Greyhaven, though no one called it the great hall anymore.

The roof still opened to the weather in three places. Rain had darkened the long table where Lord Marrow had once received taxes, petitions, and flattering reports from men who never stood in the lower yard. One wall was black with smoke. The carved crest above the hearth had been hacked away, leaving only four pale scars in the stone. Through the high windows, Elianor could see the sea striking the rebuilt harbor wall and the square below, where people waited beneath patched awnings for the day's grain allotment.

A year earlier, she had crossed that square as Lady Marrow, guarded by men who bowed before they searched the baskets of hungry women. Now she entered carrying a ledger under one arm and a bundle of keys at her belt.

The keys were not hers. That was the point.

“Are they all here?” Mara asked.

She stood at the head of the table, not seated, with a strip of red cloth tied around her wrist to mark the assembly's temporary officers. Her hair had silvered at the temples during the two years of war. Beside her, Joren leaned on his ashwood crutch and watched the doors with the habitual suspicion of a man who had survived too many negotiations by noticing who had not yet arrived.

“Everyone who agreed to come,” Elianor said.

“Which is not the same thing.”

“No,” said Master Vey from the table's far end. “It is more useful.”

The delegates came in clusters, as if the old hall still had invisible rooms dividing them. Three village speakers from Rill sat together, their coats smelling of salt and wet rope. Hallowmere sent two millers and a woman who had kept its grain accounts after the tax clerks abandoned their office. From Blackwater Reach came guild leaders with ink-stained fingers and sailors' knives at their belts. Northwatch sent a former captain and two rankers who had opened the garrison stores rather than enforce conscription. Farmers from Durn arrived mud-spattered and furious about land boundaries drawn by dead men.

There were also five minor nobles who had survived the collapse of the crown by changing sides early enough to call it conscience. They wore no crests, but their boots were too fine and their hands too unscarred. One of them, Lord Varrin, kept looking at Elianor as if her presence were an insult he had been forced to swallow.

The coastal communities had demanded seats of their own. So had the soldiers. So had the guilds. By the time all the benches were filled, there was scarcely room for the arguments.

Mara struck the table once with the butt of a wooden staff.

“We are not a court,” she said. “We are not a crown in waiting. We are not the council of one estate pretending to speak for a country. We are here to decide what must be done until the villages and towns can choose a permanent form of government.”

A fisherman from Rill gave a harsh laugh. “And who chooses the people who decide that?”

“The people who have sent delegates,” Mara answered.

“Some sent one. Some sent six.”

“Then our first decision is whether that is just.”

The argument began before the rules had been written. It moved from the number of seats to the meaning of a village, from the meaning of a village to the ownership of the fields around it, and from ownership to the question no one wished to name plainly: who had the right to command when everyone had learned that command could be resisted?

Elianor listened. She had spent two years learning how hunger altered a meeting. Men who had eaten that morning spoke of principle. Men who had not eaten spoke of time. Women with children at home measured every speech against the length of the queue outside. Soldiers spoke of order because they had seen disorder kill. Villagers distrusted order because they had seen it arrive with a tax ledger and a torch.

At noon, Bryn brought in a pot of barley stew. No one was served first. The bowls went around the table in the same order as the speakers had been seated, and when the pot was empty, Vey recorded how many had eaten and how many had not.

Lord Varrin stared at him. “Must you account for every spoonful?”

“Yes,” said Bryn. Her damaged hand trembled as she set down the ladle, but her voice did not. “That is how we know whether there is enough.”

“It is a meal, not a military campaign.”

“It was a meal under Lord Marrow too. The difference was that no one recorded where it went.”

No one answered her.

The first settlement concerned levies. The question had been carried from village to village in petitions, shouted from harbor steps, and written on the doors of abandoned tax offices. Every faction wanted the old forced levy ended, though some soldiers insisted that an emergency defense could not be maintained by goodwill alone.

A former captain from Northwatch rose. His name was Edran Holt, and he had spent eleven years wearing the crown's blue coat.

“If the sea fleet returns,” he said, “we need men. If the eastern lords gather their own troops, we need men. If raiders come because the roads are unguarded, we need men. You cannot defend a coast by declaring that no one may be compelled to stand upon it.”

“Then pay them,” said the miller from Hallowmere.

“With what?”

“With the taxes you intend to collect.”

“And if the treasury is empty?”

“Then ask.”

A murmur rolled through the room. Some people laughed. Others did not.

Joren lifted one hand. “The old levy took sons for years, not days. It took children for labor. It took men from fishing boats during storms and farmers during planting. There must be a difference between asking a citizen to defend the place where he lives and taking him because an officer needs a body.”

“A difference written by whom?” Holt asked.

“By us,” Mara said. “And reviewed by the villages that must live under it.”

The proposal that emerged was clumsy and therefore perhaps honest: no person could be conscripted for ordinary service; local councils could call a temporary defense levy during invasion or declared emergency; every call had to state its length, purpose, provisions, and pay; and the assembly could not renew it without recorded consent from the affected communities.

The former captain objected to the word “pay.” The Rill delegates objected to the word “emergency.” The nobles objected to nearly everything. But when the vote was taken, the measure passed by a narrow margin.

Elianor wrote it into the ledger.

Her hand paused over the date.

“Read it aloud,” said Sella Rusk.

Sella had come from the chapel archive carrying a copy of Arlen's petition in a leather case against the rain. She had not sat with the Rusk sympathizers, because she had refused to let a family name become a faction. She sat between a fisherwoman from Rill and a former marine who had lowered his weapon during the surrender at Greyhaven.
