Elianor read the settlement. When she finished, the hall remained silent for a breath.

Then the fisherwoman began to cry.

No one asked her why. Everyone understood.

The debate over taxation lasted until evening. The crown's collectors had left behind a country stripped by fees whose names changed whenever the treasury emptied. Harbor dues, road maintenance, grain inspection, emergency contribution, crown defense: every charge had been temporary until it became permanent.

The assembly set a limit. No community would surrender more than a fixed portion of its harvest or trade in any year, and the rate could not be raised without public hearings. Essential food would not be taxed while a settlement remained below its declared survival stores. A council could refuse collection if the accounts were not open.

“Those rules will starve the government,” Lord Varrin said.

“Then the government will learn to live on less,” Bryn replied.

Varrin turned to Elianor. “You encourage this. You know what administration costs. You know what roads, ships, courts, and walls require.”

“I know what they cost,” she said. “I also know what unrecorded costs are paid by people who have no seat in rooms like this.”

“You speak as if you alone discovered injustice.”

“No. I speak because I helped inherit it.”

That answer passed through the room more sharply than any accusation. The noble delegates looked away. The villagers did not.

The hardest matter was land.

Greyhaven's old records named fields, mills, coves, and orchards as properties of the Marrow house, though many had belonged to families before the execution of Arlen Rusk and the confiscations that followed. Vey had brought the surviving ledgers. Sella had brought depositions. Villagers brought memories, boundary stones, and the names of dead grandparents. No paper could settle every claim. Some land had passed through three owners since the crown seized it. Some families had been expelled. Others had bought farms in good faith from men who had possessed them by theft.

The room grew hot with anger.

A farmer from Durn struck the table. “My father was driven from the north fields. If a noble bought them afterward, that does not make the sale clean.”

“And if my mother bought her house with money earned at a loom?” asked a guild representative. “Do we cast her out because the first title was false?”

A young soldier shouted that all estates should be broken apart. Another answered that without large farms there would be no seed stores. Someone near the door drew a knife. Harl, seated with the guards, rose before the blade cleared its sheath.

“Put it down,” he said.

The command carried the old force of rank, and for an instant the hall obeyed out of habit. Harl seemed to feel that habit pass through him. He lowered his crutch and added, “Not because I say so. Because no one settles a land dispute by adding another name to the dead.”

The knife disappeared.

They agreed to local land boards, elected in each district and subject to public appeal. Seized lands would not be sold by the assembly to enrich itself. Families dispossessed after the crown's executions would receive first consideration, but present occupants would not be stripped without inquiry. Common fields, mills, forests, and shore rights would belong to the communities. Greyhaven's remaining lands would be held in trust until the boards could examine them.

It was not justice in the clean form people had imagined while fighting. It was a process, slow and vulnerable to bribery, memory, and revenge.

“It is the beginning of justice,” Mara said when someone called it cowardice.

“It is the postponement of justice,” the young soldier answered.

“Yes,” Mara said. “And postponement is dangerous. So is pretending that a sword can decide which starving family is innocent.”

Night had fallen when the final matter was brought forward.

Elianor stood beneath the scarred stone where the Marrow crest had been. The room seemed to tilt toward her. Even those who distrusted her wanted to see what she would surrender.

Master Vey placed a document on the table. It had been written in a clear hand and witnessed by the chapel, the coastal delegates, and three former soldiers.

Elianor removed the keys from her belt and laid them beside it.

“I was born Elianor Vale,” she said. “I was raised in this house and called Lady Marrow after my mother's death. The title carried authority because other people were denied it. The lands attached to it were enlarged by confiscation, forced payments, and records written to make violence look lawful.”

A nobleman near the window muttered, “Traitor.”

The word did not surprise her. It hurt less than it once would have.

“I renounce the title of Lady Marrow,” she continued. “I renounce any hereditary claim to Greyhaven, its harbor, its fields, its stores, and its archives. I do not give them to the assembly as my gift. They were never mine to give.”

She pushed the keys forward.

“Greyhaven will become a council house. Its hall will be open to elected delegates. Its granaries will be managed under public accounts. Its surviving archive will be copied and available for examination. The estate's remaining revenues will fund repair until the local boards determine what is owed and to whom.”

Lord Varrin rose so quickly his chair struck the floor.

“You would turn your ancestral home into a public inn and call it virtue.”

“I would turn a fortress that was used against the coast into a place where the coast can speak.”

“You claim credit for surrendering what rebellion already took.”

Across the hall, a scarred harbor captain shouted, “She still speaks as if she saved us.”

Elianor looked toward him. “I did not save Greyhaven. Tomas did not save Greyhaven. Mara did not save Greyhaven. People opened the gates, carried grain from fire, refused orders, tended the wounded, and endured long enough to make a different choice possible. If anyone writes otherwise, they are lying.”

The captain's mouth tightened, but he sat.

At the name Tomas, the room changed. It always changed. Some faces softened. Others hardened with calculation.

A delegate from Northwatch stood. “If this council house bears his name, the coast will remember what he stood for.”

“It will also remember that his blood was used to demand obedience,” Sella said. “No.”

Elianor touched the signet beneath her clothing, where it hung on a cord against her heart. “Greyhaven will bear no man's name as a crown. Not Tomas's. Not my father's. Not any ruler's.”

The resolution passed after midnight.

Not unanimously. Nothing honest in the hall had passed unanimously.

The keys were placed in a locked chest whose three locks required three different custodians: one chosen by the coastal delegates, one by the guilds, and one by the village councils. No single person, not even Elianor, could open it alone.

When the assembly adjourned, rain had stopped. The square below shone under a broken moon. People were still waiting for bread, arguing over land notices, and carrying news from villages where old officers had been dragged from hiding or forgiven by frightened communities.

Elianor stepped outside without a guard. Bryn came beside her with the ledger. Mara and Joren followed more slowly.

“Tomorrow,” Mara said, “we begin the committees.”

“Tomorrow,” Elianor agreed.

“And the day after that, someone will accuse us of betrayal.”

“Someone already has.”

Joren looked back at the hall. “That is how we know it is no longer a lord's house. People are speaking against the walls.”

Elianor listened. From the old chapel came the bell marking the night watch. From the stable came the quiet stamping of Ash. Beyond the harbor, the sea continued its ancient argument with the cliffs.

She had imagined that renouncing the title would feel like freedom. Instead it felt like setting down a weight and discovering the shape it had left in her bones.

“Do you regret it?” Bryn asked.

Elianor looked up at the ruined crest, pale beneath the moon.

“I regret that it took so many dead to teach me what it meant.”

Then she opened the ledger, and together they began recording the first expenses of Greyhaven's new life.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: Based at Greyhaven, now formally converted from the Marrow fortress into an elected council house, while continuing to travel among Rill, Bracken Cove, Northwatch, Hallowmere, Durn, Blackwater Reach, and other coastal settlements. She has renounced the title Lady Marrow and all hereditary claim to Greyhaven, its lands, stores, harbor, and archives; she retains no private authority over the estate. She works with Mara, Joren, Bryn, Vey, Orren, Harl, Sella, coastal councils, village delegates, guild leaders, former soldiers, and reformers, though former aristocrats call her a traitor and some rebels accuse her of claiming credit. She keeps public double-entry records and supports the assembly's limits on taxation, end of ordinary forced levies, humane hearings, and local land boards. Tomas's signet remains under her clothing for safekeeping, while the public archive preserves his life and principles without making his name hereditary power. She is grieving, physically exhausted, emotionally steadied by accountable work, and now faces the danger of factional capture, poverty, violence, and institutional failure.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: Based at Greyhaven's elected council house and Saint Orra's Chapel, maintaining, copying, and publicly displaying the surviving grain books, Rusk petition, depositions, land transfers, and assembly records. He is aging and smoke-marked, committed to open accounts and shared custody of Greyhaven's keys. He is allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Bryn, Orren, Harl, Sella, village delegates, guild leaders, and coastal councils. He knows the assembly has ended ordinary forced levies, limited taxation, and assigned seized-land claims to local boards. His immediate goal is to preserve the archive, circulate copies, and ensure the new institutions cannot hide their decisions.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: Based at Greyhaven's council house and inner routes, limping on an improvised crutch with an injured knee and face. He oversees security without restoring lordly command, protects delegates and prisoners, and enforces the assembly's rejection of retaliatory violence. He is allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Vey, Bryn, Orren, Sella, villagers, former soldiers, and reformers. He supports paid, time-limited emergency defense rather than ordinary forced levies. His immediate goal is to prevent factional fighting around land claims and assembly decisions while keeping Greyhaven open and safe.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: Based at Greyhaven's council house and traveling with the relief network, maintaining ration, expenditure, and assembly food records in her traveling chest. Her injured hand remains stiff but functional. She is allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Vey, Orren, Harl, Sella, coastal councils, guilds, and vulnerable dependents, while distrusted by dishonest merchants and former aristocrats. She helped ensure the assembly's meals and public accounts were transparent and supports its taxation and relief rules. Her immediate goal is to keep grain distribution honest and expose hoarding or institutional capture.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: Based between Greyhaven's new council house, coastal villages, guildhalls, forts, and assembly meetings, serving as a principal negotiator and temporary organizer of the provisional assembly. She is road-worn and fatigued but disciplined, allied with Elianor, Joren, Bryn, Vey, Orren, Harl, Sella, village delegates, guild leaders, former soldiers, and coastal councils. She helped establish rules ending ordinary forced levies, limiting taxation, and placing seized lands before local boards. She opposes both aristocratic restoration and hereditary Rusk authority. Her immediate goal is to keep the assembly functioning, prevent factional violence and elite capture, and turn temporary settlements into accountable government.

set.name: Joren Pell
set.description: Based at Greyhaven and traveling between the council house, relief routes, and coastal negotiations, permanently lame and using a crutch after his Greyhaven injury. He is allied with Elianor, Mara, Bryn, Vey, Orren, Harl, Sella, villagers, guild representatives, former soldiers, and reform factions. He supports the new limits on taxation, paid emergency defense service, humane hearings, and local land boards, and continues distinguishing culpable officers from coerced conscripts. His immediate goal is to protect assembly delegates and relief caravans while preventing revenge or factional violence from destroying the settlement.

set.name: Sella Rusk
set.description: Based between Saint Orra's Chapel, Greyhaven's council house, the Rusk archive network, and coastal councils, preserving Arlen Rusk's petition and Tomas's stated refusal of hereditary power. She is grieving but controlled, allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Vey, Bryn, Orren, Harl, village and guild delegates, and reform-minded communities. She helped reject naming Greyhaven or the new government around Tomas's bloodline. Her immediate goal is to protect the Rusk cause as a program of representation, limited levies, and humane government while ensuring the archive remains public rather than becoming a political shrine.
The provisional assembly convened at Greyhaven with village, guild, soldier, coastal, and reform-minded noble delegates and adopted initial rules for representation and recorded public decisions.
The assembly ended ordinary forced levies, allowing only time-limited, paid emergency defense service authorized through recorded consent from affected communities.
The assembly limited taxation through harvest and trade caps, public hearings, open accounts, and protection for communities below survival stores.
The assembly placed seized lands under local elected boards and established communal control of common fields, mills, forests, and shore rights while requiring inquiries into competing claims.

Elianor renounced the title of Lady Marrow and all hereditary claims to Greyhaven, its lands, stores, harbor, and archives, converting the ruined estate into an elected council house governed through shared custodianship of its keys.
The assembly rejected naming Greyhaven or establishing authority around Tomas Rusk, preserving his memory without creating hereditary or personal rule.

The provisional assembly must create and oversee local land boards, public taxation hearings, and emergency-defense procedures without allowing factional violence or wealthy former aristocrats to capture the new institutions.

chapters.name: The Unplastered Wall
chapters.content:
The wall above the old stable remained unplastered.

No one had repaired it because no one could agree what repair meant. The stones had been blackened by the fire Lord Marrow ordered in the last hours of Greyhaven, and the mortar between them had fallen away in pale scars. Rain entered through the gaps. Wind carried salt into the tack room. In winter, a strip of sea-colored light crossed the floor before dawn.

Some delegates wanted the wall rebuilt properly. Others said the smoke marks should remain. A mason from Rill had proposed covering only the deepest cracks, leaving the black stones visible. A former nobleman had called that theatrical. Bryn had answered that the difference between history and theater was whether the audience was allowed to check the accounts afterward.

The wall stayed as it was.

Five years after the uprising, Elianor still woke before the bells. She woke sometimes believing she had heard Tomas calling from the lower yard, his voice lifted above the stamping of frightened horses. In the dream he was always alive and always busy. He was asking for a bucket, arguing with a groom, laughing because she had come to the stable in a gown meant for dinner. She would turn toward him, and the dream would break before she reached his face.

That morning she lay still beneath the thin blanket and listened to the council house breathe.

Greyhaven no longer sounded like a fortress. The old portcullis had been dismantled and its iron used in the harbor wall. The watch changed at the front gate, but no sentry challenged a fisherwoman carrying mussels or a child running late for lessons. Doors that had once been locked against petitions stood open to the weather. Somewhere below, a clerk was arguing over the price of lime. From the courtyard came the clatter of carts carrying seed to Hallowmere.

Freer, Elianor thought. Not free.

A bell rang twice from the archive wing.

She dressed, fastened the sign of the council beneath her collar, and went downstairs.

Master Vey was waiting by the archive door with a ring of keys. He had grown smaller over the years without seeming less solid. His hair was white, his left eyebrow still marked by a line of fire, and his spectacles were repaired with wire at one hinge. Behind him, the archive room held shelves built from salvaged doors. Every box bore two labels: one in the old household hand and one in the newer public script.

“Rill has sent the corrected casualty list,” he said. “Three names were missing from the first copy.”

“Then the first copy is not destroyed.”

“I would never destroy a record because it embarrassed us.”

“It did not embarrass us,” said Elianor. “It failed the dead.”

Vey inclined his head. “That is the more serious form of embarrassment.”

He led her between the shelves. The archive had become the most visited place in Greyhaven, which still surprised those who remembered what the room had been. Children came to read the old grain ledgers. Delegates came to compare land transfers with village testimony. Sailors came to find the names of men executed after the Blackwater mutiny. Former soldiers came quietly, carrying letters they had been afraid to surrender while the crown held power.

The records did not make anyone agree. They made lying more difficult.

On the central table lay the five volumes of the famine register, the surviving grain books, and a stitched copy of Arlen Rusk's petition. Beside them was the book Elianor had commissioned two years earlier: *The Coast in the Years of Famine and Rising*. Its pages contained the names of the dead, the displaced, the imprisoned, the missing, and those who had survived with injuries no clerk could measure.

Tomas's life occupied twelve pages.

Not a chapter of legends. Twelve pages.

His birth as Tomas Rusk, his years under the name Tomas Vale, his work in Greyhaven's stable, his aid to Rill, his role in the coastal coordination, his terms for surrendering soldiers, and his death on the battlements were set beside the names of hundreds of others. The account recorded his mistakes as carefully as his courage. He had delayed the assault to protect prisoners; the delay had allowed Veyne's marines to kill some of them. He had accepted the Rusk name as a banner despite his fear of banners. He had not saved everyone.

Elianor had insisted on that sentence.

A young archivist named Toma—named for her grandmother, not for him—stood at the table with a blotter in one hand.

“Some visitors ask why there is no portrait,” she said.

“Because portraits make people believe they have met the dead.”

Toma smiled faintly. “They ask why there is no statue.”

“Because stone can be made to command long after a person has stopped speaking.”

Vey opened the register. “The guild delegates want a commemorative plaque for him at the harbor.”

“Then the guild delegates may put his name among the names of the harbor dead.”

“They say the coast needs a figure to rally around.”

“The coast has figures. They are called neighbors.”

Vey's mouth tightened, almost a smile. “You sound like Tomas.”

The words struck more deeply than he intended. He saw it and looked down at the page.

“I know,” Elianor said. “That is why I am careful.”

At the end of the room, a shelf held objects surrendered to public custody: the scorched petition, the execution sword that had killed Arlen and Tomas, the broken ceremonial sword with which Elianor had killed Veyne, and the signet ring. The signet lay in a shallow wooden box beneath a strip of linen. It had not been worn in five years. Its silver was dull, its engraved R nearly erased by handling and fire.

Elianor had kept it under her clothing until the assembly rejected hereditary authority. Then she had returned it to the archive, because possession could become a claim even when a person meant it as grief.

Today she asked Vey for it.

He did not move at once. “For the memorial?”

“For the hour of it.”

“And afterward?”

“It returns here.”

Vey placed the ring in her palm. It was colder than she expected. She closed her fingers around it, not as she had on the battlements, when Tomas's blood had warmed the metal, but with the careful grip of a custodian receiving something that did not belong to her.

Outside, the anniversary bells began.

They rang from Saint Orra's Chapel and were answered by the harbor bell, then by smaller bells in Rill, Hallowmere, and the settlements along the cliffs. Five years since Greyhaven opened. Five years since the gates ceased to belong to one house. Five years since the sea had carried ships against the harbor and men had decided that obedience was no longer the safest form of survival.

The memorial stood in the lower yard, where the first grain had been distributed after the surrender. It was not grand. The assembly had refused a triumphal arch. A low wall of local stone curved around a patch of grass, with a narrow opening toward the sea. Names had been cut into its inner face in no order except the order in which the committees had verified them.

Villagers. Servants. Rebels. Marines. Garrison soldiers. Children. Nobles. Those who had fought and those who had been caught in the path of fighting.

No titles appeared.

No phrase called anyone a hero.

Avelune's new ministers had come from the inland provinces for the ceremony, wearing plain coats that were more expensive than they looked. Delegates stood beside them. Mara was there, older and thinner, with a cane she refused to call a cane. Joren sat near the front on his ashwood crutch. Bryn had brought the food accounts and was already correcting a clerk who had placed the memorial bread under “ceremonial expense.” Harl, his knee permanently damaged, kept the crowd from pressing against the names without allowing anyone to be turned away.

Ash waited in the stable.

Elianor had ridden her every year on this day, though the mare had become slow and white around the muzzle. The stable had been rebuilt around the old stalls. The timber Tomas had repaired remained above Ash's doorway, darkened by smoke and polished by years of hands. Elianor touched it before taking the reins.

Ash turned her head and breathed against Elianor's shoulder.

“I know,” Elianor murmured. “You remember better than I do.”

The mare carried her along the cliff path while the bells continued below. Elianor rode without escort. The council had argued about it once, but the argument had ended when she asked whether a government that required a guard to inspect its own roads had truly changed anything.

The path passed the sea garden. Its channels worked now. Beans climbed the trellises, and a girl from Rill was teaching two younger children how to cut greens without uprooting them. At the far end, beside the wind-cut ground, Tomas's grave had no railing and no carved stone. His name was on the public wall with the others. That had been his wish, insofar as a dying man could make one: no throne, no inheritance, no life treated as expendable.

Elianor stopped Ash above the water.

For a moment she imagined dismounting and walking down to the grave. She imagined kneeling there with the signet in her hand, telling Tomas about the land boards, the tax arguments, the former lords who still called her a traitor, and the villages whose councils had begun refusing wealthy merchants permission to drain common wells.

She imagined him listening. Then she remembered that listening had belonged to the living, and that she had sometimes mistaken memory for permission.

At midday she returned to the yard.

Chaplain Orren read the names aloud. He had become almost transparent with age, though his voice remained steady. When he reached the dead whose names had not yet been recovered, he read the number recorded for them and left a space afterward. The silence was part of the ceremony. It prevented absence from becoming tidiness.

When he finished, Sella Rusk stepped forward. She carried no family banner. She spoke about Arlen's petition, not as prophecy, but as one document among many that had helped the coast demand a voice. Mara spoke about the laws that had survived their first crises. Bryn read the grain stores. A fisherwoman from Rill read the names of three children found only after the wall fell.

Then Elianor approached the memorial.

She did not speak of love. Love had once been a private room between two people, and the dead were not there to defend what she said about it. She did not speak of Tomas as the heart of the rebellion. He had been a stable servant, a son, a frightened boy, a coordinator, a man who had made brave choices and costly mistakes. He had been hers for a short time, and the world had taken him before either of them could learn what a shared life would demand.

She laid the signet beneath the lowest stone of the memorial, in a hollow prepared by the mason. Not sealed away forever: a removable stone, marked in the public register, accessible to any citizen who wished to inspect it. The ring would rest there until the ceremony ended. Then it would return to the archive.

“No claim,” she said quietly. “No throne.”

The wind took the words. Perhaps no one heard them except Mara, standing close behind.

“Are you certain?” Mara asked.

“No,” Elianor answered. “But I am responsible.”

Mara looked at the names. “That is often the nearest thing to certainty we get.”

They remained beside the wall while the crowd dispersed. Children traced letters with dirty fingers. A former marine stood before the name of a prisoner he had failed to protect. Two women argued over whether a missing fisherman belonged on the list of the drowned or the disappeared. No one told them to be quiet.

At dusk, Elianor removed the signet from beneath the stone and carried it back to the archive.

The unplastered wall caught the last light. Its cracks were still visible. Rain would enter again. Someone would eventually have to mend it, and the question of how much would remain exposed would return with every generation.

Elianor placed the ring in its box.

Her grief had not become beautiful. It had become useful only when she refused to let usefulness erase grief. Tomas was not waiting in the stable, not walking the cliffs, not hidden in the habits of the mare's breath. The love they had shared had no household, no children, no long table at which to quarrel over accounts. It had survived as an absence that altered the shape of every decision.

She closed the box and recorded its return in the ledger.

Then she went downstairs to hear the evening petitions.

Outside, Avelune remained poor, divided, and vulnerable to men who promised simple answers. The new laws could be bent. The land boards could be bought. The archive could be burned again. Freedom was not a gate one opened once, but a wall people had to keep repairing while the weather worked against it.

Elianor entered the hall without a title.

Someone was waiting with a complaint about grain.

She took up her pen.

set.name: Elianor Vale
set.description: Based at Greyhaven's elected council house and traveling among Avelune's coastal settlements, now five years after the uprising. She has permanently renounced the title of Lady Marrow and all hereditary claim to Greyhaven, its lands, stores, harbor, and archives, and governs through accountable public records, evening petitions, assembly laws, and shared custodianship rather than private authority. She works with Mara, Joren, Bryn, Master Vey, Harl, Orren, Sella, delegates, guilds, village councils, former soldiers, and reformers, while former aristocrats still call her a traitor. She maintains the public archive of the famine, rebellion, Marrow crimes, Tomas's life, and all identified dead without allowing Tomas's name or signet to become hereditary power. She rides Ash along the cliffs on the uprising anniversary and keeps Tomas's signet in the public archive after temporarily placing it beneath the common memorial. She is emotionally grieving but steadied by responsible work, aware that the new government remains poor, divided, corruptible, and vulnerable to renewed violence.

set.name: Master Vey
set.description: Based at Greyhaven's elected council house archive, five years after the uprising, where he maintains and copies open records with public access. He is elderly, smoke-marked, wire-repaired in his spectacles, and committed to recording errors as well as victories. He preserves the famine registers, grain books, land transfers, Rusk petition, casualty lists, and Tomas's twelve-page life record alongside the names of all dead, while opposing portraits, statues, or political idolization of Tomas. He shares archive custody with the council and remains allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Bryn, Orren, Harl, Sella, village delegates, guilds, and coastal councils. His immediate goal is to keep records accurate, accessible, and resistant to institutional erasure or renewed burning.

set.name: Captain Harl
set.description: Based at Greyhaven's council house and memorial grounds, five years after the uprising, limping permanently from his injured knee and using a crutch. He oversees security without restoring lordly command, keeping memorial crowds safe while refusing to silence disputes or exclude civilians. He is allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Bryn, Vey, Orren, Sella, villagers, former soldiers, and reformers. He supports paid, time-limited emergency defense, humane hearings, open public buildings, and protection against factional violence while remaining alert to attempts at aristocratic or military capture.

set.name: Chaplain Orren
set.description: Based at Saint Orra's Chapel, Tomas's burial ground, and Greyhaven's common memorial, five years after the uprising. Very old and physically frail but vocally steady, he reads the names of the dead, including unidentified and missing people, and preserves silence as part of public remembrance. He remains allied with Elianor, Harl, Vey, Bryn, Mara, Joren, Sella, villagers, servants, prisoners, and reformers. His immediate goal is to keep the chapel and memorial places of equal refuge, truthful record, and humane care rather than triumphal politics.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: Dead for five years and buried without noble honors in wind-cut ground beside Greyhaven's sea garden. His life is publicly recorded in twelve factual pages within the coastal archive, including his work as a stable servant, aid to Rill, coordinating role, humane surrender terms, mistakes, and death protecting Elianor. His signet is held in public custody: temporarily placed beneath the common memorial on the uprising's fifth anniversary, then returned to its archive box. His name remains disputed and respected, but Elianor, Sella, Mara, and the assembly continue rejecting any portrait, statue, hereditary claim, or political throne built from his bloodline.

set.name: Ash
set.description: Alive in Greyhaven's rebuilt old stable, now an elderly gray mare white around the muzzle and bearing old scars. She remains cared for by stable hands and remembers Tomas's handling, responding calmly to Elianor. On the fifth uprising anniversary she carries Elianor along the cliff path past the functioning sea garden and Tomas's grave before returning to the stable. Her ongoing need is food, shelter, and gentle care.

set.name: Bryn
set.description: Based at Greyhaven's council house and traveling through the relief network, five years after the uprising. Her injured hand remains stiff but functional. She maintains transparent food and expenditure accounts, brings grain records to public ceremonies, corrects dishonest ceremonial accounting, and works with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Vey, Orren, Harl, Sella, councils, guilds, and former soldiers. She remains suspicious of merchants and former aristocrats who might hoard grain or capture institutions. Her immediate goal is to keep public stores and government expenses honest while supporting the fragile assembly.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: Based between Greyhaven's elected council house, coastal villages, assembly meetings, and memorial work, five years after the uprising. Older, thinner, and using a cane, she remains a principal negotiator and organizer of the fragile government. She is allied with Elianor, Joren, Bryn, Vey, Orren, Harl, Sella, village and guild delegates, former soldiers, and coastal councils. She supports the assembly's limits on taxation, end of ordinary forced levies, local land boards, humane hearings, and public archives, while opposing aristocratic restoration, factional capture, and hereditary Rusk authority. She continues helping Elianor govern through accountable responsibility rather than certainty.

set.name: Joren Pell
set.description: Based at Greyhaven and traveling between council, relief, land-board, and coastal negotiations, five years after the uprising. Permanently lame and using his ashwood crutch, he remains allied with Elianor, Mara, Bryn, Vey, Orren, Harl, Sella, villagers, guild representatives, former soldiers, and reform factions. He supports the new limits on taxation, paid time-limited emergency defense, humane hearings, local land boards, and common memorial records. He helps protect delegates and vulnerable communities from factional violence, revenge, and wealthy former aristocrats seeking institutional capture.

set.name: Sella Rusk
set.description: Based between Saint Orra's Chapel, Greyhaven's public archive, council house, and coastal councils, five years after the uprising. She preserves Arlen Rusk's petition as one historical document among many and refuses family banners or hereditary authority. She is grieving but controlled, allied with Elianor, Mara, Joren, Vey, Bryn, Orren, Harl, village and guild delegates, and reform communities. Her immediate goal is to keep Tomas's and Arlen's memories tied to representation, limited levies, humane government, and public evidence rather than a cult, statue, or bloodline throne.

Five years after Greyhaven's fall, Elianor and Master Vey maintain a public archive that records the famine, rebellion, Marrow crimes, and Tomas's life alongside the names and accounts of all the dead, explicitly rejecting portraits, statues, hereditary claims, and heroic simplification.

On the fifth anniversary of the uprising, Elianor rides Ash along the cliffs, attends a common memorial bearing the names of dead villagers, servants, rebels, soldiers, marines, children, and nobles without titles, and temporarily places Tomas's signet beneath its lowest stone before returning it to the public archive.

Elianor accepts that her love for Tomas has survived as grief, responsibility, and an unresolved absence rather than a shared household or beautiful victory, and continues governing by hearing evening petitions without a title.
